### [1] [Transfer Learning for Named Entity Recognition of Classical Latin through LLM Prompting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04015)
*Callum Chan*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper describes Team uOttawa's winning system for the EvaLatin 2026 Named Entity Recognition shared task. By applying prompt engineering to commercial LLMs (Gemini-2.5-pro and Claude-Sonnet-4-5), the author demonstrates that ancient Latin can benefit from cross-lingual transfer learning, achieving first place in both coarse-grained (11 classes) and fine-grained (28 classes) NER subtasks across all evaluation metrics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To investigate whether underrepresented ancient languages like Classical Latin can leverage modern LLM advancements through cross-lingual transfer learning, thereby reducing the need for task-specific training data in low-resource language scenarios.

Method: Prompt engineering applied to two commercial large language models (gemini-2.5-pro and claude-sonnet-4-5) for Named Entity Recognition, evaluated on the EvaLatin 2026 shared task with two subtasks: coarse-grained NER (11 classes) and fine-grained NER (28 classes), assessed under both strict and fuzzy evaluation regimes.

Result: The system achieved first place in both NER subtasks, obtaining the best scores across all evaluation metrics and regimes among all submissions.

Conclusion: Underrepresented ancient languages like Classical Latin can effectively benefit from cross-lingual transfer learning enabled by modern LLMs. Prompt engineering alone, without task-specific fine-tuning, proved sufficient to achieve state-of-the-art performance on Latin NER.

Abstract: With the increase in digitized resources of Classical Latin texts and modern breakthroughs of Large Language Models (LLMs), I contribute to ancient language research by participating in EvaLatin 2026. This paper describes Team uOttawa's system description and results for the Named Entity Recognition (NER) shared task. The task is divided into two subtasks: coarse-grained NER with 11 classes and fine-grained NER with 28 classes, each evaluated under strict and fuzzy regimes. Through prompt engineering of commercial LLMs gemini-2.5-pro and claude-sonnet-4-5, I show that the underrepresented ancient Latin language can take advantage of cross-lingual transfer learning by using advancements made by the wider LLM development community. Overall, the methods discussed in this report demonstrate very strong results, placing first in both NER subtasks and achieving the best scores across all evaluation metrics and regimes among all submissions.

</details>


### [2] [When More Becomes Less: Position-Dependent Repetition Effects in Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04021)
*Han-yu Wang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Cloze probes that vary token repetition count produce qualitatively different probability curves depending on where the readout slot is placed: adjacent probes yield a monotonic increase, while displaced probes yield an inverted-U pattern, challenging the assumption that readout position is orthogonal to what is being measured.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work using cloze-style probes with varying repetition counts implicitly assumes that readout slot position does not interact with the manipulation of target token frequency. The authors demonstrate this assumption is false, calling into question the validity of standard probing methodology that treats readout position as a neutral design choice.

Method: A two-probe design: (1) adjacent probe places the readout slot immediately after a repeated-target block; (2) displaced probe embeds the slot inside a fresh sentence frame. This is tested across 13 encoder and decoder models, replicated in 4 languages (Spanish, Chinese, German, French). A six-condition causal ablation isolates lexical repetition from length, generic redundancy, and semantic-neighbour confounds. Internal attention analysis examines per-target-token attention allocation as a function of N.

Result: Adjacent probes show P(target) climbing monotonically with N then plateauing. Displaced probes produce an inverted-U: P(target) rises to an early peak then declines. The per-word drop is statistically significant (bootstrap CI excludes zero) in all 13 models and replicates across all 42 multilingual cells. Causal ablation confirms the effect is driven by exact lexical repetition, not length, redundancy, or semantic similarity. Attention analysis reveals per-target-token attention decreases with N while total budget to the repeated block grows in causal LMs but not in the masked LM tested.

Conclusion: Probes that vary repetition count cannot treat readout position as orthogonal to the phenomenon being measured. The interaction between repetition and readout placement fundamentally confounds standard probing paradigms, requiring methodological reconsideration in interpretability research.

Abstract: Cloze-style probes that vary how often a target token appears implicitly assume that more copies of a target affect prediction the same way regardless of where the readout slot sits. We show this assumption fails. Our two-probe design holds a repeated-target prefix fixed and varies only the readout position: the adjacent probe places the slot immediately after the repeated block; the displaced probe places it inside a fresh sentence frame. Adjacent repetition behaves as priming intuition predicts: $P(\text{target})$ climbs with $N$ and plateaus. Displaced repetition produces an inverted-U: $P(\text{target})$ rises to an early peak and then declines as more copies are added. The displaced inverted-U shows a per-word drop with bootstrap CI excluding zero in all 13 open-access encoder and decoder models we test, and replicates across Spanish, Chinese, German, and French in 42 of 42 multilingual cells. A six-condition causal ablation isolates the effect to exact lexical repetition rather than length, generic redundancy, or semantic-neighbour exposure. A frame-pragmatics control rules out an artefact of the readout frame. Internally, per-target-token attention falls with $N$ while the total budget assigned to the repeated block grows in causal LMs but not in the masked LM we probe. Probes that vary repetition count cannot treat the readout position as orthogonal to what they measure.

</details>


### [3] [Reconstructing Persistent Worlds from Narratives for Narrative-Grounded Interactive Experiences](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04037)
*Yi-Chun Chen*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper proposes reconstructing explicit persistent worlds from narrative descriptions as a core computational objective for building narrative-grounded interactive experiences, rather than treating the world as an implicit by-product of downstream tasks. A reference prototype demonstrates feasibility through three case studies, bridging computational narrative understanding with interactive content generation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Designing narrative-grounded interactive experiences is labor-intensive because interactive content must align with the underlying world implied by the narrative. Existing approaches (narrative planning, scene generation, gameplay generation) formulate task-specific computational representations rather than explicitly reconstructing and maintaining a persistent world, which limits coherence and reuse across downstream tasks.

Method: The authors treat explicit persistent world reconstruction from narrative descriptions as the central computational objective. Their approach reconstructs and maintains persistent entities, locations, semantic relationships, and evolving world states, inferring only the contextual information needed for coherent interactive experiences. A reference prototype was developed that reconstructs structured persistent world representations from narrative descriptions and instantiates playable tile-based environments.

Result: Three representative case studies — a procedural scenario, an original fantasy narrative, and an adapted public-domain story — demonstrate the feasibility of reconstructing persistent worlds and show how a shared world representation supports coherent gameplay while remaining grounded in the source narrative.

Conclusion: Explicitly reconstructing persistent worlds prior to interactive realization bridges computational narrative understanding and interactive content generation, providing a semantic foundation for AI-assisted game authoring, mixed-initiative design, educational simulations, and narrative-grounded interactive experiences.

Abstract: Designing narrative-grounded interactive experiences remains labor-intensive because interactive content must align with the underlying world implied by the narrative. Existing approaches formulate problems such as narrative planning, scene generation, and gameplay generation, each constructing computational representations tailored to specific downstream tasks rather than explicitly reconstructing and maintaining the persistent world that grounds them.
  We investigate reconstructing explicit persistent worlds from narrative descriptions as the central computational objective for narrative-grounded interactive realization. Rather than treating the world as an implicit by-product of downstream generation, our approach reconstructs and maintains persistent entities, locations, semantic relationships, and evolving world states while inferring only the contextual information required to support coherent interactive experiences.
  To investigate this perspective, we develop a reference prototype that reconstructs structured persistent world representations from narrative descriptions and subsequently instantiates playable tile-based environments. Through three representative case studies spanning a procedural scenario, an original fantasy narrative, and an adapted public-domain story, we demonstrate the feasibility of reconstructing persistent worlds and show how a shared world representation supports coherent gameplay while remaining grounded in the source narrative.
  By explicitly reconstructing persistent worlds prior to interactive realization, this work bridges computational narrative understanding and interactive content generation, providing a semantic foundation for AI-assisted game authoring, mixed-initiative design, educational simulations, and narrative-grounded interactive experiences.

</details>


### [4] [Learning Sexism Detection Using Multi-Agent Perspectivist Preference Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04056)
*Hadi Mohammadi,Tina Shahedi,Robert A. Bagheri,Mehdi Dastani,Masoume M. Raeissi*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: MAP-PO preserves annotator disagreement in sexism detection by clustering annotators by labeling behavior, training one LLM agent per cluster, and using both individual and team-level preference optimization to keep each agent calibrated to its cluster.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Annotators genuinely disagree when labeling text for sexism due to differing perspectives, yet most NLP systems collapse this disagreement into a majority vote, discarding valuable perspectivist information.

Method: The MAP-PO framework: (1) clusters annotators by labeling behavior (not demographics) on the EXIST 2024 dataset of English/Spanish tweets; (2) fine-tunes one LLM agent per cluster to reproduce that cluster's labeling behavior; (3) coordinates agents via preference optimization combining individual rewards (cluster fidelity) and team-level rewards (majority label reproduction). Evaluated across two languages × two backbone LMs.

Result: Two consistent findings: (1) without fine-tuning, agents behave nearly identically, confirming cluster-specific training is essential; (2) training each agent solely on its own cluster's labels causes agents to drift far beyond their intended clusters, while adding a shared team-level training signal keeps each agent properly calibrated to its respective cluster.

Conclusion: Cluster-specific training is necessary to capture annotation perspectives, but must be balanced with a shared team-level objective to prevent agents from over-drifting from their target clusters.

Abstract: When people label text for sexism, they often disagree, and not because some of them are wrong: they genuinely perceive sexism differently. Most NLP systems discard this disagreement by collapsing it into a majority vote. We propose the Multi-Agent Perspectivist Preference Optimization (MAP-PO) framework to keep these different perspectives. On the EXIST 2024 dataset of labeled English and Spanish tweets, we first cluster annotators by their labeling behavior rather than their demographic attributes. We then fine-tune one Large Language Model agent per cluster to reproduce that cluster's annotation behavior, and coordinate the agents with preference optimization that combines individual and team-level rewards. We evaluate MAP-PO in four settings defined by two languages and two backbone language models, asking whether each agent reproduces the annotations of its own cluster and whether the agents together reproduce the majority label. Two findings hold in all four settings. First, without fine-tuning the agents behave almost identically, so cluster-specific training is necessary. Second, we show that training each agent only on the labels of its own cluster pushes the agents far beyond the clusters they should represent, while adding a shared team-level training signal consistently keeps each agent calibrated to its cluster.

</details>


### [5] [Mind the Cap: Output-Budget Regimes Change the Measured Multilingual Reasoning Gap](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04160)
*Ankit Goyal,Jaideep Ray*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper demonstrates that the single-token output cap used in multilingual evaluations creates a significant experimental confound: different languages require different token counts to express equivalent content. Through systematic experiments on MGSM with Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, the authors show the native-vs-translate accuracy gap swings by up to 57 points across token budgets, and they propose treating the output cap as an independent variable with reporting across the full budget regime.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard multilingual benchmarks report accuracy at a single token output cap, but languages differ in how many tokens they need to encode the same semantic content. This makes the token cap a hidden experimental variable that can systematically distort measured performance gaps between native and translated prompts, potentially misattributing tokenization artifacts to genuine reasoning deficits.

Method: The authors conduct a comprehensive token-budget sweep on MGSM (German, Thai, Swahili) using Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct under four prompting strategies. They then freeze three peaks and a near-zero gap value at 1024 tokens, evaluating on 540,000 independently hard-capped decodes with Holm-corrected statistical tests. Additional experiments include: cross-fitted Thai vocabulary extension to isolate tokenization effects, announced-vs-enforced budget manipulation, and a correct-emission timing identity validated on three additional benchmarks.

Result: The native-vs-translate gap swings by up to 57 points across budgets. Length normalization shifts the gap by up to 38.9 points where the cap binds, and can reverse strategy rankings at tight caps. All frozen tests at swept peaks reject the null, but the frozen test at B*=1024 fails to reject because native accuracy already saturates there — the residual difference is a strategy-performance gap, not a reasoning deficit. The Thai vocabulary extension closes 0.0 points at the frozen budget but 4.9 points where 19% of traces still truncate. Announcing 128 vs. 2048 tokens shifts Thai native accuracy by 5.1 points at a fixed enforced cap. The timing identity matches pre-specified MGSM peaks to 0.65 points and tracks held-out benchmarks to 0.92 points.

Conclusion: The output token cap should be treated as an independent variable; accuracy must be reported across the budget regime, not at a single budget. Above saturation, the native-vs-translate residual is a strategy-performance gap, not an identified reasoning deficit. The findings imply that tokenization artifacts have been systematically underestimated in multilingual LLM evaluation.

Abstract: Multilingual evaluations report accuracy at a single output-token cap, but languages need different numbers of tokens to express the same content, so the cap is a hidden experimental variable. We test whether the native-vs-translate gap on MGSM (German, Thai, Swahili) is a token-budget artifact for Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct under four prompting strategies. The measured gap swings by up to 57 points across budgets, length normalization moves it by up to 38.9 points where the cap binds, and at tight caps normalization can reverse which strategy scores higher. We prospectively froze the sweep's three Qwen peaks and its near-zero value at 1024 and evaluated them on 540,000 independently hard-capped decodes: a second frozen family of six Holm-corrected tests rejects every null. The frozen test at $B^*=1024$ still fails to reject because native accuracy has already saturated there; above saturation, the residual difference is a strategy-performance gap, not an identified reasoning deficit. The same truncation channel prices a cost-ordered adaptation ladder: a cross-fitted Thai vocabulary extension closes 0.0 points of the gap at the frozen budget and 4.9 points where 19% of traces still truncate. A third frozen family varies only the announced budget at a fixed enforced cap; announcing 128 rather than 2048 tokens moves Thai native accuracy by 5.1 points, so accuracy is not a function of the enforced cap alone. A correct-emission timing identity computed from one long-cap run matches the three pre-specified MGSM peaks to 0.65 points and, in an exploratory Qwen-only analysis of three further benchmarks, tracks held-out items to 0.92 points, locating the peak exactly in five of seven cells. Treat the output cap as an independent variable and report accuracy across the budget regime, not at a single budget.

</details>


### [6] [Visualizing Graph-to-Answer Mechanism Recovery in Materials-Science Hypothesis Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04170)
*Shashwat Sourav,Subhadeep Pal,Markus J. Buehler,Sanjay Das,Fiona Y. Wang,Dominik Soos,Tirthankar Ghosal*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A graph-to-answer mechanism-tracing case study on a fine-tuned Qwen3-8B model reveals that late synthesis layers (30–36) are critical for recovering mechanistic support in AI-generated materials-science hypotheses, with earlier layers (7–10) showing minimal recovery under graph corruption.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Fluent hypothesis generation by AI co-scientists in materials science does not guarantee that the answer retains scientifically meaningful mechanisms. There is a need for diagnostic tools that trace whether and where mechanistic reasoning is preserved or lost during the model's internal processing pipeline.

Method: The authors adapt a Qwen3-8B model into Graph-PRefLexOR-8B, which exposes four structured stages: brainstorming, graph construction, pattern extraction, and synthesis. They introduce a visual diagnostic workflow combining semantic backtracking, graph corruption, activation-based recovery measurements across 37 residual-stream checkpoints, and layer-by-token-region grids. This is applied across 100 open-ended materials-science questions to trace mechanism fidelity.

Result: Final answers remain closest to the model's own synthesis stage. Under graph corruption, mechanism recovery is minimal in early transition layers (7–10) and concentrated in late synthesis and answer-start regions at layers 30 and 36. The layer-by-token-region grids visually pinpoint where mechanistic support is lost or regained.

Conclusion: The proposed diagnostic workflow effectively identifies critical layers where mechanistic support is compromised or recovered, enabling scientists and model developers to inspect hypothesis reliability before forwarding results to experimental planning.

Abstract: AI co-scientists can generate fluent materials-science hypotheses, but fluency does not show that an answer preserves a scientifically meaningful mechanism. We present a graph-to-answer mechanism-tracing case study for Graph-PRefLexOR-8B, a Qwen3-8B model adapted to expose distinct stages for brainstorming, graph construction, pattern extraction, and synthesis. We organize semantic backtracking, graph corruption, activation-based recovery measurements, and layer-by-token-region grids into a visual diagnostic workflow for inspecting this pathway. Across 100 open-ended materials-science questions, final answers remain closest to the model's own structured stages, especially synthesis. Under graph corruption, a full sweep over 37 residual-stream checkpoints, the embedding output and 36 transformer blocks, shows little mechanism recovery in the earlier transition region at layers 7--10, recovery instead concentrates in late synthesis and answer-start regions around layers 30 and 36. The workflow is intended to help scientists and model developers identify where a generated hypothesis loses or regains mechanism support before it is passed to downstream experimental planning.

</details>


### [7] [MIDAS: Multi-LLM Iterative Data-Adaptive Summarization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04307)
*Karen Lee,Dhanashree Balaram,Seojun Shon,Umair Rasheed*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: MIDAS proposes a multi-LLM framework for automatic, data-adaptive text summarization that eliminates manual prompt engineering by learning patterns from data and personalizing to specific use cases, outperforming existing methods like CriSPO and ZERA on enterprise ticket summarization tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Enterprise text summarization requires strict adherence to domain-specific guidelines, output formats, and organizational conventions. Existing automated prompt optimization methods rely on static, critique-driven refinement that cannot adapt to diverse summarization applications, making them labor-intensive and brittle as requirements evolve.

Method: MIDAS (Multi-LLM Iterative Data-Adaptive Summarization) is a multi-LLM framework that combines data-driven pattern learning with use-case-specific personalization. It automatically adapts to different summarization requirements without manual prompt engineering by iteratively learning from data patterns across multiple LLMs.

Result: Applied to enterprise customer ticket summarization across five output formats, MIDAS outperformed state-of-the-art frameworks CriSPO and ZERA, improving ROUGE-1 by up to 11.0%, ROUGE-2 by up to 18.2%, and ROUGE-L by up to 8.0%, with consistent BERTScore F1 gains. Cross-model and cross-domain generalization was demonstrated via multi-LLM configurations and finance-domain benchmarks.

Conclusion: MIDAS demonstrates that data-driven, adaptive multi-LLM frameworks can surpass static critique-driven prompt optimization for constrained enterprise summarization, offering robust generalization across models and domains.

Abstract: Text summarization is deceptively difficult. While condensing information seems straightforward, real-world enterprise summarization of support tickets, legal documents, incident reports, and more, demands strict adherence to domain-specific guidelines, output formats, and organizational conventions. Crafting prompts that reliably satisfy these constraints is labor-intensive, requiring significant human expertise and continuous maintenance as requirements evolve. Existing automated prompt optimization methods reduce this burden through Large Language Model (LLM) critique-driven refinement, yet remain limited by static prompts that cannot adapt to the diversity of summary applications. We propose Multi-LLM Iterative Data-Adaptive Summarization (MIDAS), a multi-LLM framework that extends this paradigm with data-driven pattern learning and use-case-specific personalization, enabling automatic adaptation to different summarization requirements without manual prompt engineering. Applied to enterprise customer ticket summarization across five output formats, MIDAS achieves the strongest overall performance against state-of-the-art critique-driven optimization frameworks such as CriSPO and ZERA, improving ROUGE-1 by up to 11.0%, ROUGE-2 by up to 18.2%, and ROUGE-L by up to 8.0%, while consistently improving BERTScore F1 across all formats and output types. We additionally demonstrate cross-model and cross-domain generalization through multi-LLM configurations and finance-domain summarization benchmarks.

</details>


### [8] [Test, then Route: How Language Models Execute In-Context Conditional Rules Across Models and Languages](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04183)
*Luxshan Thavarasa,Sivasuthan Sukumar*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This study investigates whether language models implement in-context conditional rules ("if P(x) then A else B") using a modular circuit with separate predicate-testing and answer-routing components. Using activation patching with a four-donor design across three models, six languages, and multiple predicate families, the authors find that a mid-stack residual band robustly encodes the predicate's truth value (modular), while the routing mechanism is token-bound and non-transferable (non-modular).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To determine whether language models internally decompose conditional rule-following into modular subcomputations — specifically, a predicate-testing module and an abstract answer-routing module — and to test whether such modularity emerges consistently across models, languages, and predicate types.

Method: Activation patching with a novel four-donor design: two swapped-rule donors are used so that the condition and the answer word disagree, allowing each layer to be classified by which signal it carries. A strict pre-specified isolation criterion is applied: predicate-outcome flip near 1.0 and mapping flip near 0.0 for the predicate module, and the reverse profile for the router. The method is applied across three open models (from two families), six languages, one fixed item bank, and five predicate families. Subspace analysis and cross-lingual/pair transfer probes are also conducted.

Result: The mid-stack residual band meets the isolation criterion for predicate encoding in 17 of 18 cells, showing robust modularity across models, languages, and predicate families. The router, however, shows the opposite profile: a learned subspace can flip A/B near-perfectly within the trained pair but transfers to a new pair at ~0 across all models. In Gemma-3-4B, cross-lingual transfer to the same pair reaches ~0.98. Router direction is token-bound and non-transferable — largely answer-readout in Gemma, pair-specific in Qwen — rather than an abstract routing module. Conclusion: the test (predicate) is modular; the route (answer selection) is not.

Conclusion: Under the probes employed, language models implement conditional rule-following with a modular predicate-testing component localized to a mid-stack residual band, but the answer-routing component lacks abstraction and modularity, instead relying on token-bound, pair-specific mechanisms. This suggests that not all subcomputations in in-context reasoning are equally modularized.

Abstract: When a language model follows an in-context conditional rule such as "if P(x) then A else B," does it assemble a runtime circuit with one module that tests the predicate and another that routes the answer? We probe this with activation patching under a four-donor design whose two swapped-rule donors make the condition and the answer word disagree, so each layer reveals which of the two it carries. Across three open models from two families and six languages sharing one fixed item bank, a mid-stack residual band carries the predicate's truth value: patching it reroutes the answer with predicate-outcome flip near 1.0 and mapping flip near 0.0, meeting a strict pre-specified isolation criterion in 17 of 18 cells, and the same localization holds across five predicate families. The router shows the opposite profile. A learned subspace flips A and B near-perfectly within the trained pair yet transfers to a new pair at approximately 0 in every model, while in Gemma-3-4B (the only model probed cross-lingually) it transfers at approximately 0.98 to the same pair in other languages. Under every probe we ran, the router direction is token-bound and non-transferable (largely answer-readout in Gemma, pair-specific in Qwen) rather than an abstract routing module. Test is modular; under these probes, route is not.

</details>


### [9] [Large Language Models for Low-Resource Languages: A Conceptual Framework for an Electronic Explanatory Dictionary of the Tajik Language](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04186)
*Mullosharaf K. Arabov*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Proposes a conceptual framework for building an electronic explanatory dictionary for Tajik by integrating LLMs with classical lexicography, using subword tokenization and parameter-efficient fine-tuning to address the language's agglutinative morphology and low-resource constraints.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Tajik lacks a comprehensive digital lexicographic resource comparable to those for high-resource languages, and modern NLP technologies remain poorly adapted to this low-resource, agglutinative language system.

Method: Systematic survey of existing linguistic, statistical, and corpus resources; proposed dictionary architecture integrating morphological analysis, lemmatization, semantic clustering, and LLM-based dictionary entry generation; subword tokenization to handle agglutinative morphology; parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) for limited annotated data settings.

Result: The paper delivers a first holistic conceptual architecture that unifies classical lexicographic methods, language statistics, and generative LLM capabilities into a single electronic dictionary framework for Tajik, establishing a methodological foundation for downstream NLP tasks.

Conclusion: The proposed framework lays the methodological groundwork for a full-featured electronic Tajik dictionary, which can serve both lexicographic purposes and as a core resource for machine translation, summarization, sentiment analysis, and other applied NLP tasks in low-resource settings.

Abstract: This paper presents a conceptual framework for developing an electronic explanatory dictionary of the Tajik language using large language models (LLMs). The relevance of the work stems from the absence of a comprehensive digital lexicographic resource for Tajik that is comparable in functionality to dictionaries for high-resource languages, and from the limited adaptation of modern natural language processing technologies to low-resource language systems. Based on a systematic survey of existing linguistic, statistical, and corpus resources, we propose a dictionary architecture that integrates modules for morphological analysis, lemmatization, semantic clustering, and dictionary entry generation using LLMs. The choice of subword tokenization is justified by the agglutinative nature of Tajik morphology and its high morphological variability, along with a parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) strategy suitable for limited annotated data. The novelty of the work lies in proposing the first holistic conceptual architecture of an explanatory dictionary for Tajik that unifies classical lexicographic methods, language statistics, and generative capabilities of LLMs into a single system. The practical significance of the study is the formation of a methodological foundation for developing a full-featured electronic dictionary that can serve both as a lexicographic tool and as a core resource for machine translation, automatic summarization, sentiment analysis, and other applied NLP tasks. The paper is intended for specialists in computational linguistics, lexicography, and developers of natural language processing systems working with low-resource languages.

</details>


### [10] [OneDayAgent: Towards a Long-Horizon Harness for Autonomous Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05013)
*Jingsheng Zheng,Xinyuan Fang,Jintian Zhang,Zhengke Gui,Huajun Chen,Ningyu Zhang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: OneDayAgent is a harness for autonomous LLM agents that manages long-horizon, cross-environment, multimodal tasks by decomposing them into subtasks, maintaining execution memory under context pressure, and verifying final deliverables. It achieves SOTA (0.821) on AgentIF-OneDay with GLM-5.2 and generalizes across five backend LLMs from three model families without tuning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM agents are increasingly deployed for open-ended, long-horizon, cross-environment, multimodal tasks. Prior work addresses failure modes like goal drift, state loss, and context overflow in isolation, but whether a single harness can jointly manage all these issues while remaining effective across different backend LLMs has been underexplored.

Method: OneDayAgent converts open-ended requests into a managed execution process with three key mechanisms: (1) task decomposition into bounded subtasks, (2) execution memory maintenance under context pressure, and (3) verification and repair of the final deliverable. The harness is evaluated on the AgentIF-OneDay benchmark (104 tasks) across five backend LLMs from three model families without any backend-specific tuning.

Result: With the GLM-5.2 backend, OneDayAgent achieves a new state-of-the-art overall score of 0.821 on AgentIF-OneDay. The same harness runs effectively across all five backend LLMs from three model families, demonstrating cross-backend generalization. Different models exhibit distinct execution styles under the identical workflow.

Conclusion: A unified harness can jointly address multiple long-horizon failure modes — goal drift, state loss, and context overflow — while generalizing across diverse backend LLMs. OneDayAgent's strong performance and cross-model portability suggest that well-designed orchestration layers can complement and enhance raw model capabilities for complex, open-ended agent tasks.

Abstract: LLM agents are increasingly applied to open-ended everyday requests that span work, study, and life. These tasks are long-horizon, cross-environment, and multimodal, forcing the agent to preserve goals and constraints across many steps while navigating heterogeneous tools and attachments. While prior work has addressed individual failure modes such as goals drift, states loss, and context overflow, whether a single harness can manage them jointly and remain effective across backends has received less study. We present OneDayAgent, a long-horizon harness for autonomous agents. OneDayAgent turns an open-ended request into a managed execution process that decomposes tasks into bounded subtasks, maintains execution memory under context pressure, and verifies and repairs the final deliverable. We evaluate OneDayAgent on AgentIF-OneDay across 104 tasks. With the GLM-5.2 backend, OneDayAgent sets a new state of the art with an overall score of 0.821. The same harness runs across five backend LLMs from three model families, indicating the harness generalizes across backends without tuning, even as different models induce distinct execution styles under the same workflow.

</details>


### [11] [Caching for the Future: Scrub Jay Episodic Memory Principles for Agent Memory Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04746)
*Kartikey Singh Bhandari,Aarya Wadhwani,Dhruv Kumar,Pratik Narang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: ScrubJay-MEM introduces type-conditioned temporal decay for LLM agent memory, inspired by western scrub jay episodic memory. Each memory is stored as a What-Where-When tuple with a learned perishability coefficient πᵢ and utility horizon τᵢ, enabling query-adaptive retrieval with retroactive O(1) updates. The new TGT benchmark with GenGap metric shows ScrubJay-MEM uniquely achieves positive temporal generalization among retrieval-based systems, with gains on EventQA but diminishing returns on fact-consolidation tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM agent memory architectures treat all stored memories as equally persistent, ignoring that validity varies enormously by content type. This causes systematic contamination of retrieved context with outdated facts. The authors draw inspiration from western scrub jays' episodic memory, which exhibits content-dependent forgetting rates, to address this gap in temporal reasoning over perishable information.

Method: ScrubJay-MEM operationalizes per-memory type-conditioned temporal decay as an auto-classified coefficient πᵢ. Each memory is encoded as a jointly-bound What-Where-When tuple with estimated perishability πᵢ and utility horizon τᵢ. Retrieval uses query-adaptive scoring, and memories can be revised retroactively at O(1) LLM calls per update. Evaluation uses the novel Temporal Generalization Test (TGT) benchmark with held-out retention intervals and a Generalization Gap (GenGap) metric, plus MemoryAgentBench EventQA-64k.

Result: On TGT, ScrubJay-MEM is the only retrieval-based system with substantially positive GenGap (+0.108). On MemoryAgentBench EventQA-64k, it improves F1 by +2.66 over Mem0 and +3.09 over Qwen3-Embedding-4B under an LLM backbone. A decay ablation collapses GenGap by 5.7×, confirming type-conditioned decay as necessary. Gains narrow with stronger backbones and reverse on fact-consolidation tasks, scoping the contribution to temporal reasoning over perishable facts.

Conclusion: Type-conditioned temporal decay is necessary and effective for temporal reasoning over perishable facts in LLM agent memory. However, the benefit is scoped specifically to perishable, temporally-sensitive information and diminishes or reverses for fact-consolidation tasks or when stronger backbone models are used.

Abstract: LLM agents that persist across sessions accumulate stored memories whose validity varies enormously by content type, yet existing memory architectures treat all memories as equally persistent and systematically contaminate retrieved context with outdated facts. We show that per-memory, type-conditioned temporal decay, a property of western scrub jay episodic memory, can be operationalized as an auto-classified coefficient $π_i$ in an external LLM-agent memory store, yielding ScrubJay-MEM: each memory is encoded as a jointly-bound What--Where--When tuple with an estimated perishability $π_i$ and utility horizon $τ_i$, retrieved by query-adaptive scoring, and revised retroactively at $O(1)$ LLM calls per update. We introduce the Temporal Generalization Test (TGT), a benchmark with held-out retention intervals and a Generalization Gap (GenGap) metric. On TGT, ScrubJay-MEM is the only retrieval-based system with substantially positive GenGap ($+0.108$); on MemoryAgentBench EventQA-64k it improves F1 by $+2.66$ over Mem0 and $+3.09$ over Qwen3-Embedding-4B under a llm backbone. A decay ablation collapses GenGap by $5.7\times$, establishing type-conditioned decay as necessary for the result. Gains narrow under stronger backbones and reverse on fact-consolidation tasks, scoping the contribution to temporal reasoning over perishable facts.

</details>


### [12] [Patients-like-me: A Variational LM--GNN Framework for Explainable Clinical Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04193)
*Xinyu Wang,Yixuan Li,Hanwei Wu,Qincheng Lu,Chi-Kuang Yeh,Xiao-Wen Chang,Ziyang Song*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: PLM combines language models and graph neural networks to improve EHR predictive modeling by integrating patient-level semantics with cohort-level structure, achieving state-of-the-art results while providing interpretable similar-patient explanations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LMs process EHR patient sequences in isolation and lack explainability; GNNs capture inter-patient relationships and offer attribution, but depend on high-quality patient representations. A unified framework is needed to leverage both strengths.

Method: PLM integrates an LM encoder (for local patient semantics) with a GNN (for global cohort structure). Training uses a Variational Expectation-Maximization algorithm that alternates between updating LM and GNN parameters under a supervised variational objective.

Result: On MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV, PLM consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods across both encoder-only and decoder-only LM backbones, with only modest additional computational cost. Edge-masking experiments confirm that top-ranked reference patients significantly influence predictions.

Conclusion: PLM effectively unifies local semantic and global structural modeling for EHRs, delivering superior predictive performance and interpretable reference-patient explanations, making it a practical and explainable solution for clinical predictive tasks.

Abstract: Language models (LMs) offer strong textual representations for electronic health records (EHRs), but they encode patient sequences in isolation and provide limited explainability. Graph neural networks (GNNs) complement LMs by incorporating inter-patient relationships and enabling reference-patient attribution, yet they rely on high-quality patient representations. We propose Patients-like-me (PLM), a unified LM--GNN framework that integrates local patient semantics with global cohort structure. To train PLM efficiently, we introduce a Variational Expectation-Maximization algorithm that alternates LM and GNN updates under a supervised variational objective. Extensive experiments on MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV show that PLM consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, with improvements generalizing across encoder-only and decoder-only LM backbones. These gains are achieved with only modest additional computational overhead. PLM also provides reference-patient explanations by retrieving influential similar patients, while edge-masking experiments confirm that the highest-ranked references have the greatest impact on model predictions.

</details>


### [13] [Hallucinations on the Board: Tool-Augmented Evaluation of LLM Chess Commentary](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04240)
*S. Ashwin Hebbar,Peiyao Sheng,Sewoong Oh,Pramod Viswanath*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: ACT-Eval is a benchmark and evaluation framework that uses chess engine tools and expert-annotated gold references to assess LLM-generated chess commentary at the atomic claim level, revealing pervasive factual hallucinations (22%+ error rates) that tool augmentation partially mitigates, though coverage of strategic concepts remains limited across all models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Superhuman chess engines provide accurate evaluations but lack natural-language explanations that are educationally useful. LLMs could bridge this gap but suffer from hallucination due to limited domain knowledge, and existing evaluation frameworks (reference-based, LLM-as-judge) cannot reliably detect these errors in domain-specific commentary.

Method: ACT-Eval decomposes chess commentary into atomic claims and routes them to engine-supported tools and expert-annotated gold references for verification. It evaluates three dimensions: factual correctness, conceptual coverage, and move-quality judgment. The accompanying benchmark comprises 325 position–move pairs (pedagogical, tournament, critical), including 125 with expert-verified gold atoms and a five-class error taxonomy.

Result: Without tools, GPT-5.4 produces incorrect sub-claims 22.0% of the time; smaller open-weight models exceed 40%. Tool augmentation substantially improves factual correctness and move-quality assessment, but coverage of expert strategic and tactical ideas remains limited across all models. Human calibration validates ACT-Eval's factual judgments (within inter-human agreement range) and coverage scores (strong correlation with human strategic completeness assessments).

Conclusion: Factual hallucination in LLM-generated chess commentary is pervasive and inadequately addressed by current models alone. Tool augmentation offers meaningful improvements but does not close the gap in strategic coverage, highlighting the need for better integration of domain expertise in LLM commentary systems.

Abstract: Superhuman game engines in domains like chess have made expert-level evaluations easily accessible, yet they communicate what is true without the natural-language explanations that make such expertise educationally useful to experts and non-experts alike. Large language models could, in principle, bridge this gap, but they frequently hallucinate due to limited domain-specific knowledge, and standard reference-based or LLM-as-a-judge frameworks cannot reliably detect these errors. In this work, we present ACT-Eval, an evaluation framework that decomposes chess commentary into atomic claims and routes them to engine-supported tools and expert-annotated gold references to assess factual correctness, conceptual coverage, and move-quality judgment. We release a benchmark of 325 position--move pairs spanning pedagogical, tournament, and critical positions, including 125 positions with expert-verified gold atoms and a five-class error taxonomy. Evaluating leading proprietary and open-weight models, we find that factual hallucinations remain pervasive in chess commentary: GPT-5.4 without tools produces incorrect sub-claims 22.0% of the time, while smaller open-weight models exceed 40%. Although tool augmentation substantially improves factual correctness and move-quality assessment, coverage of expert strategic and tactical ideas remains limited across all models. Human calibration shows that ACT-Eval's factual judgments fall within the observed range of inter-human agreement, while its coverage scores correlate strongly with human assessments of strategic completeness.

</details>


### [14] [Towards End-to-End Multilingual Metaphor Processing: Integrating Detection, Translation, and Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04260)
*Jiahui Liang,Lifeng Han*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This PhD proposal outlines a unified computational framework for multilingual metaphor processing, integrating metaphor detection, translation evaluation, and joint modeling to improve NLP systems' handling of figurative language.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Metaphorical language poses a significant challenge for multilingual NLP because it requires reasoning beyond literal meaning. Current research treats metaphor detection, machine translation, and translation evaluation as isolated tasks, lacking an integrated computational framework that connects these components.

Method: The proposal advances three interconnected research directions: (1) robust cross-lingual metaphor detection, (2) metaphor-oriented translation evaluation encompassing both human assessment and automatic quality estimation, and (3) joint modeling that bridges metaphor detection with translation evaluation. The approach combines linguistic theory with large language models to create new datasets, annotation methodologies, evaluation benchmarks, and automatic evaluation techniques.

Result: The expected outcome is a unified framework that enhances the development and evaluation of multilingual NLP systems when processing figurative language. No empirical results are reported, as this is a PhD proposal.

Conclusion: A unified end-to-end framework integrating metaphor detection with translation evaluation can substantially advance multilingual NLP's capacity to handle figurative language, addressing a critical gap in current research where these tasks remain siloed.

Abstract: Metaphorical language remains a major challenge for multilingual natural language processing because successful interpretation and translation require reasoning beyond literal lexical meaning. Existing research has largely investigated metaphor detection, machine translation, and translation evaluation as separate tasks, while little work has explored how these components can be integrated into a unified computational framework. This PhD proposal aims to develop an end-to-end framework for multilingual metaphor processing consisting of three complementary research directions: (1) robust metaphor detection across languages, (2) metaphor-oriented translation evaluation for both human assessment and automatic quality estimation, and (3) joint modelling that connects metaphor detection with translation evaluation. The proposed research will combine linguistic theory with recent advances in large language models to develop new datasets, annotation methodologies, evaluation benchmarks, and automatic evaluation approaches for metaphor-aware machine translation. The expected outcome is a unified framework that improves both the development and evaluation of multilingual NLP systems when processing figurative language.

</details>


### [15] [The Fairness Collapse Phenomenon: Bias Amplification in Language Models Trained on Synthetic Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04268)
*Irina Proskurina,Antoine Gourru,Julien Velcin*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper investigates "fairness collapse," a phenomenon where recursive training on synthetic data amplifies social biases in language models before standard performance metrics show degradation. Using the Bias in Bios dataset, the authors demonstrate that fairness degradation emerges earlier and more silently than general model collapse.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While prior work has established that training language models on synthetic data leads to model collapse (performance degradation), no studies have examined whether synthetic data contamination also affects social biases. Given that LMs are known to reproduce demographic stereotypes, recursive training on self-generated data may create a self-reinforcing feedback loop that progressively strengthens biased associations.

Method: The authors construct controlled training regimes where language models are iteratively trained on self-generated (synthetic) data. They use the Bias in Bios dataset, which contains biographical text with labeled demographic attributes, to track both standard language-modeling metrics and fairness/bias metrics across successive generations of recursive training.

Result: A consistent pattern emerges across experiments: fairness degradation (increased social bias) manifests before substantial degradation appears in standard language-modeling metrics. This indicates that bias amplifies silently, without being signaled by conventional performance monitoring.

Conclusion: Synthetic data contamination poses a critical and previously overlooked risk: social biases can intensify silently during recursive training, before obvious signs of model collapse become detectable. This has serious implications for continued pretraining on open web data increasingly polluted by synthetic content.

Abstract: Generative models trained on artificially generated data have been shown to exhibit model collapse, resulting in significant performance degradation. As synthetic content increasingly contaminates the training corpora of language models, this raises critical concerns about the use of open data in continued pretraining. Although previous work has demonstrated model collapse in language models, it remains unclear whether exposure to synthetic data amplifies or attenuates the social biases already present in pretrained models. Because language models are known to reproduce and amplify demographic stereotypes, recursive training on self-generated data may create a self-reinforcing feedback loop in which biased associations become progressively stronger across generations. We call this hypothesized phenomenon fairness collapse. In this work, we construct controlled training regimes in which models are repeatedly trained on synthetic data using the Bias in Bios dataset. Across experiments, we observe a consistent and concerning pattern: fairness degradation emerges before substantial degradation is reflected by standard language-modeling metrics. This result highlights a critical risk associated with synthetic data contamination in language model training: bias can increase silently before strong indicators of model collapse become apparent.

</details>


### [16] [Eliciting Intrinsic Hallucinations in LLMs via Semantically Equivalent Adversarial Attacks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04286)
*Atri Vivek Sharma,Brian Formento,Alessio Lomuscio*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Proposes a framework that stress-tests LLMs for intrinsic hallucinations in RAG systems using semantically equivalent adversarial query variations, showing even state-of-the-art models suffer up to 50% degradation in contextual faithfulness.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: RAG systems are still susceptible to intrinsic hallucinations — unfaithful/fabricated outputs unsupported by retrieved evidence. The authors aim to systematically assess how robust LLMs are to semantically equivalent rephrasings of queries that provoke such hallucinations.

Method: A framework that adversarially optimizes semantically equivalent query variants under strict semantic equivalence constraints, targeting an intrinsic hallucination objective. Applied across white-box, gray-box, and black-box attack settings on 5 open-source and 5 closed-source models over 3 datasets.

Result: Even state-of-the-art models are highly susceptible to meaning-preserving perturbations, with contextual faithfulness degrading by up to 50% (e.g., GPT-5-mini). Faithful grounding in retrieved evidence proves fragile across all model tiers.

Conclusion: Faithful use of in-context evidence remains fragile in LLMs regardless of capability level, motivating the need for architectures and training objectives that enforce robust grounding independent of surface query form.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are often used in conjunction with external knowledge sources to improve their factual accuracy and decrease hallucinations, through methods such as Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG). However, these systems remain susceptible to intrinsic hallucinations, where the model generates unfaithful or fabricated information that is not supported by the retrieved evidence. We propose a novel framework to assess model robustness against this phenomenon by stress-testing using natural, semantically equivalent variations of a user query found via adversarial optimization methods. We apply our framework, which enforces strict semantic equivalence constraints and an intrinsic hallucination objective, to a range of adversarial attack techniques across white-box, gray-box, and black-box adversarial settings. Evaluating these attacks on 5 open-source and 5 closed-source generator models across 3 datasets, we demonstrate that even state-of-the-art models are highly susceptible to meaning-preserving perturbations, which significantly degrade contextual faithfulness (by up to 50% for GPT-5-mini). Our findings indicate that faithful use of in-context evidence remains fragile even in state-of-the-art LLMs, motivating architectures and training objectives that enforce robust grounding independent of surface query form. Code is available at: https://github.com/atriviveksharma/intrinsic_hall

</details>


### [17] [Searching for Sound-Meaning Collisions: Graph-Based Affordance Retrieval and Multi-Evaluator Ranking for Pun Translation at CLEF 2026 JOKER Task 2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04299)
*Russell Taylor,Adam Brikman,Prateek Awate*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper computationally models pun translation as a process of discovering, exploring, and selecting target-language sound-meaning affordances, finding that successful pun translation emerges from finding new phonological-semantic collisions rather than preserving source words, though retrieval remains a key bottleneck.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To computationally test Low's 15-year-old proposal that pun translators should abandon word-equivalence searching and instead discover new points of contact between sound and meaning in the target language — a notion central to effective pun translation but never before systematically evaluated through computational modeling.

Method: A three-stage pipeline: (1) a retrieval system searches semantic and phonological neighborhoods in the target language for affordances (sound-meaning bridges enabling wordplay); (2) multiple language models generate competing translations exploiting these affordances; (3) a multi-perspective generate-and-rank architecture selects among candidate translations. The primary analysis traces how retrieved affordances propagate through each stage.

Result: Generators actively exploit retrieved affordances; evaluators progressively concentrate around stronger sound-meaning bridges; exact phonological collisions are disproportionately selected when available. However, many puns yield no usable affordances, identifying retrieval as the central bottleneck in computational pun translation.

Conclusion: The computational process closely mirrors Low's vision: successful pun translation depends not on preserving source-language words but on discovering new target-language sites where sound and meaning collide. Retrieval quality fundamentally constrains downstream performance.

Abstract: Fifteen years ago, Low proposed that pun translators should stop searching for equivalent words and instead search for new points of contact between sound and meaning. In this paper, we investigate that idea computationally. We model pun translation as a process of discovery, exploration, and selection. A retrieval system searches semantic and phonological neighborhoods for target-language affordances: sound-meaning bridges that may support new wordplay. Multiple language models then explore these opportunities by generating competing translations, while a multi-perspective generate-and-rank architecture selects among them. Beyond system development, our primary contribution is an analysis of how retrieved affordances propagate through the translation process. We find that generators actively exploit retrieved opportunities, evaluators progressively concentrate around stronger sound-meaning bridges, and exact phonological collisions are selected at disproportionately high rates when available. At the same time, many puns still yield no usable affordances, suggesting that retrieval remains the central bottleneck in computational pun translation. The resulting picture is remarkably close to the process envisioned by Low. Successful pun translation emerges not from preserving source-language words, but from discovering new places in the target language where sound and meaning collide.

</details>


### [18] [Pun Intended: Multi-Agent Translation of Wordplay with Contrastive Learning and Phonetic-Semantic Embeddings](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04311)
*Russell Taylor,Benjamin Herbert,Michael Sana*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Three LLM-based approaches for English-to-French pun translation are compared: a discriminator-guided baseline, a guided reasoning pipeline using phonetic-semantic embeddings, and a multi-agent iterative framework. The multi-agent and guided chain-of-thought systems ranked first and second in CLEF JOKER 2025 Task 2, suggesting explicit phonetic-semantic guidance and iterative evaluation outperform direct discriminator generation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Wordplay translation is notoriously difficult for both humans and MT systems because it requires preserving linguistic creativity, ambiguity, and humor rather than just literal meaning. The authors aim to move beyond vocabulary reproduction toward genuine creative equivalence in pun translation.

Method: Three approaches translating English puns to French: (1) Baseline — LLM with discriminator feedback using positive/negative French pun examples; (2) Guided reasoning — phonetic-semantic embedding retrieval for candidate generation via chain-of-thought; (3) Multi-agent — iterative evaluation and regeneration using specialized agent feedback. Evaluated via BLEU, BERTScore, and expert human judgment in the CLEF JOKER 2025 Task 2 competition.

Result: The multi-agent and guided chain-of-thought systems achieved first and second place respectively under expert human evaluation in CLEF JOKER 2025 Task 2, despite only modest improvements in automatic metrics (BLEU, BERTScore).

Conclusion: Explicit phonetic-semantic guidance and iterative multi-agent evaluation offer meaningful advantages over direct discriminator-guided generation for wordplay translation, particularly in balancing semantic fidelity, phonetic similarity, and natural target-language expression. Automatic metrics alone are insufficient to capture these gains.

Abstract: Translating wordplay across languages has long challenged both professional translators and machine translation systems. We investigate three approaches to translating puns from English to French by combining large language models with linguistic constraints for wordplay generation. Our baseline uses a large language model with feedback from a discriminator prompted with positive and negative French examples. Our guided reasoning pipeline uses combined phonetic-semantic embeddings to retrieve lexical candidates for wordplay generation. Finally, our multi-agent framework iteratively evaluates and regenerates candidate translations using specialized feedback. Moving beyond literal translation, our objective is to preserve the linguistic creativity, ambiguity, and humor of the source-text wordplay rather than simply reproduce its vocabulary. The multi-agent and guided chain-of-thought systems ranked first and second, respectively, in the CLEF JOKER 2025 Task 2 competition under expert human evaluation, despite only modest improvements in BLEU and BERTScore. These findings suggest that both explicit phonetic-semantic guidance and iterative multi-agent evaluation can improve LLM-based wordplay translation relative to direct discriminator-guided generation, particularly when balancing semantic fidelity, phonetic similarity, and natural target-language expression

</details>


### [19] [DataRx: Missingness-Aware Sampling for Safer Large Language Model Task-Specific Fine-Tuning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04322)
*Junbo Zhang,Qianli Zhou,Xinyang Deng,Wen Jiang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: DataRx is a missingness-aware sampling method that selects safety-critical fine-tuning examples by measuring gaps between model responses and safety references in hidden representation space, reducing attack success rate from 59.23% to 13.70% with only 1% additional safety data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Task-specific fine-tuning degrades LLM safety guardrails. While mixing safety data helps, the principle behind why some safety examples are more effective than others remains unknown. The authors aim to uncover this principle and leverage it for better safety-preserving fine-tuning.

Method: DataRx hypothesizes that effective safety samples fill missing parts of an LLM's safety capabilities. It quantifies the "safety signal gap" by comparing high-dimensional hidden representations of the model's native response versus a safety reference response, then selects examples that address the largest gaps (missingness-aware sampling).

Result: With only 1% additional safety samples from BeaverTails, DataRx reduced the average attack success rate of Llama3-8B-Instruct across seven downstream tasks from 59.23% (random sampling baseline) to 13.70%. DataRx also complements existing safety data synthesis methods for further defense enhancement.

Conclusion: DataRx demonstrates that strategically selecting safety examples based on representation-level safety signal gaps is highly effective for preserving alignment during fine-tuning. The work encourages further data-centric defense research.

Abstract: Task-specific fine-tuning can improve the performance of large language models (LLMs) on downstream tasks. However, our study reveals that task-specific fine-tuning can also weaken the safety guardrails of aligned LLMs. A widely adopted strategy for preserving safety during fine-tuning is to incorporate safety data. Although previous studies have shown that randomly mixing safety data can alleviate safety degradation, the underlying principle determining why some safety examples are more effective than others still remains unclear. In this paper, we propose DataRx, a missingness-aware sampling method for selecting safety-critical examples. DataRx is based on the hypothesis that a safety sample is more effective when the selected examples provide safety signals that fill the missing parts of LLMs' safety capabilities. DataRx's key insight is leveraging high-dimensional hidden representations rather than discrete tokens to quantify the safety signal gap between the target model's native response and the safety reference response. The results show that, with only 1% additional safety samples from BeaverTails, DataRx reduces the average attack success rate of Llama3-8B-Instruct across seven downstream tasks from 59.23% under random sampling to 13.70%. In addition, DataRx can be combined with the existing safety data synthesis method to further enhance safety defenses during fine-tuning. We hope that DataRx will inspire more data-centric defense research.

</details>


### [20] [Right Reset: Chunking by Prefix Removal](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04330)
*Mike Vegeto*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Prefix-removal probing reveals that causal LMs exhibit boundaries where removing left context barely alters right-side hidden-state trajectories. The proposed Right Reset (RR) metric, combined with dynamic programming, recovers document boundaries in flattened text substantially better than embedding-based baselines, without task-specific training.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: When surface-level structural cues (separators, layout) are stripped from concatenated documents, conventional boundary detection methods struggle. The authors observe that causal language models exhibit natural boundaries where context dependence drops — the model processes subsequent tokens nearly identically regardless of preceding context. This suggests a latent boundary signal intrinsic to LM representations that could be exploited for unsupervised segmentation.

Method: The paper introduces prefix-removal probing: for each token position, compare the hidden-state trajectory of right-side tokens with and without left context. The Right Reset (RR) score quantifies trajectory preservation — high RR means removing left context minimally affects right-side processing, indicating a boundary. These per-token edge scores are fed into a dynamic programming algorithm that selects cuts to form variable-length chunks. The approach is evaluated on flattened text (concatenated topical records with separators removed) and compared against embedding-based baselines (e.g., BGE), passive layer scores, and direct prompting.

Result: RR recovers 47.7% of original records as clean units vs. 25.9% for the strongest baseline (BGE embedding boundary). The advantage persists after rendering and OCR degradation. Passive scores from the same Qwen3-4B layer and direct prompting of a same-scale instruction model perform substantially worse. Across six LMs, RR-selected cuts show consistently less local output disruption than unselected candidate edges. A likelihood-ratio readout on observed tokens is competitive in some architectures.

Conclusion: The core contribution is the intervention itself: context dependence provides a robust boundary signal when surface structure is weak. RR demonstrates that causal LM representations implicitly encode document structure, and that explicitly probing context sensitivity yields a practical, training-free segmentation method competitive with or superior to trained embedding baselines.

Abstract: Removing the left context from a causal language model reveals a useful kind of boundary: an edge where the model processes the same right-hand tokens with little change. We turn this observation into prefix-removal probing and introduce Right Reset (RR), which measures preservation of the right-hand hidden-state trajectory. A dynamic program converts RR edge scores into variable-length chunks. On flattened text formed by concatenating topically similar records after deleting their separators and layout, RR recovers 47.7% of the original records as clean units, versus 25.9% for a BGE embedding boundary, the strongest tested conventional baseline without task-specific model training. The gain persists after rendering and OCR. Passive scores from the same Qwen3-4B layer and direct prompting of a same-scale instruction model perform substantially worse on flattened records. Across six language models, RR-selected cuts also undergo consistently less local output disruption than unselected candidate edges. An observed-token likelihood-ratio readout is competitive in some architectures, indicating that the central contribution is the intervention: context dependence itself can provide a boundary signal when surface structure is weak.

</details>


### [21] [Equitable System-Prompt Selection via Constrained Mixed-Strategy GroupDRO](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04339)
*Mengyu Xu,Qiaoxin Yang,Zhihan Liu,Ruiyao Xu,Zachary Liu,Kezhen Chen,Chongyang Gao*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Proposes a constrained mixed-strategy GroupDRO framework that selects weighted combinations of system prompts to minimize worst-case answer quality degradation across semantically equivalent question phrasings, achieving ~13% reduction in worst-case losses while maintaining average quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs produce inconsistent answer quality for semantically equivalent but differently phrased questions, and standard system-prompt optimization targeting average performance leaves certain phrasings with poor responses. Existing approaches optimize prompt text directly rather than selecting from an ensemble.

Method: A constrained mixed-strategy Group Distributionally Robust Optimization (GroupDRO) framework that assigns selection weights to an existing pool of system prompts. The optimization minimizes worst-case information-quality loss across both evaluation metrics and groups (question-phrasing variants), subject to a constraint that keeps mean loss close to average-based selection. Pool generation and weight selection are decoupled, enabling use of any prompt pool.

Result: Across five LLMs on bilingual medical and consumer-finance benchmarks, the method reduces Overall Mean, Worst 25% Mean, and Worst metrics by 13.1%, 13.2%, and 13.7% on average relative to no mitigation, while maintaining overall quality comparable to Average selection. Multi-prompt weights reveal complementarity across metric-group pairs.

Conclusion: Constrained mixed-strategy GroupDRO effectively addresses quality disparities across question phrasings by leveraging complementary system prompts, offering a practical post-hoc solution compatible with any prompt pool without requiring prompt-text optimization.

Abstract: Large language models are increasingly used for information seeking, yet semantically equivalent questions phrased in different ways can receive answers of considerably different quality. System prompts are widely employed to steer response behavior, but they are typically optimized for average-case quality, so some question phrasings may still receive incomplete or low-quality answers. To address this, we formulate a constrained mixed-strategy GroupDRO framework for system-prompt selection. Instead of optimizing the system-prompt text, the framework assigns weights to system prompts in an existing pool to minimize the worst-case information-quality loss across evaluation metrics and groups, while constraining the mean loss to stay close to that of average-based selection. Because pool generation and selection are decoupled, the method applies to any system-prompt pool and can leverage an ensemble of complementary system prompts rather than a single one. Across five LLMs on two bilingual medical and consumer-finance benchmarks, the constrained method reduces the Overall Mean, Worst 25% Mean, and Worst by 13.1%, 13.2%, and 13.7% on average relative to no mitigation while keeping overall quality close to Average selection. Its multi-prompt weights reveal complementarity across metric-group pairs. Code and data are available at https://github.com/Rainxu09/equitable-system-prompt-selection.

</details>


### [22] [The Calibration Floor: Format Repair Can Masquerade as Self-Correction at Small-to-Mid Scale](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04355)
*Mingguang Chen,Bo Qu,Licheng Wang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Self-revision accuracy gains in language models are often misinterpreted as reasoning improvements. The authors show that most of these gains actually come from format changes (answer parseability) rather than content changes, using both observational decomposition and causal intervention via grammar-constrained decoding across multiple model families and scales.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work interprets accuracy shifts after LLM self-revision as evidence of improved reasoning. The authors challenge this by hypothesizing that much of the measured effect is an artifact at the answer-extraction boundary—format recovery or loss—rather than genuine content-level reasoning change. They aim to test this causally, not just observationally.

Method: The authors decompose the always-revise accuracy shift into a content margin (both answers parseable) and format-recovery/loss margins (parseability changes). They then intervene causally using grammar-constrained decoding to force all answers to be parseable, comparing the naive total effect against the content-margin estimate across 29 primary cells (Qwen3.5 0.8B–9B, Gemma-4-12B, plus API models) and a frontier arm (Tencent Hy3, Nvidia Nemotron-3-Ultra-550B). They also replicate a prior confidence-gating protocol and apply a clustered model to test scale effects.

Result: In 12 cells with meaningful unparseable rates, format effects significantly exceed content effects (Wilcoxon p=1.7e-3). Grammar-constrained decoding closes a median 71% of the gap between naive total effect and content margin across 14 cells. Floor-scale models (0.8B/2B) show far higher odds of content-level change and harm than capable-scale models (p<1e-7). A verbatim replication of a prior confidence-gating protocol shows near-zero content margin. Frontier models exhibit format-dominance intensifying with scale: content margin is exactly zero in all 5 frontier cells despite total effects up to +0.275.

Conclusion: Content change is a minority share of what the field has measured as self-correction. Most reported self-revision gains are format artifacts. The calibration-floor criterion reveals a squeeze: small models have headroom but no signal, while capable models have signal but no headroom. Only one cell is marginally viable, with negligible sealed-holdout gain. The authors release their instrument, code, and derived results.

Abstract: Accuracy changes after language-model self-revision are usually interpreted as changes in reasoning. We show this can fail at the answer-extraction boundary, and test the failure causally rather than only observationally. Across Qwen3.5 (0.8B-9B), Gemma-4-12B, and two frontier models via API (Tencent Hy3, Nvidia Nemotron-3-Ultra-550B) in 29 primary cells plus a frontier arm, we decompose the always-revise accuracy shift into a content margin (both answers parseable) and format-recovery/loss margins (parseability changes). On 12 cells with meaningful unparseable-answer rates, format effects exceed content effects (Wilcoxon p=1.7e-3). To test this causally, we force already-generated reasoning through grammar-constrained decoding so every answer is parseable by construction: across 14 cells this closes a median 71% of the gap between the naive total effect and the content-margin estimate, with two cells converging exactly and a residual on the two largest-effect cells reported rather than dismissed. A clustered model confirms floor-scale (0.8B/2B) models have far higher odds of content-level change and harm than capable-scale models (p<1e-7). Replicating a cited confidence-gating protocol verbatim on Qwen3.5 does not reproduce its reported gain and shows the same near-zero content margin. A frontier check on much larger models shows format-dominance intensifying with scale: content margin is exactly zero in all 5 cells despite total effects up to +0.275, though this arm is lower-powered. The calibration-floor criterion on the content margin reveals a squeeze: floor-scale cells have headroom but insufficient signal, capable-scale cells have signal but little headroom; only one cell is marginally viable, with negligible sealed-holdout gain. Content is a minority share of what the field has measured as self-correction. We release the instrument, code, and derived results.

</details>


### [23] [FinReportBench: Measuring and Improving Institution-Grade Financial Report Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04374)
*Yinghao Tang,Tan Zhenwei,Yiyao Wang,Wanli Gu,Xiaolu Zhang,Jun Zhou,Wei Chen*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: FinReportBench introduces an expert-grounded benchmark with a 35-item rubric for evaluating institution-grade financial report generation, revealing that while basic deliverability is near-saturated, report identity and institutional completeness remain bottlenecks, and benchmark-guided skill distillation substantially improves model performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLMs produce fluent financial analysis, but fluency alone is insufficient for institutional delivery. There lacks a rigorous, expert-validated benchmark to measure whether generated reports meet professional standards for identity, sourcing, structure, and visual quality.

Method: Authors construct FinReportBench from 10,000 balanced Chinese-English financial research records, curating 244 bilingual tasks across three research objects and two input tiers. Each task contains a public query, reconstructed research trajectory, and hidden source packet. A 35-item evaluation rubric is derived via expert partial orders, multimodal evidence, and decision-boundary audits, covering deliverability (G0), report identity (G1), and institutional completeness (G2). Three independent judge families validate the rubric at near-ceiling agreement rates. They then apply benchmark-guided skill distillation to convert recurring failure patterns into reusable generation and self-review constraints.

Result: Across nine model families, G0 (basic deliverability) is nearly saturated. G1 (report identity) and G2 (institutional completeness) remain primary bottlenecks, with the largest gaps in generation-trace control, information density, and data discipline.
