Skill distillation yields mean improvements of +33.85 points on G1 and +13.83 points on G2 across five model families, without degrading G0.

Conclusion: Bounded, observable criteria can support reliable expert-aligned evaluation of financial reports. Institutional-grade report generation requires systematic attention to identity, sourcing rigor, and visual standards beyond fluency. Benchmark-guided skill distillation is an effective strategy for closing these gaps.

Abstract: Large language models can produce fluent financial analysis, but fluency alone does not establish whether a report is suitable for institutional delivery. We introduce FinReportBench, an expert-grounded benchmark for measuring and improving institution-grade financial report generation. Expert review reveals recurring gaps in report identity, institutional components, source discipline, and visual delivery. We derive a 35-item rubric through expert partial orders, multimodal evidence, and audits of decision boundaries, covering deliverability, report identity, and institutional completeness. Starting from 10,000 balanced Chinese and English financial-research source records, we curate 244 bilingual tasks across three research objects and two input tiers. Each task separates the public query, reconstructed research trajectory, and hidden source packet. Three independent judge families reproduce the expert partial order at near-ceiling rates, showing that bounded, observable criteria support reliable evaluation. Across nine model families, basic deliverability is nearly saturated, while report identity and institutional completeness remain the primary bottlenecks. The largest cross-model gaps concern generation-trace control, information density, and data discipline rather than basic report framing. We then use benchmark-guided skill distillation to turn recurrent failures into reusable generation and self-review constraints. Across five model families, the evolved skill improves mean G1 by 33.85 points and mean G2 by 13.83 points over paired no-skill runs while preserving G0 for every pair. Code and benchmark artifacts are available at https://github.com/MisterBrookT/finreportbench.

</details>


### [24] [EdgeLM: Edge Demonstrations for Language Models' Table Understanding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04390)
*Soroush Omidvartehrani,Mohammadamin Habibollah,Mohammadreza Daviran,Davood Rafiei*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: EdgeLM is a demonstration retrieval framework for LLM table-centric prediction that selects "edge evidence"—examples near decision boundaries—instead of purely similar examples. It retrieves two complementary types: data edges (nearby examples with different labels) and model edges (examples the model previously misclassified), achieving strong performance across diverse tasks, datasets, and LLMs without retraining.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing retrieval methods for in-context learning select demonstrations based on similarity to the query, but similar examples often reinforce the model's existing prediction bias rather than clarifying decision boundaries. The authors identify that difficult decisions require demonstrations that reveal distinctions between classes—edge evidence near the decision boundary—rather than prototypical examples.

Method: EdgeLM retrieves two complementary forms of edge evidence: (1) data edges—examples close to the query in embedding space but with different ground-truth labels, and (2) model edges—examples similar to the query that were previously misclassified by the deployed LLM. The framework requires no model retraining or task-specific engineering and operates as a drop-in retrieval strategy for in-context learning.

Result: EdgeLM was evaluated across five data wrangling tasks, fifteen datasets, and five LLMs (both open-weight and proprietary). It achieved the best or near-best performance in every setting. Ablation studies confirmed that data edges and model edges provide complementary benefits, with each contributing uniquely to overall performance gains.

Conclusion: Selecting edge evidence—demonstrations near decision boundaries rather than purely similar ones—is a simple yet effective retrieval paradigm for in-context learning. The complementary nature of data edges and model edges suggests both semantic proximity and model-specific weaknesses are important signals for demonstration selection.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) perform table-centric prediction through in-context learning, making demonstration selection critical to performance. Existing retrieval methods prioritize similarity to the query, but similar demonstrations often reinforce the model's likely prediction rather than reveal the distinctions needed for difficult decisions. We propose EdgeLM, a retrieval framework that instead selects edge evidence, demonstrations that are both relevant to the query and informative about the decision boundary. EdgeLM retrieves two complementary forms of edge evidence by selecting data edges, nearby examples with different ground-truth labels, and model edges, similar examples previously misclassified by the deployed model. EdgeLM requires neither model retraining nor task-specific engineering. Across five data wrangling tasks, fifteen datasets, and five open-weight and proprietary LLMs, EdgeLM consistently achieves the best or near-best performance in every setting, while ablations show that the two forms of edge evidence provide complementary benefits. Our code and datasets are publicly available at https://github.com/soroushomidvar/EdgeLM.

</details>


### [25] [NOLLI: A Difficulty-Calibrated Puzzle Benchmark for Diagnosing the English-Korean Performance Gap](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04397)
*Dasol Choi,Joonyong Park,Daegon Yu,Soo Yong Kim,Youngsook Song,Seunghyeok Hong*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: NOLLI is a procedurally generated English-Korean puzzle benchmark (15 types, 7,500 items) that uses behavioral difficulty calibration instead of structural size to diagnose Korean performance gaps. Key findings: presentation language alone causes negligible gaps; writing-system-intensive tasks show sharp Korean deficits; and structural size is an unreliable proxy for empirical difficulty.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To systematically diagnose where and why performance gaps arise in Korean language model evaluation, moving beyond anecdotal observations to a controlled, procedurally generated benchmark that isolates linguistic factors (translation, script, culture/orthography) while calibrating difficulty behaviorally.

Method: NOLLI comprises 15 puzzle types (25 tasks, 7,500 items) at three levels: (1) matched direct English-Korean translations, (2) script adaptations operating over Hangul jamo (sub-syllabic letters), and (3) Korean-only tasks grounded in Korean culture or orthography. Generators are behaviorally tuned so a fixed reference model lands in target accuracy bands, avoiding reliance on structural size as a difficulty proxy. All items are seed-regenerable, verified unique-solution, and deterministically scored. Evaluation covers 15 frontier, open-weight, and Korean-developed models (12 above a 3% accuracy floor), with TOST used to assess statistical equivalence of English-Korean accuracy.

Result: Matched English-Korean accuracy is statistically equivalent within ±10 pp (TOST), suggesting negligible cost from presentation language alone. Writing-system-intensive tasks reveal sharp gaps: Korean Cipher lags English by up to 68.7 pp, while Cryptarithmetic over the same jamo shows no systematic penalty. Jamo Composition accuracy predicts Korean Cipher accuracy. Korean-only tasks: rule-application deficits vary in sign; Kinship shows a consistent positive deficit across all 12 models. Structural size fails to grow from Easy to Hard in 7 of 15 types, making it an unreliable difficulty proxy.

Conclusion: Performance gaps in Korean LM evaluation are not driven by presentation language per se but by multi-step sub-syllabic execution demands and culturally grounded reasoning. Behavioral difficulty calibration is essential for valid cross-lingual benchmarking, as structural size is an unreliable proxy for empirical difficulty.

Abstract: We introduce NOLLI, a procedurally generated English-Korean puzzle benchmark designed to diagnose where Korean performance gaps arise. It comprises 15 puzzle types (25 tasks; 7,500 items), with every instance seed-regenerable, verified to have a unique solution, and scored deterministically. Rather than equating harder with bigger, we calibrate difficulty behaviorally, tuning each generator until a fixed reference model lands in target accuracy bands. Its three-level design combines matched direct translations, script adaptations over Hangul jamo (sub-syllabic letters), and Korean-only tasks grounded in Korean culture or orthography. We evaluate 15 frontier, open-weight, and Korean-developed models; among the 12 above a 3% overall-accuracy floor, matched English-Korean accuracy is statistically equivalent within a +/- 10 pp margin (TOST), suggesting little cost from presentation language alone. Writing-system-intensive tasks show sharper gaps: Korean Cipher falls behind English by up to 68.7 pp, whereas Cryptarithmetic over the same jamo shows no systematic penalty, and Jamo Composition accuracy predicts Korean Cipher accuracy. These contrasts are diagnostic rather than causal, consistent with difficulty in multi-step sub-syllabic execution. Korean-only tasks separate rule-application deficits, which vary in sign, from a Kinship deficit positive in all 12. Finally, a salient size measure fails to grow from Easy to Hard in 7 of 15 types, making structural size an unreliable proxy for empirical difficulty.

</details>


### [26] [Social Pressure Breaks Majority Voting in LLM Safety Panels](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04415)
*Yibo Hu,Jiaming Qu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: LLM safety panels are vulnerable to social influence: when a panel of LLMs is exposed to peers asserting a wrong "unsafe" label before voting, false-alarm rates skyrocket from 56.5% to 87.5% for individual reviewers and reach 100% under majority voting. The effect is asymmetric — models follow "unsafe" pushes (~75%) far more than "safe" pushes (~17%).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While ensemble methods combining multiple LLM judgments can correct individual errors, this paper investigates a critical vulnerability: when all models in a panel are exposed to the same misleading social cues (e.g., peer assertions of wrong labels), the benefit of aggregation may disappear. The authors aim to diagnose whether shared context creates correlated failures that undermine the safety guarantees of model panels.

Method: A controlled two-round experiment: six open-weight LLMs judge items across six safety datasets. In Round 1, each model judges alone. In Round 2, models judge the same items again after being shown simulated peer responses — either six peers asserting a wrong label (treatment) or six peers abstaining (control). Final panel decisions use majority vote. Additionally, a smaller proprietary-model probe (GPT-4o, Claude, Gemini) assessed cross-model variation.

Result: Wrong-label peer messages caused average reviewer false-alarm rate to jump from 56.5% (silent peers) to 87.5%. Majority voting raised the panel false-alarm rate to 100%. Without asserted wrong labels, panel voting outperformed individual members. The effect is highly asymmetric: reviewers conform to "unsafe" pushes ~75% of the time versus only ~17% for "safe" pushes, causing false-alarm rates to surge while harmful-miss rates remain largely unchanged. Proprietary models showed substantial variation in susceptibility.

Conclusion: Sensitivity to shared social cues represents a distinct failure mode for LLM safety panels that is not addressed by standard ensembling. The authors propose their two-round experimental paradigm as a simple pre-deployment diagnostic to measure and mitigate this vulnerability before fielding safety-review ensembles.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to detect unsafe content. A common approach is to combine judgments from a panel of models to correct individual mistakes, but this benefit may disappear when every model sees the same misleading context before voting. We study this risk in a controlled two-round experiment. Each model first judges an item alone, then judges it again after six simulated peers either assert the wrong label or abstain. We combine the final judgments by majority vote. Across six open-weight LLMs and six datasets, we find that the wrong-label peer message raises the average reviewer false-alarm rate from 56.5% under silent peers to 87.5%, and majority voting raises the panel false-alarm rate to 100%. Without an asserted label, the same panel outperforms its average member. The effect is strongly asymmetric: reviewers follow pushes toward "unsafe" far more than pushes toward "safe" (about 75% versus 17%), so the panel's false-alarm rate rises sharply while its harmful-miss rate changes little. The proprietary-model probe shows substantial variation across models. These results identify susceptibility to shared social cues as a failure mode of safety panels and provide a simple pre-deployment diagnostic.

</details>


### [27] [MERaLiON-GR: Speech Gender Recognition Model for English and SEA Languages](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04433)
*Qiongqiong Wang,Ai Ti Aw,Nancy F. Chen,Ying Lay Chiu,Yang Ding,Yingxu He,Ridong Jiang,Zhuohan Liu,Yanfeng Lu,Yi Ma,Muhammad Huzaifah,Nabilah Binte Md Johan,Nattadaporn Lertcheva,Pham Minh Duc,Sailor Hardik Bhupendra,Siti Umairah Binte Mohammad Salleh,Shuo Sun,Tarun Kumar Vangani,Jeremy H. M. Wong,Jinyang Wu,Longyin Zhang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: MERaLiON-GR is a speech gender recognition system that finetunes a pre-trained conformer-based transformer with LoRA and adds an ECAPA-TDNN downstream network, achieving SOTA on English and 7 Southeast Asian languages, outperforming Vox-Profile and a large Audio-LLM.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To develop an accurate, cross-lingual speech gender recognition system that works robustly across English and diverse Southeast Asian languages, addressing the need for dedicated paralinguistic models rather than relying on general-purpose audio LLMs.

Method: Fine-tunes MERaLiON-SpeechEncoder-2 (a large conformer-based transformer) using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) for parameter efficiency. Appends a multi-scale ECAPA-TDNN downstream network with attention pooling and a lightweight linear classifier for binary gender classification (female/male).

Result: MERaLiON-GR consistently surpasses the SOTA Vox-Profile model and a large Audio-LLM across 8 languages (English, Chinese, Malay, Tamil, Thai, Vietnamese, Indonesian, Khmer) in both full-utterance and segment-level evaluation modes.

Conclusion: Dedicated, fine-tuned speech encoder models significantly outperform general-purpose audio LLMs for paralinguistic tasks, demonstrating strong cross-lingual generalization across English and Southeast Asian languages.

Abstract: We present MERaLiON-GR, a speech gender recognition system that performs binary classification (female / male) on English and Southeast Asian (SEA) languages. The model finetunes MERaLiON-SpeechEncoder-2, a large conformer based transformer pre-trained on a broad speech corpus, and applies parameter efficient fine-tuning via Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) to adapt the encoder to the gender recognition task, and appends a multi-scale ECAPA-TDNN down stream network with attention pooling and a lightweight linear classifier. Extensive evaluations across multilingual Singaporean and Southeast Asian languages (English, Chinese, Malay, Tamil, Thai, Vietnamese, Indonesian, and Khmer) show that MERaLiON-GR consistently surpasses the state-of-the-art gender recognition model Vox-Profile and a large Audio-LLM, in both full-utterance and segment level evaluation modes. The results underscore the value of dedicated speech models in achieving accurate paralinguistic understanding and strong cross-lingual generalization.

</details>


### [28] [D$^2$F-ReAG: Dynamic Decomposition and Filtering for Multi-Hop Reasoning-Augmented Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04444)
*Jiaoyang Li,Junhao Ruan,Shengwei Tang,Kaiyan Chang,Zhengtao Yu,Tong Xiao,Jingbo Zhu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: D2F-ReAG proposes a dynamic, reliability-aware reasoning framework for multi-hop RAG that adaptively decomposes questions and filters sub-answers, improving both accuracy and efficiency over static graph-based or decomposition methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs with RAG perform well on single-hop queries but falter on multi-hop questions requiring cross-document reasoning. Existing solutions (graph-structured RAG, static question decomposition) lack dynamic decomposition and effective filtering, resulting in suboptimal efficiency and accuracy.

Method: D2F-ReAG introduces an adaptive reasoning depth mechanism: it first assesses the reliability of root-level reasoning. If reliable, the answer is generated directly. If not, the question is dynamically decomposed into sub-questions, verified reasoning from those sub-questions is filtered, and the results are used to refine the root reasoning before final answer generation.

Result: Experiments on three multi-hop benchmarks demonstrate that D2F-ReAG effectively handles complex multi-hop questions, outperforming baseline approaches.

Conclusion: Dynamic, reliability-gated decomposition combined with verified filtering significantly improves multi-hop RAG performance, offering a more efficient and accurate paradigm than prior static decomposition or graph-based methods.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often generate inaccurate answers due to their reliance on static internal knowledge. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) addresses this limitation by integrating external knowledge and excelling at single-hop queries. However, it struggles with multi-hop questions that require cross-document reasoning. Existing methods, such as graph structured RAG or question decomposition, often lack dynamic decomposition and effective filtering, which leads to lower efficiency and accuracy. To overcome these limitations, we propose Dynamic Decomposition and Filtering for Multi-Hop Reasoning-Augmented Generation (D2F-ReAG), a novel paradigm that adaptively controls reasoning depth by judging the reliability of the root-level reasoning. If the root reasoning is reliable, the model directly generates the answer. Otherwise, the question is logically decomposed into sub-questions, and the verified reasoning derived from these sub-questions is used to refine the root reasoning. Experiments on three multi-hop benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in handling complex multi-hop questions.

</details>


### [29] [The Evaluator Is Part of the Experiment: Measuring Open-Ended LLM Conformity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04463)
*Alicia Guerra,Yibo Hu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper challenges existing conformity measurements for LLMs, which rely on discrete answer flips under verifiable labels. The authors propose a new experimental protocol to measure conformity in open-ended revision settings, finding that wrong peer input degrades revision quality, evaluator neutrality is inconsistent, and anchor calibration is essential for reliable latent-scale measurement.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work on LLM conformity focuses narrowly on discrete, verifiable answer flips, which fails to capture open-ended revision scenarios where answer quality is graded, latent, and judged imperfectly. There is a need for a robust measurement framework that accounts for the nuances of open-ended revision, including peer influence, evaluator bias, and scale calibration.

Method: The authors introduce an experimental protocol using a pooled main peer-condition corpus and separately constructed decomposition corpora. This design isolates four factors: ordinary re-answering, candidate-content exposure, a bundled peer-presentation residual, and directional judge sensitivity to visible peer context. Experiments span four open-weight generators, three benchmarks, and multiple evaluators including GPT-4o and GPT-5.4-mini audits. An anchor audit checks whether terse correct anchors are misread and destabilize the latent scale.

Result: All-wrong peer input produces the lowest-quality revisions across every generator-dataset cell. Blind vs. informed ratings of identical answers diverge: one judge shifts toward the peer-endorsed position, two shift away, one is approximately neutral, and both GPT-4o and GPT-5.4-mini audits are non-neutral. Terse correct anchors are misread often enough to threaten latent-scale calibration unless explicitly checked.

Conclusion: Four conclusions emerge: (1) flip rates are insufficient as a complete measure of open-ended conformity; (2) wrong peers harm open-ended revision quality; (3) evaluators are not neutral; and (4) anchor calibration is necessary for valid measurement in open-ended conformity research.

Abstract: Prior work on LLM conformity largely measures discrete answer flips under verifiable labels. Open-ended revisions require a different measurement strategy because answer quality is graded, latent, and judged imperfectly. We introduce an experimental protocol implemented across a pooled main peer-condition corpus and separately constructed decomposition corpora, allowing us to separate ordinary re-answering, candidate-content exposure, a bundled peer-presentation residual, and directional judge sensitivity to visible peer context. Across four open-weight generators and three benchmarks, all-wrong peer input produces the lowest-quality revisions in every generator-dataset cell. Blind and informed ratings of identical answers also differ by evaluator: one judge shifts toward the peer-endorsed position, two shift away, one is approximately neutral, and GPT-4o and GPT-5.4-mini audits are likewise non-neutral. Finally, an anchor audit shows that terse correct anchors can be misread often enough to destabilize the latent scale unless calibration is checked explicitly. These results support four conclusions: flip rates are insufficient as a complete measure of open-ended conformity, wrong peers harm open-ended revision, evaluators are not neutral, and anchor calibration is necessary.

</details>


### [30] [Energy- and Memory-Efficient PEFT Methods for Personalized On-Device SLMs on Consumer GPUs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04488)
*Kuanysh Akhmetzhanov,Jurn-Gyu Park*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper compares five PEFT methods (Full Fine-Tuning, LoRA, LoRA+, QLoRA, BitFit) on four SLMs across general (GLUE) and personalization (LaMP) benchmarks using energy-focused (NetScore-E) and memory-focused (NetScore-M) metrics. LoRA+ dominates energy-constrained scenarios (selected in 18/24 configurations), while QLoRA excels in memory-constrained settings (up to 3.9× VRAM reduction), establishing a practical framework for personalized on-device deployment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deploying and personalizing LLMs on resource-constrained devices is impractical due to high VRAM, time, and energy costs. PEFT of SLMs offers a promising alternative, but few studies systematically compare PEFT methods across architectures using both general and personalization benchmarks while accounting for energy consumption — a critical metric for on-device deployment.

Method: The authors compare five fine-tuning approaches (Full Fine-Tuning, LoRA, LoRA+, QLoRA, and BitFit) on four SLMs from two architectural families — Transformer-based (TinyLlama-1.1B, Qwen3-1.7B) and SSM-based (Mamba-1.4B, Mamba-2-1.3B). Evaluation spans three GLUE tasks (SST-2, QNLI, STS-B) and three LaMP personalization tasks (LaMP-1, LaMP-2, LaMP-3). Each configuration is scored using NetScore-E (energy-focused) and NetScore-M (memory-focused). Selection follows a strict energy-first rule: highest NetScore-E, with ties broken by NetScore-M.

Result: LoRA+ achieves the highest NetScore-E in 19/24 configurations and highest NetScore-M in 13/24, and is selected in 18/24. QLoRA (Transformer-only) reduces peak fine-tuning VRAM by up to 3.9× vs. LoRA, winning NetScore-M in 5/12 Transformer configurations, but its de-quantization overhead leaves it selected in only one once energy is considered. BitFit and full fine-tuning are almost never competitive. TinyLlama-1.1B leads NetScore-E on 5/6 benchmarks and NetScore-M on 4/6.

Conclusion: Compact SLMs paired with PEFT provide a practical, energy-aware path to personalized on-device deployment. The optimal method depends on the dominant constraint: LoRA+ for energy-constrained scenarios and QLoRA for memory-constrained scenarios.

Abstract: Despite rapid advances in large language models (LLMs), deploying and personalizing them on resource-constrained devices remains impractical due to high VRAM, time, and energy costs. Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) of Small Language Models (SLMs) offers a promising alternative, yet few studies compare PEFT methods across architectures using both general and personalization benchmarks while accounting for energy consumption. We compare five fine-tuning approaches (Full Fine-Tuning, LoRA, LoRA+, QLoRA, and BitFit) on four SLMs from two families (Transformer-based: TinyLlama-1.1B, Qwen3-1.7B; SSM-based: Mamba-1.4B, Mamba-2-1.3B) across three GLUE tasks (SST-2, QNLI, STS-B) and three LaMP personalization tasks (LaMP-1, LaMP-2, LaMP-3). Each configuration is evaluated with the energy-focused NetScore-E and the memory-focused NetScore-M, the two variants that reflect the constraints binding on-device deployment. Methods are selected with a strict energy-first rule (highest NetScore-E, ties broken by NetScore#). LoRA+ achieves the highest NetScore-E in 19 of 24 configurations and the highest NetScore-M in 13 of 24, and is the selected method in 18 of 24. QLoRA, available only for the Transformer models, cuts peak finetuning VRAM by up to 3.9x relative to LoRA and therefore takes the best NetScore-M in 5 of the 12 Transformer configurations, although its de-quantization overhead leaves it selected in only one of them once energy decides. BitFit and full fine-tuning are almost never competitive on either variant, and TinyLlama-1.1B leads the energy-focused NetScore-E on five of the six benchmarks and the memory-focused NetScore-M on four. These results show that compact SLMs paired with PEFT provide a practical, energy-aware path to personalized on-device deployment, with the optimal method set by the dominant constraint: LoRA+ for energy and QLoRA for memory.

</details>


### [31] [K-EXAONE 2.0 Technical Report](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04505)
*Eunbi Choi,Kibong Choi,Sehyun Chun,Seokhee Hong,Junwon Hwang,Hyojin Jeon,Ahra Jo,Hyunjik Jo,Yeonsik Jo,Minhyeok Jung,Doyoung Kim,Heegyu Kim,Joonkee Kim,Seonghwan Kim,Soyeon Kim,Sunkyoung Kim,Yireun Kim,Yongil Kim,Byungoh Ko,Changhun Lee,Dohaeng Lee,Haeju Lee,Jinsik Lee,Kyungmin Lee,Minwoo Lee,Wonkee Lee,Sangha Park,Sungjune Park,Kwangrok Ryoo,Kijung Seo,Minju Seo,Yongwoo Song,Sejong Yang,Heuiyeen Yeen,Stanley Jungkyu Choi,Yemuk Choi,Yongchan Chun,Jiwon Ham,Dasol Hong,Sujeong Im,Kijeong Jeon,Gerrard Jeongwon Jo,Hyeongjun Jo,Yujin Jo,Jiyeon Jung,Naeun Kang,Daeseong Kim,Euisoon Kim,Hayeon Kim,Hyosang Kim,Myoungshin Kim,Unsol Kim,Youchul Kim,Chaeeun Lee,ChaeYoon Lee,Edward Hwayoung Lee,Honglak Lee,Hwansoo Lee,Minkyung Lee,Sangeun Lee,Solji Lim,Woohyung Lim,Chanwoo Moon,Jueun Mun,Jimin Park,Seojeong Park,Yongmin Park,Hyerin Seo,Donghyeon Shin,Donghyun Son,Eunyong Son,Kaehyun Um,Sihoon Yang,Chang En Yea,Sihyuk Yi,Kyungjae Yoo,Chansik Yoon*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: K-EXAONE 2.0 is an open-weight 750B-parameter MoE multilingual foundation model (37B activated per token) that upcycles its predecessor, supporting 256K-token context and 10 languages, with strong gains in agentic coding, long-context understanding, and safety.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To advance toward global frontier-scale foundation models by significantly scaling up LG AI Research's existing K-EXAONE model, expanding capacity, multilingual coverage, and practical capabilities while maintaining open-weight accessibility under Apache 2.0.

Method: Upcycling K-EXAONE into a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture with 750B total and ~37B activated parameters per token. Training proceeds through three stages: continual pre-training, difficulty-focused mid-training, and post-training. The pipeline targets reasoning, agentic coding, multilingual capability (expanded from 6 to 10 languages), long-context handling (up to 256K tokens), and Korean socioculturally grounded safety.

Result: K-EXAONE 2.0 outperforms its predecessor across nine practical evaluation categories, with the largest improvements in agentic coding and long-context understanding. It shows clearest strengths in long-context retrieval and safety, and remains competitive with other open-weight models.

Conclusion: K-EXAONE 2.0 represents a significant step—not the endpoint—in LG AI Research's pursuit of frontier-scale models. Released under Apache 2.0, it invites community evaluation, deployment, adaptation, and further development.

Abstract: This technical report presents K-EXAONE 2.0, an open-weight multilingual foundation model developed by LG AI Research as a step in our effort toward global frontier-scale foundation models. Rather than training from scratch, we upcycle K-EXAONE and expand its architecture, yielding a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model with 750B total parameters and approximately 37B activated per token---more than three times the capacity of its predecessor. K-EXAONE 2.0 supports context lengths of up to 256K tokens and expands multilingual coverage from six to ten languages. Its training pipeline combines continual pre-training, difficulty-focused mid-training, and post-training to strengthen reasoning, agentic coding, multilingual capability, and safety grounded in Korean sociocultural contexts. Across nine evaluation categories selected to reflect the conditions of practical use, K-EXAONE 2.0 improves over K-EXAONE and remains competitive with open-weight models, showing its largest gains in agentic coding and long-context understanding and its clearest strengths in long-context retrieval and safety. Released under the Apache 2.0 license, K-EXAONE 2.0 enables the wider AI ecosystem to evaluate, deploy, adapt, and build upon it, while marking the beginning---rather than the endpoint---of our challenge toward the global frontier.

</details>


### [32] [RESPClinBench: Benchmarking Multimodal Clinical Decision-Making and Longitudinal Disease Management in Respiratory Specialty Care](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04514)
*Mouxiao Bian,Zhi Chen,Ruiyao Chen,Lu Lu,Hengrui Liang,Chaoyi Huang,Yiluo Lin,Jingru Ding,Yun Zhong,Yuming Su,Jie Xu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: RESPClinBench is a clinically grounded benchmark with 623 cases (AECOPD-PIM and PNBIM) evaluating seven LLMs on respiratory decision-making. Qwen3.6-27B ranked first overall (71.22/100). Significant safety concerns emerged: imaging hallucination in 31.85% of pulmonary nodule responses and medication-safety risk in 26.93% of COPD responses.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing examination-oriented medical benchmarks fail to capture the multimodal interpretation, longitudinal risk assessment, guideline-concordant intervention, and whole-course management required in real-world respiratory specialty care. The authors sought to bridge this gap with a clinically authentic benchmark.

Method: RESPClinBench was constructed from de-identified respiratory clinical data with two sub-benchmarks: AECOPD-PIM (427 open-ended COPD cases) and PNBIM (196 multimodal pulmonary nodule cases pairing chest CT with structured clinical data). Three attending physicians and one senior specialist performed case revision, reference-answer development, and cross-adjudication. Seven models generated 4,361 responses via API (temperature=0, max output 8192 tokens). Scoring combined atomic-action recall with rubric-based LLM-as-a-Judge assessment, averaged arithmetically. Independent safety flags captured imaging hallucination, medication-safety risk, and serious medical risk.

Result: Mean final score across all 623 cases was 68.58/100. Qwen3.6-27B led overall (71.22) and on AECOPD-PIM (71.11). Qwen3.5-397B-A17B led PNBIM (72.48). Safety analysis: imaging hallucination in 31.85% and serious medical risk in 8.16% of PNBIM responses; medication-safety risk in 26.93% and serious medical risk in 1.44% of AECOPD-PIM responses.

Conclusion: RESPClinBench reveals task-specific LLM limitations in multimodal pulmonary nodule assessment and longitudinal COPD management. The combined framework of explicit clinical-action coverage, holistic rubric evaluation, and independent safety flagging offers a clinically grounded basis for model selection and prospective validation.

Abstract: Background: Respiratory specialty care requires multimodal interpretation, longitudinal risk assessment, guideline-concordant intervention, and whole-course management, which are poorly represented by examination-oriented medical benchmarks. Objective: To develop RESPClinBench, a real-world scenario-based benchmark for respiratory clinical decision-making, and evaluate seven contemporary large language models across AECOPD-PIM and PNBIM. Methods: RESPClinBench cases were adapted from de-identified respiratory clinical data. Three attending-level respiratory physicians revised cases, reference answers, and atomic clinical-action points, while one senior respiratory specialist performed cross-review and final adjudication. AECOPD-PIM comprised 427 open-ended COPD cases, and PNBIM comprised 196 multimodal pulmonary nodule cases combining chest CT with structured clinical information. Seven models generated 4,361 responses through standardized API inference with temperature 0 and a maximum output length of 8192 tokens. An automated framework calculated the final score as the arithmetic mean of atomic-action recall and rubric-based LLM-as-a-Judge assessment. Results: Across 623 cases, the mean final score was 68.58. Qwen3.6-27B ranked first overall at 71.22, Qwen3.5-397B-A17B led PNBIM at 72.48, and Qwen3.6-27B led AECOPD-PIM at 71.11. Imaging hallucination and serious medical risk occurred in 31.85% and 8.16% of PNBIM responses; medication-safety risk and serious medical risk occurred in 26.93% and 1.44% of AECOPD-PIM responses. Conclusions: RESPClinBench identifies task-specific limitations in multimodal pulmonary nodule assessment and longitudinal COPD management. Combining explicit clinical-action coverage, holistic evaluation, and independent safety flags provides a clinically grounded basis for model selection and prospective validation.

</details>


### [33] [ODRA: Synthesizing Cognitive Behavioral Therapy Sessions with Structured Chain-Of-Thought and Dynamic Patient Resistance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04524)
*Javier Rodriguez-Juan,Hiba Arnaout,Jose Garcia-Rodriguez,David Tomás,Iryna Gurevych*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: ODRA introduces a Chain-of-Thought framework grounded in Beck's CBT guidelines, augmented with a resistance orchestrator to counteract patient sycophancy, producing therapeutically structured yet behaviorally realistic synthetic therapy dialogues that outperform existing methods across clinical metrics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing synthetic CBT dialogue generation faces a tension between maintaining therapeutic structure and portraying realistic patient resistance. Script-based methods lack dynamic interaction, multi-agent systems fail to preserve CBT's sequential structure, and both suffer from sycophancy, yielding unrealistically compliant patients that undermine clinical validity.

Method: ODRA combines a Chain-of-Thought generation strategy explicitly grounded in foundational CBT guidelines (Beck, 2020) to enforce therapeutic structure, alongside a resistance orchestrator that uses steering techniques to modulate patient resistance levels, thereby preventing sycophantic compliance and eliciting clinically authentic patient behaviors.

Result: Automated and expert evaluations show ODRA significantly surpasses existing methods in therapeutic skills, CBT adherence, and patient behavioral fidelity. Licensed psychologists preferred ODRA-generated sessions on 12 of 13 clinical metrics. Models fine-tuned on ODRA data exhibited superior therapeutic performance with both cooperative and resistant patients, demonstrating that explicit resistance modeling transfers to downstream clinical robustness.

Conclusion: Explicitly modeling patient resistance via a dedicated orchestrator within a guideline-grounded CoT framework resolves the structure–realism trade-off in synthetic CBT generation. This approach not only produces higher-fidelity training data but also yields measurable improvements in real clinical model performance, validating resistance-aware synthesis as a critical design principle for clinical dialogue systems.

Abstract: Synthetic generation of Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) sessions is challenged by two competing demands: adhering to strict therapeutic structure while modeling the resistant, unpredictable behavior of real patients. Existing script-based methods fail to capture dynamic therapeutic interactions, while multi-agent approaches struggle to adhere to CBT's sequential structure; both suffer from sycophancy, producing overly compliant patients that misrepresent real clinical settings. In this work we introduce ODRA, a novel framework for synthesizing therapy dialogues through a Chain-of-Thought (CoT) strategy grounded in foundational CBT guidelines (Beck, 2020). ODRA further incorporates a resistance orchestrator to solve patient sycophancy, which employs steering techniques to elicit behaviors aligned with their resistance level. Automated and expert evaluations show that ODRA significantly outperforms existing methods across therapeutic skills, CBT alignment, and patient behavioral fidelity, with licensed psychologists preferring ODRA sessions across 12 of 13 clinical metrics. Furthermore, models fine-tuned on our dataset demonstrate superior therapeutic performance against both cooperative and resistant patients, validating that explicit resistance modeling in synthetic training data directly translates to downstream clinical robustness.

</details>


### [34] [EuroExec: Frontier Language Models Fall Short of Expert Judgment on European Executive Decision Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04549)
*Pau Arnal,Khaled Denfir,Danylo Smahliuk,Amrut Avhad,Marcus A. Castro*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: The paper introduces EuroExec, a benchmark of 413 open-ended European executive tasks evaluated by human experts over 4,000+ hours. Six frontier LLMs are assessed via multi-attribute rubrics and preference rankings. The best model achieves only a 56.9% solve rate, while expert-written references reach near-ceiling performance and are preferred over any model response in 74% of direct comparisons, revealing a significant gap between LLM capabilities and professional standards. Human evaluation proves essential, as automatic metrics fail on these real-world, subjective tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Frontier LLMs are increasingly deployed on open-ended, complex, real-world tasks that differ fundamentally from the constrained benchmarks they are typically evaluated on. Existing benchmarks fail to capture the nuanced, subjective, and high-stakes nature of professional executive work. The authors aim to rigorously measure whether current LLMs meet the bar for such tasks using authentic, expert-validated evaluation.

Method: The authors construct EuroExec, a benchmark of 413 long-form, open-ended European executive tasks authored by 47 vetted domain experts, each based on real case experience. Six frontier LLMs are evaluated. Each response undergoes manual evaluation through: (1) a multi-attribute rubric, (2) an item-specific checklist of requirements, and (3) a preference rank ordering. These are aggregated into a "Solve Rate" metric. Rigorous statistical analysis is applied to verify inter-rater consistency among human evaluators.

Result: The strongest model solves only 56.9% of tasks. Expert-written reference answers achieve near-ceiling solve rates and are preferred over every model response in 74% of head-to-head rankings. Automatic evaluation metrics are shown to correlate poorly with human judgments on these open-ended, subjective problems, underscoring their inadequacy for this evaluation paradigm.

Conclusion: Current frontier LLMs fall well below the professional standard required for real-world executive tasks, despite already being deployed in such contexts. Human evaluation, carefully validated for consistency, remains the gold standard for assessing performance on open-ended problems with subjective ground truth, as automatic metrics are insufficient.

Abstract: Frontier LLMs are increasingly put to use on open-ended complex questions, different in nature from the ones they are typically evaluated on. We dedicate more than 4,000 human expert hours to evaluate a selection of six frontier LLMs on a member of this class of problems: EuroExec, our introduced human expert-based benchmark composed of 413 open-ended long-form European executive tasks authored by 47 vetted domain experts, each question drawn from experience in a real case. Every response is manually evaluated through a multi-attribute rubric, an item-specific checklist of requirements, and a preference rank ordering, extracting an aggregate metric "Solve Rate". The strongest model solves only 56.9% of tasks, while expert-written reference answers judged blindly are solved at near-ceiling levels and are preferred over every model response in 74% of direct rankings, placing frontier generative systems well below the professional standard of work they are already used for. We see that the best way to extract this kind of conclusion is by employing human evaluators, carefully checking their consistency through rigorous statistical analysis, and observe that automatic measurements also fall short when evaluating on this case of real-world open-ended problems with a subjective ground truth.

</details>


### [35] [Relational Response Fields: A General Theory of Black-Box LLM Response Consistency and Recovery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04552)
*Song Zichen*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper formalizes the problem of recovering reliable answers from black-box language model responses by introducing the relational response field (RRF) framework. It defines γ_k(D,A) as the intrinsic difficulty of recovery, proves identifiability and stability bounds, and validates theoretical predictions via experiments on mathematics and code tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing approaches to black-box LM reliability (sampling, voting, verification, iterative revision) focus on improving individual answers but neglect a foundational question: what structural conditions determine whether a set of responses is recoverable at all? The authors aim to characterize the intrinsic difficulty of recovering ground truth from a collection of black-box responses subject to corruption, establishing identifiability conditions that separate mere consistency from actual truth.

Method: The authors model responses to typed query transformations as a relational response field (RRF), where edge transports encode how valid responses change under symmetries (paraphrase, scaling, decomposition, etc.) and anchors encode independently trusted evidence (execution, verifiers). For a relation operator D, anchor operator A, and at most k corrupted nodes, they define γ_k(D,A) as the intrinsic recovery difficulty. They prove: (1) γ_k > 0 iff every k-node corruption is identifiable, (2) a deterministic stability bound proportional to 1/γ_k, and (3) a matching minimax lower bound. They develop sparse field-repair algorithms and separate information-theoretic identifiability from stronger null-space conditions needed for convex optimization. Experiments test four theoretical predictions: consistency–truth separation, anchor phase transitions, redundancy saturation, and cross-model cross-task prediction of repair difficulty.

Result: The theory shows that relation-only methods are blind to null directions (including shared hallucinations), establishing a fundamental consistency–truth gap. Controlled theorem tests and black-box experiments on mathematics and code generation validate all four theory-fixed consequences. The results support γ_k(D,A) as a measurable, intrinsic property of a response-recovery instance rather than a heuristic-dependent score.

Conclusion: The paper establishes that black-box response recovery has an intrinsic difficulty measure γ_k(D,A) with rigorous identifiability and stability guarantees. Consistency is not truth: without anchors, shared hallucinations are unrecoverable. The framework provides a principled foundation for understanding when and why response aggregation methods can succeed or fail, with empirical support across models and tasks.

Abstract: Black-box language-model reliability is commonly pursued by sampling, prompting, voting, verifying, or iteratively revising individual answers. We ask a prior question: \emph{what determines whether a collection of black-box responses is recoverable at all?} We represent responses to typed transformations of a query as a \emph{relational response field} (RRF). Edge transports encode how valid responses must change under paraphrase, scaling, decomposition, refactoring, or other task symmetries; anchors encode independently trusted evidence such as execution or a verifier. For relation operator $D$, anchor operator $A$, and at most $k$ corrupted response nodes, we identify $γ_k(D,A)$ as the intrinsic difficulty of black-box response recovery. It is positive exactly when every $k$-node corruption is identifiable; it gives a deterministic stability bound proportional to $1/γ_k$; and a matching two-point minimax lower bound shows that no estimator can improve this dependence. Thus consistency is not truth: relation-only methods are blind to null directions, including shared hallucinations. We derive sparse field-repair algorithms while separating information-theoretic identifiability from the stronger null-space conditions required by convex optimization. Controlled theorem tests and black-box mathematics/code experiments evaluate four theory-fixed consequences: consistency--truth separation, anchor phase transitions, redundancy saturation, and cross-model, cross-task prediction of repair difficulty. The results support $γ_k(D,A)$ as a measurable property of a response-recovery instance, rather than a score attached to one repair heuristic.

</details>


### [36] [Representing Visual Evidence for Item Difficulty Prediction: Visual Textualization and Image-Native Modeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04554)
*Han Chen,Ming Li,Hong Jiao,Tianyi Zhou*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: This paper compares text-only, visual textualization, and image-native representations for predicting math item difficulty. Both visual approaches achieve the best results but are statistically tied. Textualization yields lower RMSE for LLMs, while image-native modeling excels for VLMs with broader adaptation. The two visual interfaces make partially complementary errors and differ in computational workflow, suggesting image-native modeling is a competitive alternative.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Predicting item difficulty from content helps estimate new questions before student response data accumulates. Existing methods textualize visual components in math items before applying text-based predictors, but it is unclear whether this is optimal. The paper investigates how visual evidence should be represented for difficulty prediction.

Method: The authors train LLMs and VLMs directly for difficulty regression using Eedi math items with calibrated difficulty labels. They compare three representation strategies: (1) question text alone, (2) visual textualization (expressing images in language), and (3) image-native modeling (retaining original images). Test-time interventions probe dependence on visual components.

Result: Both visual interfaces achieve the lowest RMSE point estimates but cannot be reliably ordered. Open-VLM textualization yields lower RMSE for all evaluated LLMs, while broader adaptation does so for all image-native VLMs. The two interfaces make partially complementary item-level errors and differ substantially in computational workflow.

Conclusion: Textualization should not be treated as the only practical interface; image-native modeling is a competitive alternative whose effectiveness depends on how the VLM is adapted.

Abstract: Predicting item difficulty from content can provide an initial estimate for newly developed questions before sufficient student responses are available. Existing approaches typically represent the question stem and answer choices as text. When mathematics items contain visual components, a common pipeline first textualizes that evidence and then applies a text predictor. We ask: how should visual evidence be represented for item difficulty prediction? We compare question text alone, visual textualization, which expresses visual evidence in language, and image-native modeling, which retains the original image. Using Eedi items with difficulty calibrated from student responses, we train large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs) directly for difficulty regression. Both visual interfaces achieve the lowest point estimates, although the leading systems cannot be reliably ordered. Open-VLM textualization yields lower RMSE point estimates for all evaluated LLMs, while broader adaptation does so for all image-native VLMs. Test-time interventions show dependence on the paired full-item image, but do not isolate the additional visual component. The two visual interfaces also make partially complementary item-level errors and differ substantially in computational workflow. Thus, textualization should not be treated as the only practical interface: image-native modeling is a competitive alternative whose effectiveness depends on how the VLM is adapted.

</details>


### [37] [STRIVE: Probing Reasoning Limits in Graded Plausibility Generation and Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04567)
*Bhiman Kumar Baghel,Anna Chrabaszcz,Tessa Warren,Michael Walsh Dickey,Haley C. Dresang,Xiang Lorraine Li*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: STRIVE is an LLM-based framework that automatically generates controlled event sets for psycholinguistic plausibility studies. By combining a global reasoning scratchpad with evaluator-guided refinement, it increases high-quality output from 16.7% to 75.0% compared to baseline prompting, though human input remains necessary for events near the plausibility boundary.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Psycholinguists need controlled event sets varying plausibility (plausible vs. implausible) and difficulty (easy vs. hard) to study event knowledge, but manually constructing these sets is extremely labor-intensive. Automating this process would significantly reduce researcher workload.

Method: STRIVE uses LLMs to jointly generate and evaluate controlled event sets. For a given verb, it constructs a shared event frame and produces four events by varying one slot across conditions (plausible-easy, plausible-hard, implausible-easy, implausible-hard). The framework introduces two key innovations: (1) a global reasoning scratchpad for structured planning before generation, and (2) an evaluator-guided iterative refinement loop. Six LLMs were tested across 60 verbs.

Result: Baseline GPT-5.1 achieved only 16.7% high-quality sets. Adding the reasoning scratchpad and evaluator-guided refinement boosted this to 75.0%. Greater reasoning effort correlated with improved evaluator-human agreement. However, the implausible-hard condition remained challenging, with the best evaluator reaching only 57% accuracy, and events near the plausibility boundary elicited the most human disagreement.

Conclusion: STRIVE demonstrates that LLMs can substantially automate controlled event-set generation for psycholinguistic research, but events near the plausibility boundary still require human judgment. The framework offers a scalable approach to reducing—though not eliminating—manual annotation effort.

Abstract: Event knowledge concerns who does what to whom. Psycholinguists use event-plausibility judgments to examine how this knowledge supports human language processing. To isolate plausibility effects, these studies require controlled event sets in which one event slot varies across plausibility levels while all other event features remain fixed. Constructing such sets manually is labor-intensive. We therefore introduce STRIVE, an LLM-based framework for jointly generating and evaluating controlled event sets crossing plausibility class (plausible vs. implausible) with intended classification difficulty (easy vs. hard). Given a verb, STRIVE constructs a shared event frame, then produces one event per condition by varying one slot while holding all others fixed. In experiments with six models across 60 verbs, GPT-5.1 produced high-quality sets only 16.7% of the time using the baseline generation prompt. Adding a global reasoning scratchpad and evaluator-guided refinement raised this rate to 75.0%. Greater reasoning effort also improved evaluator--human agreement. Nevertheless, events near the plausibility boundary remain most difficult. They elicit the greatest human disagreement, and the best evaluator reaches only 57% accuracy on the implausible-hard condition, indicating a need for human input. Overall, STRIVE offers a scalable approach to reducing manual effort by automating initial event-set generation and evaluation for psycholinguistic studies.

</details>


### [38] [Relevant but Incomplete: Referential Dangling as a Paradigm-Level Failure Mode in Hard Prompt Compression](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04569)
*Zhengpei Hu,Kai Li,Dapeng Fu,Xuechao Zou,Yuanhao Tang,Yue Li,Tengfei Cao,Jianqiang Huang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Hard prompt compression methods that independently select tokens/sentences/chunks under a budget create "referential dangling" — retained text containing an answer whose necessary entity definition has been deleted. This structural failure affects all six tested compressors, with up to 60% dangling rates on HotpotQA. Reinserting missing supporting paragraphs recovers 88%+ of the accuracy gap. A compact classifier trained to detect dangling references enables automatic restoration, improving accuracy by 4.7 points with negligible budget increase (0.30→0.31).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing hard prompt compression methods select text units independently based on relevance scores, ignoring structural dependencies between pieces of text. The authors identify that this independence assumption causes a systematic failure: splitting dependent evidence pairs where one piece defines an entity referenced in another, rendering the retained text uninterpretable. This problem has been overlooked in prior compression research.

Method: The paper (1) formally defines "referential dangling" using a tripartite decomposition — a dangling reference (retained), a target entity (deleted), and an independent answer path; (2) measures dangling rates across six hard compressors (Beaver, LLMLingua-2, LongLLMLingua, Jina, R2, Selective Context) on three multi-hop QA datasets (HotpotQA, MuSiQue, 2WikiMQA) and LongBench-v2; (3) evaluates the causal impact via a controlled experiment reinserting missing supporting paragraphs; (4) trains a compact binary classifier that ranks deleted sentences by whether they are required to interpret retained text, enabling automatic restoration during inference without support annotations.

Result: At 0.30 compression ratio, Beaver leaves answer paths incomplete in 34–54% of bridge examples across three datasets. All six compressors exhibit dangling on HotpotQA bridge examples at rates up to 60%. Every LongBench-v2 Single-Document QA document contains at least one dangling reference. Reinserting missing supporting paragraphs improves accuracy by 29–34 pp (p<0.0001), recovering ≥88% of the gap to full-context performance. GPT-5.5 loses 8.8 points on MuSiQue compressed contexts vs. both-paragraph contexts, showing even strong models cannot compensate. The automatic restoration classifier improves HotpotQA accuracy by 4.7 points while increasing compression ratio only from 0.30 to 0.31.

Conclusion: Referential completeness is a necessary optimization target alongside relevance for hard prompt compression. The proposed restoration classifier offers a practical, lightweight remedy that identifies dangling references at inference time without requiring support annotations, substantially recovering lost accuracy at negligible budget cost.

Abstract: Hard prompt compression reduces long-context inference cost by independently scoring tokens, sentences, or chunks and retaining the highest-scoring units under a budget. We identify a structural failure in this procedure: independent selection can split dependent evidence pairs, retaining one member while deleting the other. When retained text contains an answer but deleted text defines the entity needed to interpret it, we call the result referential dangling. At a compression ratio of 0.30, Beaver, which ranks coherent chunks using Qwen3-0.6B embeddings, leaves the answer path incomplete in 34-54% of bridge examples across three multi-hop question answering datasets. On a shared HotpotQA bridge set, all six hard compressors we test exhibit dangling at rates up to 60%, and every document in LongBench-v2 Single-Document QA contains at least one dangling reference. On dangling examples evaluated with Qwen3-8B, reinserting the missing supporting paragraph while removing nonsupporting paragraphs to maintain the token budget improves accuracy by 29-34 percentage points (p < 0.0001), recovering at least 88% of the gap to contexts retaining both supporting paragraphs. Stronger answer models do not absorb the loss: on MuSiQue, GPT-5.5 is 8.8 points less accurate on compressed contexts than on contexts retaining both supporting paragraphs. Finally, we train a compact classifier to rank omitted sentences by whether they are needed to interpret retained text and reinsert the top-ranked candidates without support annotations at inference. On HotpotQA with Qwen3-8B, this automatic restoration improves accuracy by 4.7 points while changing the compression ratio only from 0.30 to 0.31. Hard compressors should optimize both relevance and referential completeness.

</details>


### [39] [The Personalization Mirage: How LLMs Fabricate User Profiles, and Why Self-Monitoring Misleads](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04570)
*Yushi Sun,Yanjie Zhang,Rui Sheng*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: MirageBench evaluates over-inference in personalized LLMs—where models fabricate user attributes beyond evidence. Across 12 models, 35–49% of claims were over-inferred. A key finding, Self-Monitoring Inversion, shows models that self-report the least over-inference actually fabricate the most, challenging the reliability of model self-assessment for trustworthiness.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Personalized LLMs with persistent memory are increasingly deployed, yet no systematic evaluation exists for the faithfulness of their user models. The authors identify a critical gap: the phenomenon of over-inference (OI), where LLMs fabricate or hallucinate user attributes beyond what the available evidence supports, remains unexamined despite its direct implications for trustworthy personalization.

Method: The authors introduce MirageBench, a benchmark with: (1) 150 personas balanced across stereotypical, counter-stereotypical, and neutral profiles; (2) 6 personalization tasks spanning an "imagination gradient"; (3) a four-way faithfulness taxonomy judged by an independent model, validated against a blind human annotator on 400 claims (Cohen's kappa = 0.863 four-class, 0.900 binary); and (4) a leaderboard evaluating 12 models across 7 families on 143,616 judged claims. They also conduct a multi-turn pilot studying accumulation of inferred attributes.

Result: Over-inference is pervasive: all 12 models over-infer 35–49% of claims (cross-model mean 41.6%). The phenomenon is task-dependent (27–59%). A striking "Self-Monitoring Inversion" emerges: models' self-assessed OI is negatively rank-correlated with judge-measured OI (Spearman's ρ = -0.60, p = 0.044), meaning models that claim least over-inference fabricate most. Within-model self-audit retains moderate ranking ability (AUROC 0.58–0.83). In multi-turn settings, inferred attributes accumulate roughly linearly with minimal revision.

Conclusion: External verification, rather than model self-report, is the more reliable foundation for trustworthy personalization. The pervasive nature of over-inference across all evaluated models and the Self-Monitoring Inversion together suggest that current LLM personalization approaches require independent faithfulness monitoring, and MirageBench provides the infrastructure for such evaluation.

Abstract: Personalized LLMs with persistent memory are increasingly deployed, yet the faithfulness of their user models remains unexamined. We study over-inference (OI): the phenomenon where LLMs fabricate user attributes beyond what evidence supports. We introduce MirageBench, comprising 150 personas balanced across stereotypical, counter-stereotypical, and neutral profiles, 6 personalization tasks spanning an ``imagination gradient'', a four-way faithfulness taxonomy operationalized by an independent judge (validated against a blind human annotator on 400 claims: Cohen's kappa = 0.863 four-class, kappa = 0.900 binary), and a leaderboard of 12 models across 7 families on 143616 judged claims. We find that over-inference is pervasive: every one of the 12 models over-infers 35%--49% of its claims (cross-model mean 41.6%; claim-weighted 41.8%), with no model in this evaluation escaping it. Most strikingly, we surface a Self-Monitoring Inversion: at the model-selection level, models' self-assessed OI is negatively rank-correlated with their judge-measured OI (rho = -0.60, p = 0.044; exploratory, wide bootstrap CI [-0.90, +0.06], n = 12). The models that report the least over-inference tend to be flagged as fabricating the most, so self-reported confidence is a misleading signal for comparing models, even though within a single model self-audit still ranks that model's own claims moderately well (AUROC 0.58--0.83). We further show that OI is task-dependent (27%--59%) and that, in a multi-turn pilot, inferred attributes accumulate approximately linearly with little revision. MirageBench positions external verification, rather than model self-report, as a more reliable foundation for trustworthy personalization.

</details>


### [40] [When Memory Lies: An Empirical Study of Spatial Memory Staleness in VLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04574)
*Yushi Sun,Yanjie Zhang*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: Memory-augmented VLMs suffer from spatial memory staleness: models confidently act on outdated memory despite contradicting visual observations. Using a dynamic FrozenLake testbed, the paper shows that text-based staleness detection does not transfer to vision, trusting stale memory doubles agent death rates versus having no memory, and auditing mechanisms fail to fully close the safety gap—especially under unreliable visual grounding.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Memory-augmented VLM agents rely on persistent spatial knowledge that becomes stale as environments change. The core question is whether current models can detect conflicts between confident memory claims and contradictory real-time observations before these conflicts lead to safety-critical mistakes. The work frames spatial-memory staleness as an underexamined safety failure mode.

Method: The authors use a dynamic FrozenLake testbed pairing a staleness-detection task with a downstream navigation task. They evaluate three closed-source models and three open-weight VLMs under both text and image input modalities, running 1,800 detection runs and 12,000 text-mode navigation episodes across four LLM navigators at a shared 50-seed scale. They also test read-time filtering mechanisms, including oracle stale labels, to assess whether auditing can mitigate safety costs.

Result: Three key findings: (1) Text solvability does not imply visual grounding—F1 scores for vision-based staleness detection range from 0.887 to 0.067 on identical grids, with the weakest model making fluent but visually ignorant decisions. (2) Trusting stale memory is a safety liability—a GPT-4o agent trusting raw memory dies over twice as often as one with no memory. (3) Auditing reduces but does not eliminate safety costs—read-time filtering helps in text mode, but oracle labels yield no significant additional gain on current grids, and unreliable visual auditing provides no consistent benefit.

Conclusion: Spatial-memory staleness constitutes a concrete safety failure mode for memory-augmented agents. The central open challenges are achieving reliable visual grounding and robust action selection under memory-observation conflict. Bridging the gap between text-based reasoning and embodied visual perception remains critical for safe deployment.

Abstract: Memory-augmented VLM agents act on persistent spatial knowledge, yet that knowledge silently goes stale as the environment changes. We ask what happens when an agent must reconcile a confident memory claim with a contradicting observation, and whether current models can catch the conflict before it becomes a safety-relevant mistake. Using a dynamic FrozenLake testbed, we pair a staleness-detection task with a downstream navigation task across three closed-source models and three open-weight VLMs under both text and image inputs (1,800 detection runs, and 12,000 text-mode navigation episodes over four LLM navigators at a shared 50-seed scale). Three findings emerge. First, text solvability does not imply visual grounding: models that flag stale entries reliably from text nonetheless span vision F1 from 0.887 down to 0.067 on the identical grids, and the weakest keeps making fluent, confident decisions that ignore the image. Second, consuming stale memory without an audit is a safety liability: in our primary GPT-4o setting, an agent that trusts raw memory dies more than twice as often as the same agent given no memory at all. Third, auditing helps but does not close the gap: a transparent read-time filter removes much of the safety cost in text mode, yet even oracle stale labels bring no further significant gain on the current grid size, and when visual auditing is unreliable, filtering yields no consistent benefit. Together these results frame spatial-memory staleness as a safety failure mode and isolate reliable visual grounding and action selection under memory--observation conflict as the central open challenges for memory-augmented agents.

</details>


### [41] [Causal Evidence Extraction and Triangulation in Crisis Reports using Large Language Models: A ReliefWeb-based Study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04576)
*Yuanjun Zhang,Mourad Oussalah*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: A two-stage LLM pipeline extracts structured causal evidence (intervention-outcome relations with direction/strength) from humanitarian reports, achieving 94.15% weighted F1 with fine-tuned Llama-3.1-8B, and introduces a context-preserving triangulation method to aggregate evidence across disaster contexts using a Level-of-Evidence score.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Humanitarian reports are long, noisy, and multi-topic, making it difficult to systematically consolidate decision-relevant causal evidence. There is a need for automated extraction of structured intervention-outcome relationships with quantifiable direction and strength, along with a principled method to aggregate evidence across diverse disaster contexts.

Method: A two-stage LLM pipeline: (1) query-conditioned extraction restricts outputs to a specified intervention class, mitigating retrieval-induced over-extraction, and (2) snippet grounding links each relation to supporting text for auditability. A ReliefWeb corpus (2000–2024) is used. For aggregation, a context-preserving triangulation method pools strength-weighted evidence within disaster×source cells, applies Laplace smoothing, equally weights cells, and computes a Level-of-Evidence (LoE) score quantifying cross-context convergence.

Result: On an expert-annotated dataset of 100 reports, the best closed-source LLM achieved 90.73% weighted F1 with strong cost-efficiency. Supervised fine-tuned Llama-3.1-8B reached 94.15% weighted F1. Applied to cash assistance, food-related outcomes demonstrated strong positive convergence (LoE=0.865) and stable long-horizon trajectories.

Conclusion: The proposed pipeline effectively extracts structured causal evidence from humanitarian reports with high accuracy, and the context-preserving triangulation method provides a principled framework for synthesizing evidence across heterogeneous contexts, demonstrated through robust findings on cash assistance and food security outcomes.

Abstract: Humanitarian reports are long, noisy, and multi-topic, making it difficult to consolidate decision-relevant causal evidence. We present a ReliefWeb study (2000-2024) and a two-stage Large Language Model (LLM) pipeline that extracts structured intervention-outcome records with direction and strength attributes. Query-conditioned extraction restricts output to a specified intervention class, reducing retrieval-induced over-extraction, while snippet grounding links each relation to supporting text for auditability and classification. In an expert-annotated dataset of 100 reports, the best closed-source LLM achieved a weighted F1 score of 90.73% with strong cost-efficiency, while Llama-3.1-8B with supervised fine-tuning reached 94.15% weighted F1 score. We further propose context-preserving triangulation that aggregates strength-weighted evidence within disaster$\times$source cells, applies Laplace smoothing and equally weights cells to quantify cross-context convergence via a Level-of-Evidence score. Applied to cash assistance, food-related outcomes show strong positive convergence (LoE=0.865) and stable long-horizon trajectories.

</details>


### [42] [Breaking the Curse ofMultilinguality inMany-to-Many Speech-to-Text Translation via a Resource-AwareMixture of Speech Encoders](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04586)
*Yexing Du,Kaiyuan Liu,Youcheng Pan,Bo Yang,Chengpeng Fu,Yu Wang,Ming Liu*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: MSRT proposes a Mixture of Speech Encoders (MoSE) with a language router and curriculum learning to address the multilingual curse in S2TT, achieving SOTA on 45 languages with only 10h paired data per language.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In multilingual speech-to-text translation, a shared speech encoder causes the curse of multilinguality — high-resource languages dominate limited representation capacity, severely degrading low-resource language performance. Existing solutions lack a mechanism to preserve high-resource quality while adapting to low-resource speech.

Method: MSRT introduces MoSE: a resource-aware Mixture of Speech Encoders with an explicit language router that assigns utterances to either a frozen expert (preserving high-resource capabilities) or a trainable expert (specializing in medium/low-resource languages). A five-stage curriculum learning strategy reduces data requirements to only 10 hours of paired S2TT data per language.

Result: Experiments on 45 languages across all 45×44 translation directions show the 4B-parameter model achieves SOTA, outperforming much larger baselines. MoSE simultaneously improves performance across high-, medium-, and low-resource languages, with the largest gains on low-resource speech.

Conclusion: MoSE effectively breaks the curse of multilinguality in S2TT without sacrificing high-resource performance, demonstrating that resource-aware expert routing combined with curriculum learning is a scalable solution for massively multilingual speech translation.

Abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have achieved significant success in speech-to-text translation (S2TT). However, when processing multilingual speech inputs, a single speech encoder shared across all languages suffers from the curse of multilinguality: languages at different resource levels compete for limited representation capacity, leading to strong high-resource performance but substantial degradation on low-resource speech. To address this problem and improve multilingual consistency, we propose MSRT, a novel framework built around a resource-aware Mixture of Speech Encoders (MoSE). MoSE uses an explicit language router to assign each utterance to an appropriate expert encoder. A frozen expert preserves high-resource language capabilities, while a trainable expert adapts to and specializes in medium- and low-resource languages. We further introduce a five-stage curriculum learning strategy that substantially reduces data dependence, requiring only 10 hours of paired S2TT data per language for effective alignment. We conduct extensive experiments on 45 languages, systematically evaluating all $45 \times 44$ translation directions. Our 4B-parameter model achieves state-of-the-art performance, outperforming substantially larger baselines. Empirical analyses show that MoSE improves high-, medium-, and low-resource languages simultaneously, with the largest gains on low-resource speech, thereby breaking the curse of multilinguality without compromising high-resource performance. To support future multilingual S2TT research, we release our code and models.

</details>


### [43] [EASy: Towards Efficient LLM-Based Agentic System](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04588)
*Junnan Liu,Linhao Luo,Thuy-Trang Vu,Gholamreza Haffari*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: EASy is a trainable agentic framework that uses reinforcement learning to jointly optimize task performance and computational efficiency. It features an orchestrator with explicit knowledge of heterogeneous executor capabilities/costs, a milestone-plan-act workflow with dependency-aware execution graphs, and a tree-structured rollout training procedure with multi-component rewards. Experiments across math reasoning, embodied AI, and deep research benchmarks demonstrate superior performance-efficiency trade-offs over existing systems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing agentic systems prioritize task success while neglecting execution efficiency under real-world constraints (executor capability, computational cost). Router-based methods lack the ability to reason over rich, evolving task contexts, multi-step dependencies, and intermediate feedback, and they generalize poorly to unseen executors.

Method: EASy introduces: (1) an LLM-based orchestrator with explicit knowledge of heterogeneous executor capability and cost profiles for context-sensitive coordination; (2) a milestone-plan-act workflow that decomposes complex tasks into milestones, builds dependency-aware execution graphs, assigns suitable executors, parallelizes independent steps, and adapts to intermediate outcomes; (3) a tree-structured rollout procedure for training that explores alternative milestone decompositions and execution plans; (4) multi-component rewards capturing task correctness, execution efficiency, and trajectory completeness, optimized via reinforcement learning.

Result: Extensive experiments on mathematical reasoning, embodied decision-making, and deep research benchmarks show that EASy consistently achieves stronger performance-efficiency trade-offs compared to strong agentic baselines.

Conclusion: EASy demonstrates that jointly optimizing for task performance and computational efficiency via RL-based orchestration with explicit executor awareness and structured planning yields robust, generalizable agentic systems that outperform performance-only routing approaches across diverse domains.

Abstract: Agentic systems have emerged as a promising paradigm for solving complex tasks by coordinating specialized LLM-based agents. However, most existing systems primarily optimize task success while giving limited consideration to execution efficiency under practical constraints such as executor capability and computational cost. Existing router-based methods have limited ability to reason over rich, evolving task contexts, multi-step dependencies, and intermediate execution feedback, and often generalize poorly to unseen executors. We propose EASy, a trainable agentic framework that jointly optimizes task performance and computational efficiency through reinforcement learning. EASy equips an LLM-based orchestrator with explicit knowledge of the capability and cost profiles of heterogeneous executors, enabling context-sensitive coordination beyond performance-only routing. It further introduces a milestone-plan-act workflow that decomposes complex tasks into manageable milestones, constructs dependency-aware execution graphs, assigns suitable executors, and parallelizes independent steps while adapting subsequent decisions to intermediate outcomes. To train the orchestrator, we develop a tree-structured rollout procedure that explores alternative milestone decompositions and execution plans, together with multi-component rewards that capture task correctness, execution efficiency, and trajectory completeness. Extensive experiments on mathematical reasoning, embodied decision-making, and deep research benchmarks show that EASy consistently achieves stronger performance-efficiency trade-offs than strong agentic baselines.

</details>


### [44] [When Absence Is Evidence: Evaluating Completeness-Sensitive Negative Reasoning in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04591)
*Byoungjae Min,Kennedy Edemacu,Sae-Hong Cho,Yoonhyuk Choi,Beakcheol Jang,Jong Wook Kim*

Main category: cs.CL

TL;DR: CROWN-QA introduces a benchmark for completeness-sensitive negative reasoning, revealing that LLMs systematically fail to distinguish between justified negative answers (when evidence fully covers the query scope) and unknown answers (when evidence is partial), with a dominant asymmetric failure where models treat implicitly partial evidence as query-covering.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs frequently answer negative queries (e.g., "Is X absent?"), but a valid negative answer requires complete evidence coverage. When coverage is partial, the proper response is "Unknown." Prior work has not systematically probed whether LLMs can perform this completeness-sensitive reasoning, motivating the creation of a controlled benchmark to diagnose failures.
