### [73] [Echoes in the Sky: Computational Thematic Analysis of Online Public Discourse on Bluesky Across Trump's Reelection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04120)
*Qile Wang,Ali Salloum,Carolina Coimbra Vieira,Benjamin E. Bagozzi,Mikko Kivelä,Kenneth E. Barner,Matthew Louis Mauriello*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: This study analyzes 38.5 million Bluesky posts (2019–2026) related to Trump and U.S. policy, using LLM-assisted clustering to identify 14 thematic domains in English posts and 19 EO categories. It finds dominant themes like executive governance and national security, substantial variation in issue attention persistence, and increasing negative sentiment over time.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As political disruption intensifies online discourse, Bluesky has emerged as an important platform for U.S. political discussion. The authors aim to systematically characterize large-scale discourse patterns on this growing platform—specifically, what themes dominate, how attention to issues persists or fluctuates, and how sentiment evolves—in the context of Trump administration policy developments.

Method: The authors collected all available posts matching Trump-related keywords from Bluesky's historical retrieval API (2019–2026), yielding 38.5 million posts. They employed an LLM-assisted clustering pipeline combined with human validation to identify 14 interpretable thematic domains in English-language posts and 19 thematic categories across 258 executive orders (EOs) signed between January 20, 2025, and May 1, 2026. They further analyzed persistence, volatility of issue attention, and sentiment trends.

Result: Dominant themes in Bluesky discourse include executive governance, political identity, and national security. Recurring EO themes include executive task forces, border enforcement, and foreign policy. The study finds substantial variation in the persistence and volatility of issue attention, along with an overall increasing proportion of negative sentiment over the observation period.

Conclusion: Bluesky hosts rich, thematically diverse political discourse that mirrors real-world policy developments. The platform exhibits dynamic attention patterns and a trend toward more negative sentiment over time. The authors release the dataset and resources publicly to facilitate further research.

Abstract: As political disruption intensifies online discourse, Bluesky has become an important platform for political discussion and public reaction. In this study, we examine large-scale discourse on Bluesky related to U.S. policy developments associated with the Trump administration. Using the historical retrieval API, we collected all available posts matching Trump and related keywords from 2019 to 2026, yielding 38.5 million posts. We leverage a large language model (LLM)-assisted clustering pipeline, combined with human validation, to identify 14 interpretable thematic domains in English-language posts and 19 thematic categories across 258 executive orders (EOs) signed between January 20, 2025, and May 1, 2026. Our findings identify several dominant themes in Bluesky discourse, including executive governance, political identity, and national security, as well as recurring themes in EOs, including executive task forces, border enforcement, and foreign policy. We also find substantial variation in the persistence and volatility of issue attention, accompanied by an increasing proportion of negative sentiment over time. The dataset and resources are publicly available at https://github.com/Sensify-Lab/Echoes-in-the-Sky

</details>


### [74] [Enacting Constructive Conflicts with AI Agents to Enhance Reconsideration among Novice Interaction Designers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04166)
*Howard Ziyu Han,Nikolas Martelaro*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: An AI agent embodying adversarial design principles was built to provoke constructive conflict. In a 45-student experiment comparing Self Reflection, Stepwise Guidance, and Interactive Engagement (agent-enacted), both structured conditions increased self-reconsideration and design improvements over unaided reflection. The antagonistic agent uniquely introduced more conflictual perspectives and led participants to generate and discard more ideas, turning reconsideration into concrete design actions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Generative AI tools in design typically serve as ideation aids or critics following their own internal reasoning, expanding the design space. The authors identify a gap: no work has explored AI agents taking an explicitly antagonistic, adversarial role that forces designers to confront stakeholder tensions and conflicts constructively.

Method: A between-subjects experiment with 45 design students across three conditions: (1) Self Reflection — unsupported review of one's design proposal; (2) Stepwise Guidance — written prompts walking designers through a constructive-conflict framework; (3) Interactive Engagement — an AI agent that interactively enacts the same framework by synthesizing stakeholder pushback. Conditions 2 and 3 share the framework but differ in self-enacted vs. agent-enacted delivery.

Result: Both Stepwise Guidance and Interactive Engagement significantly increased self-reconsideration and design improvements over Self Reflection. The Interactive Engagement condition uniquely introduced more conflictual perspectives and led participants to generate and discard significantly more ideas than Stepwise Guidance.

Conclusion: Agent-enacted constructive conflict can transform reconsideration into tangible design actions and deepen engagement with divergent stakeholder perspectives, suggesting that antagonistic design agents offer value beyond traditional assistive or critique-oriented AI roles.

Abstract: Generative AI agents are increasingly used in interaction design to facilitate ideation and offer critique, often following their own internal reasoning. These interactions tend to add design ideas and expand the design space. Our work explores an antagonistic role for design agents, prompting designers to engage with stakeholder tension. We built an AI agent inspired by adversarial design theory that enacts constructive conflict. We examine the agent's influence in a between-subjects experiment with 45 design students across three conditions: Self Reflection (unsupported review of the design proposal), Stepwise Guidance (written prompts that walk designers through a constructive-conflict framework), and Interactive Engagement (an AI agent that enacts the constructive-conflict framework interactively by synthesizing stakeholder pushback). The latter two conditions share the framework but differ in whether it is self-enacted or agent-enacted. Results show that, compared with Self Reflection, both the Stepwise Guidance and Interactive Engagement groups reported significantly higher self-reconsideration and made more improvements to their design proposals. Compared with Stepwise Guidance, the antagonistic agent introduced more conflictual perspectives, and participants in the Interactive Engagement condition generated and discarded more ideas. These findings suggest that agent-enacted constructive conflict can turn reconsideration into concrete design actions and deepen engagement with divergent stakeholder perspectives.

</details>


### [75] [Compass: Continuously Aligning Social Media Feeds via In-Situ Reflections](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04274)
*Aadit Barua,Leijie Wang,Amy X. Zhang*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: Compass is a system embedded in YouTube Shorts that promotes reflective social media consumption through lightweight in-situ notifications and periodic feed realignment, outperforming a baseline in a 10-day field study without compromising casual browsing.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Social media recommendation feeds optimize for immediate impulses rather than reflective preferences. Existing solutions (configuration pages, in-feed controls) require user initiative and are rarely used. Users' preferences evolve and diverge from stated preferences, necessitating continuous reflection and realignment — but current approaches are effortful and impractical.

Method: Compass combines two mechanisms: (1) in-situ reflection prompts via lightweight notifications to help users articulate preferences during everyday browsing, and (2) feed alignment through periodic simulation of behavioral signals and direct manipulation of feed content. The system was embedded within YouTube Shorts and evaluated in a 10-day field study (N=15) against a baseline lacking continuous support.

Result: Compass promoted more reflective and purposeful feed consumption, enabled iterative preference adjustment, and achieved stronger feed alignment compared to the baseline, all while preserving the casual nature of feed browsing.

Conclusion: Continuous, lightweight, in-situ reflection support can effectively align recommendation feeds with users' reflective preferences without requiring burdensome user initiative, offering a practical path beyond impulse-optimized social media design.

Abstract: Social media recommendation feeds often optimize for users' immediate impulses rather than preferences they would hold after deeper reflection. Some systems address this misalignment by incorporating users' explicit preferences via a configuration page or in-feed controls instead of just behavioral signals. However, users typically have evolving preferences, and their stated preferences and behavior naturally diverge, necessitating continuous reflection and feed realignment. But existing strategies require the user to take initiative and are often effortful; as a result, in practice they are rarely invoked. We present Compass, a system that aligns a user's feed with their reflective preferences by helping users reflect on and articulate their preferences given their behavior. To enable continuous reflection during everyday browsing, Compass surfaces in-situ reflections via lightweight notifications, while feed alignment is achieved by periodically simulating behavioral signals and directly manipulating feed content. We embedded Compass within YouTube Shorts and compared it against a baseline without continuous support through a 10-day field study (N=15). We found that Compass promoted more reflective and purposeful feed consumption, iterative preference adjustment, and stronger feed alignment, without sacrificing the casual nature of feed browsing.

</details>


### [76] [LEGOUI: Designing with UI-DSL Bricks to Balance Transparency and Controllability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04293)
*Yinsi Zhou,Mingyue Yuan,Hongyue Xu,Jieshan Chen,Dong Wen,Shidong Pan,Xiwei Xu,Wenjie Zhang,Aaron Quigley,Zhenchang Xing,Gelareh Mohammadi*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: LegoUI is a staged generative UI framework that decomposes interface design into interpretable, sequential steps using a UI domain-specific language with provenance tracking, enabling user intervention and iterative refinement. It achieves >95% accuracy in requirement analysis and significantly outperforms one-shot generative tools on transparency, controllability, and intent alignment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing generative UI design tools function as black boxes with limited transparency and controllability. When outputs misalign with designer intent, users resort to trial-and-error prompt tweaking without visibility into the model's reasoning process.

Method: LegoUI structures the UI generation process into sequential, interpretable stages aligned with key design dimensions. Each stage's output is captured in a UI domain-specific language (UI-DSL) enriched with provenance metadata, exposing intermediate reasoning and enabling user intervention at any stage for iterative refinement.

Result: Technical evaluation on 40 real-world design prompts showed the requirement analysis stage achieving >95% accuracy, near-complete coverage, and zero redundancy. User studies demonstrated that LegoUI significantly improved perceived transparency, controllability, and alignment with designer intent compared to one-shot generative UI tools.

Conclusion: A staged, provenance-aware generative approach substantially improves the usability of generative UI design tools by making model reasoning interpretable and the design process controllable, addressing key limitations of black-box one-shot generation.

Abstract: Generative user interface design tools enable rapid prototyping but often operate as black boxes with limited transparency and controllability. When outputs diverge from the designer's intent, users are left tweaking prompts via trial-and-error with little insight into the model's reasoning. We present LegoUI, a staged generative framework that structures the interface design process into sequential, interpretable steps along key design dimensions, capturing each step's result in a UI domain-specific language (UI-DSL) enriched with provenance. This approach exposes the model's intermediate reasoning and enables user intervention and iterative refinement. In a technical evaluation on 40 real-world design prompts, LegoUI's requirement analysis stage captured explicit requirements with over 95% accuracy, near-complete coverage, and zero redundancy. In user studies, participants using LegoUI reported significantly greater transparency, controllability, and alignment with their intent compared to existing one-shot generative UI tools.

</details>


### [77] [An immersive micro-manipulation system using real-time 3D imaging microscope and 3D operation interface for high-speed and accurate micro-manipulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04300)
*Kenta Yokoe,Tadayoshi Aoyama,Toshiki Fujishiro,Masaru Takeuchi,Yasuhisa Hasegawa*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: The paper proposes an immersive 3D micromanipulation system for ICSI that uses real-time 3D imaging, a head-mounted display, and pen-type or glove-type 3D interfaces to enable non-experts to perform accurate micromanipulation, with experiments confirming improved speed and accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The increasing global demand for ICSI as an ART has created a shortage of skilled embryologists. Current ICSI procedures require specially trained experts, and this bottleneck motivates the development of a system that enables efficient, accurate micromanipulation without specialized skills.

Method: The authors developed an immersive micromanipulation system integrating three components: (1) a real-time 3D imaging microscope for volumetric visualization, (2) stationary pen-type and wearable glove-type 3D operation interfaces for pipette control, and (3) a head-mounted display (HMD) that immerses the operator in a virtual micromanipulation space with freely adjustable viewpoints. System performance was evaluated through two subject experiments measuring pipette operation speed and accuracy.

Result: Experimental results with human subjects demonstrated that the proposed immersive 3D system improves both the speed and accuracy of pipette manipulation compared to conventional approaches.

Conclusion: The immersive micromanipulation system successfully reduces the skill barrier for performing ICSI by providing intuitive 3D visualization and control, offering a promising solution to the shortage of skilled embryologists in ART.

Abstract: The use of intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI), an assisted reproductive technique (ART), is increasing widely. ICSI is currently performed by specially skilled embryologists. However, with the increasing demand for ART, the shortage of skilled embryologists has become a problem. Therefore, we propose an immersive micromanipulation system that requires no special skills for efficient and accurate micromanipulation. Our proposed system is composed of a real-time three-dimensional (3D) imaging microscope and 3D operation interfaces. The 3D operation interfaces are stationary pen-type or wearable glove-type interfaces. In this system, an operator wearing a head-mounted display (HMD) and using 3D operation interfaces is immersed in a virtual micromanipulation space. The operator can move the pipettes by 3D operation interface and freely change the viewpoint. We verified that the proposed system improves the speed and accuracy of operating a pipette through two types of experiments with subjects.

</details>


### [78] [IntentLint: Supporting Intent Scaffolding and Prompt-time Linting in Human-AI Collaborative Data Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04331)
*Felicia Li Feng,Jian Zhao,Anamaria Crisan*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: IntentLint introduces a rule-based coordination layer with intent scaffolding and prompt-time linting to make analytic intent explicit and checkable during human-AI collaborative data analysis, improving shared understanding and alignment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In human-AI collaborative data analysis, rapidly evolving analyses cause shared artifacts (e.g., notebooks) to become incomplete or hard to interpret, leading to undocumented assumptions, misaligned intent across users, context-poor prompts, and undesired AI agent behaviors.

Method: The authors propose (1) intent scaffolding and (2) prompt-time linting as two interaction mechanisms within a rule-based coordination layer. These are implemented in IntentLint, a proof-of-concept system that infers analytic intent from shared notebooks, represents it as structured, editable rules, and checks users' prompts against those shared rules at prompt time.

Result: A user study with 16 data analysts demonstrated that IntentLint improves awareness of collaborators' intent, encourages reflection on analytic strategies, and yields design implications for more aligned and transparent human-AI collaboration.

Conclusion: Making analytic intent explicit through structured rules and proactive prompt checking can meaningfully address coordination breakdowns in human-AI collaborative data analysis, fostering greater alignment, transparency, and reflective practice among analysts.

Abstract: In human-AI collaborative data analysis, as analyses rapidly evolve, the artifacts meant to capture shared understanding often become incomplete or difficult to interpret, leading to undocumented assumptions, cross-user misaligned intent, context-poor prompts, and unwanted agent behaviors. To address these challenges, we introduce a rule-based coordination layer with two interaction mechanisms, intent scaffolding and prompt-time linting, that make analytic intent explicit and actionable during human-AI collaborative data analysis. We implement them in IntentLint, a proof-of-concept system that infers analytic intent from shared notebooks, represents it as structured, editable rules, and checks users' prompts against shared rules. IntentLint helps analysts externalize and refine their intent and proactively checks prompts for potential conflicts. A study with 16 data analysts shows that IntentLint improves awareness of collaborators' intent and encourages reflection on analytic strategies, and provides design implications for supporting more aligned and transparent human-AI collaborative data analysis.

</details>


### [79] [Preference-Driven Online Adaptation for Personalized Interaction Initiation in Proactive AI Assistants](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04416)
*Yufeng Wang,Wei Zhang,Zhiquan Wen,Jinwu Hu,Linhui Xiao,Tianlu Pan,Qingfang Zheng,Mingkui Tan*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: EOPA is a proactive AI assistant framework that learns user-specific interaction timing preferences through online feedback using temporal and activity evidence carriers, eliminating the need for LLM-based retraining while achieving substantial gains in F1 score and massive reductions in adaptation latency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Proactive AI assistants must determine when to initiate interactions, but optimal timing is highly user-specific and difficult to predefine. Online feedback provides valuable personalization signals, yet adapting from sparse interaction-worthy moments scattered across fine-grained user states is extremely challenging. Existing approaches lack efficient mechanisms for evidence-driven, feedback-based preference adaptation.

Method: EOPA introduces two evidence carriers: (1) temporal preference anchors that capture when a user prefers interaction, and (2) evidence-bearing activity prototypes that represent context patterns associated with interaction preferences. At each polling step, EOPA performs user-prior-smoothed evidence estimation and uncertainty-guided evidence scaling, then adaptively fuses both evidence types for interaction-or-silence binary decisions. When interaction is triggered, an LLM generates context-aware responses using high-quality historical examples as demonstrations. Critically, evidence carriers and decision parameters are updated directly from online feedback without LLM-based reasoning or retraining.

Result: On a ProPerSim-based benchmark, EOPA improved the interaction-timing F1 score by 19.80 points over the strongest baseline. It substantially reduced inference latency for both silence and interaction steps, and slashed the average daily adaptation time from 11.41 seconds to 0.39 seconds.

Conclusion: EOPA demonstrates that grounding interaction-timing preferences in measurable contextual evidence enables efficient, feedback-driven personalization for proactive AI assistants, achieving state-of-the-art timing accuracy with minimal computational overhead for online adaptation.

Abstract: AI assistants are typically reactive, relying on users to initiate interactions. Proactive assistants go beyond this paradigm by autonomously initiating interactions based on users' activity contexts. However, appropriate interaction timing is user-specific and difficult to determine in advance, while online feedback offers valuable signals for personalization. Direct feedback-driven adaptation is therefore appealing, but remains challenging due to sparse interaction-worthy moments scattered across fine-grained user states. To address the issues, we propose Evidence-driven Online Preference Adaptation (EOPA), which grounds a user's interaction-timing preferences in measurable contextual evidence through two evidence carriers: temporal preference anchors and evidence-bearing activity prototypes. At each polling step, EOPA derives temporal and activity evidence from the carriers through user-prior-smoothed evidence estimation and uncertainty-guided evidence scaling, and adaptively fuses the evidence for interaction-or-silence decisions. When interaction is selected, an LLM uses high-quality historical responses as demonstrations to generate a context-aware response that better reflects user preferences. EOPA updates its evidence carriers and decision parameters from received online feedback without LLM-based reasoning or retraining. Extensive experiments on a ProPerSim-based benchmark show that EOPA improves the interaction-timing F1 score by 19.80 points over the strongest baseline in our experiments, substantially reduces inference latency for both silence and interaction steps, and lowers the average daily adaptation time from 11.41 to 0.39 seconds.

</details>


### [80] [Revisiting Channel Effectiveness: A Multi-Dimensional Evaluation with Primitive Visual Stimuli](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04435)
*Soohyun Lee,Seokhyeon Park,Minsuk Chang,Jinwook Seo*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: Channel effectiveness is multi-dimensional: rankings shift substantially across accuracy, discriminability, separability, and pop-out tasks. Spatial channels generally excel, but task context (e.g., anchor availability) dramatically alters effectiveness. The authors introduce an Anchored Harmonic Weber model for discriminability and reveal asymmetric pairwise interactions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing channel effectiveness rankings focus narrowly on magnitude estimation accuracy within complete chart contexts, neglecting other critical perceptual tasks such as discriminability, separability, and preattentive pop-out. This limits principled, context-sensitive channel selection.

Method: Crowdsourced experiments using primitive visual stimuli (isolated visual marks without chart scaffolding) across seven channels (position, length, tilt, area, curvature, luminance, saturation) evaluated on four perceptual tasks: accuracy, discriminability, separability, and pop-out. A novel Anchored Harmonic Weber model formalizes discriminability patterns. Pairwise channel interactions were also assessed.

Result: Channel effectiveness is fundamentally multi-dimensional with rankings shifting across tasks. Spatial channels retain overall advantage, but accuracy is anchor-dependent. Discriminability varies widely by channel and value range (modeled by the new Weber variant). Pairwise interactions are often strongly asymmetric. A dissociation exists between estimation accuracy and preattentive detection: length has high accuracy but modest detection; area has poor accuracy but top detection rates.

Conclusion: Channel selection should be scenario-driven and context-sensitive, not based on a single static ranking. The findings provide a richer framework for visualization designers to match channels to specific perceptual task demands.

Abstract: Established channel effectiveness rankings primarily assess magnitude estimation accuracy in complete chart contexts, often neglecting other perceptual tasks such as discriminability, separability, and pop-out. To address this gap, we conducted crowdsourced experiments on seven core visual channels (position, length, tilt, area, curvature, luminance, and saturation) using primitive visual stimuli, a set of visual marks without chart-specific scaffolding to isolate channel-level variation. We evaluated these channels across four perceptual tasks (accuracy, discriminability, separability, and pop-out) and found that channel effectiveness is fundamentally multi-dimensional, with rankings shifting substantially across tasks. For instance, while spatial channels maintain an overall advantage, accuracy depends strongly on whether a fixed spatial anchor is available. Discriminability varies dramatically across channels and value ranges, a pattern we formalized with a novel Anchored Harmonic Weber model. Pairwise channel interactions are often strongly asymmetric. Finally, we identify a dissociation between estimation accuracy and preattentive detection: length shows only moderate detection effectiveness despite top-tier accuracy, while area achieves the highest detection rates despite poor quantitative accuracy, though the latter advantage may partly reflect stimulus-level cues. We synthesize these findings into a scenario-driven perspective for context-sensitive channel selection.

</details>


### [81] [Super-Gaussian: Interactive Scene Editing for 3D Gaussian Splatting and NLI-Based Volume Visualization in Virtual Reality](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04475)
*Suemin Jeon,Kaiyuan Tang,Chaoli Wang,Won-Ki Jeong*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: Super-Gaussian introduces a VR volume visualization framework that uses hierarchical 3D Gaussian clustering and natural language interaction to enable intuitive, efficient selection and semantic editing of complex volumetric regions without fatigue-inducing manual point-by-point operations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Volume visualization in VR suffers from high rendering costs and motion discomfort. While 3D Gaussian splatting enables high-performance rendering suitable for VR, existing Gaussian-based scene editing workflows are hindered by slow offline segmentation and fatigue-inducing manual selection, creating a need for more intuitive and efficient interaction paradigms.

Method: The framework groups Gaussian primitives into higher-level semantic units via feature-aware clustering. It employs a hierarchical select-and-refine workflow combining random-walk-based region propagation, cluster selection, and point refinement for progressive ROI specification. Natural language interaction (NLI) enables on-the-fly text labeling, allowing users to semantically query and manipulate content within a visualization-perception-action loop. Multimodal interaction integrates speech, visual feedback, and spatial VR manipulation.

Result: Effectiveness is demonstrated through four case studies (e.g., medical tumor selection, cosmological filament analysis), quantitative selection benchmarks against existing Gaussian-based techniques, and system-level evaluations.

Conclusion: Super-Gaussian successfully addresses key limitations in VR volume visualization by combining hierarchical Gaussian representation with multimodal interaction (clustering, random-walk propagation, NLI), enabling intuitive exploration, editing, and scientific analysis of volumetric data with reduced user effort and discomfort.

Abstract: Despite the promise of virtual reality (VR) for intuitive spatial interaction, volume visualization (VolVis) in VR remains constrained by high rendering costs and motion discomfort. Recent advances have shown that representing volumetric scenes with 3D Gaussian splatting enables high-performance rendering, making this representation well-suited for VR. However, existing Gaussian-based scene editing workflows remain limited by slow offline segmentation and fatigue-inducing manual selection. To address these challenges, we present Super-Gaussian, a novel VolVis framework that enhances scene editing and interaction in VR through intuitive 3D Gaussian selection and natural language interaction (NLI). Our approach groups Gaussian primitives into higher-level units via feature-aware clustering, enabling efficient selection of complex volumetric regions, such as tumors in medical images or filaments in cosmological data, without point-by-point interaction. Building on this, we introduce a hierarchical select-and-refine workflow that combines random-walk-based region propagation, cluster selection, and point refinement, allowing users to progressively specify regions of interest with reduced effort. We further support on-the-fly text labeling of selected regions using NLI, allowing users to semantically query, interpret, and manipulate content within a visualization-perception-action loop. By integrating multimodal interaction, including speech, visual feedback, and spatial manipulation in VR, our framework supports intuitive exploration, editing, and scientific analysis of volumetric data. We demonstrate the effectiveness of Super-Gaussian through four case studies, quantitative selection benchmarks against existing Gaussian-based techniques, and system-level evaluations. Implementation details and experiments can be found on the project page: https://smin0136.github.io/super-gaussian-project/

</details>


### [82] [Emotion Dynamics in Social Deception Games: Analysis of Professional and Nonprofessional Players through Electrodermal Activity in Werewolf Games](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04605)
*Sho Mitarai,Chang Liu,Goshiro Yamamoto,Nagisa Munekata*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: This study compares professional and non-professional players in social deception games using electrodermal activity measurements, revealing that professionals maintain persuasion-based communication under high arousal while non-professionals shift to information-focused strategies, with professionals also demonstrating superior emotional regulation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Developing AI systems capable of emotionally resonant communication is a persistent challenge. Understanding how humans modulate their communication strategies under emotional arousal — particularly across different expertise levels — can provide design principles for emotionally intelligent artificial agents.

Method: The authors employed a comparative experimental design using social deception games. They measured electrodermal activity (EDA) as a physiological index of emotional arousal during gameplay. Communication patterns were analyzed specifically during high-arousal episodes, and statistical analyses were conducted to compare expression patterns between professional and non-professional players.

Result: Two key findings emerged: (1) Under high emotional arousal, professional players continued using persuasion-oriented communication, whereas non-professional players shifted toward information-focused communication. (2) Professional players exhibited more stable emotional states overall, indicating superior emotional regulation capacity. Statistical tests confirmed significant group differences in communication patterns.

Conclusion: The findings offer actionable insights for designing AI systems that can adapt communication strategies based on recipient characteristics and contextual emotional states, thereby advancing the development of emotionally intelligent artificial agents capable of resonant human-AI interaction.

Abstract: The development of AI systems capable of emotionally resonant communication remains a significant challenge. This study examines how humans influence emotions in social deception games by comparing professional and non-professional players. We measured electrodermal activity during gameplay to capture physiological emotional responses and analyzed communication patterns during periods of high emotional arousal. Our results revealed distinct communication strategies: professional players maintained persuasion-based approaches under high arousal, while nonprofessional players shifted toward information-focused communication. Statistical analysis confirmed significant differences in expression patterns between expertise levels. Professional players exhibited more stable emotional states during gameplay, indicating better emotional regulation. These findings inform the design of AI systems that can adapt their communication strategies based on recipient characteristics, advancing the development of emotionally intelligent artificial agents.

</details>


### [83] [LiverPlan: A Stage-Adaptive Immersive Visual Analytics Framework for Anatomical Liver Surgical Planning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04707)
*Qixuan Liu,Shi Qiu,Xiwen Wu,Yuqi Tong,Yinqiao Wang,Ruiyang Li,Jialun Pei,Shengdong Zhao,Chi-Wing Fu,Pheng-Ann Heng*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: LiverPlan is an immersive VR-based visual analytics framework for anatomical liver resection planning that decomposes the workflow into three cognitively distinct stages with tailored visualization techniques, demonstrating significant improvements over desktop tools in a user study with eight hepatobiliary surgeons.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current 2D desktop tools for ALR planning suffer from three limitations: monolithic interfaces that don't adapt to different cognitive stages, limited spatial representation creating a perceptual bottleneck, and fragmented display of safety criteria causing an attention bottleneck. These inadequacies motivate a stage-adaptive, immersive solution.

Method: An 8-month collaborative design process with two expert hepatobiliary surgeons yielded LiverPlan, which decomposes planning into three stages: (1) anatomical discovery using context-preserving focus and hue-preserving rendering, (2) plan refinement via direct 3D resection plane manipulation with real-time embedded safety feedback, and (3) anticipatory surgery preparation through explicit plane-vessel intersection visualization. A within-subjects study with eight hepatobiliary surgeons compared LiverPlan against a desktop baseline on controlled planning tasks.

Result: LiverPlan yielded large-effect-size improvements in task completion time, perceived cognitive workload (NASA-TLX), and system usability (SUS) over the desktop baseline. Qualitatively, surgeons shifted from merely satisfying safety criteria to actively optimizing them, indicating reduced cognitive barriers to complex planning.

Conclusion: Explicit spatial visualization of anatomical relationships in an immersive, stage-adaptive framework substantially lowers the cognitive burden of complex surgical planning. LiverPlan demonstrates that tailoring interface design to the distinct cognitive demands of each planning stage enables more efficient and higher-quality preoperative decision-making.

Abstract: Anatomical liver resection (ALR) surgery is the most important treatment for liver cancer, yet preoperative planning demands complex, multi-stage clinical reasoning under competing safety constraints. Current 2D desktop tools are not well equipped to support this process, exhibiting three fundamental limitations: reliance on monolithic interfaces that fail to adapt to the distinct cognitive demands of each planning stage; a perceptual bottleneck caused by limited anatomical spatial representation and missing plane-vessel intersection visualization; and an attention bottleneck stemming from fragmented critical safety criteria display across separate views. We present LiverPlan, a stage-adaptive immersive visual analytics framework for ALR planning, grounded in an 8-month collaboration with two expert hepatobiliary surgeons. Decomposing the surgical planning process into three sequential yet cognitively distinct stages, LiverPlan externalizes the cognitive demand of each stage via tailored techniques: (1) context-preserving focus and hue-preserving rendering for anatomical discovery; (2) direct 3D resection plane manipulation coupled with real-time, embedded visual feedback on critical safety criteria during plan refinement; and (3) explicit plane-vessel intersection visualization for anticipatory surgery preparation. A within-subjects study with eight hepatobiliary surgeons against a desktop baseline shows large-effect-size improvements in task completion time, perceived cognitive workload, and system usability on controlled planning tasks. Moreover, our study reveals broader insights: LiverPlan reduces cognitive burden and encourages a shift in surgeons from merely satisfying safety criteria to actively optimizing them, suggesting that explicit visualization of spatial relationships lowers the cognitive barrier to complex surgical planning.

</details>


### [84] [Reference-Based Manipulation: A Framework and Pipeline for Multimodal Spatial Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04798)
*Yangyang He,Zhuangze Hou,Yonglin Chen,Can Liu*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: This paper investigates how users naturally construct spatial references via speech and gesture in immersive VR, formalizes a Reference-based Manipulation framework (Source, Anchor, Frame), and demonstrates its utility through an LLM-based interaction pipeline.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Users naturally combine speech and gesture to reference objects, their bodies, and the environment during immersive manipulation, yet existing systems lack a systematic understanding of how these spatial references are constructed and communicated. The work aims to bridge spatial cognition theories with interaction design to better support unconstrained multimodal spatial input.

Method: The authors conducted a Wizard-of-Oz study using a custom toolkit to observe unconstrained multimodal (speech + gesture) input patterns during scene construction tasks in VR. Based on empirical findings, they developed a formal framework decomposing spatial references into three core components — Source, Anchor, and Frame — and characterized their compositional strategies and explicitness. An LLM-based pipeline implementing example interaction techniques was built and preliminarily evaluated.

Result: The framework identifies Source (the entity being referenced), Anchor (the reference point), and Frame (the coordinate system) as the three core components of spatial references, with characterized compositional strategies and varying degrees of explicitness. The LLM-based pipeline demonstrates the framework's practical utility for implementing reference-based interaction techniques.

Conclusion: The Reference-based Manipulation framework provides a principled lens for designing and implementing spatial interaction systems that accommodate natural multimodal input, with implications for future immersive interface design.

Abstract: When manipulating objects in immersive platforms through speech and gesture, users naturally construct spatial references, referring to scene entities, their bodies, or the environment. Leveraging spatial cognition theories, this work systematically examines how users construct and communicate spatial intent. Using a custom toolkit, we conducted a Wizard-of-Oz study to observe unconstrained multimodal (speech + gesture) input patterns in Virtual Reality for scene construction. Based on these findings, we formalize a framework that decomposes spatial references into three core components: Source, Anchor, and Frame, while characterizing their compositional strategies and explicitness. We demonstrate the utility of this Reference-based Manipulation framework by implementing an LLM-based pipeline featuring a set of example interaction techniques with a preliminary technical evaluation. Finally, we discuss key lessons learned for supporting reference-based spatial interaction.

</details>


### [85] [Investigating Click Behaviors On Google Search Result Pages That Produce an AI Overview](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04831)
*Athena Chapekis,Anna Lieb,Sono Shah,Aaron Smith*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: This study analyzes Google's "AI Overviews" feature using browsing data from 900 U.S. adults, finding that AI Overviews appear more for certain query types and are associated with fewer clicks, rare citation engagement (~1%), and higher session-termination rates—patterns that persist after controlling for query and user effects.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: With Google's 2024 rollout of AI Overviews—AI-generated summaries displayed atop search results—there is an urgent need to understand how this feature affects user search behavior, query patterns, and traffic to external websites. The study aims to provide empirical evidence on the real-world impact of integrating generative AI into a dominant search platform.

Method: The authors collected one month of web browsing data from a representative panel of 900 U.S. adults. They identified which Google searches triggered AI Overviews, analyzed query-level attributes (e.g., length, presence of question words, noun-verb combinations) associated with AI Overview generation, and examined user behavioral outcomes (clicks, session endings). A mixed-effects logistic regression model was used to control for random effects by panelist and for query attributes that predict AI Overview appearance, isolating the independent association between AI Overviews and user behavior.

Result: Key findings: (1) Queries that are longer, begin with a question word, or contain both a noun and verb are more likely to trigger an AI Overview. (2) Clicks to cited sources within AI Overviews are extremely rare (~1% of AI Overview visits). (3) AI Overviews are associated with fewer overall clicks and higher rates of browsing session termination. The mixed-effects logistic regression confirmed these behavioral associations remain significant even after adjusting for query characteristics and individual panelist variability.

Conclusion: AI Overviews fundamentally alter search interaction patterns by reducing click-through behavior and increasing session abandonment, while rarely driving traffic to cited sources. These findings raise important questions about the downstream effects on web publishers, the information ecosystem, and the evolving role of search engines from navigational tools to answer-providing agents.

Abstract: In 2024, Google introduced "AI Overviews," a feature that displays an AI-generated result summary at the top of many Google search pages. This study investigates the role of AI in Google search using one month of web browsing data from a representative panel of 900 U.S. adults. Our analysis of the panelists' Google searches sheds light on AI Overviews, when they appear in Google search results, and what user behaviors are associated with AI Overviews. We identify several attributes that make a search query more likely to generate an AI Overview, including the length of a query, whether the query begins with a question word, and whether the query contains both a noun and verb. When it comes to user behavior, we find that clicks to sources cited in AI Overviews are very rare, occurring in only about 1% of visits to AI Overviews. We also find that AI Overviews are associated with fewer clicks and higher rates of ending browsing sessions. Importantly, results from a mixed-effects logistic regression model indicate that these associations hold when controlling for random effects by panelist and query attributes that make AI Overviews more likely to appear.

</details>


### [86] [AutoCue: Multimodal LLM-Assisted Externalization of Implicit Inputs as Instructional Visual Cues in Screencast Tutorials](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04910)
*Shengyang Luo,Shengyao Luo,Xiaolei Guo,Fengze Zhang,James Liang,Yingjie Victor Chen*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: AutoCue is a multimodal LLM-assisted pipeline that augments software tutorial videos by automatically inferring and externalizing implicit mouse/keyboard inputs as visual cues, reducing learner breakdowns and completion time.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Learners following screencast tutorials for feature-rich software frequently get stuck or rewind because critical input information (mouse actions, keyboard modifiers) is often missing or implicit when tutorials lack input metadata, causing interaction breakdowns.

Method: AutoCue integrates frame-to-frame visual changes, narration signals, and official software manual guidance within a multimodal LLM pipeline to infer mouse and key-modifier actions. It produces aligned cue layers and editable artifacts for human refinement. A visual cue grammar grounded in multimedia learning and cognitive load theory represents mouse, keyboard, and combined inputs.

Result: In a 24-participant between-subjects study evaluating AutoCue in Autodesk Maya, the augmented tutorials reduced task completion time and interaction breakdowns while improving learner-reported experience compared to baseline tutorials.

Conclusion: AutoCue demonstrates that LLM-assisted, human-in-the-loop augmentation of tutorials with structured visual cues can effectively address the problem of implicit input information in screencasts, yielding measurable improvements in both objective performance and subjective experience.

Abstract: Tutorial videos are widely used for learning feature-rich software, yet following screencast tutorials often breaks down in practice. Through a survey and contextual inquiry, we found that learners frequently rewind or get stuck because critical input information, especially mouse actions and keyboard-modified operations, is often implicit or missing in tutorials without input metadata. To address this problem, we present AutoCue, a multimodal LLM-assisted, human-in-the-loop tutorial augmentation pipeline for externalizing implicit inputs as instructional visual cues. AutoCue integrates frame-to-frame visual changes, narration signals, and operation guidance from official software manuals to infer likely mouse and key-modifier actions, then produces aligned cue layers and editable artifacts for human refinement. Grounded in multimedia learning and cognitive load theory, we further develop a visual cue grammar for representing mouse, keyboard, and combined inputs in software-learning tutorials. We instantiate and evaluate AutoCue in Autodesk Maya, focusing automatic inference on selected UI-mediated interactions with observable visual or textual feedback while supporting more ambiguous state changes through editable authoring artifacts. In a between-subjects study with 24 participants, the AutoCue-augmented tutorial reduced task completion time and interaction breakdowns and showed improved learner-reported experience.

</details>


### [87] [Transition Techniques for Externally-Guided Multi-Scale Viewpoint Changes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04912)
*Matt Gottsacker,Mengyu Chen,David Saffo,Feiyu Lu,Benjamin Lee,Blair MacIntyre*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: This paper presents and evaluates three transition techniques for externally-guided multi-scale viewpoint changes in XR (world-in-miniature, street-level, indoor), finding that techniques which externalize reference frames and user pose improve multi-scale spatial recall compared to a fade-to-black baseline, while same-scale recall remains unaffected.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing XR viewpoint transition techniques focus on self-guided exploration, but many scenarios (presentations, guided tours) require externally-guided transitions where the user lacks control. These can cause disorientation and discomfort, yet no prior work has systematically evaluated transition techniques for externally-guided multi-scale viewpoint changes.

Method: Within-subjects study (N=20) comparing three novel transition techniques for externally-guided multi-scale XR viewpoint changes against a fade-to-black baseline. Participants transitioned across three scale levels: world-in-miniature, street-level, and indoor destination views. Evaluation combined spatial recall measures, standardized questionnaires (workload, comfort), and semi-structured interviews to assess orientation, continuity, and user experience.

Result: Techniques that externalized reference frames and the user's pose significantly improved multi-scale spatial recall compared to the fade-to-black baseline. However, same-scale spatial recall was insensitive to the choice of transition technique, suggesting the benefits are specific to cross-scale transitions.

Conclusion: Externalizing reference frames and user pose during externally-guided multi-scale transitions enhances spatial orientation without affecting same-scale recall. The authors provide design implications for building more usable multi-scale XR viewpoint transitions in guided scenarios.

Abstract: Extended reality (XR) is increasingly used to help users understand complex virtual environments through multiple viewpoints across different immersion levels, positions, and scales. While numerous techniques address viewpoint transitions for self-guided exploration, many scenarios require externally-guided transitions where a system or presenter controls the user's viewpoint, leaving the user with limited spatial knowledge and control over the transition process, which can increase susceptibility to disorientation and discomfort. We present three transition techniques for externally-guided multi-scale XR viewpoint changes and evaluate them against a fade-to-black baseline in a within-subjects study (N=20). Participants transitioned between world-in-miniature, street-level, and indoor destination views. We combined spatial recall measures, standardized questionnaires, and semi-structured interviews to assess orientation, workload, comfort, and continuity. Results showed that in our setup, techniques externalizing reference frames and the user's pose improved multi-scale spatial recall relative to a fade, while same-scale recall was insensitive to transition technique. We conclude with design implications for multi-scale XR viewpoint transitions.

</details>


### [88] [Reply, Delete, or Ignore? Examining How Content Creators Perceive and Select Comment Moderation Strategies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04951)
*Yunhee Shim,Shagun Jhaver*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: This paper investigates how content creators choose among three strategies for moderating hateful comments—deleting, replying, or ignoring—revealing that safety and impression management concerns drive their decisions, while perceived algorithmic benefits do not significantly predict their choices.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Content creators, especially those with large followings, face disproportionate online harm. Their moderation decisions shape audience experience and platform discourse, yet prior HCI research has focused mainly on safety, overlooking how impression management and algorithmic reward concerns influence creators' moderation strategies.

Method: A survey of 584 content creators was conducted, examining their perceptions of three comment moderation strategies (deleting, replying, ignoring) across three evaluative dimensions: emotional safety, impression management, and algorithmic benefits. Regression analysis was used to determine which perceived benefits predict adoption willingness for each strategy.

Result: (1) Deleting was perceived as most beneficial for safety; (2) deleting and replying both outperformed ignoring for impression management; (3) replying was perceived to yield the highest algorithmic benefits. Crucially, safety and impression management concerns significantly predicted willingness to adopt strategies, but perceived algorithmic benefits did not.

Conclusion: Creators function as middle-level governance actors, balancing safety and self-presentation. Design implications are offered to support creators in governance roles without placing the full burden of online safety on them. The disconnect between perceived and actual influence of algorithmic incentives warrants further investigation.

Abstract: Content creators on social media sites occupy highly visible positions on their channels. As a result, creators, especially those with large followings, experience disproportionate levels of online harm. To address such harm, they enact a range of moderation strategies, which in turn shape the visibility of content that their audiences encounter. This paper examines how content creators perceive three moderation strategies to address hateful comments (deleting, replying to, or simply ignoring) and how they decide which strategy to deploy. While creator moderation is usually examined through the lens of safety, creators' regulation decisions may also be shaped by concerns about how their actions appear to audiences and how they are rewarded or penalized by platforms' recommendation algorithms. Conducting a survey of 584 content creators, we found that in their view, (1) deleting is the most beneficial for achieving safety, (2) both deleting and replying produce better impression management benefits than ignoring, and (3) replying is perceived to yield the highest algorithmic benefits. Crucially, while expectations of emotional safety and impression management benefits significantly predicted creators' willingness to adopt each comment moderation strategy, perceived algorithmic benefits did not. By unpacking how creators evaluate these trade-offs, this study contributes to HCI research on understanding creator-led, middle-level governance. We conclude with design implications for supporting creators as crucial governance actors without burdening them with sole responsibility for online safety.

</details>


### [89] [Exploring Cross-Reality Transitions between Projections and Head-Mounted Displays for Immersive Digital Art](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04971)
*Xiangpeng Fu,Mads Haahr*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: Investigates how users perceive transitions between large-scale projections and MR HMDs in hybrid immersive art. A within-subjects study (N=24) compared calibrated vs. deliberately inconsistent conditions, revealing that spatial misalignment, appearance mismatch, and latency harm presence, workload, and coherence—with effects varying by asset type (rigid, animated, particle). An open-source Unreal plugin (HUICRSync) is released.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Immersive exhibitions increasingly blend large-scale projections with MR HMDs, yet user perception of transitions across these heterogeneous visualization environments remains underexplored. The authors aim to understand how inconsistencies in spatial alignment, visual appearance, and latency affect user experience during cross-reality transitions.

Method: A within-subjects study (N=24) in a hybrid immersive art installation spanning projection, AR, and VR. Participants experienced two conditions: a calibrated condition and a bundled inconsistency condition that deliberately introduced noticeable spatial misalignment, visual appearance mismatch, and cross-device latency. The inconsistency condition served as a diagnostic probe to surface and discuss transition disruptions. Measures included presence, workload, and qualitative interviews. Three asset types were tested: rigid static, animated skeletal, and particle effects.

Result: The inconsistency condition significantly reduced presence and increased workload. Spatial misalignment disrupted action-outcome predictability; appearance mismatch reduced aesthetic coherence; latency weakened perceived responsiveness. Asset type mattered: rigid static assets exposed inconsistencies most clearly, animated skeletal assets shifted attention toward motion (masking discrepancies), and particle effects often concealed small mismatches.

Conclusion: The findings clarify how users perceive projection-to-MR transitions and support asset-aware design strategies for coherent hybrid immersive art. The authors also release HUICRSync, an open-source Unreal Engine plugin for prototyping projection-MR cross-reality experiences.

Abstract: Immersive exhibitions increasingly combine large-scale projections with mixed reality (MR) head-mounted displays (HMDs), but how users perceive transitions across these heterogeneous visualization environments remains underexplored. We investigate cross-reality (CR) object- and scene-level transitions in a hybrid immersive art installation spanning projection, augmented reality (AR), and virtual reality (VR). In a within-subjects study (N=24), we compared a calibrated condition with a bundled inconsistency condition introducing noticeable differences in spatial alignment, visual appearance, and cross-device latency. This contrast was used not to establish perceptual thresholds or hardware targets, but as a diagnostic probe to make transition disruptions more perceptible and discussable. The inconsistency condition reduced presence and increased workload. Interviews showed that spatial misalignment disrupted action-outcome predictability, appearance mismatch reduced aesthetic coherence, and latency weakened perceived responsiveness. Effects also varied by asset type: rigid static assets exposed inconsistencies more clearly, animated skeletal assets shifted attention toward motion, and particle effects often masked small discrepancies. These findings clarify how users perceive projection-MR transitions and support asset-aware design strategies for coherent hybrid immersive art. We also release HUICRSync, an open-source Unreal Engine plugin for prototyping projection-MR CR experiences.

</details>


### [90] [ArtAnno: Annotating Implicit Semantics in Artworks through LLM Agent-Driven Bidirectional Human-AI Augmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05026)
*Xiaoyan Gu,Yifang Wang,Wenqing Zheng,Haozhong Liu,Yixia Zheng,Peiyi Jiang,Wenjie Ning,Wei Zhang,Wei Chen*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: ArtAnno is a multi-agent artwork annotation system that implements a Bidirectional Human-AI Augmentation (BiHAA) framework, where AI assists annotators via semantic mining and label suggestions, while human expertise continuously refines the AI by distilling annotation trajectories into reusable knowledge—demonstrating improved efficiency and reduced effort for non-expert annotators.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current AI-assisted annotation tools for artworks are limited by one-way workflows that require extensive manual calibration from experts. Extracting implicit semantics from artworks is inherently difficult because it demands culturally grounded meanings and deep contextual knowledge. There is a need for a closed-loop system where human expertise and AI capabilities mutually enhance each other in real time.

Method: The authors first conducted a formative study with 20 artwork annotators from diverse backgrounds to identify pain points. They then designed the BiHAA closed-loop framework and implemented it in ArtAnno, a multi-agent annotation system comprising two core modules: (1) a Proactive Agentic Support Module for AI-to-human augmentation via semantic mining and label suggestion, and (2) an Interaction-Driven Evolution Module for human-to-AI augmentation by distilling annotation trajectories into reusable experience. Evaluation was conducted through a user study and two case studies.

Result: The framework and ArtAnno system improved annotation efficiency, enabled knowledge accumulation, and reduced the effort of information seeking and verification, particularly benefiting annotators with limited domain expertise.

Conclusion: The bidirectional human-AI augmentation paradigm shows strong promise for computational art research. The authors discuss broader implications for human-AI collaboration and outline future research directions.

Abstract: High-quality annotation of artworks is essential for computational art research, yet extracting implicit semantics remains challenging due to the reliance on culturally grounded meanings and deep contextual knowledge behind the images. Current AI-assisted annotation tools often lack assistance or rely on one-way workflows where experts have to perform extra manual calibrations to improve AI models, resulting in limited efficiency. To address this, we propose Bidirectional Human-AI Augmentation(BiHAA), a closed-loop framework in which skills and domain knowledge base evolve through real-time interaction and bidirectional HAI augmentation. Informed by a formative study with 20 artwork annotators from different backgrounds, we implement this framework in ArtAnno, an artwork annotation system driven by a multi-agent architecture. The system includes a Proactive Agentic Support Module, where AI augments humans through semantic mining and label suggestion, and an Interaction-Driven Evolution Module, where human expertise continuously enhances the AI through distilling annotation trajectories into reusable experience. Evaluation through a user study and two case studies demonstrates that our framework and system improve annotation efficiency, enable knowledge accumulation, and reduce the effort of information seeking and verification for annotators with limited domain expertise. We conclude by discussing broader implications and future directions.

</details>


### [91] [DeepConnect: A Visual Analytics System for Bridging Interdisciplinary Research Collaborations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05134)
*Yingchaojie Feng,Zekai Shao,Yiqun Sun,Yixuan Tang,Anthony K. H. Tung*

Main category: cs.HC

TL;DR: DeepConnect is an LLM-augmented visual analytics system that helps researchers discover interdisciplinary collaborators by translating open-ended goals into domain-specific tasks, comparing candidates through coordinated visualizations, identifying terminology gaps, and enabling conversation rehearsal before outreach.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Interdisciplinary collaboration is hard to initiate due to disciplinary silos, static researcher profiles that lack context for new goals, and difficulties in evaluating fit, complementarity, and establishing common ground before contact.

Method: DeepConnect integrates LLMs with visual analytics to: (1) translate collaboration ideas into domain-specific tasks, (2) retrieve and ground relevant cross-domain papers, (3) provide coordinated visualizations for candidate exploration/comparison, (4) surface terminology gaps/overlaps, and (5) support publication-grounded conversation rehearsal for outreach preparation.

Result: Evaluated through two case studies, a user study, and component-level evaluation, demonstrating value for complementary team formation, idea refinement, and pre-contact preparation.

Conclusion: DeepConnect effectively bridges disciplinary boundaries in collaborator discovery by contextualizing the search process around specific collaboration goals and equipping researchers with tools for meaningful pre-contact groundwork. A live system is publicly available.

Abstract: Interdisciplinary research collaboration is crucial for scientific innovation, but it remains difficult to initiate in practice. Existing collaborator discovery approaches are often constrained by disciplinary boundaries and static researcher profiles that do not reflect the specific context of a new collaboration goal. As a result, researchers struggle to translate open-ended collaboration goals into domain-specific tasks, evaluate candidate researchers' fit and complementarity, and establish common ground before initial contact. To address these challenges, we present DeepConnect, an LLM-augmented visual analytics system for interdisciplinary collaborator discovery. DeepConnect translates collaboration ideas into domain-specific tasks, retrieves relevant papers to ground cross-domain exploration, and provides coordinated visualizations for exploring and comparing candidate researchers. It further reveals terminology gaps and overlaps across domains and supports publication-grounded conversation rehearsal to help users prepare for outreach. We evaluate DeepConnect through two case studies, a user study, and a component-level evaluation, showing its value for complementary team formation, idea refinement, and pre-contact preparation. The DeepConnect website is available at https://deepconnect.sg.

</details>

### [92] [Energy Efficiency in Microservice Architectures: A Systematic Literature Review](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04070)
*Eoan O'Dea,Roberta Capuano,Paris Avgeriou,Henry Muccini*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: A systematic literature review of 40 primary studies reveals that energy efficiency in microservices is predominantly treated as a runtime operational concern (monitoring, scheduling, resource management) rather than a design-time architectural consideration, with measurement relying heavily on model-based estimation and coarse-grained infrastructure monitoring.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite growing interest in sustainable software and the widespread adoption of microservice architectures, research on energy efficiency remains fragmented across operational, infrastructural, and architectural perspectives with limited synthesis. No prior review has systematically examined how energy efficiency is considered, measured, and addressed at the architectural level in microservice-based systems.

Method: A systematic literature review (SLR) following Kitchenham's guidelines, screening publications from four major digital libraries through a six-stage process incorporating backward and forward snowballing. The final corpus consists of 40 primary studies, analyzed to address where energy efficiency is considered, how it is measured, and which architectural solutions have been proposed.

Result: Energy efficiency is predominantly addressed at runtime through monitoring, scheduling, and resource management techniques. Design-time integration of energy concerns remains limited. Measurement practices are largely infrastructure-oriented, relying on model-based estimation and coarse-grained monitoring rather than fine-grained, service-level instrumentation.

Conclusion: Energy efficiency in microservices is primarily treated as an operational optimisation problem rather than a lifecycle-spanning architectural concern. The field needs earlier integration of energy considerations during architectural design and improved, finer-grained measurement practices to shift from reactive optimisation to proactive, architecture-level sustainability.

Abstract: Context. Microservice architectures are widely adopted for building scalable cloud-native systems, enabling independent deployment, fine-grained service composition, and operational elasticity. Problem. Despite growing interest in sustainable software, research on energy efficiency in microservices spans operational, infrastructural, and architectural perspectives, but these are typically addressed in isolation. Existing studies focus on optimisation techniques or measurement approaches, with limited synthesis of how energy efficiency is considered, measured, and addressed at the architectural level. Goal. This study synthesises research on energy-efficient microservices by examining where energy efficiency is considered, how it is measured, and which architectural solutions have been proposed. Method. We conduct a systematic literature review following Kitchenham's guidelines, screening publications from four major digital libraries through a six-stage process with backward and forward snowballing, resulting in 40 primary studies. Results. Energy efficiency is predominantly addressed at runtime through monitoring, scheduling, and resource management, while design-time integration remains limited. Measurement practices are largely infrastructure-oriented and rely on model-based estimation and coarse-grained monitoring. Conclusion. Energy efficiency in microservices is primarily treated as an operational optimisation problem rather than a lifecycle-spanning architectural concern, highlighting the need for earlier architectural integration and improved measurement practices.

</details>


### [93] [An Approach for Embedding-Guided Function Reuse Detection in Embedded C Software](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04137)
*A A Talha Talukder,Omar Alam,Akramul Azim*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: A domain-aware RAG pipeline with hardware-compatibility validators is proposed to detect reusable embedded C functions across microcontroller platforms, addressing the 93.6% false-positive rate of static analysis tools like SonarQube caused by hardware-environment mismatches.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reusing embedded software functions across different microcontroller platforms is economically valuable but technically challenging: high cosine-similarity functions passing SonarQube checks can be entirely hardware-incompatible. Static analysis tools lack models of peripheral interfaces, HAL dependencies, and register-map constraints, producing excessive false positives when used for reuse detection.

Method: A retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline enriches each embedded C function with inline comments, call-graph context, and project README, then embeds using eight backbone models (MiniLM, MPNet, BGE, E5, GraphCodeBERT, OpenAI text-embedding-3-small, LLaMA 3 8B, StarCoder2 3B). Four hardware-compatibility validators (peripheral token overlap, parameter count parity, call-graph dependency overlap, structural branching pattern) filter candidates directly in the retrieval stack.

Result: Evaluated on six public embedded C projects (184 functions, 4,815 above-plateau pairs), SonarQube yielded a 93.6% false-positive rate as a reuse filter; 83.5% of failures stemmed from hardware-environment mismatches undetectable by static analysis. Manual verification of 40 rejected pairs confirmed 97.5% validator accuracy. A diagnostic rule-injection variant identified dominant failure categories (McNemar chi-squared ≈ 294.0, p < 0.001).

Conclusion: Hardware-compatibility validation must be integrated into embedded software reuse pipelines, as semantic similarity and code quality metrics alone are insufficient. The proposed validator stack effectively bridges the hardware-domain gap with high accuracy.

Abstract: Reusing embedded software functions across products is economically valuable but technically difficult: the same functionality implemented for two different microcontroller platforms can be entirely incompatible at the hardware level, even when the functions score above 0.90 cosine similarity and both pass SonarQube quality checks. Static analysis tools were designed to measure code quality, not hardware-domain compatibility, and have no model of peripheral interfaces, hardware abstraction layer (HAL) dependencies, or register-map constraints. This paper presents a domain-aware retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline for embedded C software reuse detection that addresses the hardware-compatibility gap directly. The pipeline enriches each function by extracting its existing inline comments, call-graph context, and a project README before embedding it with eight backbone models (MiniLM, MPNet, BGE, E5, GraphCodeBERT, OpenAI text-embedding-3-small, LLaMA 3 8B, StarCoder2 3B) acting as feature extractors. Four hardware-compatibility validators---covering peripheral token overlap, parameter count parity, call-graph dependency overlap, and structural branching pattern---filter candidates directly in the retrieval stack. Evaluated on six public embedded C software projects (184 functions, 4,815 above-plateau pairs), the pipeline reveals that SonarQube produces a 93.6% false-positive rate as a reuse filter, with 83.5% of failures caused by hardware-environment mismatches that static analysis cannot detect. Manual verification of 40 rejected pairs confirms 97.5% validator accuracy, and a diagnostic rule-injection variant identifies the dominant failure categories (McNemar chi-squared~=~294.0, p~$<$~0.001).

</details>


### [94] [AgentForge: An Immersive Role-Playing Platform for Learning Agentic Software Engineering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04148)
*Zihan Fang,Yueke Zhang,Yu Huang*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: AgentForge is an immersive learning system where novices role-play as one of four software-engineering agents (Task Planner, Patch Author, Code Reviewer, or Test Runner) in a multi-agent code-repair workflow, with AI handling the remaining roles. A study with 37 novices showed high task-completion rates, though the Code Reviewer role demanded significantly more interaction. Participants reported substantial gains in understanding software repair and AI collaboration.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Agentic AI systems in software development offer limited transparency and assume users can effectively guide and validate AI decisions. This is especially challenging for novices, who must simultaneously learn how agentic AI works, how to collaborate with it, and how to critically evaluate its outputs.

Method: AgentForge is presented as an immersive learning system embedding novices into one of four roles (Task Planner, Patch Author, Code Reviewer, Test Runner) within a multi-agent code-repair workflow. In each session, the novice performs their chosen role while AI agents handle the other three. The system provides role-based scaffolding and metacognitive support to clarify responsibilities, visualize agent coordination and intermediate artifacts, and encourage self-monitoring. A user study with 37 novice developers evaluated task-completion rates, interaction demands (turns, reroutes, completion time), perceived difficulty, and self-reported learning gains, with statistical comparisons using adjusted p-values.

Result: Participants achieved high task-completion rates with AI-agent support. However, the Code Reviewer role required significantly more interaction turns, reroutes, and completion time (p_adj = .004) and was perceived as most challenging. Participants reported significant gains in understanding software repair and agent collaboration (p_adj < .001).

Conclusion: AgentForge can help novices develop practical software-engineering skills while learning to collaborate with agentic AI more critically and effectively. The findings highlight role-dependent differences in interaction demands, with Code Reviewer being the most demanding practice.

Abstract: Agentic AI is increasingly used to coordinate planning, implementation, review, and testing in software development, yet it often offers limited transparency into its decisions and interactions. Many such systems also assume that users can effectively guide the AI's decisions and validate its outputs. This assumption poses a particular challenge for novices, who must simultaneously learn how agentic AI works, how to collaborate with it effectively, and how to evaluate its outputs critically. To address this challenge, we present \textit{AgentForge}, an immersive learning system in which novices take on one of four software-engineering roles: Task Planner, Patch Author, Code Reviewer, or Test Runner, within a multi-agent code-repair workflow. In each practice session, the novices perform their chosen role while AI agents perform the remaining three. Through role-based scaffolding and metacognitive support, AgentForge clarifies role-specific responsibilities, makes agent coordination and intermediate artifacts visible, and encourages novices to monitor and evaluate their decisions. In a study with 37 novice developers, participants achieved high task-completion rates with AI-agent support. However, interaction demands differed significantly across practices: the Code Reviewer practice required more interaction turns, reroutes, and completion time ($p_{\mathrm{adj}} = .004$) and was perceived as the most challenging. Participants nevertheless reported significant gains in their understanding of software repair and agent collaboration ($p_{\mathrm{adj}} < .001$). These findings suggest that AgentForge can help novices develop practical software-engineering skills while learning to collaborate with agentic AI more critically and effectively.

</details>


### [95] [MergeSE: Post-Hoc Model Merging for Software Engineering Tasks Without Retraining](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04181)
*Palash R. Roy,Banani Roy,Kevin A. Schneider,Chanchal K. Roy*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: MergeSE is an open-source CLI and web tool for training-free model merging of HuggingFace encoder checkpoints, addressing catastrophic forgetting under distribution shift in SE tasks (clone detection, vulnerability detection, etc.) through five merging algorithms and supporting inspect, merge, evaluate, and export operations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Fine-tuned code models degrade severely under distribution shift (e.g., 71% F1 drop on cross-language clones, near-zero F1 on AI-generated clones). Post-hoc model merging achieves 93% of multi-task performance and 4× better OOD generalization, but no practical tool exists for SE researchers to diagnose compatibility, merge specialists, validate results, and export models — motivating the creation of MergeSE.

Method: MergeSE implements a five-operation workflow (tasks, inspect, merge, evaluate, export) supporting five merging algorithms (TIES, DARE-TIES, Wudi, PCB, averaging), with built-in cross-task classification-head mismatch detection, deterministic seedable outputs, a registry of nine SE task types, and bundled benchmark samples for reproduction. It operates on HuggingFace encoder checkpoints with CPU-only merging of 124M-parameter models in under 5 seconds.

Result: A full merge of two 124M-parameter checkpoints completes in under 5 seconds on CPU. End-to-end validation confirms that MergeSE-produced checkpoints match reference implementations and recover cross-domain performance from domain-specific specialists.
