Conclusion: MergeSE fills a practical gap in the SE research toolchain, enabling training-free model merging with validated, reproducible results. It is publicly available at mergese.usask.ca and on GitHub under srlabUsask/MergeSE.

Abstract: Fine-tuned code models often behave as domain specialists and can degrade sharply under distribution shift: in our clone-detection setting, a model trained on same-language clones drops 71\% F1 on cross-language clones, while multi-task training falls to 0.151 F1 on unseen AI-generated clones. Our companion study shows that post-hoc model merging can address this fragmentation, achieving 93\% of multi-task performance without training data while generalizing 4$\times$ better to unseen clone types. However, no practical tool exists that lets SE researchers diagnose checkpoint compatibility, merge specialists, validate results on SE benchmarks, and export models for deployment. We present \textbf{MergeSE}, an open-source CLI and web tool for training-free model merging of HuggingFace encoder checkpoints. While motivated by OOD generalization in clone detection, MergeSE supports SE classification workflows more broadly through a built-in registry of nine task types, including vulnerability detection, defect prediction, and code-smell detection. MergeSE provides five operations: \textit{tasks}, \textit{inspect}, \textit{merge}, \textit{evaluate}, and \textit{export}. It supports five merging algorithms, including TIES, DARE-TIES, Wudi, PCB, and averaging; detects cross-task classification-head mismatches; produces seedable deterministic outputs; and includes bundled benchmark samples for smoke-test reproduction. A full merge of two 124M-parameter checkpoints completes in under 5 seconds on CPU. End-to-end validation confirms that MergeSE-produced checkpoints match reference implementations and recover cross-domain performance from domain-specific specialists. The tool is available online at https://mergese.usask.ca, and the development repository is at https://github.com/srlabUsask/MergeSE.

</details>


### [96] [SONAR: Task-Aware Code Summary Evaluation for LLM Consumers Without References](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04195)
*Simantika Bhattacharjee Dristi,Matthew B. Dwyer*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: SONAR is a reference-free framework for evaluating source code summaries based on code regeneration quality. It measures four dimensions—Correctness, Abstraction, Conciseness, and Fluency—and reveals that Correctness and Abstraction strongly correlate with LLM performance on downstream SE tasks, while Conciseness and Fluency do not, challenging human-centric evaluation norms.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional evaluation of source code summaries relies on human-written references or human preferences, but this paradigm is outdated: LLM-based tools and agents increasingly consume these summaries as inputs for downstream software engineering tasks. What makes a summary useful for a consuming agent remains largely unexplored.

Method: SONAR evaluates summaries along four dimensions (Correctness, Abstraction, Conciseness, Fluency) using a novel code regeneration-based approach: a summary is used to regenerate the original code, and the quality of this reconstruction serves as an empirical, reference-free quality signal that requires neither gold-standard references nor human/LLM subjective judgments.

Result: Correctness and Abstraction significantly correlate with LLM performance across four downstream SE tasks, with correlations up to 14X higher than the best baseline. Conciseness and Fluency, though valued by human developers, are mostly insignificant for LLM consumers. A large-scale evaluation of 11 popular LLMs using SONAR identifies model-specific strengths and weaknesses across each dimension.

Conclusion: Summary usefulness is task- and consumer-dependent. The dimensions that matter for LLM agents differ from those valued by humans, suggesting the need for task-aware summarization approaches. SONAR provides both a practical evaluation framework and empirical insights to guide future research in this direction.

Abstract: Source code summaries have traditionally been evaluated from a human developer's perspective, with quality determined by how closely they resemble developer-written references and how well they align with human preferences. But this overlooks a growing reality: LLM-based tools and agents increasingly consume code summaries as inputs for software engineering (SE) tasks, and what makes a summary useful for a consuming agent on a task remains largely unexplored. To bridge this gap, we propose SONAR, a reference-free framework that evaluates source code summaries along four dimensions: Correctness, Abstraction, Conciseness, and Fluency. Rather than optimizing for a pre-written "gold standard", SONAR introduces a novel code regeneration-based approach that uses a summary to regenerate code and leverages that reconstruction as a quality signal of the summary. This provides an empirical grounding that requires neither a reference summary nor the subjective judgment of humans or LLMs. We evaluate SONAR's dimensions on their ability to influence LLM performance across four downstream SE tasks. We find that Correctness, followed by Abstraction, significantly correlates with LLM performance, with correlations up to 14X higher than the best baseline. Conciseness and Fluency, though widely valued by human developers, remain mostly insignificant to an LLM consumer, suggesting that what makes a summary useful is task- and consumer-dependent. Through a large-scale evaluation of 11 popular LLMs using SONAR, we further identify the strengths and weaknesses of different models across each quality dimension, while offering insights to facilitate future research on task-aware summarization.

</details>


### [97] [A Unified Model for Cross-Domain Clone Detection via Model Merging](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04215)
*Palash R. Roy,Banani Roy,Kevin A. Schneider,Chanchal K. Roy*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This paper investigates model merging—a post-hoc technique combining trained checkpoints without original training data—to build unified cross-domain code clone detectors. The authors evaluate five task-vector methods, architecture merging, and cross-tokenizer alignment across multiple models and benchmarks. TIES merging on a shared pre-trained base emerges as the recommended method, achieving 93% of multi-task performance (0.865 F1) while generalizing better to unseen AI-generated clones than alternatives.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Code clone detection faces a fragmentation crisis: detectors are domain specialists whose performance degrades drastically (F1 drops >70%) outside their training distribution. Deploying multiple specialized models is impractical, and training a single cross-domain model requires simultaneous access to all training data. Model merging offers a promising middle ground—combining separately trained checkpoints post-hoc without data sharing—but has been largely unexplored in software engineering.

Method: The authors systematically evaluate model merging for cross-domain clone detection using: (1) five task-vector parameter merging methods (including TIES, WUDI), (2) architecture merging via greedy layer stitching, and (3) cross-tokenizer alignment. Experiments span four code models (UniXcoder, CodeBERT, etc.), three benchmarks, and twelve configurations. They test same-base merging (models fine-tuned from identical pretrained checkpoints) and cross-base merging (different pretrained bases), measuring both in-distribution performance and out-of-distribution generalization to unseen AI-generated clones (GPTCloneBench).

Result: Same-base TIES merging achieves 0.865 combined F1 on UniXcoder (93% of multi-task training performance) without any training data at merge time. WUDI attains the highest in-distribution F1 (0.899) but TIES generalizes better to unseen AI-generated clones. Cross-base merging yields only marginal, high-variance gains across all methods, indicating that a shared pre-trained base is critical for task vector compatibility. Merged detectors outperform zero-shot code LLMs on GPTCloneBench at lower inference cost and generalize up to 4× better than multi-task training to unseen AI-generated clones.

Conclusion: Model merging, specifically TIES on a shared pre-trained base, provides a practical, data-free recipe for building cross-domain clone detectors. A key trade-off emerges between in-domain performance (favors multi-task training) and out-of-distribution robustness (favors merging). The work establishes that task vector compatibility through a shared pre-trained base is the binding factor for effective merging, offering one of the first systematic empirical studies of model merging applied to software engineering tasks.

Abstract: The growing diversity of code clone types, from syntactic copies to cross-language semantic clones to AI-generated duplicates, has created a fragmentation crisis in clone detection. Current deep learning detectors are domain specialists that degrade significantly outside their training distribution, with F1 drops exceeding 70% across domains. Deploying multiple specialized models is impractical, yet training a single cross-domain detector requires simultaneous access to all training data. To address this, we investigate model merging, a family of post-hoc techniques that operate solely on trained checkpoints. We evaluate parameter merging with five task-vector methods, architecture merging via greedy layer stitching, and cross-tokenizer alignment across four code models, three benchmarks, and twelve configurations. Same-base TIES merging creates effective cross-domain detectors, validated across two model families and three random seeds, reaching 0.865 combined F1 on UniXcoder, 93% of multi-task performance without any training data at the merging step. WUDI achieves the highest in-distribution combined F1 at 0.899, but TIES generalizes better to unseen AI-generated clones, making it our recommended method. Cross-base merging yields only marginal and high-variance gains across all five methods, indicating that task vector compatibility through a shared pre-trained base is the binding factor for effective merging. Merged detectors also outperform zero-shot code LLMs on GPTCloneBench at lower inference cost and generalize up to 4x better than multi-task training to unseen AI-generated clones, suggesting a trade-off between in-domain performance and OOD robustness. This work provides one of the first systematic empirical studies of model merging for software engineering and a practical recipe for building cross-domain clone detectors.

</details>


### [98] [Neuro-Symbolic Proof-of-Vulnerability Generation with Open-Weight Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04217)
*Yu Nong,Haipeng Cai*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: POVGEN is a low-cost neuro-symbolic framework that combines semantic focusing with LLM-guided constraint reasoning and SMT solving to automatically generate Proof-of-Vulnerability inputs. It achieves 78.98% success on a recent benchmark, significantly outperforming fuzzing and symbolic execution, and generates valid PoVs for 74.80% of 250 real-world CVEs, uncovering six flawed patches and five previously unknown vulnerabilities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Validating software vulnerabilities requires concrete proof-of-vulnerability inputs, yet public triggering inputs are often unavailable for disclosed vulnerabilities. Existing approaches (fuzzing, symbolic execution) involve tradeoffs in effectiveness, scalability, cost, and controllability, creating an opportunity for a complementary design that is both cost-effective and highly capable.

Method: POVGEN is a three-stage neuro-symbolic framework: (1) vulnerability-relevant region localization using patch diff analysis (when available) to focus the search; (2) path-sensitive reachability analysis to identify feasible execution paths leading to vulnerable code; and (3) PoV generation via constraint extraction and solving, where open-weight LLMs guide the constraint reasoning process backed by an SMT solver. Fine-tuned open-weight models match frontier commercial LLMs on core constraint-reasoning subtasks.

Result: On a recent benchmark, POVGEN achieves 78.98% PoV generation success, compared to fuzzing (up to 50.20%) and symbolic execution (2.45%). On 250 real-world CVEs without public PoVs, it generates valid PoVs for 74.80% with patch information and 65.1% without. The generated PoVs revealed six flawed CVE patches (all subsequently fixed) and five previously unreported vulnerabilities (four confirmed and fixed by developers).

Conclusion: POVGEN demonstrates that combining semantic focusing with LLM-guided constraint reasoning and SMT solving yields a cost-effective, high-performing PoV generation framework. It advances vulnerability validation capabilities, exposes flawed patches, and discovers new vulnerabilities, with open-weight models eliminating per-sample API costs while matching commercial LLM performance on key reasoning tasks.

Abstract: Software vulnerabilities are persistent, but validating them remains difficult: a Proof-of-Vulnerability (PoV) requires a concrete input that triggers the vulnerable behavior, yet public triggering inputs are often unavailable for disclosed vulnerabilities. Existing techniques make different tradeoffs in effectiveness, scalability, cost, and controllability, leaving room for complementary designs. To complement them, we present POVGEN, a low-cost neuro-symbolic framework that makes PoV generation cost-effective via semantic focusing and LLM-guided constraint reasoning using open-weight models. POVGEN first localizes vulnerability-relevant regions (utilizing patch information if available), then performs path-sensitive reachability analysis, and finally generates PoVs by extracting and solving constraints with LLM-guided reasoning backed by an SMT solver. POVGEN successfully generates PoVs for 78.98% of vulnerabilities in a recent benchmark, outperforming fuzzing (up to 50.20%) and symbolic execution (2.45%). On 250 real-world CVEs without public PoVs, it generates valid PoVs for 74.80% of cases and reproduces 65.1% when without patch information. The fine-tuned open-weight models match frontier commercial LLMs on key sub-tasks (i.e., the core constraint-reasoning steps) while running locally at no per-sample API cost. Applying the generated PoVs revealed six flawed patches in disclosed CVEs (all subsequently fixed) and five previously unreported vulnerabilities (of which four have been confirmed and fixed by the developers).

</details>


### [99] [CURATE: Leveraging LLM Agents to Compose, Catalog, and Deploy Reproducible Workflows](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04270)
*Nolan Cutler,Chia-Chen Kuo,Nanda Velugoti,Kathryn Newhart,Renato Figueiredo*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: CURATE is a human-in-the-loop multi-agent LLM system that manages composable workflows across their entire lifecycle — including deployment and sharing — featuring a module catalog for reuse and FAIR-aligned sharing, demonstrated with 6 experiments including SeBS-Flow benchmarks and an environmental engineering simulation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing agentic code generation systems focus narrowly on code generation, neglecting the full workflow lifecycle (deployment, sharing, reuse). Users must independently stitch modules together and manage deployment, creating barriers to entry in scientific and applied domains.

Method: CURATE (Composition, User-in-the-loop, Reuse, and Automated Task Execution) is a multi-agent system where LLM agents orchestrate composable workflow development end-to-end. Key innovation is a module catalog enabling storage, retrieval, and reuse of curated modules/subgraphs across workflows, aligned with FAIR principles (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable). The prototype uses Claude Opus 4.8.

Result: The prototype was validated through 6 experiments: reproducing and adapting 4 workflows from the SeBS-Flow benchmark suite, and automating development and scaling of a complex mechanistic model for anaerobic digestion simulation in environmental engineering.

Conclusion: CURATE demonstrates feasibility of multi-agent systems that span the full workflow lifecycle beyond code generation, with catalog-based reuse showing promise for FAIR-aligned scientific workflow development.

Abstract: Agentic code generation has shown promise in automating and accelerating software development by utilizing Large Language Models (LLMs) to generate, test, and deploy code. For engineers and scientists, such systems have the potential to accelerate the development of applied and scientific workflows while reducing barriers to entry in domains that have yet to fully realize their benefits. However, a key gap remains: existing coding agents primarily focus on code generation and do not address the entire workflow lifecycle, including deployment and sharing. As a result, users develop and stitch modules independently while managing deployment on their own. To address this gap, we propose CURATE - Composition, User-in-the-loop, Reuse, and Automated Task Execution - a novel human-in-the-loop multi-agent system that uses LLM agents to manage and develop composable workflows across their entire lifecycle. A key feature of the system is a catalog that allows for the storage and reuse of modules across workflows. Module catalogs provide a foundation that can be expanded to support FAIR principles by facilitating the sharing and reuse of curated modules and subgraphs. We demonstrate the feasibility of our system with an initial prototype using Claude Opus 4.8, comprising 6 experiments: reproducing and adapting 4 workflows derived from the SeBS-Flow benchmark suite, and automating the development and scaling of a workflow that leverages a complex mechanistic model in environmental engineering used to simulate anaerobic digestion.

</details>


### [100] [LLM-based Vulnerability Discovery in Business Process Documentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04271)
*Ben Falchuk,Himanshu Garg,Euthimios Panagos,Sioan Zohar*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: MIRABELLE is a system that uses AI/ML, particularly LLMs, to detect business logic vulnerabilities in process documentation by extracting attributed graph representations, with this paper focusing on evaluating LLM performance across stages from error-flagging to full process structure recovery.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Business processes suffer from vulnerabilities (conflicting requirements, ambiguous documentation, missing quality checks, etc.) that cause quality issues, delays, and cost overruns. Extracting business logic from natural-language process documentation is challenging due to domain expertise requirements, process complexity, and large information volumes, motivating the need for automated AI/ML-based approaches.

Method: MIRABELLE processes business process artifacts (ISO 9000/9001 docs, user guides, work instructions, execution logs) using LLMs and AI/ML to generate attributed graph representations of business logic. These graphs are then analyzed via graph-based and formal logic approaches to identify vulnerabilities. The paper specifically experiments with multiple LLMs across key stages: grammatical/technical error-flagging in short phrases and complete process structure recovery/extraction.

Result: The paper reports on the comparative performance of several LLMs across the vulnerability detection pipeline stages, though specific quantitative results are not detailed in the abstract.

Conclusion: LLMs play a vital role within MIRABELLE for extracting business logic from natural language artifacts, and their performance varies across different stages of the vulnerability detection workflow.

Abstract: Just like software and hardware, business processes are susceptible to vulnerabilities that can lead to product quality issues, delays, and increased costs. Business process vulnerabilities can arise from a variety of sources, including conflicting requirements, ambiguous documentation, invalid measurement spec-ifications, omission of quality checks, or implementations that differ from speci-fications. MIRABELLE is a system that identifies and characterizes business logic (BL) vulnerabilities from available business process representations, in-cluding ISO 9000/9001 documentation, user guides, work instructions, and pro-cess execution logs. MIRABELLE leverages recent advances in AI/ML to pro-cess available business process documentation and generate attributed graph rep-resentations of the business logic that can be processed using both graph and for-mal logic approaches for identifying potential vulnerabilities. However, extract-ing the business logic (e.g., operation execution sequences, decisions, input/out-put resources) from mostly natural language artifacts is challenging due to the required domain expertise, inherent process complexity, and the sometimes very large volumes of information. This paper focuses on our experimentation with Large Language Models (LLMs) and their role within MIRABELLE. We report on the performance of several LLMs across vital stages of vulnerability detection, from grammatical and technical error-flagging in short phrasings, to complete process structure recovery and extraction.

</details>


### [101] [EA-Graph: Artifact-Anchored Verification Memory for Coding Agents under Upstream Drift](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04278)
*Hwai-Jung Hsu,Cheng-Jan Chi,Hanna Everett*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: EA-Graph introduces artifact-anchored memory for coding agents, linking verification claims to specific file content at sub-path granularity. When upstream code changes, claims are classified as unaffected, affected, or unprovable rather than silently invalidated. Experiments across 42 sessions show significant improvement for a smaller model (Haiku), while a larger model (Sonnet) performed near ceiling, and no sessions fabricated missing content.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Coding agents working across sessions accumulate verification claims (e.g., "this function is correct"), but prose notes preserve conclusions without the program state that supported them. After upstream changes, prior claims may become invalid yet go undetected because the repository still builds. The authors argue that memory systems for coding agents need to anchor claims to the specific artifact content used to establish them, track freshness independently from evidence strength, and gracefully handle missing upstream content by marking claims unprovable rather than guessing.

Method: EA-Graph represents code artifacts at sub-path granularity, resolves aliases to leaf definitions, and anchors each verification claim to the content used when the claim was established. Evidence strength and freshness are maintained as separate dimensions. The system is evaluated on synthetically generated repositories with known behavior-to-artifact ground truth. The task is to classify prior claims as unaffected, affected, or unprovable after three types of drift: value drift, logic drift, and deliberately withheld upstream content. The study covers 42 sessions across 7 clean worlds, 14 model-world instances, and 3 memory conditions (artifact-anchored, prose notes, no persistent memory), using Haiku and Sonnet model tiers. Wilcoxon signed-rank tests are used for paired comparisons.

Result: In the Haiku (smaller model) round, artifact-anchored memory outperformed both prose notes and no persistent memory across all 7 worlds, with exact paired Wilcoxon tests yielding p = 0.0156 for each comparison. In the Sonnet (larger model) round, the anchored condition achieved perfect performance, but frequent ceiling effects in control conditions rendered the preregistered contrasts non-significant. Critically, no session in any condition fabricated withheld content. An exploratory comparison suggests structured claim memory may narrow capability gaps by externalizing in-session re-derivation, though it does not establish cross-model equivalence.

Conclusion: The results support a bounded claim: artifact-anchored memory improved the smaller model's provability judgments in this testbed. The approach prevented hallucination of missing content and showed promise for externalizing reasoning to narrow capability gaps. The authors explicitly disclaim any conclusions about efficiency or repair quality, scoping the contribution strictly to memory-aided claim classification under drift.

Abstract: Coding agents increasingly work across sessions, but prose notes can preserve a conclusion without the program state that supported it. After an upstream change, a repository may still build even though earlier verification claims are no longer valid. EA-Graph is an artifact-anchored memory for verification claims. It represents artifacts at sub-path granularity, resolves aliases to leaf definitions, anchors each claim to the content used to establish it, and keeps evidence strength separate from freshness. When replacement content is unavailable, the claim becomes unprovable rather than guessed.
  EA-Graph is evaluated on generated repositories whose behavior-to-artifact ground truth is known by construction. The task is to classify prior claims as unaffected, affected, or unprovable after value drift, logic drift, and deliberately withheld upstream content. The analysis covers 42 sessions across seven clean worlds, 14 model-world instances, three memory conditions, and two model tiers. In the Haiku round, artifact-anchored memory outscored prose notes and no persistent memory in all seven worlds; each exact paired Wilcoxon comparison yielded p = 0.0156. In the Sonnet round, the anchored condition was perfect, but frequent control ceilings left the preregistered contrasts non-significant. No session fabricated withheld content. These results support a bounded claim: artifact-anchored memory improved the smaller model's provability judgments in this testbed. An exploratory comparison further suggests that structured claim memory may narrow a capability gap by externalizing in-session re-derivation, but it does not establish cross- model equivalence. The study makes no claim about efficiency or repair quality.

</details>


### [102] [COMPAS: Difficulty-Aware Joint Search for Optimizing Code Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04336)
*Jingzhi Gong,Jie M. Zhang,Gunel Jahangirova,Dong Huang,Mohammad Reza Mousavi,Mark Harman*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: COMPAS jointly optimizes model selection, prompts, and decoding settings for code generation, using difficulty-aware routing to learn quality-cost Pareto fronts. It achieves 52.8% pass@1 on LiveCodeBench (vs. 45.9% baseline) at $4.92 cost (vs. $36.57), and 76.0% on SWE-bench (vs. 70.0%).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing optimization methods for LLM code generation tune only subsets of choices (model, prompt, decoding settings) in isolation or use a single fixed configuration for all tasks. The joint, group-specific interactions among these three factors remain unexplored, limiting both quality and cost efficiency.

Method: COMPAS is a difficulty-aware optimization method that first learns group-specific quality-cost fronts through low-cost model selection and joint prompt-decoding search. It then routes each test task online to its matching Pareto front without further search, exploiting observed interactions: prompts and decoding settings interact, tuning effects vary by model, and optimal configurations differ by task difficulty.

Result: Under matched search budget on LiveCodeBench, COMPAS improves pass@1 from 45.9% (best baseline) to 52.8% while reducing cost from $36.57 to $4.92. On SWE-bench repository-level code generation, COMPAS resolves 76.0% of tasks vs. 70.0% for the best baseline.

Conclusion: Joint optimization over models, prompts, and decoding settings with difficulty-aware routing significantly outperforms partial or global tuning approaches, achieving both higher accuracy and lower cost. The method also transfers effectively from function-level to repository-level code generation.

Abstract: Code generation systems make each LLM call with a model, a prompt, and decoding settings. However, existing optimization methods usually tune only part of these choices or use one fixed configuration for all tasks: global optimizers search one configuration for all tasks, routers choose only a model, and prompt optimizers keep the model and decoding settings fixed. This leaves their joint, group-specific interactions unclear. We therefore examine how these choices interact and observe that prompts and decoding settings interact, tuning effects vary by model, and the best configuration varies by task difficulty. Guided by these observations, we introduce COMPAS (Code-generation Optimization over Models, Prompts, And Decoding Settings), a difficulty-aware method that learns group-specific quality-cost fronts through low-cost model selection and joint prompt-decoding search, then routes each test task to its matching front online without further search. Under a matched search budget on LiveCodeBench, COMPAS improves pass@1 from 45.9% for the best baseline to 52.8% while reducing cost from $36.57 to $4.92. This also transfers to repository-level code generation on SWE-bench, resolving 76.0% of tasks versus 70.0% for the best baseline. Code and the reproducibility artifact are available at https://github.com/gjz78910/COMPAS.

</details>


### [103] [ExeCRE: Execution-Consistency Guided Reliability Estimation for Self-Correcting Code Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04439)
*Yiru Dong,Richong Zhang,Fanshuang Kong,Si Chen*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: ExeCRE estimates the reliability of LLM-generated code by statistically analyzing execution output consistency across many random inputs, using the Dawid-Skene model to infer latent reliability, thereby reducing misleading feedback in self-correction pipelines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Self-correction pipelines for code generation rely on supervision signals (e.g., test cases, LLM feedback) whose reliability is often unknown, leading to misleading feedback, unnecessary revisions, and incorrect final answers. A principled method is needed to assess code reliability before using it in correction loops.

Method: ExeCRE collects execution outputs from generated code over a large set of randomly generated inputs, projects these outputs into consistency signals (agreement/disagreement patterns), and applies the Dawid-Skene probabilistic model to infer latent code reliability from the observed consistency structure. This reliability estimate is then integrated into self-correction pipelines to filter or weigh feedback.

Result: On LiveCodeBench with GPT-5.2, ExeCRE reduces misleading feedback on already-correct code from 113.2 (representative baseline) to 14.0 cases on average. The method consistently improves both effectiveness and stability of self-correction, and similar benefits are observed when applied to code-based mathematical reasoning.

Conclusion: ExeCRE demonstrates that execution-consistency-based reliability estimation enables more trustworthy use of generated code in execution-based pipelines, mitigating the problem of unreliable supervision signals in self-correction.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have made notable progress in code generation, but they still struggle on challenging tasks that require sophisticated algorithms or complex implementations. Recent methods increasingly use code execution as feedback, especially in self-correction pipelines that construct verification signals from generated code. However, these pipelines often depend on supervision signals whose reliability is unknown, which can introduce misleading feedback, unnecessary revisions, and incorrect final answers. To address this issue, we propose ExeCRE, an Execution-Consistency guided code Reliability Estimation framework. Instead of judging candidate code by tests or LLM feedback, ExeCRE estimates code reliability by statistically analyzing consistency patterns in execution outputs over a large number of randomly generated inputs. It collects execution outputs over generated inputs, projects them into consistency signals, and applies the Dawid-Skene model to infer latent code reliability. We integrate ExeCRE into self-correction for code generation. Experiments show that ExeCRE consistently improves both effectiveness and stability, while substantially reducing misleading correction signals. Under GPT-5.2 on LiveCodeBench, the average number of misleading feedback cases on already correct code drops from 113.2 with a representative self-correction baseline to 14.0 with ExeCRE. As an additional study, we apply the same reliability estimation strategy to code-based mathematical reasoning and observe similar benefits. These results suggest that ExeCRE enables more reliable use of generated code in execution-based pipelines.

</details>


### [104] [AdaptAgent: A Multi-agent, Domain-Guided Reasoning Framework for Code Adaptation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04459)
*Xiaokai Rong,Hridya Dhulipala,Aashish Yadavally,Tien N. Nguyen*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: AdaptAgent is a multi-agent framework that decomposes code adaptation—integrating external snippets into existing repositories—into specialized agents (Intent Summarizer, Policy Agent, Domain Planner, Context Miner, Code Adapter, and Verifier) that collaborate through typed artifacts, outperforming baselines in semantic correctness on real-world data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Integrating LLM-generated code or online code snippets into existing projects is a manual, error-prone process that requires more than simple copy-paste; it demands context-aware patches at specific repository locations. Existing single-shot prompting approaches lack the structured reasoning needed for robust adaptation.

Method: AdaptAgent employs a multi-agent architecture with domain-guided reasoning. The Intent Summarizer extracts goals from Q&A; the Policy Agent derives policies from six adaptation categories; the Domain Planner produces self-ordered plans; the Context Miner extracts sibling-method semantics; and the Code Adapter generates minimal unified diffs, iteratively refined by a compiler-based Verifier. Agents communicate through typed artifacts rather than raw text.

Result: On a real-world dataset, AdaptAgent outperforms strong baselines in semantic correctness and produces patches that mirror actual developer adaptation patterns. Ablation confirms each agent's necessity, with planning critical for code-hardening and exception-handling, and intent summarization essential for logic customization.

Conclusion: A structured, multi-agent decomposition with domain-specific policies and iterative compiler-driven refinement significantly improves the quality and correctness of code adaptation compared to monolithic prompting approaches.

Abstract: Developers often need to adapt into their projects the code generated from LLMs or code snippets from online forums. However, integrating them into an existing repository remains challenging in a manual process. A successful integration typically requires more than copying code as a user must produce correct adapting changes at a designated location in the target repository. We formalize this as the code adaptation problem: given a snippet, functional intent, a target repository, and an adaptation location, generate a patch that adapts the snippet into the repository. We present AdaptAgent, a multi-agent, domain-guided reasoning framework for code adaptation. Rather than relying on single-shot prompting, AdaptAgent decomposes adaptation into specialized agents that communicate via typed artifacts: an Intent Summarizer extracts adaptation goals from Q&A text; a Policy Agent derives domain policies from six adaptation categories; a Domain Planner generates a self-ordered plan; a Context Miner distills sibling-method semantics from the target codebase; and a Code Adapter realizes the plan as a minimal unified diff, iteratively refined using a compiler-based Verifier. This division of labor enables robust, policy-aligned adaptations and supports adapting code snippets into a project. On a real-world dataset, AdaptAgent outperforms strong baselines in semantic correctness and produces patches that mirror developers' actual adaptation patterns. Our ablation study shows each agent's necessity, especially planning for code-hardening and exception-handling, and intent for logic customization.

</details>


### [105] [Energy Efficient AI-Enabled Wireless Sensor Networks for Mission Critical Environments: A Systematic Review across Smart Grid, AI, and Urban Infrastructure Applications](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04499)
*Alexandros Gazis,Valeri Mladenov,Kleanthi SantamourI,Stylianos Pappas*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: This systematic review (2023–2026) analyzes 50 DOI-indexed studies on AI-enabled energy-efficient wireless sensor networks for mission-critical applications, finding that AI improves energy behavior through routing, edge AI, reinforcement learning, and metaheuristics, but concludes that energy efficiency must be co-optimized with security, latency, and reliability in lightweight, explainable, field-tested architectures.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Mission-critical environments (power electronics, urban infrastructure) demand WSNs with continuous monitoring, autonomous operation, reliable communication, and rapid decision-making. Traditional approaches treat energy efficiency in isolation, but real-world deployments reveal intertwined requirements across energy, security, latency, and reliability that necessitate an integrated, AI-driven solution.

Method: Systematic review of 50 DOI-indexed studies published between 2023 and 2026, selected via defined inclusion criteria. Eligible studies underwent qualitative thematic coding and comparative analysis. Additional references provided historical/methodological/technical context but were excluded from the core review corpus.

Result: AI improves WSN energy behavior via six key techniques: (1) routing and clustering optimization, (2) edge AI processing, (3) reinforcement learning, (4) fuzzy logic, (5) metaheuristic optimization, and (6) AI-based security. Critically, energy efficiency cannot be decoupled from security, latency, and reliability in mission-critical systems.

Conclusion: Future research should abandon isolated protocol optimization and instead pursue lightweight, explainable, secure, and field-validated AI-driven WSN architectures designed for real operational environments where energy, security, latency, and reliability are jointly addressed.

Abstract: Advanced wireless sensor networks powered by artificial intelligence are increasingly required for applications demanding continuous monitoring, autonomous operation, reliable communication, and fast decision support. This systematic review examines recent work from 2023 to 2026 on energy-efficient, AI-enabled wireless sensor networks (WSNs) in mission-critical environments, with particular focus on power electronics, and urban infrastructure systems. The authors synthesise a corpus of 50 DOI indexed studies satisfying inclusion criteria that received qualitative thematic coding and comparative analysis. Other references were only cited to provide historical, methodological, or technical context and were not included in the systematic review corpus. As such, our results show that AI can improve WSN energy behaviour through routing and clustering, edge AI, reinforcement learning, fuzzy logic, metaheuristic optimisation, and AI-based security. At the same time, energy efficiency cannot be treated as an isolated performance target. In mission-critical systems, security, latency, and reliability are closely interlinked requirements. The review concludes that future work should move away from optimising protocols in isolation, and instead focus on building lightweight, explainable, secure, and field-tested AI-driven WSN architectures suited to real operational environments.

</details>


### [106] [The Order Is the Guarantee: Verifier-Budgeted Code Deletion with Static-First Learned Proposals](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04611)
*Ruitong Li,Binjie Guo,Aisheng Mo,Guowei Su,Han Wang,Jie Li,Ru Zhang*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: DELSCOUT frames redundant-code removal as a budgeted proposal-scheduling problem, where candidate ordering—not model confidence—is the key control surface. Two schedules (deterministic shortest-first plus learned, vs. static-prefix-first) improve verified-deletion coverage by 9.5% relative in-domain while maintaining verifier-call efficiency, with an auditable division of labor between models, ordering, and execution.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Frontier coding models excel at generating code but lack mechanisms for removing redundant or obsolete logic. "Vibe coding" produces additive changes where guards, branches, and fallbacks accumulate. The paper addresses the inverse problem: how an AI system should delete code when execution-verification capacity (test suite runs) is finite and costly.

Method: The problem is formalized as proposal scheduling: a ranker orders single-statement deletion candidates, an execution suite accepts the first candidate that passes all tests, and a budget B limits how many candidates can be tested. Candidate order is identified as the deployable control surface. DELSCOUT provides two schedules: (1) with in-domain validation, a five-slot budget allocates three slots to deterministic shortest-first candidates and two to complementary learned candidates; (2) without validation, the complete static prefix is evaluated first, with learned candidates appended afterward, making coverage non-decreasing by construction. Experiments span nine MBPP replications using 0.5B, 0.6B, and 8B rankers.

Result: The hybrid schedule (three static + two learned slots) raises verified-deletion coverage by 9.5% relative (+6.7 accepted tasks) while consuming slightly fewer verifier calls than the matched static baseline. Under distribution shift without validation, the static-prefix-first schedule guarantees non-decreasing coverage and character reduction, at a measured 4.8–62.5% increase in verifier calls. MBPP+ erases the in-domain advantage, demonstrating that scheduling governs search while the test suite alone defines behavioral preservation.

Conclusion: The work establishes an auditable division of labor: models widen the search for removable code, ordering bounds the damage a mis-ranked proposal can do, and execution (test suites) retains final authority over every committed deletion. Scheduling rather than confidence-based gating is the principled control mechanism for safe, budgeted code removal.

Abstract: Frontier coding models now match or exceed strong human reference points on programming benchmarks, yet benchmark success does not imply maintainable software. Prompt-driven "vibe coding" is additive: new branches, guards, and fallbacks accumulate faster than obsolete logic is removed. We study the inverse problem-how an Al system should remove code when execution-verification capacity is finite. We formulate redundant-code reduction as proposal scheduling: a ranker orders single-statement deletion candidates, an execution suite accepts the first candidate that passes, and a budget bounds how many candidates may be tested. Our central observation is that candidate order, not model confidence, is the control surface a deployment can reason about. DELSCOUT instantiates two schedules. Given representative target-domain validation, a five-slot budget spends three slots on deterministic shortest-first candidates and two on complementary learned candidates; across nine MBPP replications with 0.5B, 0.6B, and 8B rankers this raises verified-deletion coverage by 9.5% relative (+6.7 accepted tasks) while consuming slightly fewer verifier calls than the matched static baseline. Without such validation the same rankers can lose coverage under shift, so we instead evaluate the complete static prefix first and append learned candidates only afterwards; for a deterministic verifier this makes coverage and character reduction non-decreasing by construction, at a measured 4.8-62.5% increase in verifier calls. MBPP+ then erases the in-domain advantage, showing that scheduling governs search while the test suite alone governs what "preserving behavior" means. The result is an auditable division of labor: models widen the search for removable code, order bounds the damage a mis-ranked proposal can do, and execution retains authority over every committed deletion.

</details>


### [107] [An Exploratory Study of Agent Plans for Agentic AI Coding Tools in Open-Source Software](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04661)
*Muhammad Auwal Abubakar,Seyedmoein Mohsenimofidi,Jai Lal Lulla,Jie M. Zhang,Christoph Treude,Sebastian Baltes,Matthias Galster*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: An exploratory study of Agent Plans in open-source repositories finds them to be rare but highly concentrated, task-oriented artifacts that guide AI coding agents through implementation steps, file references, and testing information across various software engineering activities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While prior work has studied repository-level context files like AGENTS.md for project-level instructions, little is known about more task-oriented artifacts such as Agent Plans. The authors aim to characterize how these plan files are preserved, what development activities they support, and what execution guidance they provide.

Method: The authors screened 36,710 GitHub repositories belonging to engineered software projects and identified 85 Markdown plan files from 10 repositories. They then conducted a qualitative analysis to categorize the types of software engineering work supported and the forms of task-oriented execution guidance provided.

Result: Agent Plans were found in only 10 of 36,710 repositories, indicating high concentration. The plans supported diverse activities: maintenance, design, construction, quality-related work, and process support. Execution guidance most commonly took the form of implementation steps, concrete file/location references, and testing/validation information.

Conclusion: Repository-preserved Agent Plans under tool-specific directories represent a narrow but informative artifact class for studying task intent and execution guidance in human-agent collaborative workflows.

Abstract: Repository-level configuration artifacts allow developers to provide guidance for agentic AI coding tools, such as Claude Code, Gemini, etc. Although prior research has examined repository-shared context files that capture project-level instructions and conventions (e.g., AGENTS.md files), little is known about more task-oriented artifacts such as Agent Plans. We present an exploratory study of Agent Plans in open-source software repositories, examining how plan files are preserved, which development activities they support, and what information they provide to guide agent execution. We screened 36,710 GitHub repositories belonging to engineered software projects and identified 85 Markdown plan files from 10 repositories. Within this highly concentrated corpus, Agent Plans supported several kinds of software engineering work, including maintenance, design, construction, quality-related work, and process support. They also provided task-oriented execution guidance, most commonly through implementation steps, concrete files and locations, and testing and validation information. Overall, repository-preserved Agent Plans under these tool-specific directories appear to be a narrow but informative artifact for studying task intent and execution guidance in human-agent workflows.

</details>


### [108] [Active-SWE: Benchmarking Coding Agents for Proactive Bug Fixing without Issue Reports](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04682)
*Haobin Li,Ping Deng,Weizhong Qian,Liang Jiang,Zhenyu Huang,Mouxing Yang,Xi Peng*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: Active-SWE is a new benchmark evaluating LLM-based coding agents on proactive bug discovery and fixing across 1,663 tasks in 8 languages, without relying on pre-written issue reports. Current agents perform poorly on these tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing SWE benchmarks unrealistically assume high-quality, detailed issue reports are always available. In practice, such reports are costly and difficult to obtain. There is a need to evaluate coding agents on proactively discovering and fixing bugs without report guidance, and to assess their capability in multi-bug and potential-bug scenarios.

Method: The authors construct Active-SWE, a benchmark with 1,663 tasks spanning six bug categories and eight programming languages. They introduce a difficulty-aware task formulation pipeline and a dual-track evaluation framework. The benchmark shifts evaluation from reactive single-bug fixing to proactive discovery and fixing of multiple bugs, including potential (unrecorded) bugs.

Result: Extensive experiments show that most state-of-the-art coding agents struggle significantly with proactive bug-fixing: they exhibit limited performance in locating and resolving recorded bugs, handling multiple-bug scenarios, and discovering valid potential bugs.

Conclusion: Proactive bug fixing represents a major open challenge for current LLM-based coding agents. Active-SWE provides a more realistic and rigorous evaluation framework that highlights these limitations and can guide future research.

Abstract: Coding agents powered by large language models (LLMs) are increasingly adopted in software engineering (SWE) scenarios, capable of fixing a specific bug in large-scale codebase. However, existing SWE benchmarks typically assume that high-quality issue reports with detailed information are always available, which is easily violated in practice due to the complexity of report acquisition and curation. To address this, we introduce Active-SWE, a benchmark for evaluating coding agents on proactively discovering and fixing multiple bugs without report guidance, covering 1,663 tasks across six bug categories and eight languages. Beyond shifting the focus from existing reactive bug fixing to proactive bug fixing, Active-SWE enables a more in-depth evaluation by expanding the scope from fixing a specific recorded bug to multiple-bug fixing and potential bug discovery scenarios. To construct Active-SWE, we propose a novel difficulty-aware task formulation pipeline with a dual-track evaluation framework, facilitating comprehensive evaluation of proactive bug-fixing capability. Extensive experiments reveal that most state-of-the-art coding agents struggle with proactive bug-fixing tasks, demonstrating limited performance in locating and resolving recorded bugs, handling multiple bug fixing scenarios, and discovering valid potential bugs.

</details>


### [109] [What We Observe as LLM Behavior Can Be a Side-effect of Inference Backend](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04714)
*Shahed Masoudian,Passant Shafaei,Monorama Swain,Markus Schedl*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: Benchmark scores are not backend-agnostic: the choice of inference framework (HuggingFace, vLLM, Ollama, etc.) significantly and structurally alters model performance, accounting for ~39% of out-of-the-box variability, even under deterministic decoding. Authors recommend full disclosure of backend, version, and generation configuration.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Inference frameworks (backends) used to generate benchmark scores are almost never disclosed in publications, treated as interchangeable black boxes. The authors challenge this assumption by systematically quantifying how much backend choice influences model output and benchmark results.

Method: A fully-crossed experimental design: 3 instruction-tuned models × 5 inference frameworks (HuggingFace, vLLM, Ollama, and two others) × 6 benchmarks (spanning factual and social-bias tasks) × 4 generation modes (including greedy decoding to eliminate sampling noise). Variance decomposition is used to partition score variability into backend effects, sampling noise, and default hyperparameter differences.

Result: Backend choice is a non-negligible, structural, and strongly model-dependent factor. Approximately 39% of out-of-the-box variability stems from the backend itself, with the remainder from sampling noise and default parameter discrepancies. Effects are more pronounced on factual benchmarks than on social-bias benchmarks. Even under greedy, noise-free decoding, changing backends significantly alters performance.

Conclusion: Benchmark scores are not backend-agnostic. The field should mandate disclosure of backend, version, and complete generation configuration. Deterministic decoding should be used for cross-backend comparisons to eliminate avoidable sources of variability.

Abstract: Benchmark scores are reported as properties of a model, yet the inference framework used to produce them, such as HuggingFace, vLLM, or Ollama, are considered non-influential and their names and versions are almost never disclosed. In this work we investigate how much this choice can influence the model output. In a fully-crossed study (three instruction-tuned models x five inference frameworks x six benchmarks x four generation modes) we investigate how different tools (wrappers/backend) influence benchmark scores and how their score changes is influenced by generation hyper-parameters. We find backend to be a non-negligible factor where even under greedy, sampling-noise-free decoding, changing the backend can significantly alter models performance and this effect is structural and strongly model-dependent. Decomposing the variance according to generation mode reveal that considerable portion of the variability (roughly 39\%) a practitioner sees out-of-the-box can stem from the backend, while the remaining stems from sampling noise and each framework's default generation parameters, both of which are avoidable by disclosing and matching the generation configuration. These divergences are more pronounced on factual than on social-bias benchmarks. Overall, benchmark numbers are not backend-agnostic therefore, we recommend disclosing the backend, its version, and the full generation configuration, also using deterministic decoding for cross-backend comparison.

</details>


### [110] [RepoProbe: Benchmarking Architecture-Aware Repository Comprehension with Checklists](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04783)
*Yuexi Yang,Alyssa Wu,Ji Luo,Richeng Xuan,Zhichao Hu,Yuhong Liu,Zhen Qin*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: RepoProbe introduces a benchmark for repository-level code understanding using GitHub Discussions (architectural Q&A) instead of GitHub Issues (bug reports). It employs a Checklist-Based Verification Protocol for objective, atomic-fact evaluation, revealing that SOTA LLMs exhibit high clarity but low technical correctness, suffer from "edit bias" (premature code generation over architectural analysis), and that the protocol improves evaluation reliability over scalar scoring.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing benchmarks for repository-scale LLM evaluation rely on GitHub Issues, which enable models to bypass genuine understanding through pattern matching on error logs. This under-measures "Edit Bias" — the tendency to prematurely generate code rather than analyze architecture. Additionally, LLM-as-a-Judge scalar scoring suffers from high variance and low interpretability, necessitating a more rigorous evaluation paradigm.

Method: The authors introduce RepoProbe, a benchmark built from GitHub Discussions that poses open-ended architectural inquiries. For evaluation, they propose a Checklist-Based Verification Protocol that decomposes LLM answers into atomic, verifiable facts, enabling objective binary verification instead of subjective scalar ratings.

Result: Evaluation of SOTA LLMs reveals: (1) a persistent gap between high clarity/fluency and evidence-grounded technical correctness; (2) quantitative confirmation of edit bias, where models prioritize code generation over architectural analysis; (3) the verification protocol significantly improves evaluation reliability compared to traditional scalar scoring.

Conclusion: RepoProbe and its Checklist-Based Verification Protocol provide a more reliable, interpretable, and rigorous framework for evaluating repository-level code understanding. The findings highlight that current LLMs, despite fluent outputs, lack genuine architectural comprehension and are prone to edit bias, underscoring the need for benchmarks that emphasize understanding over generation.

Abstract: The integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) into software engineering has shifted the focus from function-level generation to repository-scale assistance. However, existing benchmarks largely rely on bug reports from GitHub Issues, which often allow models to bypass genuine understanding via pattern matching on error logs. This misalignment under-measures Edit Bias, which refers to premature generation, where models prematurely propose code modifications instead of understanding the existing repository architecture. Furthermore, current LLM-as-a-Judge scalar scoring suffers from high variance and low interpretability. This work introduces RepoProbe, a novel benchmark for evaluating repository-level code understanding through open-ended Q&A using GitHub Discussions, which focuses on open-ended architectural inquiries rather than defect reporting. To ensure rigorous evaluation, we propose a Checklist-Based Verification Protocol that decomposes answers into atomic, verifiable facts, thereby replacing subjective ratings with objective verification. Our evaluation of state-of-the-art (SOTA) LLMs reveals a persistent gap between high clarity and evidencegrounded technical correctness. It also quantitatively confirms the prevalence of edit bias, in which models prioritize code generation instead of architectural analysis. Finally, we demonstrate that our verification protocol significantly improves evaluation reliability compared to traditional evaluations with scalar scoring.

</details>


### [111] [Scrouting: Cost-Aware Routing of Coding Agents by Scouting the Repository First](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04804)
*Ishaan Bhola,Adithyan Krishnan,Mukunda NS*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: SuperScout introduces a two-stage approach to repository-level code repair: a 7B "searcher" model scouts the repository, produces verified claims, and its hidden states feed a router that dispatches tasks to frontier fixers. On SWE-bench Pro, it matches the best single model's solve rate at ~5x lower cost per solve, but ablation shows the handoff (not the router) drives results, redistributing solving ability across cheaper fixers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Frontier LLMs can solve repository-level software issues, but each inference attempt is expensive. Existing model routers select a fixer based solely on issue text, ignoring repository structure. The authors aim to reduce cost while maintaining solve rates by first "scouting" the repository to inform both routing and repair.

Method: SuperScout uses a 7B "searcher" model that explores the repository and produces a structured handoff with reproduction claims, which are sandbox-verified to strip false claims. The searcher's hidden states, combined with task text, feed a resume-based router that dispatches to one of four frontier fixers. Adding a new fixer requires no retraining. Evaluated on SWE-bench Pro's Python slice (266 tasks) under the official capped budget tier, with ablations (no-router, cheapest fixer only) and a paired calibration study (N=99).

Result: SuperScout solves 159/266 tasks vs. 158/266 for the best single model, matching solve rate at ~1/5 the cost per solve. It sits above the random traffic-splitting baseline. However, the no-router ablation (always using the cheapest fixer with the handoff) ties the routed system, indicating the handoff drives gains rather than routing. The paired calibration study (N=99) suggests the handoff redistributes solving ability: lifting three cheaper fixers while slightly hurting the strongest (directional only). Searcher hidden states improve cost routing on calibration labels, while the handoff text alone does not. Searcher compute adds <$0.005 GPU time per task.

Conclusion: The handoff mechanism, not the router, is the primary contributor to SuperScout's cost-efficiency gains, redistributing solving ability toward cheaper models. The searcher's hidden states show promise for cost-aware routing, but the current routing contribution is minimal. Future work may need to better leverage routing signals.

Abstract: Frontier language models can resolve repository-level software issues, but each attempt is expensive, and existing routers select a model from the issue text alone. We present SuperScout, which routes after scouting the repository: a 7B searcher, SuperScout-7B, first explores the repository and produces a structured handoff whose reproduction claims are sandbox-verified, with false claims stripped before delivery. The searcher's hidden states, together with the task text, then feed a resume-based router that dispatches the task to one of four frontier fixers. Adding a new fixer requires no retraining. On the full Python slice of SWE-bench Pro (266 tasks) under the benchmark's official capped budget tier, SuperScout matches the best single model's solve rate (159 of 266 for SuperScout, 158 for the best model) at about a fifth of the total cost per solve, and the reported configuration sits above the random traffic-splitting baseline. A no-router ablation, always the cheapest fixer with the handoff, ties the routed system on this benchmark, so the handoff rather than the routing decision carries the result. A paired calibration study points to the mechanism: the handoff appears to redistribute rather than add solving ability, lifting the three cheaper fixers while slightly hurting the strongest, though at $N=99$ the per-fixer effects are directional only; the searcher's hidden states improve cost routing on the calibration labels while the handoff's own text does not. The searcher's compute adds less than half a cent of GPU time per task.

</details>


### [112] [A Chain Is Only as Strong as Its Weakest Link: A Scoping Review of System Integration Audits in AI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04921)
*Leah Davis,Dominic Martin,AJung Moon*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: A scoping review of 4,259 documents (n=58 included) reveals that system integration in AI auditing is an emerging but fragmented field. The paper identifies three integration sites (inter-component, system-environment, multi-system), four audit functions (risk exploration, risk determination, coordination, procedural regularity), and three integration-specific qualities (compatibility, completeness, oversight), while highlighting significant gaps in measures and resource access.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Model-centric AI audits are insufficient because they fail to capture risks that emerge from interactions between AI system components and their deployment environments. While system integration has long been a cornerstone of software auditing in safety-critical fields like aerospace, its role in AI auditing remains underexplored. The authors aim to map this gap systematically.

Method: A scoping review was conducted, scanning 4,259 documents and ultimately including 58 papers that treat system integration as a core tenet of AI evaluation. Reflexive thematic analysis was applied to examine the elements, actors, enablers, and constraints characterizing these audits.

Result: The corpus represents an emerging yet fragmented form of AI auditing: (1) few existing measures specifically target integration-specific risks; (2) large gaps remain in meeting traditional audit expectations; (3) access to information and resources significantly influences audit design. Three integration sites were identified—inter-component, system-environment, and multi-system—each serving four functions: risk exploration, risk determination, coordination, and procedural regularity. Three integration-specific qualities were distinguished: compatibility, completeness, and oversight.

Conclusion: The AI community should prioritize system integration as a core strategy for addressing AI risk and develop audit practices that can capture failures across components, environments, and systems—failures that component-level evaluation cannot reach.

Abstract: As AI systems become increasingly integrated into diverse interfaces and applications, model-centric audits are insufficient to address risks arising from interactions among system components and deployment environments. System integration has long been central to software audits in safety-critical domains such as aerospace. However, its role in AI auditing remains underexplored. Scanning through 4,259 documents, we present a scoping review of AI audits that treat system integration as a core tenet of evaluation (n = 58). Using reflexive thematic analysis, we analyze their elements, actors, enablers, and constraints. We find that the corpus represents an emerging yet still fragmented form of AI auditing: few existing measures target integration-specific risks; large gaps remain in meeting traditional audit expectations; and access to necessary information and resources significantly influences audit design. Nonetheless, integration can be categorized across three sites (inter-component, system-environment, and multi-system), each serving the functions of risk exploration, risk determination, coordination, and procedural regularity. Deviating from other types of evaluations, these audits assess qualities specific to system integration, including compatibility, completeness, and oversight. This review calls on the AI community to prioritize system integration as a core strategy for addressing AI risk, and to develop audit practices capable of capturing failures across components, environments, and systems beyond the reach of component-level evaluation.

</details>


### [113] [SciCode-Verified: How Benchmark Defects Underestimated the Scientific-Coding Ability of Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04975)
*Sihan Hu,Lyuhan Huang,Youjin Deng,Kun Chen*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: SciCode, a benchmark for evaluating language models' scientific coding abilities, has shown stagnating scores. An expert audit found 263 defects across 91% of its problems, mostly causing correct solutions to be wrongly rejected. After correction (SciCode-Verified), re-evaluation showed frontier models' subproblem accuracy jumping from 45–60% to 84–98%, revealing that the bottleneck was benchmark quality, not model capability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Scores on the SciCode benchmark have plateaued, with top 2026 models clustering around 60% subproblem accuracy and successors failing to improve. The authors suspected these stagnating scores were not due to genuine limits in model scientific coding ability, but rather defects in the benchmark itself that suppressed true performance.

Method: A per-problem, domain-expert audit was conducted on all 65 test problems, identifying and categorizing 263 defects. Defects included non-reproducible gold answers, overly tight tolerances, and self-contradictory specifications. 78% of score-suppressing defects required specialized physics or mathematics knowledge to detect. Every confirmable defect was corrected, with each change justified and independently verified by a second domain expert. Twelve frontier model snapshots were then re-evaluated on the corrected SciCode-Verified benchmark.

Result: The audit uncovered 263 total defects, with 192 score-suppressing defects across 91% of main problems. After correction, subproblem accuracy rose from 45–60% to 84–98%, and main-problem accuracy from 9–27% to 69–92%. This demonstrates that state-of-the-art models are far more proficient in scientific coding than previously measured, and the true bottleneck was evaluation instrument quality.

Conclusion: The stagnation in SciCode scores was attributable to benchmark defects, not model limitations. SciCode-Verified is released with a complete audit trail as the corrected public standard, providing a more accurate measure of language models' scientific coding capabilities.

Abstract: SciCode is the standard measure of the scientific-coding ability of language models: research-level problems that demand both frontier scientific theory and its implementation as working numerical code. It is a component of the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index and a standing evaluation in government and national-laboratory suites. Yet its scores have recently plateaued: the strongest 2026 models cluster tightly around 60\% subproblem accuracy, and a successor model ties its predecessor. We trace this stagnation to defects in the benchmark itself. A per-problem, domain-expert audit of all 65 test problems uncovers 263 defects; 192 of them, spread across 91\% of the main problems, cause correct, instruction-following solutions to be wrongly rejected---through non-reproducible gold answers, over-tight tolerances, or self-contradictory specifications. Critically, 78\% of these score-suppressing defects require specialized physics or mathematics knowledge to detect, not mere clerical proofreading. We corrected every confirmable defect to produce SciCode-Verified. The corrections add only the specifications a well-posed problem requires, repair grading, and tighten the tests that were too lenient; every change is recorded with its justification and independently re-checked by a second domain expert. We re-evaluate twelve frontier model snapshots on the corrected benchmark and find a substantial recovery: subproblem accuracy rises from 45--60\% to 84--98\%, and main-problem accuracy from 9--27\% to 69--92\%. State-of-the-art models are far more proficient in scientific coding than SciCode has suggested---the bottleneck was not model capability, but the quality of the evaluation instrument. We release SciCode-Verified with its complete audit trail as the corrected public standard.

</details>


### [114] [RepairFormer: Automated Repair of Structured Inputs Using Transformers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05060)
*Ovi Paul,Tom J King,Ali Shokri*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: RepairFormer is a transformer-based framework that formulates structured input repair as a supervised sequence generation task, using format tags, oracle validation, and boundary-localized repair to fix malformed files (JSON, DOT, OBJ, etc.) while preserving original content, achieving 88% repair and 94% recovery rates with 5x faster runtime than prior methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Structured input files (JSON, DOT, OBJ, INI, S-expressions, TinyC) are pervasive in software systems, but even minor corruptions cause parsers to reject otherwise useful data. Existing repair techniques can produce structurally valid inputs but often rely on deletion or repeated search, leading to loss of original content and semantic incorrectness. There is a need for a repair method that both restores structural validity and preserves as much original content as possible.

Method: RepairFormer casts structured input repair as a supervised sequence generation task using a transformer architecture. Key innovations include: (1) format tags to encode the target grammar/syntax, (2) oracle validation during training to ensure generated outputs are syntactically correct, and (3) a boundary-localized repair workflow that focuses generation on the detected fault region, reducing input size and enabling repair of longer files.

Result: RepairFormer achieves 88% repair rate and 94% recovery rate overall, with strongest content preservation when repairs succeed. On a benchmark dataset, it achieves 97.57% repair and 94.29% recovery while running 5x faster than the state-of-the-art.

Conclusion: Transformer-based sequence generation with boundary-localized repair is an effective approach for structured input repair, outperforming existing methods in both repair accuracy and runtime efficiency while better preserving original content.

Abstract: Structured input files such as JSON, DOT, OBJ, INI, S-expression, and TinyC are widely used in software systems, but small corruptions can cause parsers to reject otherwise useful data. Repairing such inputs is important because malformed configuration, program, and data files can interrupt testing, analysis, deployment, and downstream automation even when most of the original content remains intact. Existing repair techniques can produce structurally valid inputs, but they often rely on deletion or repeated search, which may lose original content and result in semantic incorrectness. This paper presents RepairFormer, a transformer-based framework for structured input repair. The approach formulates repair as a supervised sequence generation task and uses format tags, oracle validation, and boundary-localized repair to generate valid outputs while preserving content. The boundary workflow focuses generation on the detected fault region, reducing the input size, and supporting repair of longer files. In evaluation, RepairFormer achieves a 88% in repair and 94% in recovery, showing strongest content preservation when repairs are successful. Additional experiments on our benchmark shows RepairFormer repairs 97.57% and recovers 94.29% with 5x faster runtime compared to state of the art.

</details>


### [115] [Characterizing Visual Accessibility Issues in AI Developer Tools: An Empirical Study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05116)
*Sabrina Haque,Christoph Csallner*

Main category: cs.SE

TL;DR: A study analyzing 2,652 candidate issues/discussions across five AI developer tool ecosystems (GitHub Copilot, Cursor, Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, OpenCode) identified 600 visual accessibility reports. Three recurring barrier categories emerged: screen-reader/assistive-technology issues, visual presentation/contrast problems, and readability/scaling limitations. These concerns varied by ecosystem and interaction surface, shaped by both design and reporting/maintenance practices.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI-assisted developer tools increasingly use chat panels, terminal agents, generated diffs, and streaming output — interaction surfaces that may create visual accessibility barriers for blind, low-vision, and color-vision-deficient developers. However, little prior work has examined how such barriers manifest and are reported in public tool ecosystems.

Method: The authors collected 2,652 keyword-retrieved candidate issues and forum discussions from five ecosystems (GitHub Copilot in VS Code, Cursor, Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, OpenCode). A three-model ensemble classified reports, yielding 600 unanimously positive visual accessibility reports. Stratified manual sanity checks validated this conservative selection. Topic modeling and qualitative analysis identified barrier categories, and exploratory metadata analysis examined reporter activity, maintainer participation, and closure processes.

Result: Three recurring categories of visual accessibility barriers were identified: (1) screen-reader and assistive-technology barriers; (2) visual presentation, contrast, and differentiation problems; and (3) readability, scaling, and control limitations in AI-specific interfaces. The relative prominence of these concerns varied across ecosystems, reflecting differences in editor, terminal, chat, diff, and agent interaction surfaces. Metadata analysis revealed differences in reporter activity and, for GitHub-based ecosystems, maintainer participation and closure processes.

Conclusion: The accessibility record of AI developer tools is shaped by both interaction design choices and the reporting/maintenance practices of their surrounding ecosystems. Addressing these barriers requires attention to both the design of AI-specific interaction surfaces and the responsiveness of ecosystem maintenance workflows.

Abstract: AI-assisted developer tools increasingly mediate programming through chat panels, terminal agents, generated diffs, and streaming status output. These interaction surfaces may create visual accessibility barriers for blind, low-vision, and color-vision-deficient developers, yet little is known about how such barriers are reported in public tool ecosystems. We analyze issues and forum discussions from five AI developer tool ecosystems: GitHub Copilot in VS Code, Cursor, Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, and OpenCode. From 2,652 keyword-retrieved candidates, a three-model ensemble identified 600 unanimously positive visual accessibility reports. A stratified manual sanity check supported this conservative selection. Topic modeling and qualitative analysis identified three recurring categories: screen-reader and assistive-technology barriers; visual presentation, contrast, and differentiation problems; and readability, scaling, and control limitations in AI-specific interfaces. The relative prominence of these concerns varied across ecosystems and reflected differences in editor, terminal, chat, diff, and agent interaction surfaces. An exploratory metadata analysis further identified differences in reporter activity and, across the GitHub-based ecosystems, maintainer participation and closure processes. These findings show that the accessibility record of AI developer tools is shaped by both their interaction design and the reporting and maintenance practices of their surrounding ecosystems.

</details>
