Our work underscores the potential of integrating global coordination mechanisms into deep learning systems to advance robust, adaptive continual learning. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/RoozbehRazavi/NeuMoSync.

</details>


### [137] [Improving Auto-Design of Neural PDE Solvers with a Domain-Specific Language](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04384)
*Shengxin Kong,Liwen Xu,Jingwen Fu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ADSL-PDE introduces a structured intermediate representation (search state) between solver concepts and executable code, compiled deterministically to valid solvers. This reshapes the search space by eliminating invalid programs, enabling an evolutionary agent to propose, evaluate, and refine designs efficiently, achieving >52% improvement within ten iterations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In the unrestricted space of Python programs, valid neural PDE solvers are extremely sparse; most candidates are syntactically incorrect, semantically incompatible, or numerically unstable. Direct code generation via LLMs wastes search capacity on implementation failures rather than solver quality reasoning.

Method: ADSL-PDE defines a structured search state capturing functional decisions (architecture, physical constraints, objectives, sampling, optimization) while abstracting low-level implementation. A deterministic compiler maps each valid search state to executable solver code. An evolutionary agent then iteratively proposes, evaluates, and refines these search states using empirical feedback.

Result: Across multiple PDE benchmarks, ADSL-PDE improves both search efficiency and optimization stability, achieving over 52% improvement within the first ten evolution iterations.

Conclusion: Effective LLM-driven auto-design depends not merely on stronger reasoning but on a search representation that concentrates exploration on valid and consequential decisions. ADSL-PDE exemplifies this principle for neural PDE solver design.

Abstract: Neural PDE solver auto-design is fundamentally a search-space representation problem. In the space of unrestricted Python programs, valid solvers form an extremely sparse subset: most candidate programs are syntactically incorrect, semantically incompatible, or numerically unstable. Direct code generation therefore forces an LLM to spend most of its search capacity navigating implementation failures rather than reasoning about solver quality. ADSL-PDE addresses this challenge by introducing a structured search state between solver concepts and executable code. It represents the functional decisions that determine a neural PDE solver (architecture, physical constraints, objectives, sampling, and optimization) while abstracting away low-level implementation details. A deterministic compiler maps each valid search state to an executable solver. In effect, ADSL-PDE reshapes the search space: it removes large regions of invalid programs, increases the density of meaningful candidates, and preserves the compositional freedom needed to discover previously unseen designs. Solver evolution can thus operate over design decisions rather than code artifacts. Built on this representation, our evolutionary agent iteratively proposes, evaluates, and refines solver search states using empirical feedback. Across multiple PDE benchmarks, ADSL-PDE improves both search efficiency and optimization stability, achieving an improvement of more than 52% within the first ten evolution iterations. These results suggest a broader principle for LLM-driven auto-design: effective agents do not merely require stronger reasoning, but rather a search representation that concentrates exploration on valid and consequential decisions.

</details>


### [138] [Architectural Implications of Agentic AI Workflows](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04458)
*Jirong Yang,Peizhe Liu,Chaojie Zhang,Jovan Stojkovic*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Agentic AI workloads exhibit fragmented, heterogeneous execution patterns that create architectural mismatches with conventional uniform servers. The paper characterizes these patterns via production and controlled studies, then presents Agora, a prototype that dynamically optimizes CPU-GPU resource allocation, improves utilization, and preserves tail latency for agentic workflows.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Agentic AI is rapidly emerging in datacenters, but its architectural implications remain unexplored. Conventional uniform server designs are mismatched to the fragmented, bursty, and heterogeneous resource demands of agentic workflows, leading to stranded capacity, inefficient CPU provisioning, and degraded microarchitectural locality when multiplexing agents.

Method: The authors first develop a taxonomy of agentic workflows and conduct two studies: a production study at Microsoft Azure and a controlled study of open-source agentic frameworks. They characterize execution patterns (fragmentation, burstiness, model composition, tool diversity) and identify architectural mismatches. Based on these findings, they design Agora, a prototype that (1) dynamically harvests idle CPU cores for co-located throughput work while protecting agentic tail latency, (2) oversubscribes GPU memory with state prefetching to hide swap latency, (3) pools cores by role with affinity-aware scheduling, and (4) auto-tunes mechanisms to workload characteristics.

Result: Agentic execution is fragmented across CPU-GPU boundaries with the CPU on the critical path. Load is bursty (low baseline with sudden spikes), and model composition determines GPU utilization evenness. Tool and task diversity widens resource demand variability. Agora improves server utilization and throughput while preserving agent tail latency under these conditions.

Conclusion: Conventional uniform servers are architecturally mismatched for agentic AI. Agora demonstrates that dynamic resource harvesting, GPU memory oversubscription with prefetching, and role-based affinity scheduling can bridge this gap. The findings also point toward future server architectures purpose-built for agentic workloads.

Abstract: Agentic AI is emerging in datacenters, but its architectural implications remain unexplored. We organize agentic workflows in a taxonomy and present its first architectural characterization with a production study at Microsoft Azure and a controlled study of open-source frameworks. We show that agentic execution is fragmented and heterogeneous. Requests expand into a workflow of LLM inferences, tool invocations, and orchestration decisions that repeatedly cross the CPU-GPU boundary. Our taxonomy explains how this fragmentation turns into resource demand. As orchestration and tools run on the host, the CPU sits on the critical path. Execution structure sets the load over time, which stays low with sudden spikes. Model composition sets how evenly the workflow uses the GPUs. Diversity in tasks and tools widens this range even further. These characteristics expose architectural mismatches of conventional uniform servers. Fragmented execution strands CPU and GPU capacity despite bursty demand. Different software roles make homogeneous CPU provisioning inefficient. Finally, multiplexing many agents onto shared cores degrades microarchitectural locality. Guided by our findings, we derive implications for agentic servers and examine them through Agora, our prototype for commodity servers. Agora dynamically harvests idle CPU cores for co-located throughput work, while protecting agentic tail latency against tool spikes. It oversubscribes GPU memory by placing more agents on each GPU, prefetching the next agent's state to hide swap latency. To match the machine to the heterogeneous roles, Agora pools cores by role and applies affinity-aware scheduling to restore locality. It automatically tunes mechanisms to the workload. Agora improves utilization and server throughput while preserving agent tail latency. Our insights also identify key directions for future server architectures for agentic AI.

</details>


### [139] [CARGO-VL: Counterfactual Arbitration with Risk-Constrained Group Optimization for Vision-Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04509)
*De Jiang,Zhengyang Zhang,Kehong Yuan,Shaohua Ma*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CARGO-VL is a group-relative training framework that optimizes vision-language models across four matched evidence states (aligned, image-correct, text-correct, both-wrong) simultaneously, using transition rewards and primal-dual risk control to improve multimodal conflict handling and abstention.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing post-training objectives for vision-language systems score instances independently, failing to enforce coherent behavior when evidence sources change counterfactually. Models need to identify trustworthy sources and abstain when neither image nor text is adequate, but current pointwise training does not couple decisions across matched evidence variants.

Method: CARGO-VL bundles four evidence states (A/V/T/N: Aligned, Vision-correct, Text-correct, Neither) as a group. It optimizes condition-wise correctness jointly with transition rewards enforcing answer invariance, source equivariance, and answer-to-abstention switching. A primal-dual controller balances unsafe answers against excessive deferral. The authors also introduce XMC, a four-condition conflict training dataset, and evaluate on CMC-Bench and Modality-Bias benchmarks.

Result: Across multiple seeds, CARGO-VL improves conflict handling, unsupported-answer avoidance, and modality balance compared to pointwise baselines. Ablations show complementary benefits from relational transition signals and adaptive risk control.

Conclusion: Counterfactual consistency, enforced through group-relative training with transition rewards and adaptive risk control, is a practical and effective objective for reliable multimodal evidence arbitration in vision-language systems.

Abstract: Vision-language systems combine images with retrieved text, but these sources can disagree or jointly fail to support an answer. Reliable models must identify the trustworthy source and abstain when neither is adequate. Existing post-training objectives score instances independently and therefore do not enforce coherent behavior under counterfactual evidence changes. We introduce CARGO-VL, a group-relative framework that optimizes matched variants covering aligned, image-correct, text-correct, and both-wrong (A/V/T/N) evidence states as one bundle. Its objective couples condition-wise correctness with transition rewards for answer invariance, source equivariance, and answer-to-abstention switching, while a primal-dual controller balances unsafe answers against excessive deferral. We also contribute XMC (eXtended Modal Conflict), a four-condition conflict training resource, and evaluate transfer on CMC-Bench and Modality-Bias. Across multiple seeds, CARGO-VL improves conflict handling, unsupported-answer avoidance, and modality balance over pointwise baselines. Ablations identify complementary benefits from relational transition signals and adaptive risk control, supporting counterfactual consistency as a practical objective for reliable multimodal evidence arbitration.

</details>


### [140] [Leak-Resistant Unlearning: A New Benchmark for Evaluating Multi-Hop Reasoning Consistency and Recovery Robustness](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04519)
*Haoting Qian,Qingjie Zhang,Zhicong Huang,Cheng Hong,Han Qiu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces a novel benchmark for evaluating LLM unlearning that tests robustness across diverse multi-hop reasoning paths and recovery attacks, revealing that existing unlearning methods are vulnerable to knowledge leakage and recovery.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current unlearning benchmarks suffer from two key limitations: (1) they fail to account for knowledge leakage through diverse multi-hop reasoning paths, and (2) static evaluation cannot detect whether unlearned knowledge can be recovered via lightweight post-unlearning adaptation attacks. This motivates a more comprehensive, robustness-focused benchmark.

Method: The authors introduce a benchmark that systematically evaluates LLM unlearning methods across diverse multi-hop reasoning paths and recovery attacks. Experiments are conducted on 3 models, 6 unlearning methods, and 2 carefully curated datasets to assess forget quality, robustness, and model utility trade-offs.

Result: Existing unlearning methods are shown to be vulnerable to both multi-hop reasoning paths (which can induce knowledge leakage) and recovery attacks (which can partially recover supposedly unlearned knowledge).

Conclusion: LLM unlearning remains fragile; robust evaluation must account for multi-hop reasoning leakage and recovery attacks. There exists a trade-off among forget quality, robustness, and model utility that requires further exploration.

Abstract: Benchmarking machine unlearning methods is critical to understand whether sensitive knowledge is removed from large language models (LLMs) or not. Current unlearning benchmarks include mainly single-hop questions and a narrow set of multi-hop questions. Although effective, they still face two challenges. (1) Knowledge is not isolated, whereby diverse multi-hop reasoning paths can potentially induce knowledge leakage than normal queries. (2) Unlearning may be fragile: unlearned knowledge can be partially recovered through recovery attacks such as lightweight post-unlearning adaptation, making static evaluation insufficient. Therefore, in this paper, we introduce \unlearning as a novel benchmark to understand robust LLM knowledge removal across diverse reasoning paths and recovery attacks. We experiment with this benchmark on 3 models, 6 unlearning methods, and 2 carefully curated datasets. Results show that existing methods are vulnerable to multi-hop reasoning paths and recovery attacks. We further explore the trade-off among forget quality, robustness, and model utility for LLM unlearning.

</details>


### [141] [What Is a Skill Worth? Structure-Aware Shapley Valuation of Agent Skills](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04562)
*Tao Li,Junfeng Liu,Qinghua Zhao,Yifan Li,Lei Wang,Bo Shao,Xuejun Liu,Linjun Shou*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SkillSV introduces a structure-aware Shapley-value framework for assigning credit to internal units (rules, examples, scripts) of agent skills, accounting for dependencies, hierarchy, and prompt context costs. It uses paired deletion with length-neutral padding to separate content value from context cost, validated on four benchmarks for pruning and compression.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Agent skills — long, structured artifacts like rules, examples, scripts, and heuristics — are increasingly produced by automated feedback loops, but the internal contribution of each component remains opaque. Existing data or prompt-span valuation methods fail because skill units are structured (interdependent, hierarchical, behavior-triggering, context-consuming), motivating a dedicated structure-aware valuation approach.

Method: SkillSV compiles a skill into units, dependencies, and a document hierarchy. It restricts counterfactual evaluations to only valid skill subsets respecting these constraints. To disentangle content value from context cost, it employs paired deletion: removing a unit vs. replacing it with length-neutral padding. Shapley values are estimated using a rollout-budgeted estimator designed for noisy agent evaluations.

Result: On four agentic benchmarks, SkillSV recovers unit interactions, preserves aggregate skill lift, and enables safe pruning and compression of skills. The method demonstrates faithfulness, actionability, and provides interpretable explanations of unit contributions.

Conclusion: SkillSV provides a principled, structure-aware method for skill valuation that respects internal dependencies and separates content value from context cost, enabling practical downstream applications like safe pruning and compression of agent skills.

Abstract: Agent skills are increasingly optimized by automated feedback loops, producing long structured artifacts whose internal value remains unclear. We study skill valuation: assigning credit to the internal units of a fixed skill, such as rules, examples, scripts, and heuristics, under a fixed agent and held-out task distribution. Skill valuation differs from data or prompt-span valuation because skill units are structured: they may depend on other units, belong to a document hierarchy, trigger agent behavior, and consume limited prompt context. We introduce SkillSV, a structure-aware Shapley-style framework for skill valuation. SkillSV compiles a skill into units, dependencies, and hierarchy, so that only valid counterfactual skills are evaluated. It uses paired deletion and length-neutral padding to separate content value from context cost, and estimates the resulting values with a rollout-budgeted estimator for noisy agent evaluations. On four agentic benchmarks, we assess the faithfulness, actionability, and explanation of SkillSV: it recovers unit interactions, preserves aggregate skill lift, and guides safe pruning and compression.

</details>


### [142] [Joint UAV Flight and Opportunistic Routing under Reinforcement Learning for Delay-Tolerant Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04590)
*Xiao Wang,Shun-Ren Yang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: JUROR proposes a joint optimization framework integrating UAV flight control with decentralized opportunistic routing for DTNs, using a PPO-based CTDE approach with factored POMDP formulation, achieving performance gains over PRoPHET and MaxProp.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Delay-tolerant networks suffer from sparse connectivity, intermittent contacts, finite buffers, and limited TTL, causing sparse delivery and congestion that degrade end-to-end performance. Existing solutions lack joint optimization of routing and controllable UAV mobility under contact-limited observations.

Method: The problem is formulated as a factored partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP) with sequential motion–routing coupling and per-step team reward. JUROR employs the PPO framework under centralized training and decentralized execution (CTDE), where decentralized actors use local observations, a training-time critic leverages global statistics, and an optional multi-horizon hotspot predictor provides auxiliary supervision.

Result: Simulation results across four traffic modes show effective performance gains over PRoPHET and MaxProp, while maintaining contact-limited decentralized execution.

Conclusion: Joint UAV flight control and opportunistic routing via CTDE-based reinforcement learning effectively addresses DTN performance degradation, outperforming established protocols like PRoPHET and MaxProp.

Abstract: The growing deployment of delay-tolerant networks (DTNs) has made store-carry-forward (SCF) communication indispensable under sparse connectivity.
  However, intermittent contacts, finite buffers, and limited message time-to-live (TTL) often give rise to sparse delivery and congestion, leading to substantial end-to-end performance degradation.
  To address this challenge, this study explores the joint optimization of decentralized opportunistic routing and controllable unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) flight, aiming to enlarge future contacts through discrete UAV headings while enabling per-node replication under contact-limited observations.
  Building upon this architecture, we study cooperative factored routing--UAV control under centralized training and decentralized execution (CTDE) and propose JUROR (Joint UAV flight and Opportunistic Routing, based on the proximal policy optimization (PPO) framework.
  In our design, we first cast the problem as a factored partially observable Markov decision process with sequential motion--routing coupling and a per-step team reward; subsequently, decentralized actors act on local observations while a training-time critic uses global statistics, and an optional multi-horizon hotspot predictor provides auxiliary supervision.
  Simulation results over four traffic modes demonstrate effective gains over PRoPHET and MaxProp, while retaining contact-limited decentralized execution.

</details>


### [143] [Agreement Before Diversity: Verification-First Complementarity for Heterogeneous Language-Model Coordination](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04618)
*Ruitong Li,Binjie Guo,Aisheng Mo,Guowei Su,Jie Li,Ru Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ABD is a frozen, label-free decision rule for heterogeneous LM ensembles that uses agreement of two trusted samples to retain an anchor answer, or else synthesizes a heterogeneous replacement. It yields exact accuracy-gap identities and achieves strong blind evaluation results on LiveCodeBench-v6 and GPQA-Diamond.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Heterogeneous LM ensembles broaden candidate responses but lack a principled criterion for when a new answer should replace an already supported one. The authors aim to decouple candidate headroom from replacement authority, making the latter explicit and auditable.

Method: Agreement-Before-Diversity (ABD): a frozen, label-free gating rule. An anchor answer is retained if two additional trusted samples corroborate it under a fixed equivalence relation; otherwise, a heterogeneous synthesis replaces it. The authors prove two exact identities: (1) the accuracy gap relative to unconditional synthesis is determined by agreement coverage and anchor advantage on the protected subset; (2) the gap relative to never-synthesizing reflects a contrast between authorized recovery and authorized destruction. Neither identity assumes independence or calibrated confidence.

Result: On LiveCodeBench-v6 (n=175), ABD achieves 59.43% vs. Single9 (52.57%) and HAC (52.00%). On GPQA-Diamond (n=180), ABD scores 75.00% vs. both controls at 72.78%. The identities localize aggregate differences to an enumerable protected stratum: 0 discordant items among 3 protected cases on LiveCodeBench; 13 vs 8 discordant among 132 on GPQA-Diamond; 12 vs 0 among 71 under frozen anchor perturbation. Expected inference cost is approximately 8 – 5×coverage calls.

Conclusion: Diversity supplies potential; verification structure supplies authority. ABD provides a principled, auditable mechanism for replacement decisions in heterogeneous LM ensembles, with provable identities that localize performance differences to an enumerable protected stratum, without requiring independence or calibration assumptions.

Abstract: Heterogeneous language-model ensembles expand the space of candidate responses, yet they lack a principled criterion for when a newly generated answer should supersede an already supported one. We decouple candidate headroom from replacement authority, rendering the latter as an explicit, auditable object. Our proposed method, Agreement-Before-Diversity (ABD), is a frozen, label-free decision rule: an anchor answer is retained if two additional trusted samples corroborate it under a fixed equivalence relation; otherwise, it is replaced by a heterogeneous synthesis. For this gating mechanism, we prove two exact identities. The first shows that the accuracy gap relative to unconditional synthesis is determined jointly by the agreement coverage and the anchor's advantage on the protected subset. The second shows that the gap relative to never synthesizing reflects a contrast between authorized recovery and authorized destruction. Neither identity assumes independence or calibrated confidence, and the expected inference cost is approximately eight minus five times the coverage in number of calls. Under blind, exact-ID evaluation, ABD achieves 59.43% on the complete LiveCodeBench-v6 (vs. 52.57% for Single9 and 52.00% for HAC; n = 175) and 75.00% on an untouched GPQA-Diamond split (both controls at 72.78%; n = 180). Furthermore, these identities localize every aggregate difference to an enumerable protected stratum: no discordant items occur among the 3 protected cases on LiveCodeBench, where coverage bounds the gate's contribution to 1.71 points a priori; 13 versus 8 discordant cases among 132 on GPQA-Diamond; and 12 versus 0 among 71 under a frozen anchor perturbation. Diversity supplies potential; verification structure supplies authority.

</details>


### [144] [A/B Agent: A Self-Evolving Agent for Strategy Iteration in Industrial A/B Testing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04625)
*Zhuohang Jiang,Yuxin Chen,Yongsen Pan,Zheng Hu,Wenqi Fan,Qing Li,Hongyang Wang,Jun Wang,Wenwu Ou*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A/B Agent is a closed-loop framework for industrial recommendation strategy optimization that organizes historical experiments into a hierarchical experience tree, retrieves transferable knowledge via multi-path Tree-RAG, and autonomously refines strategies through sequential A/B feedback, achieving a 4.829% GMV improvement in a real-world short-video e-commerce system.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional industrial recommendation strategy iteration relies on manual A/B experimentation, which is labor-intensive, time-consuming, and fails to systematically reuse fragmented historical knowledge. Existing RAG agents organize experience in a flat manner, ignoring hierarchical relationships among business scenarios, recommendation stages, optimization objectives, and experimental contexts, leading to mismatched retrieval, limited cross-scenario transfer, and inability to continuously refine strategies through sequential A/B feedback.

Method: The A/B Agent framework consists of three tightly coupled components: (1) Historical Strategy Knowledge Organization — structures past strategies into a hierarchical experience tree capturing scenario-stage-objective-context relationships; (2) Autonomous Target-Aware Strategy Generation — employs multi-path Tree-RAG to retrieve transferable evidence from the experience tree and generate executable strategies; (3) Experiment-Guided Strategy Self-Evolution — continuously analyzes online A/B feedback to guide autonomous parameter tuning and updates the experience tree for iterative self-improvement.

Result: Extensive offline and online evaluations demonstrate the framework's effectiveness, including a 4.829% improvement in GMV in a real-world short-video e-commerce recommendation system while maintaining positive gains across all guardrail metrics.

Conclusion: The A/B Agent provides an effective closed-loop solution for industrial recommendation strategy optimization by hierarchically organizing historical knowledge, enabling targeted retrieval via Tree-RAG, and supporting continuous self-evolution through A/B feedback, significantly outperforming flat RAG-based baselines in both strategy quality and cross-scenario transferability.

Abstract: Industrial recommendation strategy iteration heavily relies on large-scale A/B experimentation. Traditional tuning requires experts to repeatedly design strategies, configure experiments, analyze results, and adjust parameters, making the process labor-intensive and time-consuming. Meanwhile, valuable knowledge from historical experiments is often fragmented, making systematic reuse difficult through manual expert effort alone. Existing RAG agents partially alleviate this burden by retrieving prior strategies, but typically organize experience in a flat manner, overlooking the hierarchical relationships among business scenarios, recommendation stages, optimization objectives, and experimental contexts. This often results in mismatched retrieval and limited cross-scenario transfer, while preventing agents from continuously refining strategies and parameters through sequential A/B feedback. %
To address these limitations, we propose A/B Agent, a closed-loop A/B agent for industrial recommendation strategy optimization. The framework comprises three tightly coupled core components: Historical Strategy Knowledge Organization, Autonomous Target-Aware Strategy Generation, and Experiment-Guided Strategy Self-Evolution. It organizes historical strategies into a hierarchical experience tree, retrieves transferable evidence through multi-path Tree-RAG to generate executable strategies, and continuously analyzes online A/B feedback to guide autonomous tuning and update the experience tree for self-evolution. Extensive offline and online evaluations demonstrate its effectiveness, including a 4.829% improvement in GMV in a real-world short-video e-commerce recommendation system while maintaining positive gains across all guardrail metrics.

</details>


### [145] [AI Literacy for Legal Translation: Developing Digital Resilience](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04641)
*Łucja Biel*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This chapter proposes a four-dimensional AI literacy framework (foundational, procedural, critical, strategic) for legal translation, arguing that AI does not alter legal translation's core objectives but requires extending professional competence through transversal AI literacy to foster digital resilience, with pedagogical activities for translator education.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Generative AI introduces both opportunities and multifaceted risks (linguistic, technical, legal, ethical, cognitive) to legal translation, creating an urgent need to define how professional translators can critically and responsibly integrate AI without compromising professional standards.

Method: The chapter develops a conceptual framework for AI literacy in legal translation, structured around four mutually reinforcing dimensions, and derives pedagogical implications by proposing concrete classroom activities for legal translator education.

Result: The resulting framework conceptualizes AI literacy as a transversal competence component woven across existing legal translation competence models, comprising foundational (understanding AI systems), procedural (operational skills), critical (evaluative judgment), and strategic (adaptive, goal-oriented deployment) dimensions that collectively enable digital resilience.

Conclusion: AI does not change the fundamental objectives of legal translation; rather, the profession must extend its competence model through AI literacy. Integrating this framework into legal translator education will equip future practitioners to use AI critically, responsibly, and in line with professional norms.

Abstract: Generative AI is transforming legal translation by introducing opportunities alongside linguistic, technical, legal, ethical and cognitive risks. This chapter examines the implications of AI for professional legal translation and proposes an AI literacy framework tailored to the profession. It argues that AI does not change the fundamental objectives of legal translation but requires an extension of professional competence through AI literacy. The proposed framework comprises four mutually reinforcing dimensions, foundational, procedural, critical and strategic, and conceptualises AI literacy as a transversal component of legal translation competence that fosters digital resilience. It further discusses the pedagogical implications of this framework by proposing classroom activities designed to develop AI literacy in legal translator education, enabling future translators to integrate AI critically, responsibly and in accordance with professional standards.

</details>


### [146] [Calibrating Artificial Guilt: Neurally Grounded Reward Shaping for Prosocial Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04663)
*Aaditya Mehta,Arya Shah*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether a guilt signal derived from human fMRI data can calibrate prosocial reward shaping in multi-agent reinforcement learning, finding that neurally calibrated agents match human social behavior more closely than hand-tuned or selfish alternatives.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In cooperative multi-agent RL, social reward-shaping weights are typically chosen arbitrarily by hand, lacking principled, empirically grounded calibration. The authors ask whether neurobehavioural data from humans can provide a quantitative basis for setting these weights, bridging cognitive neuroscience and multi-agent RL.

Method: Using the SoDec responsibility fMRI dataset (N=40), the authors fit a subject-fixed-effects regression of momentary happiness changes onto outcome-type counts, extracting a guilt weight as the Partner-negative minus Social-negative contrast (ŵ=1.118, Cohen's d=0.214). This weight is embedded into a two-agent Social Lottery environment with independent PPO actor-critics under four shaping conditions: neurally calibrated, uniform constant, zero (selfish baseline), and a unit-coefficient oracle. Evaluation spans 1,000 episodes per condition, with KL divergence used to compare agent behavior against human Social safe-choice rates.

Result: The neurally calibrated agents achieve a social safe-choice rate of 0.459, closely matching the human rate of 0.484 (KL=0.0012). The other three conditions diverge by one to three orders of magnitude in KL divergence, demonstrating that the neurobehaviourally derived weight yields substantially better alignment with human prosocial behavior than arbitrary or absent shaping.

Conclusion: Human neurobehavioural priors can serve as quantitative constraints for prosocial reward shaping in artificial agents, offering a data-driven alternative to hand-tuned social terms in multi-agent RL.

Abstract: Cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning often adds social terms to individual rewards, yet the scale of those terms is usually chosen by hand. We ask whether a guilt signal can instead be calibrated from human neural and behavioural data and transferred to artificial agents. Using the public SoDec responsibility fMRI dataset (40 participants), we fit a subject-fixed-effects regression of momentary-happiness changes on outcome-type counts and recover a guilt weight as the Partner-negative minus Social-negative contrast ($\hat{w}=1.118$, Cohen's $d=0.214$). We embed this weight in a two-agent Social Lottery environment and train independent Proximal Policy Optimization actor-critics under four shaping regimes: neurally calibrated, uniform constant, zero (selfish), and a unit-coefficient oracle. Across 1{,}000 evaluation episodes per condition, the calibrated agents track the human Social safe-choice rate most closely ($0.459$ vs.\ human $0.484$; $\mathrm{KL}=0.0012$), while the other three conditions deviate by one to three orders of magnitude in KL. Human neurobehavioural priors can therefore act as quantitative constraints on prosocial reward shaping.

</details>


### [147] [Traceable LLM-Generated Hazard Scenarios for Operational Safety Analysis of Aviation Systems Using ASRS Reports](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04697)
*Cristian Mascia,Roberto Pietrantuono,Daniel Rodriguez,Stefano Russo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: An AI-assisted method using LLMs generates structured hazard scenarios and narratives from NASA ASRS data, with a hybrid evolutionary abduction approach improving correctness and reducing variability in operational hazard analysis for aviation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Operational hazard analysis in aviation requires reasoning about interactions across weather, ATC, airspace, aircraft, and human factors—a challenge distinct from aircraft-level functional hazard assessment. Existing methods lack systematic, data-driven scenario generation with traceability to real incident reports.

Method: The system generates structured hypotheses (categorical factors) and narrative scenarios from a target adverse outcome using ASRS data. Scenarios are scored by historical co-occurrence plausibility and similarity to held-out reports. A hybrid variant conditions narrative generation on structured hypotheses derived via evolutionary abduction. Evaluation spans multiple LLMs, zero-shot vs. few-shot prompting, and optional fine-tuning.

Result: The hybrid evolutionary abduction variant improves structural correctness and reduces output variability compared to purely generative approaches. Prompting strategy and model choice significantly affect validity and realism of both structured factor combinations and generated narratives.

Conclusion: AI-assisted scenario generation from ASRS data is viable for operational hazard analysis. Conditioning narrative generation on abduced structured hypotheses enhances correctness and consistency, suggesting a promising human-AI collaborative workflow for aviation safety analysis.

Abstract: Operational hazard analysis of aviation system operations must consider interactions among weather, ATC actions, airspace constraints, aircraft operations, and human factors - distinct from the functional hazard assessment applied at the aircraft-system level. We present an AI-assisted approach that generates candidate hazard scenarios from NASA's Aviation Safety Reporting System (ASRS). Given a target adverse outcome, it produces a structured hypothesis as categorical factors and a narrative scenario describing an operational event sequence consistent with the structure. Each scenario includes by a plausibility score from historical co-occurrence evidence and traceability to the most similar held-out ASRS reports. We then propose a hybrid variant, conditioning narrative generation on a structured hypothesis produced via evolutionary abduction, improving correctness and reducing variability. We evaluate multiple large language models, zero-shot versus few-shot prompting, and optional fine-tuning, measuring how prompting and model choice affect the validity and realism of the generated structures and narratives.

</details>


### [148] [OctoLong: Mid-Training On Cross-Repository Code Contexts Enhances Long-Context Modeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05141)
*Indraneil Paul,Falko Helm,Goran Glavaš,Iryna Gurevych*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: OctoLong introduces a pipeline that recursively retrieves code references to create dependency-rich, million-token code contexts. Training long-context LMs with just 12% OctoLong data significantly improves long-range retrieval, state tracking, code understanding, and agentic tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing long-context corpora (books, articles, code repos) are finite and lack long-distance dependencies. The authors address the need for dependency-rich, ultra-long training data to improve LM performance on long-horizon agentic workflows, in-context learning, and repository-level code understanding.

Method: OctoLong is a context engineering pipeline combining an AST parser, a language server backend, and a package manager for recursive retrieval of code references (functions, imports, types). This generates code contexts spanning millions of tokens with rich cross-file dependencies. OctoLong-Instruct models (600M–14B parameters) are then trained via: (1) context-extension mid-training on a ~50B-token mixture (~6.2B tokens of OctoLong data, ~12% of the mix), and (2) ~10B tokens of instruction tuning. Evaluation covers 18 open-weight long-context LMs.

Result: Replacing just 12% of traditional context-extension data with OctoLong yields substantial improvements in: long-range retrieval, long-term state tracking, repository-level code understanding, and downstream agentic tasks. Short-context API usage in coding is also enhanced. Ablations confirm the efficacy of the pipeline.

Conclusion: Synthetically constructed dependency-rich code contexts (OctoLong) are a highly data-efficient method for improving long-context LM capabilities. The approach complements traditional corpora and unlocks stronger performance on both long-range and short-range code understanding tasks.

Abstract: Context lengths of language models (LMs) have dramatically increased, driven by the demands for in-context learning, self-improvement, and long-horizon agentic workflows. Existing long-context corpora, however, are dominated by books, academic articles, and code repositories, which are finite resources and often scarce in long-distance dependencies. In this work, we introduce OctoLong, a context engineering pipeline that instruments an AST parser, a language server backend, and a package manager to facilitate the recursive retrieval of code references, enabling the curation of dependency-rich code contexts of millions of tokens in length. We then train OctoLong-Instruct, a suite of capable long-context open LMs, derived from base models ranging in size from 600M to 14B parameters, via context-extension mid-training on a ~50B-token mixture containing ~6.2B tokens of OctoLong code contexts, followed by ~10B tokens of instruction tuning. Our training ablations and experimental evaluations against 18 state-of-the-art open-weight long-context LMs show that supplanting just 12% of traditional context-extension corpora with OctoLong data yields substantial gains in long-range retrieval, long-term state tracking, repository-level code understanding, and downstream agentic tasks, while also enhancing API usage in short-context coding scenarios.

</details>


### [149] [Diagnosing Tool-Selection Reasoning in LLM Agents with Canary Tools](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04719)
*Atul Anand,Sourav Chattaraj*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces "canary tools" — diagnostic probes embedded in MCP tool sets that diagnose why agents choose wrong tools. A six-type taxonomy (semantic decoys, parameter traps, capability mirages, prerequisite blindness, temporal decoys, granularity traps) profiles tool-selection reasoning. Evaluation across 8 models and 120 tasks (8,640 runs) shows susceptibility drops sharply with capability, but capability tier alone doesn't predict safety. Capability mirages trap frontier models; other types discriminate by capability. The framework is released publicly.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current agent evaluations only tell us a model selected the wrong tool, but provide no diagnostic insight into *why* the error occurred. This opacity hinders targeted improvement of tool-use reasoning in LLM agents.

Method: The authors design "canary tools" — diagnostic probes planted in MCP tool sets, each engineered to test one specific tool-selection weakness. They define a six-type taxonomy: semantic decoys (confusing similar tools), parameter traps (misleading parameter schemas), capability mirages (tools that appear capable but aren't), prerequisite blindness (ignoring dependencies), temporal decoys (time-based confusion), and granularity traps (wrong abstraction level). Eight models (six hosted, two 8B open-weight) across three capability tiers are tested on 120 tasks under three canary-density conditions, three seeds (8,640 runs), plus a 2,880-run subtlety ablation. Task success is graded by a provider-independent judge with a second judge for corroboration (Cohen's κ = 0.75).

Result: Three key findings: (1) Canary Susceptibility Rate (CSR) varies ~36x across models, with Claude Opus 4.8 lowest and Llama 3.1 8B highest. (2) Capability tier alone does not predict safety — the most susceptible hosted model is mid-tier, and cheaper models can be safer within a provider. (3) Taxonomy is capability-stratified: capability mirages most reliably trap frontier models; other types fire mainly on small open models, discriminating by capability rather than being weak. Softening canary give-away phrases leaves frontier CSR unchanged, indicating probes measure reasoning, not surface-level phrase-spotting. Susceptibility predicts task failure (Spearman ρ = -0.34); the most robust models are not significantly degraded by canary pressure.

Conclusion: Canary tools provide a principled, fine-grained diagnostic method for evaluating tool-selection reasoning in LLM agents. The framework enables developers to profile specific weaknesses rather than merely counting wrong-tool errors. Findings reveal that stronger models are not uniformly safer, and that diagnostic taxonomies can stratify by capability. The authors release the framework, schemas, tasks, and logs for community use.

Abstract: Agent evaluations tell us that a model picked the wrong tool, but rarely why. We introduce canary tools: diagnostic probe tools planted in an agent's Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool set, each engineered to probe one specific tool-selection weakness. A six-type taxonomy (semantic decoys, parameter traps, capability mirages, prerequisite blindness, temporal decoys, and granularity traps) turns a single "wrong tool" outcome into a multi-dimensional profile of how a model reasons about tools. We evaluate eight models -- six hosted and two 8B open-weight -- spanning three capability tiers, on 120 tasks across three canary-density conditions and three seeds (8,640 runs), plus a 2,880-run subtlety ablation. Task success is graded by a provider-independent judge, corroborated by a second independent judge (Cohen's kappa = 0.75). We report three findings. First, susceptibility drops sharply as models get more capable: the per-task canary susceptibility rate (CSR) ranges about 36x across models, lowest for Claude Opus 4.8 and highest for Llama 3.1 8B. Second, capability tier alone does not predict safety: the most susceptible hosted model is mid-tier, and within a provider the cheaper model can be the safer one. Third, the taxonomy is capability-stratified: capability mirages most reliably trap frontier models, while the other types are largely inert on strong models but fire on small open models, so they discriminate by capability rather than being weak. Softening each canary's give-away phrase leaves frontier CSR essentially unchanged, evidence that the probes measure reasoning, not phrase-spotting. Susceptibility also predicts task failure (Spearman rho = -0.34), while the most robust models are not significantly degraded by canary pressure. We release the framework, canary schemas, tasks, and logs.

</details>


### [150] [When Prompts Become Pixels: Prompt-Region Grounding for Multimodal Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04726)
*Yongxin Wang,Ruizhe Zhou,Yueling Tang,Yingying Zhu,Xuemin Zhao,Xiaojun Chang,Xiaodan Liang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces Visualized Task Semantics (VTS) to test whether MLLMs reason equally well when task instructions appear in pixels vs. text. Finds a 17.8-point average accuracy drop across 24 model-task pairs. Proposes prompt-region grounding to close this semantic channel gap, improving VTS accuracy from 58.0 to 66.3 while preserving original performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: MLLMs increasingly process screenshots/documents where tasks are embedded in pixels, yet benchmarks present questions in text. It is unclear whether models interpret pixel-based instructions as effectively as text-based ones. The work aims to isolate and measure a potential "semantic channel gap" — the failure to use correctly transcribed visual instructions for reasoning.

Method: (1) VTS intervention: moves the question into the image while keeping the source problem and ground-truth answer fixed, enabling controlled comparison across text and visual instruction channels. (2) Prompt-region grounding: aligns the visual question region with typed semantics and recovers a clean representation from a masked view. Trained at matched cost, requires no OCR or region metadata at inference.

Result: Across 6 MLLMs and 4 benchmarks, VTS causes accuracy drops in all 24 model-task pairs, averaging 17.8 points. Models often transcribe the visual question correctly but fail to utilize it. The proposed prompt-region grounding raises 4-benchmark VTS accuracy from 58.0 to 66.3 while preserving original-interface accuracy.

Conclusion: Reading task-bearing text from pixels and grounding it as an instruction for reasoning are distinct capabilities. Current MLLMs exhibit a semantic channel gap that goes beyond OCR quality. Prompt-region grounding effectively narrows this gap without inference-time overhead, demonstrating that explicit alignment between visual question regions and typed semantics is critical for robust multimodal instruction following.

Abstract: Multimodal large language models increasingly reason over screenshots and documents where the task itself may be written in pixels. Yet benchmarks usually place questions in text, leaving it unclear whether models use the same instruction equally well across channels. We introduce Visualized Task Semantics (VTS), a controlled intervention that moves the question into the image while keeping the source problem and answer fixed. Across six MLLMs and four benchmarks, accuracy drops in all 24 model-task pairs, by 17.8 points on average. Models often transcribe the visual question correctly yet fail to use it, exposing a semantic channel gap beyond OCR. To reduce this gap, we present prompt-region grounding, whose core design aligns the question region with typed semantics and recovers its clean representation from a masked view. At matched training cost, our method raises four-benchmark VTS accuracy from 58.0 to 66.3 while preserving accuracy on the original interface, and requires no OCR or region metadata at inference. Reading task-bearing text and grounding it as an instruction for reasoning are distinct capabilities.

</details>


### [151] [Chain-of-Thought Monitoring Can Be Unreliable in Implicit-Influence Settings](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04735)
*Agatha Duzan,Asa Cooper Stickland*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CoT monitoring effectively detects behavior shifts under explicit influence (60-94%), but detection drops dramatically (41-46 pp) under implicit influence. Realistic system prompts further reduce implicit detection to as low as 5%, suggesting explicit-influence evaluations overestimate real-world monitorability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current Chain-of-Thought (CoT) monitoring evaluations focus almost exclusively on explicit-influence settings where models are directly instructed to hide something. However, real-world deployment also involves implicit-influence settings — where subtle contextual features shape model behavior without any concealment instruction. The gap between these two regimes has not been systematically studied, raising concerns that monitorability estimates may be misleadingly optimistic for practical safety applications.

Method: The authors introduce a benchmark spanning four task formats (binary choice, numeric rating, multiple-choice QA, open-ended coding) and seven frontier extended-thinking models. In each task, a "nudge" is introduced to bias the model toward a particular option. The nudge is delivered either implicitly (as a casual aside) or explicitly (as a direct instruction to act on it and conceal doing so). CoT monitorability is then compared across both regimes by measuring how well monitors detect the resulting behavior shifts. The benchmark also tests the effect of realistic system-prompt additions designed to reduce off-topic bias.

Result: Under explicit influence, CoT monitors detect 60-94% of behavior shifts. Under implicit influence, detection falls by 41-46 percentage points in two of the four settings. Adding realistic system prompts further reduces implicit detection to as low as 5%, even though the behavioral influence itself persists. This reveals that well-intentioned deployment mitigations can inadvertently undermine monitorability.

Conclusion: Monitorability estimates derived from explicit-influence settings likely overestimate real-world CoT monitoring efficacy. Implicit influence is both harder to detect and made even harder by standard deployment practices. Safety evaluations must account for implicit-influence regimes to provide realistic assessments of CoT monitoring as a safety layer.

Abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) monitoring is increasingly treated as an important safety layer for frontier reasoning models. Most monitorability evaluations study explicit-influence settings: setups where the prompt directly incentivizes the model to hide something, e.g., by instructing it to perform a hidden side-task. A complementary axis for CoT-monitor evaluations is implicit-influence settings, where the prompt contains no instruction to hide, but the model's behavior is still shaped by features of the task or context, e.g. an irrelevant detail about a candidate that biases a hiring rating.
  We introduce the first benchmark that directly compares CoT monitorability under the two regimes. We test how model behavior changes in the presence of a nudge to choose a particular option. The nudge is delivered either as a casual aside (implicit), or as a direct instruction to act on the nudge and to conceal having done so (explicit). The benchmark spans four task formats (binary choice, numeric rating, multiple-choice QA, open-ended coding) and seven frontier extended-thinking models.
  Under explicit influence, a CoT monitor detects 60-94% of behavior shifts: even models instructed to conceal it leak the instruction into their CoT. Under implicit influence, the same factors still shift behavior, but detection falls by 41-46 percentage points in two of our four settings. Realistic system-prompt additions (of the kind a developer might deploy to reduce off-topic bias) lower implicit detection further, to as low as 5%, while preserving the behavioral influence itself.
  These results suggest that monitorability estimates obtained in explicit-influence settings may over-estimate monitorability, and that monitorability can be further decreased by well-intentioned deployment choices. Our benchmark and code are available at https://github.com/agatha-duzan/implicit-vs-explicit-influence

</details>


### [152] [EviGraph: Evidence-Guided Autonomous Research Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04738)
*Zhenjiang Ren,Ruiji Li,Xujing Zhang,Ziliang Pang,Shuo Ren,Jiajun Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: EviGraph introduces a typed evidence graph as the operational state for autonomous research agents, enabling explicit validation of claim-evidence chains. It detects inconsistencies, localizes weak nodes, regenerates downstream subgraphs, and uses checkpointing to prevent corruption. The system significantly outperforms baselines, improving Claim Support Rate by 40.19% and achieving 87.73% Experimental Data Consistency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current autonomous research agents produce outputs with unsupported claims and inconsistencies across research questions, experiments, results, and conclusions. The authors argue this stems from a flawed architectural paradigm where research is treated as a sequential pipeline without explicit maintenance or validation of the evolving claim-evidence structure across stages.

Method: EviGraph models the research process as a typed evidence graph with six node types: Problem, Gap, Hypothesis, Experiment, Finding, and Claim. The graph serves as the agent's live operational state. The system inspects evidence chains for missing dependencies, semantic misalignment, and result-claim inconsistencies; localizes the earliest weak node; and regenerates the affected downstream subgraph. Graph checkpointing prevents unsuccessful repairs from corrupting previously validated evidence. Manuscripts are generated only after every retained claim is grounded in a validated evidence chain.

Result: On ARC-Bench-ML and NanoResearch-20 benchmarks, EviGraph outperforms all compared end-to-end research-agent baselines in overall research performance. It improves Claim Support Rate by 40.19% over the strongest baseline and achieves 87.73% Experimental Data Consistency.

Conclusion: Explicit evidence-state maintenance via a typed evidence graph is a valuable architectural approach for improving the reliability of autonomous research agents, as demonstrated by EviGraph's strong performance gains in claim grounding and data consistency.

Abstract: Autonomous research agents can generate hypotheses, execute experiments, and draft manuscripts, yet their outputs often contain unsupported claims and inconsistencies between research questions, experiments, results, and conclusions. We argue that this problem is partly architectural: existing systems organize research as sequential pipelines but do not explicitly maintain or validate the evolving claim-evidence structure across stages.In this paper, we introduce EviGraph, an autonomous research framework that represents the research process as a typed evidence graph containing Problem, Gap, Hypothesis, Experiment, Finding, and Claim nodes. The graph serves as the operational state of the agent rather than a post-hoc record. EviGraph inspects evidence chains for missing dependencies, semantic misalignment, and result-claim inconsistencies, localizes the earliest weak node, and regenerates its affected downstream subgraph. Graph checkpointing prevents unsuccessful repairs from corrupting previously validated evidence. Manuscripts are generated only after every retained claim is grounded in a validated evidence chain.Experiments on ARC-Bench-ML and NanoResearch-20 show that EviGraph outperforms the compared end-to-end research-agent baselines in overall research performance, improves Claim Support Rate by 40.19% over the strongest baseline, and achieves 87.73% Experimental Data Consistency. These results demonstrate the value of explicit evidence-state maintenance for reliable autonomous research.

</details>


### [153] [Fewer Tokens, Smaller Cache: Reward-Coordinated Efficient Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04771)
*Qiyuan Zhu,Dezhi Li,Pengyu Cheng,Tianle Chen,Jiacheng Wang,Ruijie Shen,Hao Gu,Sida Lin,Zirui Liu,Jiacheng Liu,Sirui Han*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ReCo coordinates KV-cache compression and generation-side penalties under a unified process reward signal to reduce overthinking in large reasoning models, achieving 37-65% token reduction and 2.08-2.35x speedup while preserving accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large Reasoning Models suffer from overthinking — generating excessively long chain-of-thought trajectories that inflate inference cost. Existing KV-cache compression methods apply uniform policies and ignore generation-side effects, where smaller caches paradoxically cause models to generate more tokens, offsetting savings. The authors observe that (1) tolerance to context loss varies across reasoning steps (high-reward steps tolerate more compression) and (2) compression on the KV-cache side affects generation length on the output side, necessitating joint optimization.

Method: ReCo is a step-wise framework with three components driven by a lightweight process-reward estimator: (1) Reward-adaptive KV-cache compression — more aggressive cache eviction at high-reward steps, conservative retention at low-reward steps; (2) Reward-banded penalty on reflection tokens — discourages redundant/cyclical generation when reward is already high; (3) Confidence-based early stopping — terminates reasoning once the process reward indicates reliable reasoning. All components are coordinated by the same process reward signal.

Result: Across three reasoning models and six benchmarks, ReCo reduces generated tokens by 37%-65% and end-to-end latency by 2.08x-2.35x over Full CoT, while largely preserving accuracy.

Conclusion: Coordinating KV-cache compression and generation-side behavior under a unified process reward is an effective strategy for mitigating overthinking in LRMs, enabling substantial inference cost reduction without sacrificing reasoning quality.

Abstract: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) excel on complex tasks through long chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning, but their lengthy intermediate steps cause severe overthinking that inflates inference cost. KV-cache compression is a common solution, yet existing reasoning-oriented methods apply a uniform policy across the trajectory and judge compression only by what it removes from the cache. Two observations point the other way. First, a reasoning state's tolerance to context loss varies along the trajectory, and process reward tracks it: deleting tokens at high-reward steps preserves accuracy far better than deleting the same budget at random. Second, compression is not free on the generation side, since a smaller cache leads the model to generate more tokens, partly canceling the saving. Together these motivate coordinating both sides under a single process reward. We propose ReCo (Reward-Coordinated Compression), a step-wise framework in which a lightweight process-reward estimator scores each completed step and drives three components: (1) reward-adaptive KV-cache compression that shrinks the retained cache harder at high-reward steps and less at low-reward ones, (2) a reward-banded penalty on reflection tokens that curbs redundant generation, and (3) confidence-based early stopping that triggers when the reasoning is reliable. Across three reasoning models and six benchmarks, ReCo reduces generated tokens by 37%-65% and end-to-end latency by 2.08x-2.35x over Full CoT, all while largely preserving accuracy.

</details>


### [154] [NSF-HRPT: Neural Semantic Field meets Hierarchical Risk Perception Tree for Safety-Critical Scenario Assessment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04776)
*Yu Zhao,Jiangyu Pan,Tao Hu,Ming Yin,Fan Yang,Jiangfan Liu,Xiubo Liang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: NSF-HRPT is a monocular risk assessment framework that combines a Neural Semantic Field for learning TTC distributions with a Hierarchical Risk Perception Tree for efficient multi-agent spatial reasoning, enhanced by a foundation-model-based Sim2Real strategy, achieving state-of-the-art risk assessment on both synthetic and real-world benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Monocular vision-based quantitative risk assessment in autonomous driving is challenging due to complex multi-agent interaction dynamics and real-world uncertainty. Existing collision prediction methods struggle to accurately quantify risk levels from monocular inputs alone.

Method: The framework comprises three components: (1) a Neural Semantic Field (NSF) trained on simulation data to model scene semantics, trajectory predictions, and probabilistic TTC distributions; (2) a Hierarchical Risk Perception Tree (HRPT) that uses the pre-trained NSF as a prior for efficient parallel spatial reasoning about multi-agent risks; and (3) a Sim2Real enhancement strategy that leverages priors from foundation models to improve real-world generalization without retraining.

Result: The framework achieves state-of-the-art performance on synthetic benchmarks and competitive near-state-of-the-art results on real-world datasets for both TTC estimation accuracy and risk localization precision.

Conclusion: NSF-HRPT provides an effective real-time risk awareness solution using monocular camera inputs, successfully bridging learning-based perception with structured reasoning for safety-critical autonomous driving applications.

Abstract: The ability to accurately assess and anticipate risks in safety-critical scenarios is crucial for autonomous driving systems. While existing research has made progress in collision prediction, accurately quantifying risk levels from monocular vision inputs remains challenging due to the complex dynamics of multi-agent interactions and the inherent uncertainty in real-world environments. To address these challenges, we present NSF-HRPT, a novel framework that combines learning-based perception with structured reasoning for quantitative risk assessment. Our approach features a Neural Semantic Field (NSF) that learns to model scene semantics, trajectory predictions, and probabilistic Time-to-Collision (TTC) distributions from simulation data. During inference, the pre-trained NSF serves as a prior for our Hierarchical Risk Perception Tree (HRPT), which enables efficient parallel computation and spatial reasoning about multi-agent risks. Additionally, we introduce a Sim2Real enhancement strategy that improves real-world applicability without retraining by incorporating priors from foundation models. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that our framework achieves state-of-the-art performance on synthetic benchmarks and delivers competitive, near-state-of-the-art results on real-world datasets for both TTC estimation accuracy and risk localization precision. The proposed method provides an effective solution for real-time risk awareness from monocular camera inputs.

</details>


### [155] [Privileged, but Biased: How PI-Conditioned Teachers Break Self-Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04794)
*Sarthak Harne,Chinmay Karkar,Yash Pandya,Ahmed Awadallah,Akshay Nambi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Self-distillation (SD) alone, without reward signals, fails to improve reasoning on difficult tasks. The teacher's privileged information biases its supervision toward a specific reference trajectory, causing the student to optimize a loss decoupled from task success — loss falls on low-information tokens while penalizing exploratory reasoning, yielding a flatter, less decisive model.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work reports gains from self-distillation (e.g., SDPO, OPSD) but almost exclusively in narrow, low-difficulty settings. This raises a fundamental question: does SD, as a standalone objective without any verifiable reward term, actually teach anything useful on genuinely difficult tasks?

Method: The authors reproduce SDPO's reported gains in its original easy setting, then apply the identical SD setup to difficult tasks spanning question answering, mathematics, coding, and multi-turn agentic tool use, across reasoning modes (CoT, tool-augmented), model sizes, and forms of privileged information. They analyze the causal mechanism via a PI Bias Score quantifying teacher target deviation toward a reference trajectory, and examine per-token loss distributions across token types (stopwords, punctuation, uncertainty markers, exploratory tokens).

Result: Across all difficult-task settings, per-token loss falls steadily during SD training, but validation accuracy does not improve and typically degrades. The failure is traced to PI bias: the teacher's targets are pulled toward one reference solution rather than general correctness. The student becomes nearly blind to rollout correctness, with loss concentrated on low-information tokens; within correct rollouts, exploratory tokens incur the highest divergence, penalizing the hesitation reasoning requires. The result is a flatter, less decisive model.

Conclusion: As a lone objective, self-distillation optimizes a signal fundamentally decoupled from task success. The per-token loss reduction is illusory — it reflects matching surface-level token patterns rather than acquiring reasoning capability. SD should not be used in isolation for difficult tasks.

Abstract: Self-distillation (SD) has emerged as a compute-efficient alternative to reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards: a self-teacher, conditioned on privileged information (PI) about the answer such as a reference solution, supplies dense per-token supervision to a student that never sees it. Reported gains, however, come almost exclusively from narrow, low-difficulty settings, leaving open a basic question: as a lone objective, with no reward term, does SD teach anything? We reproduce SDPO's reported gains in its easy setting, then apply the identical setup to difficult tasks and find that it does not. Across question answering, mathematics, coding, and multi-turn agentic tool use, across reasoning modes, model sizes, and forms of PI, and under both the SDPO and OPSD recipes, the per-token loss falls steadily while validation accuracy does not improve and typically degrades. We explain this failure through a single causal chain from the loss to the model it produces. The chain begins with PI bias: having seen one particular reference solution, the teacher's per-token target is pulled toward that trajectory rather than toward correctness in general, an effect we quantify with a PI Bias Score. Trained to match this target everywhere, the student's objective becomes nearly blind to whether a rollout is correct, and the loss it assigns falls mostly on low-information tokens like stopwords, punctuation, uncertainty markers, rather than those that determine the answer; within correct rollouts the exploratory tokens incur the highest divergence, so it penalizes the hesitation that reasoning requires. The result is a flatter, less decisive student that is no better at reasoning: as a lone objective, SD optimizes a signal decoupled from task success.

</details>


### [156] [ContextWeave: A Real-World Workflow Benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04830)
*Bo Wang,Yuqian Yao,Enxi Wang,Luozhijie Jin,Yang Liu,Yiran Suo,Yuxuan Cai,Enyu Zhou,Yufei Gao,Honglin Guo,Tianyu Huai,Li Ji,Zhikai Lei,Bufan Li,Lizhi Lin,Jinxiu Liu,Jie Yang,Jiazheng Zhou,Maosen Zhou,Pengfang Qian,Shichun Liu,Guanshan Liu,Hao Zheng,Yunhao Yu,Hang Yan,Jihua Kang,Xinchi Chen,Xipeng Qiu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ContextWeave is a longitudinal benchmark that evaluates whether recalled past experiences improve downstream agent performance on realistic, multi-month office workflows. It finds that experience-rich memory significantly boosts both workspace and preference alignment scores, but is more susceptible to misleading recall, motivating memory systems that balance retrieval relevance with reliable execution.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing memory evaluations for language agents are limited to retrieval accuracy or question answering, failing to assess whether memory actually improves performance on long-horizon, stateful, real-world workflows. There is a gap in understanding how recalled experience translates to better downstream task execution.

Method: The authors introduce ContextWeave, a benchmark built from privacy-preserved, multi-month office-work streams of 14 participants, yielding 1,005 executable tasks (568 core evaluation tasks) with instructions, containerized environments, trajectories, and task-specific rubrics. They evaluate six memory component configurations under a fixed model and test five base models with a fixed memory component, measuring Workspace Score (task output quality), Preference Score (alignment with participant-specific preferences), and diagnostics like relevance, continuity, solvability, and robustness to misleading recall.

Result: The strongest memory configuration improved Workspace Score from 68.08 to 78.20 and Preference Score from 41.50 to 70.60. Recall improved outcomes for all five tested base models under a fixed memory component. Experience-rich memory better supported workflow continuation and reduced redundant exploration compared to compact summaries, but was more susceptible to misleading recall.

Conclusion: Memory systems for language agents should be optimized not only for retrieval relevance but also for reliable use during execution. Actionable, experience-rich memory supports long-horizon workflows effectively, but robustness to misleading or irrelevant recall remains a critical design challenge.

Abstract: Memory is essential as language agents move from isolated tasks to long-horizon, stateful workflows, yet existing evaluations often reduce it to retrieval or question answering. We introduce ContextWeave, a longitudinal benchmark that evaluates whether recalled experience improves downstream agent performance in realistic office-work streams. ContextWeave reconstructs privacy-preserved, multi-month workflows of 14 participants into 1,005 executable tasks, including 568 core evaluation tasks, with instructions, containerized environments, trajectories, and task-specific rubrics. It measures workspace quality and alignment with participant-specific preferences, complemented by diagnostics of relevance, continuity, solvability, and robustness to misleading recall. Across six memory components under a fixed model, the strongest configuration raises Workspace Score from 68.08 to 78.20 and Preference Score from 41.50 to 70.60. With a fixed memory component, recall improves both outcomes for all five tested base models, although gains vary substantially. Our analysis shows that actionable, experience-rich memory supports workflow continuation and reduces redundant exploration more effectively than compact summaries, while it can also be more susceptible to misleading recall. These findings motivate memory systems that optimize not only retrieval relevance but also reliable use during execution.

</details>


### [157] [When Shared Rollouts Fail in Defensive Driving Evaluation: A NAVSIM Score Basis Audit](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04896)
*Ziang Wei,Minjun Yu,Zheyuan Lai,Mingjie Pang,Wei Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper audits NAVSIM v2.2's defensive driving scoring, revealing that reference-conditioned forgiveness combined with numerical instability in the shared velocity refit allows blind/actor-blind probes to outrank human replay and PDM-Closed. Replacing the solver eliminates the divergence, confirming the numerical trigger. The authors propose an audit protocol requiring score basis disclosure, blind probes, overwrite reporting, and rollout stability tests.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Defensive driving scores must distinguish between policies that observe surrounding actors and those that do not. The paper identifies a risk: reference-conditioned forgiveness in re-simulation benchmarks can propagate shared reference failures into broad compliance credit when agent and reference share an unstable rollout transformation, undermining the validity of such scores.

Method: An audit of NAVSIM v2.2 original scene single-stage scoring is conducted. The authors test a route-blind Ignore-All probe and a route-aware actor-blind probe against human replay and PDM-Closed on the full 12,146-token navtest split. A fresh installation on a fixed 32-token diagnostic set reproduces rollout divergence. A same-source dependency stack control and exact-input diagnostic isolate the numerical instability to the shared velocity refit. A 450-token control pool confirms that replacing only the solver eliminates rollout divergence and restores blind-last ordering.

Result: Under the affected documented-stack condition, blind probes outrank human replay and PDM-Closed over the complete navtest split. Rollout divergence is reproduced on a diagnostic set. The numerical instability in the shared velocity refit is identified as the direct trigger. Replacing only the solver eliminates divergence and restores correct blind-last ordering while forgiveness remains enabled.

Conclusion: Reference-conditioned forgiveness propagates shared reference failures from numerical instability into compliance credit, undermining defensive driving score validity. The authors contribute an audit protocol requiring score basis and stack disclosure, blind probes, overwrite reporting, and rollout stability tests before using such scores for defensive driving claims.

Abstract: Defensive driving scores are useful only when they preserve distinctions between policies that observe surrounding actors and those that do not. Re-simulation benchmarks may use reference-conditioned forgiveness, under which an agent receives credit when the logged human reference fails a compliance channel. When agent and reference share an unstable rollout transformation, this rule can propagate shared reference failures into broad compliance credit.
  We audit this risk in NAVSIM v2.2 original scene single-stage scoring. Under the affected documented-stack condition on the audited numerical backend, the route-blind Ignore-All probe and a route-aware actor-blind probe outrank human replay and PDM-Closed over the complete 12,146-token navtest split. A fresh installation following the public specification reproduces rollout divergence on a fixed 32-token diagnostic set. A same-source dependency stack control and an exact-input diagnostic isolate dependency-sensitive numerical behavior in the shared velocity refit. On a 450-token control pool, replacing only the solver eliminates rollout divergence and restores blind-last ordering while keeping forgiveness enabled. Thus, the numerical instability is the direct trigger. Reference-conditioned forgiveness propagates the resulting shared reference failures into compliance credit. We contribute an audit protocol requiring score basis and stack disclosure, blind probes, overwrite reporting, and rollout stability tests before using such scores for defensive driving claims.

</details>


### [158] [WorldCycle: Self-Verifiable Reinforcement Learning for Long-Horizon Video World Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04964)
*Bohai Gu,Yueyang Yuan,Taiyi Wu,Dazhao Du,Jian Liu,Xiaoyi Pang,Jie Zhang,Xiaocheng Lu,Haobin Zhong,Xiaotong Zhao,Alan Zhao,Song Guo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: WorldCycle is a self-verifiable RL framework that improves interactive video world models by enforcing consistency over closed action cycles — sequences that return to the initial state — reducing long-horizon drift without ground-truth supervision and dramatically improving composite-action accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Interactive video world models suffer from compounding errors over long horizons. While RL-based post-training can help, there is no ground-truth future state for arbitrary action sequences, creating a verification bottleneck that makes measuring and correcting long-term drift infeasible.

Method: The core insight is that reversible action cycles (a sequence composed with its inverse) must analytically return to the initial state, enabling annotation-free supervision. WorldCycle constructs closed action cycles from ordinary sequences and optimizes two rewards: (1) a spatial closure reward that enforces symmetry between mirrored forward and reverse segments, and (2) a temporal consistency reward that aligns states across repeated cycle executions. These force the model to learn actions as consistent state operators rather than memorized temporal patterns, and generalize to out-of-distribution composite action cycles. The authors also release CycleBench, a diagnostic benchmark for state-returning ability.

Result: WorldCycle reduces state-returning drift by up to 44% and improves composite-action accuracy by nearly 4x over the base model.

Conclusion: Self-verification via reversible action cycles provides a principled and effective way to enforce long-horizon consistency in video world models without requiring ground-truth future states, offering a crucial foundation for physically grounded world modeling.

Abstract: Interactive video world models are essential for long-horizon planning and exploration, yet they suffer from compounding errors. Post-training methods such as reinforcement learning (RL) can improve these models, but they hit a verification bottleneck: for arbitrary action sequences, no ground-truth future state exists to measure long-term drift. Our key insight is that reversible action cycles make this verification possible: a sequence composed with its inverse must analytically return to the initial state, yielding annotation-free supervision on long-horizon correctness.
