However, label-aware dense masking is stronger for accuracy alone (85.2/83.7). SpecDrop achieves 58%/100% branch-category alignment with masking gains of 0.00/+1.06, indicating the output-space restriction is largely internalized during training. On fuzzy-partition tasks, routing reduces to the No-Routing control within seed noise, confirming the granularity-alignment thesis.

Conclusion: Granularity alignment between training signals and target categories, not routing algorithm choice, determines when routing helps in MoE networks. SpecDrop demonstrates that category supervision can be converted into trained-in modular structure, but the benefit is contingent on crisp category boundaries in the training objective.

Abstract: Mixture-of-experts (MoE) networks pursue specialization through learned routers, gates, and load-balancing losses, yet at matched total-parameter budgets learned routers can underperform equal-weight No-Routing baselines. Is the bottleneck the routing algorithm, or the alignment between training-signal granularity and the target categories? We probe the question with SpecDrop, a fixed parameter-free routing scheme: each of $K$ branches receives weight $p_a$ for its assigned category and a small leakage $p_i > 0$ otherwise, merged through a category-independent fixed denominator, with no learned routing parameters and no auxiliary losses; the category label is required at inference. On vision tasks where each image has one superclass label (CIFAR-100 on ResNet-110; ImageNet-1K on ViT-S/16), SpecDrop reaches 79.23% on CIFAR-100 and 79.89% on ImageNet-1K, exceeding parameter-matched baselines that do not use the label (+4.75 over dense on CIFAR-100; +6.53 over the No-Routing+SE control on ImageNet-1K). These gains quantify what category supervision buys when deployed through routing -- not an advantage over label-aware deployments of the baselines: given the same label, masking a dense model's outputs is stronger for accuracy alone (85.2 / 83.7). SpecDrop's contribution is converting the label into trained-in modular structure: 58%/100% branch-category alignment, and masking gains of 0.00 (CIFAR) / +1.06 (ImageNet) -- the output-space restriction is largely internalized during training. On fuzzy partitions, where training units span multiple categories (SlimPajama-6B language modeling with a 30M Transformer; SuperNI instruction tuning over Llama-3.2-1B with LoRA), the routing mechanism reduces to the matched No-Routing controls within seed noise, the null our thesis predicts. Granularity alignment, not algorithm choice, localizes when routing helps. Code: https://github.com/Beryex/SpecDrop

</details>


### [181] [Out-Of-The-Loop Multi-Fidelity Bayesian Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04113)
*Gustavo Sutter,Hao Wang,Luis Ricardez-Sandoval,Pascal Poupart,Agustinus Kristiadi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Standard multi-fidelity Bayesian optimization (MF-BO) fails when the highest-fidelity function is too expensive for the optimization loop. The authors propose incorporating historical high-fidelity data with task descriptors to improve performance, demonstrating effectiveness on synthetic and real-world tasks in chemistry and hyperparameter optimization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In many real-world MF-BO settings, the highest-fidelity function is prohibitively expensive to query during optimization, yet practitioners often possess "gold standard" historical data (e.g., top-k candidates from prior experiments). Standard MF-BO algorithms perform suboptimally in these scenarios, even under ideal assumptions, because they cannot leverage this offline high-fidelity information effectively.

Method: The authors incorporate historical high-fidelity data into MF-BO by using task descriptors—which can be explicitly provided or extracted from unstructured metadata—to transfer knowledge from prior related tasks. This enables the model to condition on past gold-standard observations when optimizing a new task, mitigating the reliance on expensive online queries of the highest-fidelity function.

Result: The proposed method outperforms standard MF-BO algorithms on synthetic functions and real-world problems in molecular optimization and hyperparameter optimization, where historical high-fidelity data is available but the true highest-fidelity function remains too costly for online evaluation.

Conclusion: Incorporating historical high-fidelity data with task descriptors significantly improves multi-fidelity Bayesian optimization in settings where online access to the highest-fidelity function is infeasible, addressing a critical limitation of standard MF-BO in practical applications.

Abstract: Black-box optimization is a ubiquitous problem in science and engineering, often dealing with expensive objective functions with cheaper lower-fidelity proxies available. Multi-fidelity Bayesian optimization (MF-BO) is a principled approach to this problem, leveraging correlations across different fidelities when querying the objective. However, for many important MF-BO tasks, the true highest-fidelity function is prohibitively expensive to be part of the optimization loop. Nevertheless, practitioners often have gold standard data (observations of the highest-fidelity function) obtained from previous experiments that might provide information for the current task. For instance, in molecular optimization, chemists often pick the top-$k$ candidate molecules using various computer simulations, and later reveal their true objective function values. In this work, we demonstrate the suboptimality of standard MF-BO algorithms in the real-world scenarios above, even under ideal assumptions. Next, we mitigate this problem by incorporating historical high-fidelity data accompanied by task descriptors---which can be explicitly given or extracted from unstructured metadata. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our methods on synthetic functions, as well as real-world problems in chemistry and hyperparameter optimization.

</details>


### [182] [LiNC: Lightweight Noise Correction via Per-Sample Trust and Gaussian Mixture Modeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04147)
*Abhishek Moturu,Babak Taati,Anna Goldenberg*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: LiNC introduces per-sample trust parameters that learn to interpolate between observed labels and model predictions during training, using a 3-component GMM to separate clean, ambiguous, and noisy samples, followed by soft-then-hard correction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Label noise in medical imaging—from inter-rater variability, annotation errors, and ambiguous cases—degrades model reliability and clinical utility. Existing noise-robust methods often incur significant computational overhead, motivating a lightweight alternative.

Method: LiNC augments standard training with one trainable trust parameter per sample. The loss uses a convex combination of the observed label and the model's predictive distribution, weighted by this trust value. Early-training gradient dynamics naturally separate clean (trust → 1) from noisy (trust → 0) samples. A 3-component Gaussian Mixture Model is then fit to trust values to classify samples as clean, ambiguous, or noisy. A short soft-correction phase (using a blend of label and prediction) is applied to noisy samples, followed by hard correction (using the model's prediction as the target).

Result: On ten 2D MedMNISTv2 datasets under up to 50% label noise, LiNC achieves consistent accuracy gains and strong mislabel detection performance. Overhead is negligible: asymptotic training complexity matches the base network, with additional memory linear in dataset size.

Conclusion: LiNC provides an effective, lightweight mechanism for handling label noise in medical imaging by learning per-sample trust parameters that naturally separate noisy from clean samples, enabling targeted correction with minimal computational cost.

Abstract: Label noise is common in medical imaging datasets due to factors such as inter-rater variability, annotation errors, and ambiguous cases. This can severely undermine the reliability and clinical effectiveness of machine learning models trained using those datasets. To address this challenge, we introduce Lightweight Noise Correction (LiNC), which adds a single trainable trust parameter per training sample and learns when to use the observed label and when to defer to the model during a standard training loop. The key idea is to train using a convex combination of the observed label and the model's own predictive distribution, controlled by a per-sample trust parameter. We show that the gradient of this objective drives trust values in opposite directions for clean versus noisy samples in the early training phase, yielding separable trust distributions. We use a 3-component Gaussian Mixture Model over the trust values to separate them into clean, ambiguous, and noisy cases and then execute a short soft-correction phase on the noisy cases and a final hard correction phase. Experiments on ten 2D datasets from MedMNISTv2 under label noise of up to 50% show consistent gains in accuracy and strong mislabel detection. LiNC adds negligible asymptotic overhead: the training-time complexity remains dominated by the base network, with additional memory growing linearly with the size of the training set.

</details>


### [183] [MINT: Tensor Decomposition on Stacked Recurrence Matrices for Time Series Data Mining](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04157)
*Kaamil Kaka,Audrey Der,Evangelos E. Papalexakis,Zachary Zimmerman,Vikram Jayaram*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes tensorized self-similarity matrices (a generalization of recurrence plots) for mining univariate time series datasets. The method computes N×(n-m+1)×(n-m+1) dot plots and applies tensor decomposition to discover co-clustered patterns across multiple time series, demonstrated on transit, electricity, wind turbine, and traffic data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional recurrence plots and self-similarity matrices are limited to analyzing individual time series in isolation. There is a need for a primitive that can simultaneously mine patterns across multiple time series in a dataset, capturing cross-sensor relationships and co-clustered motifs at regular intervals.

Method: The MINT pipeline: (1) Given an N×n dataset (N time series, length n) with subsequence window m, compute dot plots producing a 3-way tensor of size N×(n-m+1)×(n-m+1); (2) Apply tensor decomposition methods to this tensor to extract co-clustered patterns across the N time series; (3) The tensor-based formulation is naturally extensible to multivariate datasets.

Result: The MINT pipeline effectively co-clusters cross-sensor patterns in highly regular datasets containing motifs at regular intervals. Successful demonstrations are reported across four domains: mass rapid transit, electricity demand, wind turbine, and car traffic data.

Conclusion: Tensorized self-similarity matrices serve as an effective primitive for multi-time-series pattern mining, with tensor decomposition enabling joint discovery of co-clustered motifs across sensors in regular, motif-rich datasets.

Abstract: Recurrence plots are a time series data mining primitive applied to a variety of domains (e.g. star light curves, sound waveforms, CCT telemetry). This work proposes tensorized self-similarity matrices as a primitive for univariate time series datasets ($N\times n$) of $N$ time series of length $n$ with a subsequence window of length $m$, and whose tensor-based nature is naturally extensible to multivariate datasets. The proposed method to compute this primitive computes dot plots of size $N \times (n-m+1) \times (n-m+ 1)$ from these datasets, where the subsequent tensor is mined using tensor decomposition methods to mine for co-clustered patterns. We demonstrate our results in mass rapid transit, electricity demand, wind turbine, and car traffic data, finding the MINT pipeline effectively co-clusters cross-sensor patterns in highly regular datasets containing motifs at regular intervals.

</details>


### [184] [Understanding Fault Tolerance of Adversarially Robust Pruned Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04173)
*Manali Dangarikar,Cory Merkel*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper empirically studies the combined effects of pruning, adversarial training, and hardware-induced stuck-at-zero weight faults on CNN robustness. Key finding: adversarial training improves perturbation robustness but increases fault sensitivity; surprisingly, pruning has negligible impact on fault tolerance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Neuromorphic hardware-deployed DNNs simultaneously face three challenges: model compression (pruning), adversarial attacks, and hardware weight faults (stuck-at-zero). These factors have been studied separately, but their interactions and combined effects on reliability remain unexplored.

Method: The authors use a compact three-layer CNN trained on MNIST. Three experiments are conducted: (1) comparing fault tolerance of naturally vs. adversarially trained models under simultaneous hardware faults and adversarial attacks; (2) evaluating pruning's effect on adversarial robustness; (3) mapping the joint accuracy surface across fault rates, adversarial perturbation magnitudes, and pruning levels.

Result: Adversarial training improves robustness against input perturbations but increases sensitivity to stuck-at-zero weight faults. Pruning does not significantly increase fault sensitivity, contrary to intuition. Varying pruning level had minimal effect across different fault rates and attack strengths.

Conclusion: Adversarial robustness and hardware reliability must be jointly considered when deploying DNNs on resource-constrained neuromorphic hardware, as adversarial training introduces a trade-off with hardware fault tolerance.

Abstract: Deep neural networks (DNNs) deployed on resource-constrained neuromorphic hardware face three concurrent challenges: the need for model compression through pruning, vulnerability to adversarial input perturbations, and susceptibility to hardware-induced weight faults such as stuck-at-zero errors. While each of these factors has been studied in isolation, their combined effects on model reliability have received little attention. This paper presents an empirical investigation of how pruning, adversarial training, and hardware fault injection interact to affect the robustness of convolutional neural networks. Using a compact three-layer CNN trained on MNIST, we conduct three experiments: (1) comparing the fault tolerance of naturally and adversarially trained models under simultaneous hardware faults and adversarial attacks, (2) evaluating how pruning affects adversarial robustness, and (3) characterizing the joint accuracy surface across fault rates, adversarial perturbation magnitudes, and pruning levels. Our results show that adversarial training improves robustness against input perturbations but increases sensitivity to stuck-at-zero weight faults. Contrary to intuition, pruning did not significantly increase fault sensitivity, and varying the pruning level had little effect across fault rates and attack strengths. These results highlight the need to jointly consider adversarial robustness and hardware reliability.

</details>


### [185] [TS2TabPFN: Time Series Classification and Extrinsic Regression through Feature Extraction and a Tabular Foundation Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04174)
*Gabriel da Costa Merlin,Diego Furtado Silva*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: TS2TabPFN bridges the gap between feature engineering and end-to-end deep learning for time series by integrating explicit feature extraction with TabPFN 2.5, a tabular foundation model, achieving state-of-the-art results on both time series classification (TSC) and extrinsic regression (TSER).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing time series methods are bifurcated: feature-based approaches offer control and interpretability, while deep learning models provide automated predictive power from raw data. Neither paradigm alone achieves optimal performance, creating a gap between engineered features and end-to-end architectures that the authors aim to close.

Method: TS2TabPFN extracts explicit, structured features from time series data and feeds them into TabPFN 2.5, a state-of-the-art foundation model designed for tabular data. This hybrid approach combines handcrafted feature extraction with the powerful in-context learning and predictive capabilities of a pretrained tabular foundation model.

Result: TS2TabPFN significantly outperforms state-of-the-art models on TSER tasks with statistical significance. For TSC, it surpasses most current best-performing algorithms, establishing a new benchmark for time series tasks.

Conclusion: Combining structured feature extraction with foundation models overcomes the limitations of single-paradigm approaches. This integration establishes a new state-of-the-art for time series analysis and suggests a promising direction for future research at the intersection of feature engineering and foundation models.

Abstract: Time series data are ubiquitous in practical applications, where classification (TSC) and extrinsic regression (TSER) have emerged as essential tasks for obtaining value from temporal sequences. While the literature has seen significant progress through feature-based and deep learning models, existing methods often focus either on the quality of feature extraction or on the intrinsic predictive power of complex architectures applied to raw data. This division creates a gap between the control offered by feature engineering and the automated performance of end-to-end models. This paper proposes TS2TabPFN, a framework that bridges this gap by integrating explicit feature extraction with TabPFN 2.5, a cutting-edge foundation model for tabular data, to leverage its predictive capabilities. Our extensive experimental evaluation demonstrates that TS2TabPFN significantly outperforms state-of-the-art models in TSER tasks with statistical significance, providing a robust and efficient alternative for TSC and surpassing most of the currently best-performing algorithms. These results suggest that combining foundation models with structured features overcomes single-paradigm limitations, establishing a new time series state-of-the-art.

</details>


### [186] [A Comparative Study of Feature Selection Methods for EHR Diagnosis Codes in Opioid Use Disorder Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04180)
*Zihan Ding,Yinan Liu,Tengfei Ma,Rachel Wong,George Leibowitz,Benjamin Littenberg,Xia Zheng,Richard N. Rosenthal,Fusheng Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper compares five feature selection methods — recurrence enrichment, NTK-motivated early gradient sensitivity, LightGBM-SHAP, Elastic Net, and LLM-guided semantic selection — for predicting opioid use disorder (OUD) from EHR diagnosis codes. NTK sensitivity offers the best accuracy-stability trade-off, while LLM-guided selection adds clinically meaningful complementary signals.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: EHR-based predictive modeling suffers from high-dimensional, sparse, noisy, and redundant features, leading to computational burden, overfitting, and poor interpretability. The authors aim to systematically compare feature selection paradigms to identify methods that yield compact, stable, and clinically useful feature sets for OUD prediction.

Method: The authors evaluate five feature selection paradigms under a unified preprocessing and evaluation framework: (1) recurrence enrichment, (2) NTK-motivated early gradient sensitivity, (3) LightGBM-SHAP, (4) Elastic Net, and (5) LLM-guided semantic selection. Methods are assessed on downstream predictive performance, resampling stability, and representation of infrequent diagnosis codes across varying feature budgets.

Result: Predictive performance improves with larger feature budgets but shows diminishing returns beyond a moderate size. NTK sensitivity achieves the best overall balance of accuracy and stability. LLM-guided selection, while having lower standalone performance, contributes complementary clinically meaningful signals not captured by other methods.

Conclusion: NTK-motivated early gradient sensitivity is recommended as the most balanced feature selection approach for EHR-based OUD prediction. LLM-guided semantic selection can serve as a complementary strategy to inject clinical domain knowledge, and feature budget should be moderate to avoid diminishing returns.

Abstract: Feature selection is a critical step in electronic health record (EHR)-based predictive modeling, where input variables are often high-dimensional, sparse, noisy, and redundant. Large feature sets not only increase computational burden and overfitting risk, but also make model interpretation difficult, leading to limited usefulness in clinical settings. In this study, we focus on diagnosis-related features and compare five feature selection paradigms for opioid use disorder (OUD) prediction: recurrence enrichment, NTK-motivated early gradient sensitivity, LightGBM-SHAP, Elastic Net, and large language model (LLM)-guided semantic selection. We use a unified preprocessing and evaluation framework and assess each method by downstream predictive performance, resampling stability, and representation of infrequent diagnosis codes. Our results demonstrate that performance improves with larger feature budgets with diminishing returns beyond a moderate size. NTK sensitivity provides the best overall balance of accuracy and stability, and LLM-guided selection contributes complementary clinically meaningful signals despite lower standalone performance.

</details>


### [187] [Unscented KalmanNet: a hybrid deep learning filter with calibrated posterior covariance for nonlinear state estimation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04201)
*Minhyeok Ko,Abdollah Shafieezadeh*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Unscented KalmanNet (UKN) augments the UKF with two learned neural components—NoiseNet for adaptive time-varying noise covariance estimation and GainNet for residual Kalman gain correction—trained with a calibration-aware loss. UKN achieves 26.4–49.7% RMSE reduction over UKF on synthetic benchmarks and 22.4–34.3% improvement on real-flight data, with superior covariance calibration.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The UKF is widely used for nonlinear state estimation but suffers degradation from unknown, time-varying noise statistics and model mismatch, which harm both accuracy and covariance calibration. Existing learned filters (mostly EKF-based) improve accuracy but either discard explicit covariance or fail to correct mismatch-induced gain bias.

Method: UKN wraps the UKF's sigma-point covariance recursion with two learned modules: (1) NoiseNet, which predicts time-varying process/measurement covariances as bounded multiplicative corrections to fixed baselines, ensuring positive definiteness; (2) GainNet, which applies a bounded residual correction to the analytical Kalman gain. Training uses a calibration-aware objective combining state-error, covariance-consistency, and innovation-consistency terms with adaptive weights, optimized end-to-end via backpropagation through the UKF recursion.

Result: UKN achieves the lowest aggregate RMSE across all four test scenarios (three synthetic, one real UZH-FPV). Synthetic-case RMSE reductions: 26.4–49.7% vs. UKF. Real-flight LOOCV over 11 flights: 22.4% mean position RMSE reduction, 34.3% mean velocity RMSE reduction. UKN shows lowest fold-to-fold variability, with normalized NEES and empirical coverage closest to nominal values among UKF, KalmanNet, and Bayesian KalmanNet.

Conclusion: UKN demonstrates that augmenting the UKF with structurally constrained, physically interpretable neural corrections yields simultaneous improvements in state estimation accuracy and uncertainty calibration, outperforming both classical UKF and existing learned filtering approaches on synthetic and real-world nonlinear estimation tasks.

Abstract: State estimation for nonlinear dynamical systems is commonly performed with the Unscented Kalman filter (UKF), which propagates the state moments through deterministic sigma points and reports a posterior covariance at every step. In practice, however, unknown and time-varying noise statistics and model mismatch degrade both estimation accuracy and covariance calibration. Existing learned filters improve accuracy but are largely built on the extended Kalman filter and either forgo an explicit covariance or learn uncertainty without correcting mismatch-induced gain bias. This paper introduces the Unscented KalmanNet (UKN), a hybrid recursive estimator that augments the UKF with two structurally distinct learned components while preserving its explicit sigma-point covariance recursion. NoiseNet predicts time-varying process and measurement covariances as bounded multiplicative corrections to fixed baselines, guaranteeing positive definiteness, while GainNet applies a bounded residual correction to the analytical gain. A calibration-aware training objective combines state error with covariance- and innovation-consistency terms through adaptive weights, jointly optimizing accuracy and calibration. UKN is benchmarked against UKF, KalmanNet, and Bayesian KalmanNet on three synthetic systems and UZH-FPV real-flight data. It achieves the lowest aggregate state-estimation error in all four examples and reduces RMSE by $26.4$-$49.7\%$ compared to UKF in the synthetic cases. Leave-one-sequence-out cross-validation over 11 flights shows $22.4\%$ and $34.3\%$ reductions in mean position and velocity RMSE, respectively. UKN also yields the lowest fold-to-fold variability, with normalized NEES and empirical coverage closest to nominal values among the other filters.

</details>


### [188] [From Non-Convex Self-Concordant Regularization to Scalable Quasi-Newton Training of PINNs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04206)
*Chenhao Si,Kang An,Shiqian Ma,Ming Yan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SCORE is a self-concordance-inspired quasi-Newton method for PINN training that uses a single quasi-Newton decrement to jointly determine step selection and shifted secant geometry, avoiding Hessian construction while achieving lower final errors than BFGS and self-scaled Broyden baselines on multiple PDE benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: PINNs require high-accuracy quasi-Newton refinement for reliable PDE solutions, but their residual objectives exhibit indefinite, nearly singular, and poorly scaled local curvature — conditions that destabilize standard quasi-Newton methods. Existing regularized quasi-Newton methods offer stabilization mechanisms and self-concordant methods provide curvature-dependent step rules, but these two lines of work have not been integrated for PINN training.

Method: SCORE combines: (1) a learned inverse metric that produces a quasi-Newton decrement, which simultaneously determines a strong-Wolfe-tested candidate step and an adaptive shift for the next secant geometry; (2) a shifted displacement representing the action of an averaged shifted metric along the accepted step, requiring no Hessian construction or Hessian-vector products; (3) strong Wolfe acceptance, fallback line search, and standard curvature safeguards for globalization. Under a local spectral-equivalence condition, the decrement and candidate step recover the normalized self-concordant rule in the matched-metric case.

Result: Experiments on viscous Burgers, Kuramoto-Sivashinsky, Korteweg-de Vries, and complex Ginzburg-Landau equations demonstrate that SCORE achieves lower final errors than tested BFGS and self-scaled Broyden baselines. A Burgers ablation study shows that shifted curvature stabilization and decrement-based step selection make complementary contributions to high-accuracy refinement.

Conclusion: SCORE effectively integrates self-concordant step selection with regularized quasi-Newton secant updates for PINN training, providing robust high-accuracy refinement without Hessian access. The complementary roles of curvature stabilization and decrement-based step selection suggest both components are necessary for optimal performance.

Abstract: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) often require high-accuracy quasi-Newton refinement to obtain reliable partial differential equation solutions, but their residual objectives can exhibit indefinite, nearly singular, and poorly scaled local curvature. Regularized quasi-Newton methods provide established mechanisms for stabilizing secant models, while self-concordant methods provide local-metric rules for curvature-dependent step selection. Building on these two lines of work, we propose SCORE, a self-concordance-inspired quasi-Newton method with decrement-coupled shifted secant geometry for PINN training. Its distinguishing mechanism is that a single quasi-Newton decrement computed from the learned inverse metric jointly determines a strong-Wolfe-tested candidate step and an adaptive shift used to define the next secant geometry. The shifted displacement represents the action of an averaged shifted metric along the accepted step, while requiring neither Hessian construction nor Hessian-vector products. Under a local spectral-equivalence condition, we show that the quasi-Newton decrement and candidate step remain comparable to their counterparts in a positive shifted metric, and recover the normalized self-concordant rule in the matched-metric case. Strong Wolfe acceptance, fallback line search, and standard curvature safeguards provide globalization without modifying the underlying PINN objective. Experiments on the viscous Burgers, Kuramoto--Sivashinsky, Korteweg--de Vries, and complex Ginzburg--Landau equations show that SCORE attains lower final errors than the tested BFGS and self-scaled Broyden baselines. The Burgers ablation further indicates that shifted curvature stabilization and decrement-based step selection make complementary contributions to high-accuracy refinement.

</details>


### [189] [Attention-Only White-Box Transformer via LeJEPA-Based Self-Supervised Pretraining](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04213)
*Yang Bai,Linyuan Wang,Haoyang Jiang,Nuolin Sun,Libin Hou,Bin Yan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper unifies self-supervised learning (LeJEPA) with white-box Transformer optimization (sparse rate reduction), deriving an attention-only Transformer via ADMM that drops ISTA/MLP layers. The resulting model matches CRATE performance on CIFAR-10/100 with ~31% fewer parameters. Extending to standard ViTs, replacing MLPs with ReLU under distillation removes ~66% of parameters while maintaining accuracy, suggesting MLP redundancy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing white-box network research treats the derivation of network architectures via optimization algorithms and self-supervised learning paradigms as separate, decoupled problems. The authors aim to unify these two components by revealing a conceptual equivalence between LeJEPA's isotropic Gaussian embedding assumption and the expansion term in the sparse rate reduction objective, thereby enabling a joint optimization perspective that can simplify white-box Transformer design.

Method: The authors observe that the LeJEPA self-supervised framework's assumption of an isotropic Gaussian optimal embedding distribution is conceptually equivalent to the expansion term R(Z) in the sparse rate reduction objective used for white-box Transformer optimization. They then use LeJEPA to optimize R(Z) and derive the remaining terms (the compression term R^c(Z|U_[K]) plus the L0 sparsity penalty) via the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM). This derivation yields an attention-only Transformer architecture that eliminates the ISTA structure and MLP layers present in the original CRATE design. Additionally, they investigate standard ViTs by replacing all MLP blocks with ReLU activations under knowledge distillation.

Result: The attention-only white-box Transformer achieves 88.88% on CIFAR-10 and 63.54% on CIFAR-100 at Base scale under LeJEPA, closely matching CRATE's 89.18% and 63.56% respectively, while reducing parameters by ~31%. In the standard ViT setting, replacing MLP blocks with ReLU under knowledge distillation removes ~66% of parameters while preserving competitive accuracy.

Conclusion: The joint perspective on self-supervised learning and white-box network derivation yields a simplified attention-only Transformer that is competitive with CRATE while being more parameter-efficient. The findings also suggest significant redundancy of MLP modules in standard ViT architectures, warranting further investigation into their necessity.

Abstract: Existing studies on self-supervised learning for white-box networks typically decouple the derivation of white-box networks via optimization algorithms from self-supervised learning paradigms. In this work, we instead revisit the two components from a joint perspective. The LeJEPA-based self-supervised framework assumes an isotropic Gaussian distribution as the optimal embedding distribution for downstream tasks, which is conceptually equivalent to the expansion term $R(Z)$ in the sparse rate reduction objective guiding white-box Transformer optimization. Building on this observation, we use the LeJEPA self-supervised paradigm to optimize $R(Z)$, and derive the remaining terms $R^{c}(Z\mid U_{[K]})+λ\lVert Z\rVert_{0}$ via the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) into an attention-only Transformer that dispenses with the ISTA structure or MLP layers of the original design. Experimental results demonstrate that our attention-only white-box Transformer achieves classification accuracies of $88.88\%$ on CIFAR-10 and $63.54\%$ on CIFAR-100 at the Base scale under the LeJEPA self-supervised paradigm, while the original white-box Transformer CRATE achieves classification accuracies of $89.18\%$ on CIFAR-10 and $63.56\%$ on CIFAR-100. Our model achieves competitive performance while reducing the parameter count by roughly $31\%$. Beyond the white-box setting, we further investigate standard ViTs and find that replacing all MLP blocks with ReLU activations under knowledge distillation removes approximately 66\% of the parameters while preserving competitive accuracy, motivating further investigation into the potential redundancy of MLP modules in standard ViT architectures.

</details>


### [190] [Random features for Grassmannian kernel approximation with bounded rank-one projections](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04227)
*Rémi Delogne,Laurent Jacques*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes a random feature framework for scalable kernel learning on the Grassmannian manifold, using rank-one projections with bounded nonlinear transforms to approximate rotation-invariant kernels without computing full Gram matrices.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Classical Grassmannian kernels (projection, Binet-Cauchy) require full Gram matrices, causing prohibitive computational and memory costs for large, high-dimensional subspace datasets. A scalable approximation is needed.

Method: Random features are generated via rank-one projections of subspace projection matrices, followed by bounded nonlinear transforms (periodic or binary). Structured rank-one projections using randomized FFT further reduce computation. Inner products in the random feature space approximate rotation-invariant Grassmannian kernels depending on principal angles.

Result: With sufficiently many features relative to intrinsic subspace dimension, the approximation holds uniformly over fixed-dimensional subspaces with high probability. Periodic transforms yield a closed-form kernel tunable between inverse Binet-Cauchy and Gaussian regimes. Binary transforms give compact one-bit features. Experiments on synthetic data and ETH-80 confirm accurate geometry preservation with reduced computation, memory, and storage.

Conclusion: Rank-one embeddings provide a practical, scalable alternative to classical Grassmannian kernels for subspace-based learning tasks.

Abstract: We propose a family of random feature maps for scalable kernel machines on low-dimensional subspaces, ie on the Grassmannian manifold. Such representations are useful when data classes or clusters are well described by the span of a few samples. Classical Grassmannian kernels, including the projection and Binet-Cauchy kernels, require full Gram matrices, which leads to prohibitive computational and memory costs for large high-dimensional subspace datasets. We address this limitation using random features based on rank-one projections of subspace projection matrices followed by bounded non-linear transforms, either periodic or binary, to control the resulting distributions.
  We show that inner products in the random feature space approximate well-defined rotation-invariant Grassmannian kernels that depend only on the principal angles between subspaces. When the number of features is sufficiently large relative to the intrinsic subspace dimension, the approximation holds uniformly over all fixed-dimensional subspaces with high probability. For periodic transforms, the approximated kernel has a closed-form expression with tunable behaviour between inverse Binet-Cauchy and Gaussian-type regimes. Binary transforms yield compact one-bit subspace features, although no closed-form kernel is known. Structured rank-one projections based on randomised fast Fourier transforms further reduce computation without sacrificing practical accuracy. Experiments on synthetic data and ETH-80 classification tasks show that these features accurately preserve Grassmannian geometry while reducing computation, memory, and storage. Rank-one embeddings therefore provide a practical and scalable alternative to classical Grassmannian kernels.

</details>


### [191] [Transferable Dual-Stream Representations for Mesoscale-Preserving Sea Surface Temperature Downscaling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04230)
*Parth Doshi,Priyanka Aravindan,Vaishnav Vaidheeswaran,Md Mahbub Alam,Gabriel Spadon*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: EddyFlow is a representation learning framework for kilometer-scale sea surface temperature downscaling that balances accuracy, scale-dependent structure, and regional generalization. It reduces zero-shot RMSE by 21%, achieves 85.6% skill relative to persistence on unseen domains, and maintains near-ideal spectral fidelity (PSD ratio ≈1.00).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing deep learning models for spatio-temporal downscaling minimize reconstruction error but produce overly smooth outputs that lack mesoscale variability (e.g., eddies), critical for regional ocean dynamics. Current methods rely on pixel-wise objectives or single-context conditioning, limiting spectral fidelity and cross-region generalization.

Method: EddyFlow is a representation learning framework that incorporates physics-informed constraints to preserve multi-scale structure. It is trained on the Gulf of St. Lawrence and evaluated in zero-shot and few-shot settings on the Bay of Fundy and the Gulf of Mexico.

Result: EddyFlow reduces zero-shot RMSE by 21%, achieves up to 85.6% skill relative to persistence on unseen domains, and maintains near-ideal spectral fidelity with a power spectral density (PSD) ratio of approximately 1.00.

Conclusion: Physics-informed representation learning effectively addresses the spectral fidelity and generalization limitations of conventional downscaling methods, producing physically plausible, multi-scale SST predictions that transfer robustly to unseen ocean regions.

Abstract: Deep learning models for scientific spatio-temporal downscaling often minimize reconstruction error while failing to preserve physically meaningful multi-scale structure. For sea surface temperature prediction, this can yield outputs that are numerically plausible yet overly smooth, missing mesoscale variability critical to regional ocean dynamics. Existing methods often focus on pixel-wise objectives or single-context conditioning, which limits their ability to preserve spectral fidelity and generalize across regions. To address this, we propose EddyFlow, a representation learning framework for kilometer-scale sea surface temperature downscaling that balances predictive accuracy, scale-dependent structure, and regional generalization. EddyFlow is trained on the Gulf of St.~Lawrence and evaluated in zero-shot and few-shot settings on the Bay of Fundy and the Gulf of Mexico. EddyFlow demonstrates that physics-informed representation learning reduces zero-shot RMSE by 21%, achieves up to 85.6% skill relative to persistence on unseen domains, and maintains near-ideal spectral fidelity with a PSD ratio of $\approx 1.00$.

</details>


### [192] [Physics-informed reduced-order modelling with equivariant spectral submanifolds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04239)
*Georg Maierhofer*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces equivariant spectral submanifold (eSSM) reduction, which incorporates symmetries of full-order models into SSM-based model reduction, yielding faster computation and improved robustness, demonstrated on benchmark problems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: SSM reduction is a mathematically rigorous method for nonlinear reduced-order modeling that outperforms linear techniques like DMD, but its computation is prohibitively expensive for high-dimensional systems. The authors aim to address this computational bottleneck by leveraging inherent symmetries in the full-order model.

Method: The authors establish mathematical foundations proving that SSMs are naturally equivariant submanifolds, with charts and reduced dynamics inheriting appropriate induced group actions. They develop a novel equivariant SSM reduction algorithm that explicitly exploits these symmetries during the reduction process.

Result: The eSSM approach achieves substantially faster computations and improved model robustness compared to standard SSM reduction. Advantages are demonstrated on several benchmark problems, including a test from the Common Task Framework for Science.

Conclusion: Incorporating symmetries into the SSM framework via equivariant SSM reduction significantly reduces computational cost while enhancing robustness, making nonlinear reduced-order modeling more practical for high-dimensional systems.

Abstract: Spectral submanifold (SSM) reduction has emerged as a mathematically principled route to reliable nonlinear reduced-order models, capturing dynamics beyond the reach of linear techniques such as Dynamic Mode Decomposition (DMD). The computation of SSMs, however, remains computationally expensive, particularly for high-dimensional systems. In this work, we introduce equivariant spectral submanifold (eSSM) reduction, a novel extension of the SSM framework that explicitly incorporates symmetries of the full-order model into the reduction process. We establish the mathematical foundations of this approach by showing that SSMs are naturally equivariant submanifolds and that the associated charts and reduced dynamics inherit the appropriate induced group actions. Building on this framework, we develop a novel equivariant SSM reduction algorithm that exploits these symmetries to achieve substantially faster computations while also improving model robustness. We demonstrate the advantages of this approach on several benchmark problems including a test from the Common Task Framework for Science.

</details>


### [193] [Attention-based representations for multi-task computation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04243)
*Daniel Hsu,Mingyue Xu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper establishes theoretical bounds on the number of attention heads required for multi-task learning in Transformers. It proves that for computing min/max of a list, one head requires exponentially larger embedding dimension or precision compared to two heads. For XOR and general symmetric Boolean functions, it derives lower bounds relating the product of head count and polynomial degree to input size, and constructs matching upper bounds.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Understanding the representational power and limitations of multi-head attention is fundamental to Transformer architectures. While multi-head attention empirically benefits multi-task learning, formal theoretical justification for why multiple heads are necessary in certain scenarios is lacking. The paper aims to provide rigorous lower bounds demonstrating that some tasks inherently require multiple heads, thus offering a theoretical foundation for the multi-head design.

Method: The paper uses a theoretical framework analyzing attention heads through the lens of representation theory and polynomial threshold functions. Two concrete multi-task scenarios are analyzed: (1) simultaneously computing min and max via linear predictors, where lower bounds on embedding dimension/precision are derived for single-head attention; (2) computing XOR (and general symmetric Boolean functions) via polynomial threshold functions, where lower bounds on the head-count × degree product are established using communication complexity and threshold degree arguments. Matching constructions are provided for the upper bounds.

Result: For the min/max scenario: a single attention head requires either embedding dimension or bit precision to grow exponentially relative to the two-head solution. For XOR: the product of number of heads and polynomial degree must be at least n for n-bit XOR, and matching multi-head constructions achieving this bound are provided. Results generalize to arbitrary symmetric Boolean functions with bounds expressed in terms of threshold degree.

Conclusion: Multi-head attention is not merely an empirical convenience but a theoretical necessity for certain multi-task learning problems. The paper formalizes trade-offs between number of heads, embedding dimension, precision, and polynomial degree, showing that reducing heads forces exponential blow-up in other resources. These results provide concrete lower bounds that justify the multi-head design paradigm in Transformers.

Abstract: Multi-head attention layers produce vector representations that support multiple downstream tasks. We establish bounds on the number of heads required in two simple and concrete multi-task scenarios. In the first scenario, a vector representation is sought so that linear predictors can compute both the smallest and largest numbers in a given list. In this case, it is known two attention heads with small embedding dimension and bit precision level suffice. We prove that a single attention head requires exponentially higher embedding dimension or precision level. In the second scenario, a vector representation is sought so that a polynomial threshold function can compute the XOR of a given string of $n$ bits. This scenario is analogous to the first one for $n=2$, since XOR is readily computed by a linear function using a vector representation that encodes both the AND and the OR of the two bits. We observe that $n$-bit XOR requires the product of the number of heads and the polynomial degree to be at least $n$, and we construct multi-head attention layers that match this lower bound. These results generalize to arbitrary (symmetric) Boolean functions, where the bound is given in terms of the threshold degree.

</details>


### [194] [Geometry-Informed Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning of Pre-trained Molecular GNNs for Blood-Brain Barrier Permeability Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04257)
*Marco Vieto Vega,Long D. Nguyen,Binh P. Nguyen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: BBBP-GeoPEFT is a parameter-efficient fine-tuning framework that enhances pre-trained molecular GNNs for blood-brain barrier permeability prediction by incorporating 3D geometric information via distance-based graphs and line graphs with cutoff attention and gated residual connections, achieving competitive performance while updating only ~10% of parameters.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Blood-brain barrier permeability (BBBP) prediction is critical for CNS drug discovery but is hampered by limited, class-imbalanced datasets. While pre-trained molecular GNNs offer transferable knowledge, full fine-tuning is parameter-inefficient and overfitting-prone, and existing PEFT methods focus only on node features or 2D covalent graphs, failing to capture 3D geometry and second-order edge interactions relevant to permeability.

Method: BBBP-GeoPEFT constructs distance-based graphs at multiple cutoffs and corresponding line graphs from molecular conformers to capture spatial atom-level and second-order edge-level interactions. Lightweight auxiliary geometric graph encoders produce cutoff-specific representations, which are integrated into each pre-trained GNN layer via node-wise cutoff attention and gated residual connections, preserving pre-trained knowledge while injecting geometric information with minimal trainable parameters.

Result: On a curated BBBP dataset under both random and scaffold splitting, BBBP-GeoPEFT achieves competitive or improved ROC-AUC and accuracy compared to full fine-tuning and representative PEFT baselines, while updating only 10.1% of model parameters.

Conclusion: BBBP-GeoPEFT demonstrates that incorporating 3D geometric and second-order interaction information via a lightweight, geometry-informed PEFT framework is an effective strategy for BBBP prediction, offering a favorable trade-off between predictive performance and parameter efficiency.

Abstract: Blood-brain barrier permeability (BBBP) prediction is a critical screening task in central nervous system drug discovery, where candidate molecules must be assessed for whether they can cross, or should be prevented from crossing, the blood-brain barrier. However, this task remains challenging because of limited, class-imbalanced datasets and sensitivity to molecular structure. Recent advances in deep learning have established graph neural networks (GNNs) as a powerful approach for molecular representation learning, while pre-trained molecular GNNs provide transferable knowledge for downstream tasks. However, full fine-tuning is often parameter-inefficient and prone to overfitting, whereas existing parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods mainly adapt node features or the two-dimensional covalent graph, limiting their ability to capture three-dimensional geometry and second-order interactions. To address these limitations, we propose BBBP-GeoPEFT, a geometry-informed PEFT framework for pre-trained molecular GNNs. BBBP-GeoPEFT constructs distance-based graphs at multiple cutoffs and their corresponding line graphs from molecular conformers to capture spatial atom and second-order edge interactions. Lightweight auxiliary geometric graph encoders generate cutoff-specific representations, which are incorporated into each pre-trained layer through node-wise cutoff attention and gated residual connections. This design preserves pre-trained knowledge while incorporating permeability-relevant geometric information with a small trainable-parameter budget. Experiments on a curated BBBP dataset show that BBBP-GeoPEFT achieves competitive performance compared with full fine-tuning and representative PEFT baselines. Under both random and scaffold splitting, BBBP-GeoPEFT achieves competitive or improved ROC-AUC and accuracy in most experiments while updating only 10.1% of the model parameters.

</details>


### [195] [Sample Complexity of Multicalibration for Multilevel Properties](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04288)
*Jiuyao Lu,Krishnakumar Balasubramanian,Aleksandr Podkopaev,Shiva Prasad Kasiviswanathan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper studies multicalibration for sequences of identifiable statistical properties (e.g., mean → variance → skewness), establishing tight sample complexity bounds of Θ̃(ε^{-(k+2)}) for k properties, with applications to variance, skewness, and conditional value at risk.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Many prediction tasks require estimating multiple related features of a conditional outcome distribution (e.g., variance depends on mean, skewness on both). Standard multicalibration guarantees apply to single properties or Bayes pairs from a single loss function. The authors generalize this to sequences of k identifiable properties, where each property becomes fixed once preceding ones are known, accommodating richer distributional descriptions without requiring a common loss.

Method: The authors formalize a framework for multicalibration of property sequences where each property is identifiable given its predecessors. They derive matching upper and lower sample-complexity bounds: a lower bound of Ω̃(ε^{-(k+2)}) via information-theoretic arguments, and a randomized learner achieving O(ε^{-(k+2)} + ε^{-2} log|G|) samples for any finite group family G, using techniques from online learning and property elicitation.

Result: For fixed k ≥ 2, under regularity conditions, achieving multicalibration error ε requires Ω̃(ε^{-(k+2)}) samples. The proposed randomized learner uses O(ε^{-(k+2)} + ε^{-2} log|G|) samples, yielding Θ̃(ε^{-(k+2)}) for polynomial-size group families. The theory is instantiated on three canonical cases: mean-variance, mean-variance-skewness, and quantile-CVaR.

Conclusion: The paper provides a tight characterization of the sample complexity for multicalibrating sequences of identifiable properties, showing an unavoidable polynomial dependence on k in the exponent. The framework significantly extends multicalibration beyond single-property or Bayes-pair settings, with practical relevance for distributional forecasting tasks.

Abstract: Calibration requires a predictor to be unbiased after conditioning on its own predictions. Multicalibration asks for this guarantee simultaneously across a collection of groups. Many prediction tasks ask for several related features of the same conditional outcome distribution: variance is defined relative to the mean, skewness relative to both mean and variance, and conditional value at risk relative to a quantile. We study multicalibration for a sequence of $k$ properties in which each property is identifiable once the preceding properties are fixed. This framework includes Bayes pairs but does not require the properties to arise from a single loss.
  For every fixed $k\ge2$, we establish matching upper and lower sample-complexity bounds up to logarithmic factors under regularity conditions. Even with only polylogarithmically many binary groups, achieving multicalibration error $\varepsilon$ requires $\widetildeΩ(\varepsilon^{-(k+2)})$ samples. Conversely, for any finite group family $\mathcal G$, we give a randomized learner using $O(\varepsilon^{-(k+2)}+\varepsilon^{-2}\log|\mathcal G|)$ samples. Thus the sample complexity is $\widetildeΘ(\varepsilon^{-(k+2)})$ for polynomial-size group families. We instantiate the theory for three canonical examples.

</details>


### [196] [Adaptive Finite-Budget Training for CVaR Risk-Aware Q-Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04305)
*Yifan Wu,Junjie Lei,Wenjie Huang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: An adaptive training controller with six coordinated mechanisms is proposed for CVaR-based Risk-aware Q-learning, dramatically reducing Bellman residuals (~85%) and improving risk-adjusted trading performance on Bitcoin, without modifying the underlying risk estimator or fixed point.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Risk-aware Q-learning (RaQL) for dynamic risk objectives suffers from fragile finite-budget behavior: fixed inner-loop hyperparameters cause unstable value estimates, persistent Bellman residuals, and inefficient sample reuse. These issues undermine reliability in practical financial applications where sample budgets are limited.

Method: The authors preserve the original CVaR estimator and Bellman fixed point but redesign the training procedure via six coordinated mechanisms: (1) per-cell inner-step sizing, (2) outer-rate-matched decay synchronization, (3) a short early correction for the VaR-like inner variable, (4) a coverage-first-then-greedy sample allocation rule, (5) progressive suffix aggregation of mature inner estimates, and (6) data-driven calibration of key scales from online-observable quantities. Evaluated on a daily Bitcoin trading task across 20 random seeds and 856,000 inner-transition samples.

Result: The adaptive controller reduced mean empirical CVaR Bellman residual by ~85% relative to the fixed-parameter baseline (MeanBEQ: 1.2202→0.1854; MeanBEV: 1.1624→0.0535). Stability was maintained across CVaR levels, discount factors, and training budgets. On out-of-sample test data, the learned policy achieved a Sharpe ratio of 0.9281 with 6.46% max drawdown after costs, with far lower volatility (9.57% vs. 47.93%), drawdown, and CVaR loss compared to buy-and-hold.

Conclusion: Adaptive finite-budget training design, applied solely to the training procedure without altering the risk objective, can materially improve reliability and risk-adjusted performance of risk-aware Q-learning in financial applications, even when raw cumulative returns trail a buy-and-hold benchmark.

Abstract: Risk-aware Q-learning (RaQL) provides a model-free, two-timescale estimator for dynamic risk objectives, but its finite-budget behavior remains fragile: fixed inner-loop hyperparameters can produce unstable value estimates, persistent Bellman residuals, and inefficient sample reuse. This paper proposes an adaptive training controller for Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) RaQL and evaluates it on a daily Bitcoin trading task. The controller preserves the original CVaR estimator and Bellman fixed point; instead, it redesigns the training procedure through six coordinated mechanisms: per-cell inner-step sizing, outer-rate-matched decay synchronization, a short early correction for the VaR-like inner variable, a coverage-first-then-greedy sample allocation rule, progressive suffix aggregation of mature inner estimates, and data-driven calibration of key scales from online-observable quantities. Across 20 random seeds and 856,000 inner-transition samples, the controller reduces the mean empirical CVaR Bellman residual by approximately 85% relative to the fixed-parameter baseline (MeanBEQ: 1.2202 to 0.1854; MeanBEV: 1.1624 to 0.0535) and maintains stability across CVaR levels, discount factors, and training budgets. On the chronological out-of-sample test set, the learned policy attains a Sharpe ratio of 0.9281 with a maximum drawdown of 6.46% after transaction costs. Although buy-and-hold yields a higher cumulative return (35.43% vs. 23.61%), the adaptive policy achieves far lower volatility (9.57% vs. 47.93%), drawdown, and CVaR loss. These results demonstrate that adaptive finite-budget training design, applied solely to the training procedure without altering the risk objective, can materially improve the reliability and risk-adjusted performance of risk-aware Q-learning in financial applications.

</details>


### [197] [ArborEnum: Decision Tree Rashomon Sets over Continuous Features](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04310)
*Zakk Heile,Hayden McTavish,Margo Seltzer,Cynthia Rudin*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper presents the first exact algorithm for enumerating Rashomon sets of decision trees on continuous features without requiring prior binarization, along with approximate and anytime variants that dramatically accelerate computation while maintaining high recall.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior methods for enumerating decision-tree Rashomon sets depend on binarizing continuous features, which either restricts allowable splits or inflates combinatorial complexity. This motivates an algorithm that directly exploits the ordered nature of continuous features to enable full, exact enumeration without these limitations.

Method: The authors introduce an exact enumeration algorithm for continuous-feature decision-tree Rashomon sets that leverages ordered feature structure. They also develop a relaxation for approximate enumeration and an anytime algorithm that iteratively refines candidate threshold sets, producing progressively more accurate approximations converging to the exact Rashomon set.

Result: Experiments demonstrate that coarse binarization misses many trees, important features, and predictive multiplicity. The proposed algorithms achieve orders-of-magnitude speedups over existing enumeration methods, and the approximate variants provide further acceleration with near-perfect recall.

Conclusion: Directly handling continuous features for Rashomon set enumeration is both feasible and substantially more effective than binarization-based approaches, enabling accurate recovery of model multiplicity, feature importance, and robustness insights that coarse discretization would otherwise obscure.

Abstract: The Rashomon effect describes the phenomenon that many models can achieve nearly equivalent performance on the same learning task, with significant ramifications for robustness, feature importance, and customizability. These use cases motivate the computation of Rashomon sets: the set of all models whose regularized loss is near-optimal. Decision trees are one of the few model classes for which Rashomon sets can be fully enumerated, but this computation has always been conditional on a binarization of the original data, either restricting which splits each tree is allowed to make or substantially increasing the complexity of an already difficult combinatorial problem. We introduce the first algorithm that exactly enumerates decision-tree Rashomon sets while exploiting the ordered structure of continuous features. We further develop a relaxation for approximate enumeration and an anytime algorithm that progressively refines the set of candidate thresholds, producing increasingly detailed approximations that converge to the continuous-feature Rashomon set. Experiments show that coarse binarization can miss many trees, important features, and predictive multiplicity; our algorithms achieve orders-of-magnitude speedups over existing enumeration methods, with approximations providing further speedups while maintaining near-perfect recall.

</details>


### [198] [Efficient Online Lexicographic Generalized Low-Rank Matrix Bandits](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04324)
*Bo Xue,Ji Cheng,Haodong Jing,Hongzong Li,Shuang Qiu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes Lexi-LowGLM, an efficient online algorithm for generalized low-rank matrix bandits with multiple prioritized objectives. It uses online Newton steps for per-objective estimation, reducing computational complexity from O(T²) to O(T), and achieves regret bounds that scale with the low-rank dimension rather than ambient dimension.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing low-rank matrix bandit algorithms focus on single-objective settings and require repeatedly solving batch generalized linear estimators using all historical data, leading to O(T²) computational complexity. Real-world applications often involve multiple objectives with lexicographic priorities, and no existing method efficiently handles this multi-objective, low-rank setting with affordable computation.

Method: The authors propose Lexi-LowGLM, which first estimates objective-specific low-rank subspaces via an online Newton step for each objective, maintaining per-objective estimators incrementally. It then performs lexicographic learning in the reduced feature spaces, where arms are selected by iteratively optimizing higher-priority objectives before considering lower-priority ones (lexicographic preference order). Crucially, the online Newton update replaces batch GLM estimation, slashing per-round complexity.

Result: Lexi-LowGLM achieves a regret bound of Õ(W_i^lex √m (d₁+d₂)r√T) for each objective i, where r bounds the rank and W_i^lex captures lexicographic trade-off effects. The bound depends on the effective low-rank dimension (d₁+d₂)r instead of the ambient d₁d₂. The estimator-update complexity is reduced from O(T²) to O(T) over T rounds. Numerical experiments confirm both effectiveness and computational efficiency.

Conclusion: Lexi-LowGLM provides the first efficient solution to multi-objective generalized low-rank matrix bandits with lexicographic preferences, combining computational tractability (online Newton steps) with statistically optimal regret scaling in the low-rank dimension. The framework opens directions for multi-objective bandit problems with structured parameter spaces.

Abstract: This paper studies generalized low-rank matrix bandits with multiple prioritized objectives. At each round, the learner selects a matrix-valued arm and observes a vector-valued reward, whose components correspond to multiple objectives with different priority levels. Each objective is governed by an objective-specific generalized low-rank matrix model, and the learner evaluates arms according to a lexicographic preference order, prioritizing higher-level objectives before lower-level ones. We propose \textsc{Lexi-LowGLM}, an efficient online algorithm that first estimates objective-specific low-rank subspaces and then performs lexicographic learning in the reduced feature spaces. Unlike existing single-objective algorithms that repeatedly solve a batch generalized linear estimator using all historical observations, \textsc{Lexi-LowGLM} updates each objective-specific estimator via an online Newton step, reducing the estimator-update complexity over $T$ rounds from $O(T^2)$ to $O(T)$. We establish a regret bound of $\widetilde O\left(W_i^{\rm lex}\sqrt{m}\,(d_1+d_2)r\sqrt{T}\right)$ for each objective $i\in[m]$, where $r$ is an upper bound on the ranks of the objective-specific parameter matrices and $W_i^{\rm lex}$ characterizes the lexicographic trade-off effect. This bound depends on the effective low-rank dimension $(d_1+d_2)r$ rather than the ambient dimension $d_1d_2$. Numerical experiments further validate the effectiveness and computational efficiency of the proposed method.

</details>


### [199] [Real-time probabilistic tsunami forecasting via generative AI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04327)
*Yusuke Oishi,Takashi Furumura,Fumihiko Imamura*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A generative AI-based conditional diffusion model enables probabilistic tsunami inundation forecasting, shifting from deterministic predictions to calibrated uncertainty quantification, validated against the 2011 Tohoku earthquake.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deterministic onshore tsunami inundation forecasts may create a false sense of safety outside predicted boundaries, especially for near-field tsunamis with high uncertainty. Current warnings focus on coastal height rather than inundation, and even machine learning–based instant predictions lack uncertainty quantification.

Method: A probabilistic ensemble model based on a conditional diffusion model (a generative AI architecture) that produces calibrated, uncertainty-aware inundation predictions and tracks uncertainty reduction over time post-earthquake.

Result: The model, validated on 2011 Tohoku-oki earthquake data, accurately predicts inundation depth and extent while faithfully tracking the post-earthquake decrease in prediction uncertainty over time.

Conclusion: Generative AI can shift tsunami forecasting from deterministic to probabilistic paradigms, laying the foundation for next-generation early warning systems that incorporate uncertainty quantification.

Abstract: Explicit onshore tsunami inundation forecasting can improve public risk awareness, but deterministically predicted inundation boundaries under highly uncertain conditions, such as near-field tsunamis generated by megathrust earthquakes, may falsely imply safety outside the boundaries. Consequently, current warnings primarily target coastal tsunami height, not onshore inundation. Although machine learning enables instant inundation predictions, they remain deterministic, lacking uncertainty quantification. Here, we develop a probabilistic ensemble model based on a conditional diffusion model (a type of generative AI) that reconciles accuracy with calibration. Validated with the 2011 Tohoku-oki earthquake data, our model faithfully tracks the postearthquake uncertainty decreasing over time while accurately predicting inundation depth and extent. Our framework shows that generative AI can shift tsunami forecasting from determinism to probabilism, providing a foundation for next-generation early warning.

</details>


### [200] [Cost-Aware Multi-Objective Bandits: Theory and Application to Budgeted LLM Configuration Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04333)
*Bo Xue,Zhi Hong,Jiayi Li,Yuanyu Wan,Ji Cheng,Shuang Qiu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper frames LLM configuration evaluation as a cost-aware multi-objective bandit problem, proposing a hypervolume-based UCB algorithm for online selection and a cost-aware empirical gap elimination algorithm for Pareto identification, both with theoretically proven regret and error probability bounds that scale efficiently with budget.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM configuration evaluation is difficult because evaluation budgets are limited, different configurations incur varying costs, and there are multiple competing objectives (e.g., accuracy, latency, cost). Existing bandit approaches do not adequately handle configuration-dependent costs alongside multi-objective trade-offs.

Method: The authors formulate the problem as a cost-aware multi-objective bandit. For online configuration selection, they propose a hypervolume-based UCB (Upper Confidence Bound) algorithm that maximizes an optimistic hypervolume-per-cost index. For fixed-budget Pareto identification, they develop a cost-aware empirical gap elimination algorithm. Both algorithms are analyzed theoretically to establish performance guarantees.

Result: The hypervolume-based UCB achieves a budgeted regret bound of O(∑_{i≠i*} (log B)/Δ_i), retaining logarithmic dependence on budget B. The Pareto identification algorithm achieves an error probability of O(exp(-B/H_{μ,c})), decaying exponentially with budget. Experiments on LLM configuration tasks confirm efficient online decision-making and accurate Pareto identification under limited budgets.

Conclusion: The proposed cost-aware multi-objective bandit framework effectively balances multiple objectives under configuration-dependent costs, offering theoretically grounded and empirically validated algorithms for both online configuration selection and Pareto set identification in LLM evaluation.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM) configuration evaluation is challenging due to limited evaluation budgets, varying costs, and multiple competing objectives. In this paper, we formulate LLM configuration evaluation as a cost-aware multi-objective bandit problem, where each configuration evaluation incurs a configuration-dependent cost and yields a noisy vector-valued outcome. Under this framework, we study two fundamental problems: online configuration selection and Pareto configuration identification. For online configuration selection, we propose a hypervolume-based UCB algorithm that optimizes an optimistic hypervolume-per-cost index. We establish a budgeted regret bound of order $O\bigl(\sum_{i\ne i^\star}\frac{\log B}{Δ_i}\bigr)$, where $B$ is the evaluation budget, $i^\star$ is the optimal configuration in terms of hypervolume efficiency, and $Δ_i$ is the corresponding efficiency gap of configuration $i$. This bound retains the logarithmic budget dependence of classical single-objective budgeted bandits. For fixed-budget Pareto identification, we develop a cost-aware empirical gap elimination algorithm and prove that its error probability is of order $O\bigl(\exp(-\frac{B}{H_{μ,c}})\bigr)$, where $H_{μ,c}$ is a cost-aware Pareto identification complexity depending on configuration costs and Pareto classification gaps. This error probability decays exponentially with the evaluation budget and recovers the standard Pareto set identification guarantee when all configuration costs are identical. Experiments on LLM configuration evaluation tasks demonstrate that the proposed framework enables efficient online decision-making and accurate cost-aware Pareto identification under limited budgets.

</details>


### [201] [ATLAS: Adaptive Topological Learning with Abstract Successors for Continual Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04334)
*R. Blake Lawlor,Daniel S. Brown*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ATLAS combines a Grow When Required network with Successor Features to achieve sample-efficient and robust model-based RL that adapts near-instantaneously to new goals and mitigates catastrophic forgetting in non-stationary environments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Model-free RL suffers from low sample efficiency and poor robustness to environmental changes. Model-based methods improve sample efficiency but still fail under distribution shift. Both paradigms struggle with catastrophic forgetting in non-stationary settings. The authors aim to address all three limitations simultaneously.

Method: ATLAS integrates a Grow When Required (GWR) self-organizing network with Successor Features (SF). The GWR network learns a topological representation of the environment's transition dynamics, while Successor Features decouple this dynamics model from the reward signal. This structural separation enables rapid policy re-evaluation when goals change, without recomputing the transition model.

Result: Empirical evaluation in spatial navigation tasks shows ATLAS achieves near-instantaneous adaptation to new goals, exhibits positive backward transfer, and significantly outperforms both on-policy and off-policy baselines in non-stationary environments.

Conclusion: Structurally decoupling transition dynamics from reward signals via the ATLAS architecture yields a model-based agent that is simultaneously sample-efficient, robust to environmental non-stationarity, and capable of rapid goal adaptation with positive transfer.

Abstract: Contemporary model-free reinforcement learning algorithms can achieve very high performance, but have low sample efficiency and are not robust to changes in the environment. Model-based algorithms have much higher sample efficiency, but still fail when the environment shifts. This paper introduces Adaptive Topological Learning with Abstract Successors (ATLAS) to combat these challenges. ATLAS uses a Grow When Required network with Successor Features in order to achieve high sample efficiency while also robustly tackling catastrophic forgetting. We evaluate ATLAS in spatial navigation tasks, benchmarking its performance against common on-policy and off-policy algorithms. Our empirical results demonstrate that by structurally decoupling transition dynamics from the reward signal, ATLAS achieves near-instantaneous adaptation to new goals and can exhibit positive backward transfer, significantly outperforming baseline methods in non-stationary environments.

</details>


### [202] [Looking in the Mirror: Introspecting Side-Effect Misalignments Induced by Fine-Tuning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04347)
*Kotaro Yoshida,Laura Gomezjurado Gonzalez,Yukinori Yamamoto,Yuji Naraki,Ryotaro Shimizu,Wenya Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces "side-effect introspection," a novel problem setting where models must detect unintended alignment degradation caused by fine-tuning on non-safety tasks. The authors construct a dedicated dataset and propose DAIA, a Delta-Aware Introspection Adapter that processes both base-model activations and fine-tuning-induced activation differences, outperforming existing introspection adapters in generalizing to unseen models and safety categories.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing introspection methods only evaluate on datasets where behaviors are explicitly implanted via fine-tuning, which fails to reflect real-world deployment scenarios. In practice, the critical concern is side-effect misalignment—unintended degradation of safety/alignment properties when fine-tuning on seemingly innocuous, non-safety-related tasks. This gap motivates a new problem formulation and dataset.

Method: The authors formulate the side-effect introspection problem and construct a corresponding dataset. They propose DAIA (Delta-Aware Introspection Adapter), a LoRA-based module that explicitly processes both (1) activations from the base model and (2) activation differences (deltas) between the base and fine-tuned model, thereby enhancing sensitivity to internal model changes caused by fine-tuning.

Result: Empirical evaluation demonstrates that introspection learning generalizes to unseen fine-tuned models and safety categories. DAIA consistently outperforms existing introspection adapters in detecting and describing side-effect alignment shifts.

Conclusion: Side-effect introspection is a practically important and previously underexplored setting. Explicitly modeling activation deltas via DAIA yields superior performance over prior introspection adapters, offering a path toward more robust detection of unintended alignment degradation in deployed fine-tuned models.

Abstract: Fine-tuning enables a source model to acquire desired capabilities and behaviors in a target domain while retaining much of its general-purpose competence. However, this adaptation process can also degrade alignment properties that were present in the source model. Recent work has shown that large language models can be trained using LoRA-based modules known as introspection adapters (IAs) to describe behavioral changes induced by fine-tuning. However, existing studies primarily consider settings in which the model is fine-tuned on datasets explicitly designed to implant a specific behavior and is then asked to explain the implanted behavior. This differs from practical deployment scenarios, where the central concern is often side-effect misalignment: unintended degradation of alignment caused by fine-tuning on tasks that are not obviously related to safety or alignment. To bridge this gap, we formulate a novel problem setting called \emph{side-effect introspection}, in which the target of introspection is not a behavior explicitly implanted through fine-tuning, but rather alignment shifts that emerge as unintended side effects, and we construct a dataset for this setting. Furthermore, to enhance sensitivity to internal model changes, we propose the Delta-Aware Introspection Adapter (DAIA), a novel mechanism designed to explicitly process both base-model activations and activation differences induced by fine-tuning. Our empirical evaluation shows that introspection learning generalizes to unseen fine-tuned models and safety categories, and that DAIA consistently outperforms existing introspection adapters.

</details>


### [203] [Manipulation-Proof Oblivious Audits against Deceptive Model Providers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04365)
*Augustin Godinot,Sofiane Azogagh,Julien Ferry,Sébastien Gambs*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes an oblivious audit protocol using Private Information Retrieval (PIR) to prevent model providers from manipulating fairness evaluations.
