Experiments on chaotic and real-world time-series benchmarks show that DMP improves or preserves forecasting accuracy while reducing redundant reservoir components. Our results suggest that dynamical influence is a useful criterion for reservoir refinement beyond static structural importance alone.

</details>


### [225] [Why Ranking Anomaly Detection Algorithms Isn't as Reliable as You May Think](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04613)
*Simon Klüttermann,Jérôme Rutinowski,Frederik Polachowski,Alice Kirchheim*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Anomaly detection benchmarks are unreliable: algorithm rankings fluctuate dramatically depending on dataset selection, hyperparameters, evaluation metrics, and random seeds. The authors quantify this instability using a novel rank instability metric across 690 datasets and 7 algorithms, finding that dataset choice and hyperparameters are the dominant sources of ranking uncertainty.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite numerous anomaly detection algorithms claiming state-of-the-art results, benchmarking practices are inconsistent across studies. This lack of standardized comparison raises serious concerns about reproducibility and whether claimed performance improvements are genuine or artifacts of benchmark design choices.

Method: The authors systematically evaluate seven representative anomaly detection algorithms on 690 datasets from the OddBench suite. They vary dataset selections, evaluation metrics, hyperparameter configurations, and random seeds to observe ranking changes. A rank instability metric is introduced to quantitatively measure the variability of algorithm rankings across different benchmark settings.

Result: Algorithm rankings in anomaly detection are highly unstable — nearly every competitive algorithm can emerge as the top performer under some benchmark configuration. Dataset selection and hyperparameter choice contribute most strongly to ranking uncertainty, while random seeds and evaluation metrics have comparatively limited impact. Reliable benchmarking requires substantially larger and more diverse dataset collections than typically used.

Conclusion: The anomaly detection community must adopt more rigorous and standardized benchmarking protocols. Relying on small, cherry-picked dataset collections or single hyperparameter settings can produce misleading rankings. Larger, more diverse benchmarks and transparent reporting of all experimental choices are essential for meaningful progress.

Abstract: Anomaly detection is a safety-critical machine learning problem with applications ranging from fraud detection to network intrusion prevention and industrial monitoring. Despite the large number of proposed anomaly detection algorithms, many novel methods claim state-of-the-art performance. However, many authors do so under benchmark settings that are not aligned with one another. This lack of comparability raises concerns regarding the reproducibility and reliability of anomaly detection benchmarks.
  In this work, we study the impact of common benchmarking choices on the stability of algorithm rankings. Using seven representative anomaly detection algorithms and 690 datasets from the OddBench benchmark suite, we analyze how rankings change under varying dataset selections, evaluation metrics, hyperparameter configurations, and random seeds. To quantify this effect, we introduce a rank instability metric measuring the variability of algorithm rankings across benchmark settings.
  Our results show that algorithm rankings in anomaly detection are highly unstable. In many cases, almost every competitive algorithm can appear as the best-performing method under some benchmark configuration. Among the studied factors, dataset selection and hyperparameter choice contribute most strongly to ranking uncertainty, while random seeds and evaluation metrics have a comparatively limited impact. We also observe that reliable benchmarking requires substantially larger and more diverse dataset collections than the ones commonly used in prior work.

</details>


### [226] [An entropic explanation of insistence on sameness in autism](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04616)
*Przemysław Śliwiński*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Proposes an information-theoretic framework that explains autism's insistence on sameness as a strategy to minimize a combined entropy metric (surprise + uncertainty), offering a formal definition, therapeutic guidelines, and a validation approach based on a Turing test-like method.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To provide a formal, quantitative explanation for insistence on sameness in autism, framing it as an instance of a general behavior pattern aimed at reducing surprise and uncertainty, and to establish a theoretical foundation for designing effective therapies and care routines.

Method: The paper constructs an information-theoretic framework centered on the metric D_H(R, M) = H(R|M) + H(M|R), where R denotes random stimuli sequences and M denotes memory. Conditional entropies are interpreted as surprise H(R|M) and uncertainty H(M|R). The framework infers that minimizing this metric can be achieved either by learning about R (updating M) or by restricting R to match already-known M — the latter identified as insistence on sameness. The framework further quantifies related concepts (anxiety, sensory overload, comfort zone, etc.), derives optimization-based therapeutic guidelines, and proposes validation via a Turing test-like approach without direct human subject experiments.

Result: The framework shows that insistence on sameness emerges naturally as a constrained entropy-minimization strategy. It successfully quantifies multiple autism-related phenomena (sensory overload, deprivation, anxiety, pedantry, rigidness, aberrant precision, etc.) in information-theoretic terms. It yields actionable guidelines for learning therapies and daily care routines, which can be formalized as optimization algorithms and implemented in robotic caregivers. A Turing test-like validation paradigm is proposed, enabling testing without experiments involving autistic individuals.

Conclusion: If positively validated, the framework provides formal foundations and design guidelines for therapies that improve self-reliance of individuals with autism in activities of daily living. The information-theoretic approach offers a principled, quantitative lens for understanding and addressing core behavioral features of autism.

Abstract: An information theory-based framework is proposed in attempt to explain insistence on sameness in autism as an instance of a general behavior pattern in which an individual tries to reduce surprise and uncertainty. It offers a new definition of autism as an impairment in which cognitive functions are restricted to discrimination, memorization and prediction of tangible properties of the environment. An analogy between insistence on sameness and constrained minimization of the entropy metric is observed and examined for a set of assumptions that describe cognitive limitations of a person with autism. The metric is given by the formula $D_H(R, M) = H(R|M) + H(M|R)$, where $R$ represents sequences of random stimuli, $M$ is a memory that stores and retrieves them, and where $H(.|.)$ denotes their conditional entropies interpreted as surprise and uncertainty, respectively. It is first inferred that to minimize the metric an individual can learn about $R$ (and store that knowledge in $M$) or can restrict $R$ to the already known $M$. Then, it is concluded that insistence on sameness is a manifestation of the latter. Moreover, it is shown that the proposed framework: (1) Helps to quantify the concepts of surprise, uncertainty, sensory overload and deprivation, anxiety, comfort zone, disappointment, disorientation, pedantry, rigidness, observance or aberrant precision. (2) Leads to a list of guidelines for learning therapies and daily care routines, and allows them to be defined as optimization algorithms and implemented as programs for robotic live-in caregivers. (3) Can be validated with the help of a Turing test-like approach that requires no experiments involving individuals with autism. The framework-if positively validated-will provide formal foundations and design guidelines for therapies aimed at improving self-reliance of individuals with autism in basic activities of daily living.

</details>


### [227] [Active Learning Guided Design Space Refinement for Scalable Multi-Objective Bayesian Optimization in Materials Discovery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04651)
*Alexandros Ntagiantas,Panagiotis Tsilimidos,George Giannakopoulos,Christoforos Rekatsinas,Panagiotis Krokidas*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Proposes an active-learning-guided adaptive search-space refinement framework combined with multi-objective Bayesian optimization to accelerate materials discovery. The method halves the candidate space while retaining >99% of the original hypervolume, improving early convergence and Pareto-front discovery in large discrete design spaces.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Conventional Bayesian optimization becomes inefficient as candidate spaces grow large, often wasting evaluations on low-value regions before reaching informative areas. There is a need for methods that can focus computation on promising regions of the design space while preserving Pareto-optimal candidates.

Method: An active-learning (AL)-guided adaptive search-space refinement framework integrated with multi-objective Bayesian optimization. The AL component iteratively prunes the candidate space by identifying and discarding low-value regions while safeguarding Pareto-relevant areas. Validated on two case studies: CH4/N2 separation in covalent-organic frameworks and pressure-vessel design with material-direction stress components and thickness objectives.

Result: The AL-guided refinement reduces the candidate space by approximately 50% while preserving more than 99% of the original hypervolume. The reduced-space strategy improves both early convergence and cumulative Pareto-front discovery compared to conventional BO applied to the full candidate space.

Conclusion: The proposed framework enables efficient large-scale materials optimization under constrained autonomous discovery settings by adaptively focusing the search on high-value regions without sacrificing Pareto-optimal solutions.

Abstract: Advanced materials discovery increasingly relies on machine learning and Bayesian optimization to explore large discrete design spaces under limited evaluation budgets. However, conventional Bayesian optimization (BO) can become inefficient as candidate spaces grow, often evaluating low-value regions before reaching informative areas. We propose an active-learning (AL)-guided adaptive search-space refinement framework combined with multi-objective BO to accelerate materials optimization while preserving Pareto-relevant regions. We evaluate the approach on CH4/N2 separation in covalent-organic frameworks and pressure-vessel design with material-direction stress components and thickness objectives. Results show that the AL-guided refinement reduces the candidate space by approximately half while preserving more than 99 percent of the original hypervolume. The reduced-space strategy improves early convergence and cumulative Pareto-front discovery from the BO, demonstrating efficient large-scale materials optimization across constrained autonomous materials discovery settings.

</details>


### [228] [Differentiating Through Dual Prices: End-to-End Policy Learning Under Capacity Constraints](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04669)
*Mohammadsaeed Haghi,Mahdi Salmani,Nima Kelidari*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper addresses learning resource-constrained assignment policies (e.g., housing, hospital interventions) from observational data, where arrivals must be served immediately and long-run resource capacities must be respected. The authors propose end-to-end training of outcome models by differentiating through dual prices in an off-policy evaluation framework, contrasting with the standard decision-blind pipeline. They introduce an exact nonconvex formulation and a convex relaxation with bounded suboptimality, and demonstrate via queueing simulations on six datasets that end-to-end methods achieve superior deployment-adjusted value and better capacity compliance compared to decision-blind baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In social services, scarce resources must be allocated sequentially under immediate-decision and capacity constraints. The conventional pipeline—fitting outcome models per arm, pricing resources, and assigning greedily—is decision-blind and can lead to capacity violations and poor deployment performance. The authors aim to bridge this gap by directly optimizing the deployed policy's value through end-to-end learning, ensuring that capacity constraints are respected in practice.

Method: The authors propose training outcome models end-to-end by backpropagating through an off-policy estimate of the deployed policy's value, with resource dual prices computed from the fitted models. Two formulations are studied: (1) an exact nonconvex optimization, and (2) a convex relaxation whose optimal solution always satisfies expected capacity constraints, with suboptimality bounded by a term linear in the smoothing temperature and logarithmic in the number of arms. Evaluation uses a queueing simulation with resources replenished at capacity rates, tested across six datasets including a 70K-patient hospital cohort.

Result: The two end-to-end variants consistently rank highest on a deployment-adjusted value index across all delay costs (including zero delay cost). Under binding capacity constraints, decision-blind baselines frequently violate capacities and incur significantly longer queueing delays. On the largest hospital dataset, end-to-end training achieves significantly higher policy value, outperforming even a capacity-matched neural baseline. However, flexible decision-blind regression remains the stronger pure predictor when ground truth is measurable.

Conclusion: End-to-end training with differentiable dual prices is best suited to settings where resources are genuinely scarce and capacity feasibility is critical. While decision-blind regression excels as a pure predictor when outcomes are directly measurable, end-to-end methods yield higher deployed policy value and better constraint satisfaction in capacity-constrained, real-world allocation scenarios.

Abstract: Many social services assign scarce resources, such as housing assistance or hospital interventions, to people who arrive one at a time: each arrival must receive a decision immediately, and the long-run usage of every resource must stay within its capacity. We study how to learn such an assignment policy from logged observational data. The standard pipeline is decision-blind: fit one outcome model per arm by regression, price each capacitated resource from the fitted models, and assign each arrival the arm whose predicted outcome minus price is largest. We instead train the outcome models end-to-end, differentiating an off-policy estimate of the deployed policy's value through the dual prices themselves. We study two formulations: an exact nonconvex one, and a convex relaxation whose optimum always satisfies the capacity constraints in expectation and which is suboptimal by at most a term linear in the smoothing temperature and logarithmic in the number of arms. Every method is evaluated in a queueing simulation with resources replenished at their capacity rates. Across six datasets, the two end-to-end variants take the top slots on a deployment-adjusted value index at every delay cost, including zero; when capacities are binding, decision-blind baselines frequently violate them and incur much longer queueing delays. On the largest dataset, a hospital cohort of seventy thousand patients, end-to-end training also achieves significantly higher policy value, a margin that survives a capacity-matched neural baseline. Flexible decision-blind regression remains the stronger pure predictor where ground truth is measurable; end-to-end training is best suited to settings where resources are genuinely scarce and feasibility matters.

</details>


### [229] [Diverse and Plausible Algorithmic Recourse via Tractable Recourse Distributions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04677)
*Anagha Sabu,Hrithik Suresh,Narayanan C. Krishnan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes TRD (Tractable Recourse Distributions), a probabilistic framework that models the entire space of feasible algorithmic recourses as a probability distribution using exponentially tilted probabilistic circuits, enabling closed-form sampling of diverse, plausible, and feasible counterfactuals without retraining.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing recourse methods construct only one or a few counterfactuals via optimization, forcing trade-offs among diversity, plausibility, and feasibility. No prior approach models the full space of feasible alternatives, which is essential since different individuals can act on different recourse paths.

Method: The framework represents the space of feasible recourse alternatives as a probability distribution over favorable outcomes using probabilistic circuits. For proximity-based and feature-change count cost functions, this distribution admits an exact closed-form representation via exponential tilting of the circuit. Sampling from the tilted distribution yields diverse and plausible recourses, with tilting parameters controlling proximity and sparsity.

Result: Experiments on standard algorithmic recourse benchmarks show the framework simultaneously achieves diversity, plausibility, and feasibility. Rejection sampling remains practical due to sufficient probability mass over feasible counterfactuals. A visual MNIST study demonstrates how tilt strength trades proximity against validity.

Conclusion: Modeling recourse as a tractable probability distribution rather than as point-valued optimization resolves the longstanding diversity-plausibility-feasibility trade-off, providing individuals with multiple realistic paths to favorable outcomes in a principled, closed-form manner.

Abstract: Algorithmic recourse seeks to help individuals reverse unfavorable automated decisions by recommending actionable changes that achieve a desired outcome. As an individual usually has several distinct routes to a favorable decision, and different people can act on different ones, a recourse system should offer multiple realistic alternatives rather than one. Existing approaches formulate recourse as an optimization problem that constructs one or a small set of counterfactuals rather than modeling the underlying space of feasible solutions, and in practice each sacrifices diversity, plausibility, or feasibility to secure the others. We propose Tractable Recourse Distributions, a probabilistic framework that represents the space of feasible alternatives for a given factual instance as a probability distribution over favorable outcomes. For commonly used cost functions based on proximity and the number of feature changes, we show that this distribution admits an exact representation as a probabilistic circuit, obtained by exponentially tilting the circuit; each individual's distribution is therefore available in closed form, without retraining the model. Sampling from these distributions naturally produces diverse and plausible recourses, while the tilting parameters provide explicit control over their proximity and sparsity. Experiments on standard algorithmic recourse benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed framework attains diversity, plausibility, and feasibility simultaneously, while retaining sufficient probability mass over feasible counterfactuals for rejection sampling to be practical. A visual study on MNIST illustrates how the tilt strength trades proximity against validity.

</details>


### [230] [The Sample Complexity of Distributionally Robust PAC Learning under Cressie--Read Divergences](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04686)
*Elad Aigner-Horev,Daniel Rosenberg,Roi Weiss*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper establishes tight sample-complexity bounds for distributionally robust PAC learning under Cressie-Read divergence constraints. It reveals a sharp phase transition in the agnostic case at k=2, where robustness alters the ε-dependence for 1<k<2 but preserves the classical ε⁻² rate for k≥2, while in the realizable case robustness always worsens the rate from ε⁻¹ to ε^{-k/(k-1)}.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work on distributionally robust PAC learning focused primarily on specific divergences (e.g., χ²) and produced bounds that fail to recover standard PAC rates as the robustness radius ρ→0. The authors aim to provide a unified, tight analysis for the entire Cressie-Read family (k>1), close existing gaps between upper and lower bounds, and properly interpolate to the classical non-robust limit.

Method: The analysis builds on a known scalar reduction that connects robust 0-1 risk to ordinary classification error. The authors analyze this reduction at a finer scale, revealing how statistical estimation error in classification interacts with the amplification effect of robustness. They derive both upper bounds (achieved by empirical risk minimization up to logarithmic factors) and matching lower bounds for hypothesis classes with finite VC dimension d.

Result: In the realizable setting, sample complexity is Θ̃(max{1/ε, ρ^{1/(k-1)}/ε^{k/(k-1)}}·d). In the agnostic setting, it is Θ̃(max{1/ε², ρ^{1/(k-1)}/ε^{(k/(k-1))∨2}}·d). For k<2, the exponent transitions from 2 to k/(k-1); for k≥2, the exponent remains 2 but with non-trivial ρ-dependence. As ρ→0, the bounds recover classical non-robust rates, correcting a flaw in prior work.

Conclusion: The paper provides the first complete characterization of sample complexity for distributionally robust PAC learning under general Cressie-Read divergences. The phase transition at k=2 in the agnostic case is a key insight: robustness only worsens the rate when the divergence is sufficiently "soft" (1<k<2). The tight bounds and correct ρ→0 interpolation significantly advance the theoretical understanding of robust learning.

Abstract: We study distributionally robust PAC learning for the $0$--$1$-loss, where adversarial perturbations of the data distribution are constrained by a Cressie--Read divergence of order $k>1$ and radius $ρ\geq 0$. For hypothesis classes with VC dimension $d$, we establish realizable and agnostic sample-complexity bounds tight up to constant and logarithmic factors, respectively; ordinary empirical risk minimization attains both rates up to logarithmic factors. For target accuracy $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$ and confidence $δ\in(0,1)$, their respective orders are \[ \max\!\left\{\frac{1}{\varepsilon}, \frac{ρ^{\frac 1{k-1}}}{\varepsilon^{k_\star}} \right\}\cdot(d+\log δ^{-1}) \qquad\text{and}\qquad \max\!\left\{\frac{1}{\varepsilon^2}, \frac{ρ^{\frac1{k-1}}}{\varepsilon^{k_\star\vee 2}} \right\}\cdot(d+\log δ^{-1}), \] where $k_\star={k}/{(k-1)}$. For every fixed $ρ>0$, robustness changes the realizable $\varepsilon$-dependence from $\varepsilon^{-1}$ to $\varepsilon^{-k_\star}$ as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$. In the agnostic case, for $1<k<2$, robustness changes the $\varepsilon$-dependence from $\varepsilon^{-2}$ to $\varepsilon^{-k_\star}$, whereas for $k\geq2$ the exponent remains the classical $2$, with nontrivial $ρ$-dependence.
  Building on the known scalar reduction of robust $0$--$1$ risk to ordinary classification error, our analysis reveals a scale-sensitive interaction between the statistical estimation of classification error and its amplification by robustness, sharply explaining the transition in the agnostic rate. We extend the previously studied $χ^2$-divergence case to every Cressie--Read order $k>1$, close its upper--lower gaps, and recover standard PAC learning rates as $ρ\to0$, unlike previous bounds that fail to interpolate correctly in this limit.

</details>


### [231] [Personalized Federated Sparse Adaptation of Time-Series Foundation Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04695)
*Priyanka Nihalchandani,Naman Srivastava,Varun Ojha,Pandarasamy Arjunan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A personalized federated sparse adaptation framework for time-series foundation models (TSFMs) is proposed for building energy forecasting, using a heterogeneous temporal mixture-of-experts adapter. Experiments across 50 buildings and 3 TSFM backbones show personalization outperforms global and local strategies, with optimal sparse-adaptation varying by backbone, highlighting the need for both client-aware and backbone-aware federated adaptation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Building energy forecasting involves private, distributed, and highly non-IID meter data, making federated adaptation of TSFMs attractive. However, existing parameter-sharing strategies are inadequate: fully shared adapters suppress building-specific temporal patterns, while fully local adaptation loses cross-building transfer benefits. There is no one-size-fits-all strategy across different pretrained backbones and heterogeneous building clients.

Method: A personalized federated sparse adaptation framework with a heterogeneous temporal mixture-of-experts (MoE) adapter placed after the pretrained TSFM representation. A sequence-level router maps each 168-hour context window to a top-k subset of experts specialized for periodicity, long-range interactions, local variation, trend-residual structure, and multi-resolution behavior. The framework is evaluated by comparing global FL, local training, and personalized FL variants with globally shared or client-private expert banks across three TSFM backbones and 50 buildings.

Result: Personalization consistently outperforms Global FL-MoE and Local MoE across 50 buildings and three TSFM backbones. The optimal sparse-adaptation strategy varies by backbone and metric. Routing analysis reveals client-level expert specialization, expert concentration, and near-uniform routing across backbones.

Conclusion: Federated TSFM adaptation for building energy forecasting should be both client-aware and backbone-aware. A personalized federated MoE approach with sparse adaptation effectively balances cross-building transfer and building-specific modeling, though the best configuration depends on the specific pretrained backbone and evaluation metric.

Abstract: Federated adaptation of time-series foundation models (TSFMs) is attractive for building energy forecasting because meter data are private, distributed, and highly non-IID. However, a single parameter-sharing strategy is unlikely to serve all pretrained TSFMs or building clients: fully shared adapters can suppress building-specific temporal behavior, while fully local adaptation discards cross-building transfer. We propose a personalized federated sparse adaptation framework with a heterogeneous temporal mixture-of-experts (MoE) adapter placed after the pretrained TSFM representation. A sequence-level router maps each 168-hour context window to a top-$k$ subset of experts specialized for periodicity, long-range interactions, local variation, trend-residual structure, and multi-resolution behavior. We compare global FL, local training, and personalized FL variants with globally shared or client-private expert banks. Across 50 buildings and three TSFM backbones, personalization consistently outperforms Global FL-MoE and Local MoE, while the best sparse-adaptation strategy varies by backbone and metric. Routing behavior further reveals client-level expert specialization, expert concentration, and near-uniform routing across backbones, showing that federated TSFM adaptation should be both client-aware and backbone-aware.

</details>


### [232] [Design Choices That Matter: A Functional ANOVA Analysis for Remote Sensing Multi-Label Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04702)
*Maryam Gholami Shiri,Eva Tuba,Sašo Džeroski,Tome Eftimov,Ana Nikolikj*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper applies fANOVA to quantify how individual design choices (architecture, fine-tuning, learning strategy, initialization) and their interactions drive performance variability in multi-label classification of remote sensing images, revealing that datasets cluster by sensitivity profiles linked to intrinsic properties like scale and label complexity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional benchmarking of DL models for MLC of RSI produces dataset-specific rankings that fail to generalize. The authors seek to move beyond rankings by systematically attributing performance variance to specific design decisions, enabling principled model selection guided by dataset characteristics.

Method: The authors employ functional analysis of variance (fANOVA) across two empirical studies (48 and 20 DL models) spanning seven multi-label remote sensing datasets. fANOVA decomposes performance variance into marginal contributions of design choices (architecture, fine-tuning strategy, learning strategy, initialization) and their interactions. Dataset meta-representations — design-choice sensitivity profiles — are constructed and then hierarchically clustered to reveal natural groupings tied to intrinsic dataset properties (scale, spatial resolution, label space complexity).

Result: fANOVA reveals that for large-scale datasets, fine-tuning strategy and architecture dominate performance; in data-limited regimes, initialization becomes decisive; and in intermediate regimes, the architecture–learning strategy interaction governs outcomes. Hierarchical clustering of sensitivity profiles yields dataset groupings strongly correlated with intrinsic properties such as dataset scale, spatial resolution, and label space complexity.

Conclusion: Moving beyond rankings to variance decomposition offers a principled framework for understanding how design choices interact with dataset properties in remote sensing MLC. This enables more informed model selection and highlights which design dimensions warrant tuning under different data regimes.

Abstract: Benchmarking deep learning (DL) models for multi-label classification (MLC) of remote sensing images (RSI) typically yields rankings that do not generalize beyond the evaluated datasets. In this work, we move beyond rankings by employing functional analysis of variance (fANOVA) to systematically quantify the contributions of individual design choices and their interactions to performance variability. We conduct two empirical analyses covering 48 and 20 DL models, respectively, spanning design choices such as network architecture, fine-tuning strategy, learning strategy, and initialization. By applying fANOVA across seven MLC RSI datasets, we construct dataset meta-representations that capture design-choice sensitivity profiles. Hierarchical clustering of these meta-representations reveals that datasets naturally group according to how they respond to design decisions, with patterns strongly linked to intrinsic dataset properties such as scale, spatial resolution, and label space complexity. Our findings show that for large-scale datasets, fine-tuning strategy and architecture are dominant factors, while in data-limited regimes, initialization becomes decisive. For intermediate regimes, the interaction between architecture and learning strategy governs performance.

</details>


### [233] [Benchmarking Deep Learning Models for Dense Event Classification of Offshore Wind Infrastructure in Sentinel-1 Time Series](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04706)
*Thorsten Hoeser,Felix Bachofer,Claudia Kuenzer*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A structured comparison of ten deep learning variants for classifying offshore wind infrastructure deployment from Sentinel-1 SAR time series. The supervised BiLSTM achieves the best performance (AUC: 0.8509 vs. 0.7853 rule-based baseline). Combined with rule-based labels via a label-transition-minimising ensemble, the method enables global-scale isolation of turbine deployment phases, revealing median deployment durations of 84d (China), 242d (EU), and 258d (UK) across 2016–2025.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Offshore wind energy infrastructure is expanding rapidly, and stakeholders need automated, scalable monitoring tools to track deployment life cycles. ESA's Sentinel-1 SAR archives offer dense global time series, but converting these massive data volumes into actionable event labels requires automated algorithms beyond existing rule-based approaches, motivating the exploration of deep learning for dense time series classification.

Method: The authors compare ten deep learning model-training variants — LSTM, Transformer, and fully connected architectures — each with monotemporal, unidirectional, and bidirectional context, with and without self-supervised pretraining. The best model (supervised BiLSTM) is combined with rule-based baseline labels using a label-transition-minimising ensemble. The resulting labels are used for global-scale isolation of turbine deployment phases and subsequent regional/subregional spatiotemporal analysis.

Result: The supervised BiLSTM raises AUC from 0.7853 (rule-based) to 0.8509 and perfect match rate from 0.3508 to 0.5063. The ensemble further improves agreement with test data. Global analysis (2016-01-01 to 2025-03-31) yields median deployment durations of 84 days (China), 242 days (EU), and 258 days (UK), with deployment drivers such as subsidies and environmental conditions clearly emerging across spatial scales.

Conclusion: Deep learning, particularly BiLSTM architectures, substantially improves dense classification of offshore wind deployment events from Sentinel-1 SAR time series over rule-based methods. The approach enables reliable global-scale, high-resolution monitoring of offshore wind infrastructure deployment, providing stakeholders with valuable insights into deployment dynamics influenced by regulatory and environmental factors.

Abstract: Monitoring of offshore wind energy infrastructure life cycles, especially during the deployment phase, is an important contribution for stakeholders to make informed decisions in a phase of increasing deployment activities. ESA's Sentinel-1 Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) mission produces large data archives that enable the global monitoring of offshore wind infrastructure. Turning these high-volume archives into information requires algorithms that automatically extract single event labels from dense time series at a global scale. In this study, we present a structured comparison of ten deep learning model-training variants for the dense classification of Sentinel-1 based offshore wind infrastructure time series, aiming to advance rule-based event classification of this task. We trained LSTM, Transformer, and fully connected model variants with monotemporal, unidirectional, and bidirectional context awareness, each with and without self-supervised pretraining. Among these, the supervised BiLSTM performs best, raising the target AUC score from 0.7853 for the rule-based baseline to 0.8509, and the perfect match rate from 0.3508 to 0.5063. Combining the BiLSTM predictions with the existing baseline labels in a label-transition-minimising ensemble further improves agreement with the test data. Using these improved labels, we isolate the deployment phase of individual turbines at a global scale and conduct a regional and subregional analysis covering 2016-01-01 to 2025-03-31, reporting median deployment durations of 84 d (China), 242 d (EU), and 258 d (UK). Deployment-related drivers, including legal regulations such as subsidies, and environmental conditions, emerge clearly from the analysed results across multiple spatial scales.

</details>


### [234] [A 6G Integrated Sensing and Communication Framework for Railway Intrusion Detection and Collision Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04710)
*Ajeet Kumar Yadav,Sankaran Balasubramaniam,Aritra Chatterjee,Vinod Aduru,Yogesh Simmhan,Pandarasamy Arjunan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A machine learning model combining 3D CNN and BiLSTM achieves 99.57% accuracy in detecting railway track intruders and predicts their position, velocity, and time-to-collision using ISAC-based CSI data from a synthetic 3D railway environment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Railway track intrusions by objects such as wildlife pose serious collision risks. 3GPP Release 19 identifies railway intrusion detection as a key ISAC use case, motivating the development of a CSI-based sensing solution that leverages 5G-Advanced/6G infrastructure for real-time intruder detection and trajectory prediction.

Method: A 3D-rendered railway environment coupled with the Sionna radio simulator generated 22,695 CSI matrices with ground-truth labels. A hybrid deep learning architecture combining a 3D Convolutional Neural Network (3D CNN) for spatio-temporal feature extraction and a Bidirectional LSTM (BiLSTM) for temporal sequence modeling was trained to detect intruders in the danger zone and estimate position, velocity, and time-to-collision.

Result: The model achieved 99.57% intruder-detection accuracy on a balanced test set and a combined Mean Absolute Error (MAE) of 0.4240 across position, velocity, and time-to-collision prediction tasks on synthetic CSI data.

Conclusion: CSI-based ISAC sensing powered by machine learning shows strong potential for reliable railway intrusion detection. The codebase is publicly available to facilitate further research.

Abstract: Integrated Sensing and Communication (ISAC) combines sensing and communication to efficiently utilize wireless resources and is emerging as a key paradigm for next-generation wireless networks. By leveraging the wide bandwidth, high frequencies, and massive antenna arrays of 5G-Advanced and 6G systems, ISAC enables physical-layer sensing using Channel State Information (CSI). The 3rd Generation Partnership Project (3GPP) Release 19 identifies 32 potential ISAC use cases, with particular emphasis on detecting and tracking moving objects. In this work, we address the Sensing for Railway Intrusion Detection use case, where intruders, including wildlife, entering a railway track can pose serious collision risks. We generated 22,695 CSI matrices with corresponding ground truth using a 3D-rendered railway environment and the Sionna radio simulator. We developed a machine learning model combining a three-dimensional Convolutional Neural Network (3D CNN) and Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (BiLSTM) network to detect intruders in the track danger zone and estimate their real-time position relative to the train, velocity, and time to collision. On synthetic CSI data, the model achieves 99.57% intruder-detection accuracy on a balanced test set and a combined Mean Absolute Error (MAE) of 0.4240 for position, velocity, and time-to-collision prediction. These results demonstrate the potential of CSI-based ISAC sensing with machine learning for reliable railway intrusion detection. The complete codebase for CSI generation, preprocessing, and model development is publicly available at https://github.com/EdgeIntelligenceLab/6g-isac-railway-intrusion-detection.

</details>


### [235] [Attention, Anomalies! Handling Attention Layers in Unsupervised Federated Outlier Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04753)
*Mihailo Ilić,Miloš Savić,Vladimir Kurbalija,Mirjana Ivanović,Giancarlo Fortino,Dušan Jakovetić*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes novel federated aggregation techniques tailored for Memory Augmented Autoencoders (MemAE) in unsupervised anomaly detection, demonstrating improved robustness on non-IID data across numerous edge nodes, even with shallow architectures suitable for resource-constrained environments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing Federated Learning (FL) frameworks lack specialized aggregation methods for Memory Augmented Autoencoders. While attention-based MemAE models excel at unsupervised outlier detection in centralized settings, no FL-specific aggregation strategies account for the unique architectural characteristics of these models, creating a gap for distributed, privacy-preserving anomaly detection.

Method: The authors analyze the architectural intricacies of MemAE models and propose guided, specialized aggregation schemes for federated scenarios. These schemes are designed to handle the memory module and attention mechanisms during model averaging across distributed clients. Evaluation is conducted on non-IID datasets with numerous edge nodes in unbalanced data environments.

Result: The proposed aggregation schemes demonstrate improved robustness over standard FL aggregation when handling non-IID, unbalanced data distributions across many edge nodes. Notably, the approach enables even very shallow autoencoders to perform effectively, making them viable for resource-constrained deployment.

Conclusion: Specialized federated aggregation techniques for MemAE models significantly improve unsupervised anomaly detection under non-IID conditions. The method extends the applicability of attention-augmented autoencoders to federated settings, including resource-limited edge environments.

Abstract: Attention layers are the backbone of today's most powerful and impactful models. Models with multi-million and billion parameters rely on contextual knowledge provided by attention layers. However, their use goes well beyond just being the core component of large language models. One particularly interesting application is in Memory Augmented Autoencoders (MemAE), specifically for unsupervised representation learning in outlier detection tasks. It was shown that attention helps these models be more effective in centralized learning scenarios. Our work aims to address the lack of specialized aggregation techniques in Federated Learning (FL) when it comes to MemAE models. In this paper we analyze the intricacies of the architecture behind Memory Augmented Autoencoders, and propose novel, guided approaches to effectively aggregate these models in federated scenarios. We demonstrate our approach on non-IID datasets and show that these novel aggregation schemes are more robust when dealing with numerous edge nodes in environments with unbalanced datasets, specifically for unsupervised anomaly detection scenarios. This approach improves the performance of even very shallow autoencoders, allowing them to be used in resource constrained environments.

</details>


### [236] [IMFACT: Counterfactual Explanations for Time Series via Intrinsic Mode Function Substitution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04777)
*Udo Schlegel,Julian Rakuschek,Thomas Seidl,Andreas Holzinger,Tobias Schreck,Javier Del Ser*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: IMFACT generates plausible counterfactual explanations for time series classifiers by progressively substituting Intrinsic Mode Functions (IMFs) from a Nearest Unlike Neighbour (NUN) until classification flips, with variance-based IMF selection and multi-NUN cycling outperforming baseline methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing counterfactual methods that perturb oscillatory signals in raw feature space destroy temporal structure and produce physically implausible results. There is a need for a counterfactual generation approach that respects the inherent oscillatory nature of such signals while producing class-discriminative changes.

Method: The IMFACT framework first decomposes input signals into Intrinsic Mode Functions (IMFs) via Empirical Mode Decomposition. It then progressively substitutes selected IMFs with those from a Nearest Unlike Neighbour (NUN) until the classifier predicts the target class. Six IMF-selection strategies are evaluated, along with a multi-NUN cycling extension that rotates across multiple NUNs for improved proximity.

Result: On the UCR benchmarks FaultDetectionA and FruitFlies, the variance-based IMF-selection strategy with three NUNs outperforms two prominent baseline techniques on both reliability and plausibility metrics. Cycling across three NUNs yields the best proximity across both datasets.

Conclusion: Operating in the EMD decomposition space enables generation of counterfactuals that preserve temporal structure and physical plausibility for oscillatory signals. The variance-based selection strategy combined with multi-NUN cycling provides the best trade-off between reliability, plausibility, and proximity.

Abstract: Oscillatory signals, such as vibration, carry class-discriminative information in specific frequency bands; perturbing them in raw feature space for counterfactual analysis easily destroys their temporal structure and produces physically implausible results. In this work, we introduce IMFACT (IMF-based counterfACTuals), a model-agnostic framework for generating plausible counterfactual explanations for time series classifiers that operates in the decomposition space of Empirical Mode Decomposition. An input signal is split into Intrinsic Mode Functions (IMFs), and selected IMFs are progressively substituted with those of a Nearest Unlike Neighbour (NUN) until the classifier flips to the target class. We evaluate six IMF-selection strategies and a multi-NUN cycling extension on two UCR benchmarks (FaultDetectionA, FruitFlies). The variance-based strategy with three NUNs outperforms two prominent baseline techniques on reliability and plausibility metrics, while cycling across three NUNs yields the best proximity across both datasets.

</details>


### [237] [Continual-Learning Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Parameterized Partial Differential Equations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04778)
*Xujia Chen,Xinyue Hu,Letian Chen,Yi Liu,Wenhui Fan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CL-PINN introduces continual learning to parameterized physics-informed neural networks, using Bayesian active parameter selection, dynamic loss weighting, and sparse replay to efficiently learn PDE solutions across broad parameter domains without observational data, achieving higher and more balanced accuracy than fixed-sampling baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing ParamPINNs suffer from inefficient training, uneven accuracy across parameter values, and overfitting to sampled parameters, limiting generalization to unseen parameters. Current approaches lack mechanisms to allocate limited training capacity effectively across a parameter domain.

Method: CL-PINN treats PDEs at different parameter values as sequential tasks in a continual learning framework. It integrates four components: (1) Bayesian-optimization-based active parameter selection to choose which parameter to train next, (2) task-wise dynamic loss weighting for balanced optimization, (3) sparse physics-constrained replay using a small buffer of collocation points from prior tasks to mitigate catastrophic forgetting, and (4) an optional parameter subnetwork for enhanced parameter encoding. No observational data is required.

Result: Evaluated on one continuous function and four parameterized PDE benchmarks under multi-seed protocols: Bayesian selection significantly reduces objective-loss queries compared to grid-greedy search; sparse replay effectively mitigates forgetting of earlier tasks; CL-PINN yields higher and more balanced solution accuracy than fixed-sampling and grid-greedy baselines under bounded active-task capacity.

Conclusion: CL-PINN offers a practical and resource-efficient framework for learning parametric PDE solutions that generalize across physical parameters, with potential for reusable physics-informed surrogates in large-scale engineering parameter studies.

Abstract: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) incorporate governing equations into neural-network training and can approximate PDE solutions without requiring large observational datasets. Parameterized PINNs (ParamPINNs) further take physical parameters as inputs, allowing a single model to represent a family of PDE solutions over a parameter domain. Existing ParamPINNs, however, still face inefficient training, uneven accuracy across parameters, and overfitting to a limited set of sampled parameter tasks, which can impair generalization to unsampled parameters. To address these issues, we propose a continual-learning physics-informed neural network (CL-PINN), which treats PDE instances at different parameter values as related tasks and learns them sequentially. CL-PINN combines Bayesian-optimization-based active parameter selection, task-wise dynamic loss weighting, sparse physics-constrained replay, and an optional parameter subnetwork to improve task allocation and knowledge retention under bounded active-task capacity. It requires no observational data and is designed to solve parameterized PDEs over relatively broad parameter domains under limited computational resources. Multi-seed evaluations on five benchmarks, including one continuous function and four parameterized PDEs, show that Bayesian selection substantially reduces objective-loss queries relative to grid-greedy search, while sparse replay mitigates forgetting of earlier tasks. Under the prescribed within-case resource protocols, CL-PINN generally provides higher and more balanced solution accuracy than fixed-sampling and grid-greedy baselines. CL-PINN offers a practical route toward learning PDE solutions that generalize across physical parameters and has the potential to support reusable physics-informed surrogates for large-scale engineering parameter studies.

</details>


### [238] [Agentic Reinforcement Learning with Observation-Calibrated Self-Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04788)
*Yi Yang,Cong Qin,Xiaodan Liu,Chishui Chen,Qing Dong,Yan Zhang,Cao Liu,Zhao Yang,Lu Pan,Jiaye Lin,Yi Feng*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: OCSD proposes a method to improve RL training of LLM agents by calibrating token-level supervision. It resolves confounding in prior work (OPSD) where replay scaffold artifacts obscure the signal from privileged future observations, using a contrastive residual between Full and Observation-Ablated replay views to modulate GRPO updates.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In RL-trained LLM agents, sparse trajectory-level rewards provide poor token-level guidance. On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD) uses a privileged replay view for dense token-level supervision, but suffers from a confounding issue: token score changes reflect both the privileged information and artifacts from the replay scaffold itself. This is especially severe when future observations serve as privileged information, since replaying them requires an extended scaffold that perturbs token scores.

Method: OCSD contrasts two structurally matched replay views — Full (with actual future observation) and Observation-Ablated (without it) — to compute an observation residual that discounts scaffold-induced score changes. This calibrated residual modulates token-level GRPO updates specifically at high-uncertainty steps, while preserving the original trajectory-level update direction.

Result: Experiments on ALFWorld, WebShop, and Search-QA across three Qwen3 model scales demonstrate that OCSD consistently outperforms strong baselines. Diagnostic analyses confirm that the calibrated residual aligns better with local environment feedback.

Conclusion: OCSD effectively isolates the genuine signal from privileged future observations by canceling out replay scaffold artifacts via contrastive replay views, yielding superior token-level credit assignment and improved agent performance across diverse interactive benchmarks.

Abstract: Large language model agents are commonly trained through reinforcement learning with sparse trajectory-level rewards, which offer limited guidance on how strongly individual tokens should be updated. On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD) addresses this by re-scoring generated tokens under a privileged replay view to obtain dense, token-level supervision. However, we identify a confounding issue: the resulting support may reflect both the privileged information contained in the replay view and score shifts induced by the replay scaffold, making it difficult to attribute the support specifically to that information. This issue is especially pronounced when future environment observations serve as privileged information, since replaying them requires reconstructing an extended scaffold that itself perturbs token scores. To resolve this confounding, we propose Observation-Calibrated Self-Distillation (OCSD), which contrasts two structurally matched replay views, Full and Observation-Ablated, differing only in whether the actual future observation is present, to derive an observation residual that discounts score changes shared by the replay scaffold. OCSD then applies this residual to modulate token-level GRPO updates at high-uncertainty steps, while preserving the trajectory-level update direction. Experiments on ALFWorld, WebShop, and Search-QA across three Qwen3 model scales show that OCSD consistently outperforms strong baselines. Diagnostic analyses further confirm that the calibrated residual aligns better with local environment feedback. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/yiy1x/OCSD.

</details>


### [239] [Above-ground Biomass Estimation with Geospatial Foundation Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04792)
*Ghjulia Sialellia,Linus Scheibenreif,Jan Dirk Wegner,Konrad Schindler*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper benchmarks Geospatial Foundation Models (GFMs) for global-scale above-ground biomass (AGB) estimation. It finds that GFMs used as frozen encoders underperform compared to a supervised SOTA model, while pre-computed embedding products (AlphaEarth Foundations, TESSERA) are highly effective — an MLP on AEF embeddings surpasses the SOTA model, with further gains from combining embeddings with raw features.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Accurate global-scale AGB estimation from satellite imagery is critical for carbon stock monitoring but remains challenging. GFMs offer promising general-purpose representations from Earth observation data, yet their utility for quantitative regression (as opposed to classification/segmentation) is largely unexplored. This gap motivates a rigorous benchmark.

Method: The authors benchmark 11 GFMs from the PANGAEA framework (evaluated as frozen encoders) and two pre-computed embedding products (AlphaEarth Foundations/AEF and TESSERA) using the AGBD dataset. They compare these against a fully supervised SOTA model across multiple dimensions: overall predictive performance, geographical and temporal generalization, and agreement with the ESA CCI biomass product on independent reference data. They also test augmenting embeddings with selected raw features.

Result: Frozen-encoder GFMs substantially underperform relative to the supervised SOTA baseline. In contrast, pre-computed embedding products prove highly effective: an MLP trained solely on AEF embeddings outperforms the SOTA model trained on AGBD features. The best overall result is achieved by the SOTA model trained on AEF embeddings augmented with selected raw features, which also generalizes better across space and time.

Conclusion: Pre-computed embedding products (particularly AEF) are a viable and effective pathway for applying GFMs to global-scale biomass regression, outperforming both frozen-encoder approaches and traditional fully supervised baselines, with superior spatial and temporal generalization.

Abstract: Accurate estimation of Above-Ground Biomass (AGB) from satellite imagery is essential for the large-scale monitoring of carbon stocks, yet it remains a challenging regression task at global scale. Geospatial Foundation Models (GFMs) have recently emerged as a promising machine learning paradigm to derive general-purpose representations from Earth observation data, but their utility for quantitative regression tasks like biomass estimation remains largely unexplored, as most benchmarks emphasize classification and segmentation. Here, we present a comprehensive benchmark of GFMs for global-scale AGB estimation using the AGBD dataset, a machine learning-ready benchmark spanning diverse biomes and geographies. We distinguish two ways in which GFMs reach practitioners: (i) models distributed as weights to be run by the user, which we evaluate as frozen encoders within the PANGAEA benchmarking framework; and (ii) models distributed as ready-to-use, pre-computed embedding products, for which we evaluate AlphaEarth Foundations (AEF) and TESSERA. We compare 11 GFMs available on PANGAEA and both embedding products against a fully supervised state-of-the-art (SOTA) model, assess their geographical and temporal generalization abilities, as well as agreement with the ESA CCI biomass product on independent reference data. Our results show that GFMs run as frozen encoders substantially underperform with respect to the supervised SOTA model, whereas pre-computed embedding products prove highly effective. An MLP trained on AEF embeddings outperforms the supervised SOTA model trained on AGBD features, and the same SOTA model trained on AEF embeddings (optionally augmented with selected raw features) achieves the best overall result, while also generalizing better across space and time.

</details>


### [240] [MGSB: Manifold Gated Signature Branch Pressure-Domain Baseline Architecture for Two-Phase Pipeline Flows Under Distributional Shift](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04805)
*Issah Suleiman,Sormeh Serpoosh,Nadine Elkholy,Hicham Ferroudji,Mohammad Azizur Rahman,Matthew Hamilton*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MGSB, a regime-aware architecture with TT-RoughPath encoding and Mean-Teacher consistency, achieves strong leak detection under distribution shift (OOD F1: 0.783), with architecture rather than training procedure driving robustness.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Leak detection models for multiphase pipelines degrade under flow regime shifts (e.g., bubble-to-slug), and standard in-distribution evaluation masks these failures.

Method: Proposes MGSB architecture combining regime-conditioned feature fusion, a TT-RoughPath encoder, and Mean-Teacher consistency regularization. Evaluated via leave-one-group-out cross-validation with Mahalanobis-distance OOD confirmation and ablation studies.

Result: MGSB achieves detection F1 of 0.930 and OOD F1 of 0.783, significantly outperforming CNN-LSTM and fully connected baselines under severe feature corruption. Ablations attribute OOD robustness primarily to architecture, not training procedure.

Conclusion: Explicit regime-aware modeling is a practical path toward robust, sensor-agnostic leak detection in industrial multiphase pipelines.

Abstract: Leak detection models for multiphase pipelines often degrade when deployed under flow regimes that differ from training. Existing evaluations typically assess performance under in-distribution operating conditions, masking failures caused by regime transitions such as bubble-to-slug flow. We propose the Manifold Gated Signature Bias (MGSB), a regime-aware architecture combining regime-conditioned feature fusion, a TT-RoughPath encoder, and Mean-Teacher consistency regularization to improve robustness under distribution shift. Under leave-one-group-out evaluation, MGSB achieves a detection F1 of 0.930 and an OOD F1 of 0.783, substantially outperforming CNN-LSTM and fully connected baselines under severe feature corruption. Ablations show the proposed architecture, not the training procedure, is the primary contributor to OOD robustness, while Mahalanobis-distance analysis confirms the held-out conditions are genuinely out-of-distribution. These results show that explicit regime-aware modelling is a practical path toward robust, sensor-agnostic leak detection in industrial multiphase pipelines.

</details>


### [241] [Robust Control under Stationary Ambiguity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04832)
*Konrad J. Mueller,Amira Akkari,Ben Wood,Lukas Gonon*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Simulator-trained policies fail when parameter uncertainty is underestimated. The paper proposes "stationary ambiguity"—a principle where simulator ambiguity is state-dependent but does not systematically decay—so that policies maintain continual robustness to latent parameter shifts. Demonstrated on hedging problems, this approach yields policies that perform well on real market data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Policies optimized in simulation often fail in real systems because simulator parameters are estimated from limited data and the resulting uncertainty is not represented. While randomizing parameters can help, policies that progressively observe the system tend to infer and over-specialize to parameter estimates, losing robustness. This is problematic when latent factors shift over time (e.g., volatility regimes in financial markets), requiring continual rather than diminishing robustness.

Method: The authors formalize "stationary ambiguity": constructing simulators such that the filtering process over the latent state is stationary, meaning ambiguity varies with the system's state but does not systematically decay. They provide a construction methodology for such simulators and train policies under this stationary ambiguity regime. The approach informs simulator design decisions including model selection, parameter randomization strategies, and initialization of both simulator and policy.

Result: Policies trained under stationary ambiguity preserve robustness to latent factors over time. In hedging experiments, these policies demonstrate strong performance on real market data compared to alternatives where ambiguity vanishes as the policy infers parameters.

Conclusion: Stationary ambiguity serves as a general modeling principle for simulator design in sequential control problems driven by exogenous stochastic processes with shifting latent structure. While validated on hedging, the approach may extend to other domains with similar characteristics.

Abstract: Control policies optimized in simulation can perform poorly in the real system when the parameters $x$ of the simulator are estimated from limited data but the resulting parameter uncertainty is not represented inside the simulation. A common way to incorporate such ambiguity is to simulate each trajectory of the system under a randomly drawn value for $x$. Since the policy cannot observe the drawn value, it must initially choose controls that perform well across many possible parameter values. However, if the policy progressively observes the system, it can often gradually infer the value of $x$, so that ambiguity vanishes. Over time, the policy then specializes to its estimate of $x$ and loses its robustness. This is undesirable in many real systems, where latent factors are expected to shift. In financial markets, for example, a policy hedging a derivative payoff should remain robust to changes in the volatility regime. To induce such continual robustness, we propose training policies in simulators where ambiguity varies with the system's state but does not systematically decay over time. We formalize this requirement as stationary ambiguity: the simulator should induce a stationary filter process over the latent state. We show how to construct such simulators and demonstrate, on hedging problems, that policies trained under stationary ambiguity preserve robustness to latent factors over time, leading to strong performance on real market data. As a modeling principle, stationary ambiguity informs many simulator design decisions: which models make realistic simulators, how their parameters should be randomized, and how simulator and policy should be initialized. While our experiments focus on hedging, stationary ambiguity may also be useful for other sequential control problems driven by exogenous stochastic processes with shifting latent structure.

</details>


### [242] [Training Crossroads for Recurrent Vision Transformers: Recurrence, Neural ODEs, and Deep Supervision](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04879)
*Grzegorz Gruszczynski,Pawel Olszowiec,Michal Byra,Grzegorz Stefanski,Alberto Presta*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A controlled empirical study of single-block recurrent Vision Transformers (bViT) examining when recurrence beats depth, whether ODE solver order acts as numerical refinement or architectural bias, and how deep supervision affects robustness beyond the training horizon.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Vision Transformers scale parameters linearly with depth. Single-block recurrent ViTs eliminate this growth by reusing one block, but the trade-offs between independent depth, recurrence, parameter memory, FLOPs, and out-of-distribution robustness are poorly characterized. The authors aim to provide a rigorous empirical characterization under a fixed, controlled protocol.

Method: The authors fix a single-block recurrent ViT architecture and evaluate three regimes on CIFAR-100: (1) recurrence vs. independent depth at matched FLOPs and matched parameter memory; (2) residual recurrent blocks trained as ODEs with varying solver orders, analyzing the continuous-time analogue (state-subtracted vector field); (3) stage-wise deep supervision to probe accuracy-robustness trade-offs beyond the training horizon.

Result: Standard ViTs win under FLOP constraints; recurrent ViTs offer better accuracy-per-parameter under memory constraints. Higher-order ODE solvers act as architectural bias rather than numerical refinement, with non-uniform gains. Improper black-box wrapping of the residual block as a vector field costs ~few accuracy points. Stage-wise deep supervision does not boost nominal accuracy but enables graceful degradation far beyond the training horizon, where naive recurrence collapses to near-random performance.

Conclusion: Recurrent ViTs are advantageous under parameter-memory constraints but not FLOP constraints. ODE solver order introduces architectural bias, not numerical improvement. The state-subtracted formulation matters in practice. Deep supervision provides robustness to extended recurrence at test time without nominal accuracy gains.

Abstract: Vision Transformers (ViTs) achieve strong image-recognition performance, but their parameter count grows linearly with depth when each block is independently parameterized. Single-block recurrent ViTs (bViT) remove this growth by repeatedly applying one shared block. Rather than proposing a new architecture, we fix a bViT and provide a controlled empirical characterization of three training and inference regimes under a common CIFAR-100 protocol, asking: (i)~when does recurrence beat independently parameterized depth---at matched FLOPs or at matched parameter memory? (ii)~when a residual recurrent block is trained through an ODE solver, does solver order act as numerical refinement or as an architectural bias? and (iii)~what does robustness beyond the training horizon cost in nominal accuracy? We find that standard ViTs remain preferable when FLOPs are the primary constraint, whereas recurrent ViTs offer a better accuracy--parameter trade-off under memory constraints. Consistent with the standard view of residual networks as Euler discretizations of ODEs, the continuous-time analogue of a residual recurrent block is the state-subtracted vector field $\dot{z}=F_θ(z)-z$; although known in principle, this distinction is easy to violate when the block is wrapped as a black-box vector field, and we qualify the cost at few accuracy points. Because the vector field is learned jointly with the solver, higher-order solvers act as a solver-induced architectural bias rather than a numerical-accuracy improvement, and their gains are not uniform. Finally, stage-wise deep supervision traces an accuracy--robustness frontier: it does not improve nominal accuracy, but degrades gracefully far beyond the training horizon, where naive recurrence collapses to near-random performance.

</details>


### [243] [Variational Bounds for Perceptron Learning from Structured Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04882)
*Francesco Camilli,Pierluigi Contucci,Federica Gerace,Emanuele Mingione*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces a variational framework for analyzing a finite-temperature continuous-spin perceptron trained on Gaussian mixture data. Using interpolation, log-concavity, and concentration methods, the authors derive matching lower and upper minimax variational bounds for the limiting quenched pressure, with the bounds differing only in optimization order. When optimizations commute, the solution is fully characterized, yielding fixed-point equations for ground-state energy, training loss, and generalization error.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To develop a rigorous variational characterization of the thermodynamic limit of a continuous-spin perceptron at finite temperature under general concave utilities and log-concave priors, providing a unified framework for computing key observables such as the quenched pressure, ground-state energy, training loss, and generalization error.

Method: The authors employ a variational approach combining the interpolation method with log-concavity and concentration estimates. They derive lower and upper minimax variational bounds for the limiting quenched pressure. The bounds differ only in the order of optimization of two variational parameters, while the concave-convex structure of the variational potential governs the remaining extrema. When optimizations commute, the bounds coincide, yielding the exact solution via stationarity (fixed-point) conditions.

Result: The two derived minimax variational bounds differ solely in the order of optimization of two variational parameters. When these optimizations commute, the bounds match and uniquely identify the model's solution. The variational potential yields fixed-point equations as stationarity conditions and provides a unified route to computing ground-state energy, training loss, and generalization error.

Conclusion: The variational framework provides a rigorous and unified method for solving the finite-temperature continuous-spin perceptron with general concave utilities and log-concave priors. Commutativity of the two variational optimizations is the key condition for the bounds to coalesce, fully characterizing the model's thermodynamic and learning behavior.

Abstract: We introduce a variational approach to a finite-temperature continuous-spin perceptron trained on a Gaussian mixture. The model allows for a broad class of concave utilities and log-concave separable prior measures on the spins. By combining the interpolation method with log-concavity and concentration estimates, we derive lower and upper minimax variational bounds for the limiting quenched pressure. Remarkably, the two bounds differ only in the order of optimization of two variational parameters, while all remaining extrema are controlled by the concave--convex structure of the variational potential. Whenever the two optimizations commute, the two bounds match and identify the solution of the model. The same potential yields the fixed-point equations as stationarity conditions and provides a unified route to the computation of the ground-state energy, training loss, and generalization error.

</details>


### [244] [Consistency-Driven Co-Evolution for Self-Supervised Cross-Representation Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04926)
*Xuehang Guo,Pengyuan Li,Tom Hope,Tirthankar Ghosal,Manling Li,Qingyun Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CoCoEvolve introduces a consistency-driven framework for cross-representation understanding among charts, tables, and code by enforcing explicit one-to-one correspondences and optimizing via inter-representation agreement, effective at both training and test time.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Cross-representation understanding across chart images, tabular data, and visualization code is challenging due to inherent one-to-many mappings, ambiguous and costly supervision, and the lack of a principled optimization signal that is both direction-adaptive and generalizable across representations beyond task-specific objectives.

Method: CoCoEvolve defines explicit one-to-one correspondences among chart, table, and code representations and optimizes models through agreement-based consistency without additional annotations. CoCoEvolve@Train performs co-evolution across the chart-table-code cycle during training, while CoCoEvolve@Test applies the same consistency objective at inference for test-time co-optimization. CoCoEvolve@Eval provides a comprehensive evaluation suite spanning all six cross-representation tasks.

Result: Across four benchmarks, CoCoEvolve improves performance in both training-time and test-time settings compared to baselines.

Conclusion: Enforcing one-to-one consistency through co-evolution across chart, table, and code representations provides an effective, annotation-free optimization signal that generalizes across all cross-representation directions and can be applied at both training and inference stages.

Abstract: As chart images, tabular data, and visualization code play increasingly important roles across diverse domains, cross-representation understanding across these modalities poses fundamental challenges for AI systems: the relationships across representations are inherently \textit{one-to-many}, supervision is ambiguous and costly, and model optimization lacks a principled signal that is both direction-adaptive and representation-generalizable beyond task-specific objectives. We introduce CoCoEvolve to improve consistency across chart, table, and code representations. Instead of treating cross-representation mapping as a one-to-many problem, we define explicit one-to-one correspondences and optimize models using agreement between representations, without additional annotations. During training, CoCoEvolve@Train performs co-evolution across the chart-table-code cycle, while CoCoEvolve@Test applies the same consistency objective at inference time for test-time co-optimization. We also present CoCoEvolve@Eval, an evaluation suite covering all six cross-representation tasks. Across four benchmarks, CoCoEvolve improves performance in both training-time and test-time settings. Our project page: https://xhguo7.github.io/CoCoEvolve/.

</details>


### [245] [Optimal Training-Time Scaling in Gradual Adaptation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04927)
*Zonghuan Xu,Krishna Harish*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: For gradual adaptation with overparameterized linear regression, optimal per-task training time scales as Θ(N⁻¹) — meaning total training time across all tasks should be constant as the number of intermediate tasks increases. Both under-training and over-training harm progress.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In gradual / continual adaptation, practitioners face a key resource-allocation question: as a smooth task shift is divided into more intermediate steps, how should per-task training time be adjusted? Prior work lacks theoretical guidance on this scheduling problem.

Method: The authors formalize the problem using overparameterized linear regression with smoothly shifting tasks that share a zero-loss solution. They analyze the limit where number of tasks N → ∞ and per-task training time s_N → 0 such that N·s_N → τ (total training time). The learning dynamics are studied via gradient flow, and the final progress is characterized asymptotically.

Result: The limiting progress scales as Θ(τ) for small τ and Θ(τ⁻¹) for large τ, implying a non-monotonic relationship with a finite optimum. Consequently, optimal per-task time is s_N* = Θ(N⁻¹), i.e., total time N·s_N* = Θ(1). Experiments on gradually rotated MNIST and the Yearbook temporal dataset confirm that finer discretization requires less per-task training.

Conclusion: When adapting along a smooth task continuum, one should not allocate fixed training time per task. Instead, total training budget should remain roughly constant regardless of how many intermediate tasks are introduced, with each task receiving proportionally less training.

Abstract: In gradual adaptation, how should the training time on each task change as the number of intermediate tasks increases? We study this question for overparameterized linear regression tasks that change smoothly and share a zero-loss solution. With $N$ tasks and training time $s_N$ on each, the final learning progress converges to a continuum curve when $Ns_N\toτ$. The limiting progress is $Θ(τ)$ for small $τ$ and $Θ(τ^{-1})$ for large $τ$, so both very short and very long training produce little progress. It follows that optimal per-task training times scale as $s_N^\star=Θ(N^{-1})$, equivalently $Ns_N^\star=Θ(1)$. Experiments on gradually rotated MNIST and a natural Yearbook time shift are consistent with less per-task training as the path is divided more finely.

</details>


### [246] [SVI-DAG: A Structured Variational Inference Approach to Bayesian Causal Discovery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04930)
*Shrenik Zinage*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SVI-DAG proposes a structured variational inference method for Bayesian causal discovery that uses normalizing flows to model edge dependencies and Stein variational gradient descent with an acyclicity-space kernel to improve mode coverage, outperforming 5 baselines in uncertainty quantification.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing Bayesian causal discovery methods fail to (1) encode dependencies between edges in DAGs and (2) incorporate domain knowledge as principled inductive biases during search. These limitations hinder expressive posterior learning and uncertainty quantification over causal structures.

Method: SVI-DAG employs structured variational inference with normalizing flows to capture dependencies between edges, enabling expressive and multimodal posterior distributions over DAGs. To address mode-seeking behavior in standard ELBO optimization, the method applies Stein variational gradient descent (SVGD) to update node potentials using a kernel defined in acyclicity space, promoting better mode coverage. Prior beliefs are incorporated as inductive biases.

Result: SVI-DAG demonstrates superior uncertainty quantification compared to 5 state-of-the-art Bayesian DAG learning methods while maintaining competitive structural accuracy.

Conclusion: The combination of normalizing flows for edge dependency modeling and SVGD with an acyclicity-space kernel effectively addresses key limitations in Bayesian causal discovery, yielding better-calibrated posterior uncertainty without sacrificing graph recovery performance.

Abstract: Bayesian causal discovery seeks to determine the posterior distribution of causal theories, which are interpreted as directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) that explain the observed data. The resulting posterior allows systematic reasoning regarding epistemic uncertainty within these theories. Nonetheless, finding such graphs is difficult due to identifiability problems and limited observational data. Furthermore, precisely approximating posterior over graphs is challenging given vast range of potential DAGs.
