Recent Bayesian approaches have addressed some of these challenges, yet they remain limited as they fail to encode dependencies between edges, and lack principled ways to incorporate domain knowledge as inductive biases during the search process. To overcome these limitations, we propose SVI-DAG, a structured variational inference approach to Bayesian causal discovery using observational data and prior beliefs that uses normalizing flows to model dependencies between edges, supporting expressive and multimodal posterior learning over DAGs. To mitigate mode seeking behaviour in evidence lower bound optimization and promote mode coverage, we use stein variational gradient descent to update the node potentials using a kernel in acyclicity space. We evaluate SVI-DAG against 5 state-of-the-art Bayesian DAG learning methods and demonstrate superior performance in uncertainty quantification while remaining competitive in terms of structural accuracy.

</details>


### [247] [CheMLFlow: An Open-Source Platform for Cheminformatics and Materials Informatics Applications](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04942)
*Brendan Smith,Susana Lopez-Moreno,Eric Dolores-Cuenca,Sangil Kim,Jose L. Mendoza-Cortes,Nijamudheen Abdulrahiman*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CheMLFlow is an open-source platform that streamlines end-to-end scientific ML workflows by providing modular, reproducible pipelines for data handling, model training, evaluation, and reporting, with demonstrated performance on molecular property prediction and time series tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Researchers building scientific ML applications face significant orchestration overhead when assembling full reproducible pipelines spanning data acquisition, curation, representation, training, validation, screening, and reporting, even when their core contribution targets only one stage. There is a need for a unified platform that reduces this burden and enables benchmarking across methods and datasets.

Method: CheMLFlow provides modular workflow components, ready-to-run reference pipelines, standardized artifacts, and structured evaluation outputs. It features pluggable representations and models, deterministic data splits, explicit run artifact tracking, batch execution, and automated report generation. The platform is configuration-driven, extensible, and supports agentic interaction through structured outputs that enable coding agents to assist with experiment construction and result summarization under human supervision.

Result: Benchmarks demonstrate literature-competitive performance for quantum mechanical, physicochemical, and bioactivity property prediction tasks. Additional use cases with time series datasets validate applicability beyond molecular chemistry domains.

Conclusion: CheMLFlow successfully addresses the pipeline orchestration bottleneck in scientific ML by delivering a reproducible, extensible, and automation-friendly platform that supports both traditional high-throughput workflows and emerging agent-assisted experimentation paradigms across diverse scientific domains.

Abstract: CheMLFlow is an open-source platform for building and executing end-to-end, high-throughput, and agentic workflows for scientific and technological applications. CheMLFlow targets a common bottleneck in scientific machine learning development, where researchers often need to assemble data acquisition, curation, representation, model training, validation, screening, interpretation, and reporting into a reproducible pipeline, even when their primary research contribution concerns only one stage. CheMLFlow provides modular workflow components, ready-to-run reference pipelines, standardized artifacts, and evaluation outputs that reduce orchestration overhead and support benchmarking across methods and datasets. The platform is designed to be extensible, reproducible, and automation friendly, with pluggable representations and models, deterministic splits, explicit run artifacts, batch execution, and report generation. As scientific software increasingly moves toward agent assisted experimentation, CheMLFlow's configuration driven workflows and structured outputs also provide a practical interface for coding agents to help users construct experiments, inspect results, and summarize findings under human supervision. This article describes the system architecture, core workflows, and benchmarks that reach literature performance for quantum mechanical, physicochemical and bioactivity property prediction, and use cases involving time series datasets demonstrating applications beyond molecular chemistry datasets.

</details>


### [248] [SpecRoll: Fast-Slow Verifier-Feedback Adaptation for Speculative Reinforcement Learning Rollouts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04962)
*Nhat Minh Pham,Duy Tung Doan,Thi Duyen Ngo,Vinh Van Nguyen,Khac-Hoai Nam Bui*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SpecRoll is a speculative rollout engine for RL post-training of LLMs that accelerates autoregressive generation by 1.26–2.15× while preserving exact target distribution, using dual-timescale adaptation: fast hidden-state corrections via a Reflex module and slow head parameter updates only when degradation is detected.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: RL post-training enhances LLM reasoning, but autoregressive rollout generation is a major efficiency bottleneck. Speculative decoding can help, but applying it during RL is challenging because the target policy continuously evolves — static proposers become stale, and frequent drafter updates incur prohibitive overhead.

Method: SpecRoll operates at two timescales: (1) A fast path using lightweight future-token heads for parallel proposals, combined with a Reflex module that applies bounded, trajectory-local hidden-state corrections using delayed verifier feedback without backpropagation. (2) A slow path that updates head parameters only when sustained degradation is detected. These are integrated with concurrency-aware sparse-tree verification and exact target verification, keeping the GRPO objective and target rollout distribution unchanged.

Result: Across 5 models (1.5B–14B) and 3 math reasoning datasets, SpecRoll achieves 1.26–2.15× generation speedup and 1.21–2.04× end-to-end speedup over vanilla GRPO. It outperforms FastGRPO in all 15 matched settings with an average pairwise end-to-end gain of 1.18×. Ablations confirm complementary benefits of the fast and slow adaptation paths.

Conclusion: SpecRoll effectively bridges speculative decoding and online RL training by solving the stale-proposer problem through dual-timescale adaptation, delivering significant practical speedups without altering the training objective or distribution.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training improves the reasoning capabilities of large language models, but autoregressive rollout generation remains a major efficiency bottleneck. Speculative decoding can accelerate generation, yet applying it during RL is difficult because the target policy continually evolves: static proposers become stale, while frequent drafter updates add substantial overhead. We introduce SpecRoll, a speculative rollout engine that preserves the target model's sampling distribution while adapting at two timescales. Lightweight future-token heads generate parallel proposals, while our proposed Reflex module uses delayed verifier feedback to perform bounded, trajectory-local hidden-state corrections without backpropagation. A complementary slow path updates the head parameters only when sustained degradation is detected. SpecRoll combines these mechanisms with concurrency-aware sparse-tree verification and exact target verification, leaving the target rollout distribution and GRPO objective unchanged. Across five models ranging from 1.5B to 14B and three mathematical reasoning datasets, SpecRoll achieves 1.26-2.15x generation speedup and 1.21-2.04x end-to-end speedup over vanilla GRPO. It also outperforms FastGRPO in both generation and end-to-end time across all 15 matched settings, with an average pairwise end-to-end gain of 1.18x. Controlled ablations show that the fast and slow adaptation paths provide complementary benefits. Our source code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/SpecRoll-26062006.

</details>


### [249] [EvolveNet: Collaborative Harness Evolution for Agent Self-Improvement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04968)
*Jun Nie,Yonggang Zhang,Qianshu Cai,Yiu-ming Cheung,Xinmei Tian,Bo Han*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: EvolveNet proposes a decentralized paradigm for evolving LLM agent harnesses collaboratively across isolated data streams, using scope-typed, evidence-guided program aggregation to compose locally-evolved adaptations into a shared harness, achieving gains across five benchmark settings especially under heterogeneous workloads.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Real-world agent deployments produce isolated streams of experience that cannot be centrally pooled (due to privacy, organizational boundaries, etc.), yet existing harness evolution methods assume a single centralized optimizer. The experience most worth learning from is precisely the experience that cannot be directly centralized.

Method: EvolveNet broadcasts a shared harness to data-local agent deployments, each evolving it on its own workload. Only the resulting program adaptations (not raw data) are sent back and composed into an updated shared harness via scope-typed, evidence-guided program aggregation. This addresses the fact that independently modified programs cannot be averaged like model parameters and may conflict when composed.

Result: Across five settings (text-to-SQL, data-science coding, competitive programming, software engineering, and agentic workflows), EvolveNet improves the shared harness in all five, with largest gains under heterogeneous workloads. Ablations show improvement stems from composition of adaptations rather than mere selection among them.

Conclusion: Shifting the aggregation boundary from raw workloads to learned program adaptations enables collaborative harness evolution in privacy-constrained, heterogeneous agent ecosystems, with composition-based aggregation outperforming selection-based alternatives.

Abstract: The capabilities of an LLM agent depend not only on its model but on the harness: the executable program that constructs context, invokes tools, verifies results, and recovers from failure. Recent work shows that evolving the harness yields persistent improvements without updating model weights. Existing approaches, however, assume that all execution experience can be routed to a single optimizer, which evolves one harness along a sequential trajectory. Real agent ecosystems violate that assumption: users, organizations, and environments generate isolated streams of experience that cannot be pooled, so the experience most worth learning from is exactly the experience that cannot be directly centralized. We introduce EvolveNet, a paradigm of collaborative harness evolution that moves experience extraction to the data. A shared harness is broadcast to data-local agent deployments, each of which evolves it on its own workload. Only the resulting program adaptations are composed into an updated shared harness and redistributed, so that every participating agent inherits operational experience discovered by the others. By shifting the aggregation boundary from raw workloads to learned adaptations, EvolveNet keeps workloads local and allows multiple evolutionary searches to proceed concurrently with reduced serial depth. Because independently modified programs cannot be averaged like model parameters and may conflict when composed, EvolveNet introduces scope-typed, evidence-guided program aggregation. Across five settings spanning text-to-SQL, data-science coding, competitive programming, software engineering, and agentic workflows, EvolveNet improves the shared harness in all five, with the largest gains under heterogeneous workloads, and ablations attribute the improvement to composition of adaptations from different agents rather than to selecting among them.

</details>


### [250] [Stochastic Emulation using Generalized Stratified Sampling for Performance-Based Risk Optimization of Structures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05006)
*Isabela D. Rodrigues,Seymour M. J. Spence,Henrique M. Kroetz,André T. Beck*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes combining Generalized Stratified Sampling (GSS) with Stochastic Polynomial Chaos Expansion (SPCE) to improve tail-region accuracy in structural reliability analysis, then applies this framework to performance-based risk optimization of a steel building.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: SPCE is attractive for stochastic emulation because it avoids replications at fixed inputs, but it struggles to accurately represent extreme responses in distribution tails—a critical region for reliability analysis. This motivates the need for an enhanced framework.

Method: The GSS-SPCE framework partitions the input space into strata based on hazard intensity. Independent SPCE emulators are trained within each stratum. Conditional exceedance probabilities from each stratum are then combined via the total probability theorem to evaluate probabilistic constraints. The framework is demonstrated on optimal design of buckling-restrained braces in a two-story steel building, minimizing construction cost under probabilistic performance constraints.

Result: The proposed GSS-SPCE framework accurately estimates structural response distributions, including tail regions, while substantially reducing the number of nonlinear model evaluations required for performance-based risk optimization.

Conclusion: GSS-SPCE offers an effective solution for computationally efficient PBRO by overcoming SPCE's tail-region limitations through stratified sampling of the hazard intensity space, enabling accurate probabilistic constraint evaluation with fewer simulations.

Abstract: Metamodels are instrumental in reducing the computational burden associated with nested reliability analyses and optimization loops in Performance-Based Risk Optimization (PBRO) of structures under stochastic loads. In this context, stochastic emulators are particularly useful because they approximate response distributions while accounting for the intrinsic stochasticity of the simulator. Among these methods, Stochastic Polynomial Chaos Expansion (SPCE) is especially attractive because it does not require replications of nonlinear analyses at fixed input conditions. However, SPCE may present limitations in accurately representing extreme responses in the tails of structural response distributions. To address this limitation, this study proposes a framework that combines Generalized Stratified Sampling (GSS) with SPCE. The GSS scheme partitions the input space into strata according to the intensity of the hazard, improving the representation of extreme responses, while independent SPCE emulators are trained within each stratum. The conditional exceedance probabilities estimated in each stratum are then recombined using the total probability theorem to evaluate the probabilistic constraints. The proposed GSS-SPCE framework is applied to the optimal design of buckling-restrained brace cross-sectional areas in a two-story steel building. The objective is to minimize the initial construction cost while satisfying prescribed probabilistic performance constraints. Results show that the proposed framework accurately estimates structural response distributions, including their tail regions, while substantially reducing the number of nonlinear model evaluations required for PBRO.

</details>


### [251] [Canonical Joint Energy-Based Model on CIFAR-10: failure modes and practical indistinguishability of Predictor-Corrector and SGLD samplers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05025)
*Dmytro Knopov*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A reproduction study of canonical Joint Energy-Based Models (JEM) finds that the Predictor-Corrector (PC) sampler offers no practical advantage over standard SGLD across generation, classification, and OOD detection tasks, with theoretical analysis showing PC's guarantees do not transfer under fixed noise schedules.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The PC sampler has theoretical motivations but had never undergone a systematic replication test on canonical JEM. The authors aim to determine whether PC retains its theoretical advantages over SGLD in practice under the canonical JEM training setup without annealed noise schedules.

Method: The authors reproduce canonical JEM on WideResNet-28-10 without normalization layers across two independent runs. They test PC versus SGLD across three protocols: (1) PC replacing SGLD throughout ~130 training epochs, (2) cold-start FID generation evaluation, and (3) refinement-style multi-OOD detection using AUROC. Statistical analysis includes hierarchical seed-by-image bootstrap with 95% confidence intervals and seed-level equivalence testing.

Result: Reproduction achieves 92.88% test accuracy and 44.46 buffer-FID (canonical: 92.9%, 38.40). Two failure modes are documented: catastrophic late-training divergence via the outlier-buffer mechanism (both SGLD and PC runs) and run-dependent SVHN OOD-discrimination dynamics. No method-level advantage of PC over SGLD is observed: absolute AUROC difference <0.007 across all checkpoint-OOD pairs, FID difference <0.5. The 95% CI on macro-averaged AUROC difference contains zero; equivalence testing cannot establish formal equivalence. Data are consistent with both equivalence and a small directional effect.

Conclusion: PC and SGLD are practically indistinguishable in canonical JEM. This is theoretically expected because under fixed noise the PC predictor step degenerates by construction, so its theoretical guarantees do not transfer to the canonical JEM setting.

Abstract: Joint Energy-Based Models (JEM) unify classification and generation within a single network and support out-of-distribution (OOD) detection. Canonical JEM training relies on stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics (SGLD); a theoretically motivated alternative, the Predictor-Corrector (PC) sampler, has not previously undergone a systematic replication test on the canonical model. We reproduce canonical JEM on WideResNet-28-10 without normalisation layers on two independent runs and test whether PC retains its theoretical advantage without an annealed noise schedule, across three protocols: PC replacing SGLD throughout the roughly 130 training epochs; cold-start generation (FID); and refinement-style multi-OOD detection (AUROC). The reconstruction reaches 92.88% test accuracy and buffer-FID 44.46 (canonical: 92.9% and 38.40). We document two failure modes: catastrophic late-training divergence via the canonical outlier-buffer mechanism (both SGLD runs and, with the same signature, both PC runs), and run-dependent SVHN OOD-discrimination dynamics. No method-level advantage of PC over SGLD is observed on any protocol: at inference the absolute AUROC difference stays below 0.007 across all ten checkpoint-OOD pairs and the FID difference below 0.5; on the training protocol a hierarchical seed-by-image bootstrap gives a 95% confidence interval on the macro-averaged AUROC difference that contains zero, while a seed-level equivalence test with two runs per method cannot establish formal equivalence. The data are consistent both with equivalence and with a small directional effect. This practical indistinguishability is theoretically expected: under fixed noise the PC predictor step degenerates by construction, so its guarantees do not transfer to canonical JEM.

</details>


### [252] [MultiPathFormer: Towards a Foundation Model for Multipath Wireless Propagation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05076)
*Blessed Guda,Kayley Sze,Carlee Joe-Wong*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MultiPathFormer is an autoregressive foundation model that pretrains on ordered multipath tokens (rather than channel tensors) using next-path prediction, augmented with Environmental RAG and a first-path codebook. It achieves superior performance across channel estimation, beam prediction, localization, and LOS classification, demonstrating that path-level pretraining captures reusable wireless propagation representations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing wireless foundation models pretrain on channel tensors via masked reconstruction (over subcarriers, antennas, or time) but overlook the physical characteristics of wireless propagation, specifically multipath structure. The authors argue that multipath — the fundamental physical phenomenon underlying wireless channels — should serve as the core pretraining object to learn more meaningful and transferable representations.

Method: The paper proposes MultiPathFormer, an autoregressive transformer that represents each TX-RX link as an ordered sequence of continuous-valued path tokens (capturing delay, power, angle, etc.) and pretrains with next-path prediction. Two key innovations are introduced: (1) an Environmental RAG mechanism that retrieves and incorporates environment-specific knowledge to improve path statistics estimation; (2) a first-path codebook for structured representation learning. The model is pretrained on 27 environments and can be fine-tuned for downstream tasks including localization, beam prediction, LOS classification, and channel estimation.

Result: MultiPathFormer achieves 5.57 m mean localization error, 0.914 top-3 beam accuracy, 0.994 LOS classification accuracy, and 0.561 NMSE for channel estimation, outperforming state-of-the-art channel-based foundation models. The Environmental RAG mechanism improves path statistics estimation (delay and power) by up to 59%. The model transfers effectively to unseen users and, after scenario-specific fine-tuning, outperforms models trained from scratch in new environments.

Conclusion: Path-level pretraining on multipath propagation produces reusable representations that generalize across environments and downstream tasks, offering a physically grounded alternative to channel-tensor-based foundation models for wireless systems.

Abstract: Recent advances in machine learning have enabled training of wireless foundation models, which aim to support tasks such as channel estimation, beam prediction, and localization based on wireless signals. Existing wireless foundation models typically pretrain on channel tensors using masked reconstruction over subcarriers, antennas, or time but ignore the physical characteristics of wireless propagation. In this work, we propose to instead use multipath propagation as the fundamental pretraining object. We present MultiPathFormer, an autoregressive foundation model that represents each transmitter-receiver link as an ordered sequence of continuous-valued path tokens and pretrains with next-path prediction. We introduce an Environmental RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) mechanism and a first-path codebook on top of the transformer backbone, leveraging environment knowledge to improve path statistics estimation like delay and power by up to 59%. MultiPathFormer pretrained on 27 environments transfers to unseen users and, after scenario-specific fine-tuning, outperforms training the corresponding models from scratch in new environments. Across downstream tasks, it outperforms SOTA channel-based foundation models, achieving 5.57 m mean localization error, 0.914 top-3 beam accuracy, 0.994 line-of-sight classification accuracy, and 0.561 channel estimation NMSE. These results show that path-level pretraining can learn reusable representations of wireless propagation.

</details>


### [253] [Optimizing What Policies Learn From: Recoverability-aware Rollout Intervention Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05080)
*Zheyuan Zhang,Manqing Mao,Hong Wang,Zhuoer Wang,Samson Koelle,Jie Yuan,Yanjun Lin,James Feng,Nikki Lijing Kuang,Yanfang Ye,Wei Niu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: RAIL is a training-time framework that learns adaptive rollout generation for RL-based LLM post-training by modeling intervention selection as an online contextual-bandit problem, using a recoverability controller that co-evolves with the policy to produce more informative rollouts under limited budgets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing group-based RL methods for LLM post-training waste compute by allocating equal rollouts to all tasks/states, ignoring that some rollouts yield far richer learning signals. Prior adaptive methods rely on fixed heuristics that cannot adapt as the policy evolves and lack fine-grained control over where and how to intervene.

Method: RAIL frames intervention selection as an online contextual-bandit problem. A recoverability controller is trained using a shadow-to-live procedure: intervention traces are collected from a shadow policy, and the controller learns to predict the improvement each intervention yields. The controller then operates live during training, dynamically deciding where and how many rollouts to generate, and continues learning as the underlying policy evolves.

Result: Across multiple settings, RAIL consistently improves performance under limited rollout budgets, demonstrating superior effectiveness, adaptivity, expressiveness, and efficiency compared to baselines.

Conclusion: Recoverability-aware intervention offers a principled mechanism for generating more informative, less redundant rollouts, yielding stronger learning signals during LLM post-training.

Abstract: Critic-free group-based reinforcement learning has become a scalable approach for post-training large language models. However, most existing methods allocate the same number of rollouts to every task and trajectory state, even though some rollouts provide much more useful learning signals than others. Recent work has started to treat rollout generation as an adaptive decision, but two important limitations remain. First, intervention strategies are often based on fixed heuristics and therefore cannot adjust as the policy changes during training. Second, these methods usually decide only how many rollouts to generate, without explicitly controlling where and how to intervene. To address these limitations, we propose Recoverability-Aware Intervention Learning (RAIL), a training-time framework that learns how to generate rollouts based on the improvement produced by each intervention. RAIL models intervention selection as an online contextual-bandit problem and trains a recoverability controller using intervention traces collected through a shadow-to-live procedure. This allows the controller to keep learning while the underlying policy evolves. We evaluate RAIL in terms of effectiveness, adaptivity, expressiveness, and efficiency. Across multiple settings, RAIL consistently improves performance under limited rollout budgets. These results show that recoverability-aware intervention provides a principled way to generate more informative and less redundant rollouts, leading to stronger learning signals during post-training.

</details>


### [254] [Learning When to Stop: Prefix-Optimal Dynamic Diffusion Policies for Continuous Control](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05084)
*Rohit Kumar Salla,Manoj Saravanan,Simon Stepputtis*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: POGP learns a prefix value function at each denoising step via Bellman recursion over the diffusion chain, enabling both auxiliary training that improves action quality and a test-time stopping rule that cuts denoising steps by ~2.7× while maintaining near-full performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Diffusion policies for continuous control suffer from a computational bottleneck due to the iterative denoising process. Reducing inference cost requires adaptively determining the number of denoising steps per action based on difficulty, without degrading task performance.

Method: POGP introduces a prefix value function learned at every intermediate denoising step through a Bellman-style recursion over the denoising chain. This serves dual purposes: (1) an auxiliary training objective that pushes intermediate outputs toward high-quality actions, and (2) a test-time early-stopping rule that halts denoising when further steps yield negligible improvement.

Result: Across four MuJoCo environments and 12 baselines, POGP reduces denoising iterations by ~2.7× while retaining near-full task performance, and improves final task performance by ~3.5% over state-of-the-art dynamic diffusion baselines.

Conclusion: Supervising intermediate denoising steps via a prefix value function is beneficial both for adaptive early stopping and as an auxiliary objective that improves the learned policy itself.

Abstract: Diffusion policies are a powerful policy class for continuous control, but their iterative denoising process creates a substantial computational bottleneck. Reducing this cost requires adapting the number of denoising steps to the difficulty of each action while preserving task performance. We introduce Prefix-Optimal Generative Policies (POGP), a framework that learns a prefix value function at every intermediate denoising step through a Bellman-style recursion over the denoising chain. The prefix value function serves two purposes: it provides an auxiliary training objective that encourages intermediate outputs to become high-quality actions, and it enables a test-time stopping rule that terminates denoising when additional steps are unlikely to produce meaningful improvement. Across four MuJoCo environments and comparisons with 12 baselines, POGP reduces the required number of denoising iterations by approximately 2.7-fold while retaining near-full task performance. Compared with state-of-the-art dynamic diffusion baselines, prefix training also improves final task performance by approximately 3.5%. These results indicate that supervising intermediate denoising steps is useful not only for adaptive early stopping, but also as an auxiliary objective that improves the learned policy.

</details>


### [255] [Capability-Gated Planning: Cost-to-Goal Discovery and the Limits of Myopic Experiment Selection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05085)
*Ahmed Hassoon,Mark Dredze*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Myopic information-gain scoring fails when discovery requires constructive actions (building tools, assays, simulators) that yield no immediate information but unlock future experiments. This "capability gating" creates a structural hardness distinct from submodularity or adaptivity, provably defeating bounded-horizon planners. The authors propose CG-Plan with a capability-aware heuristic to address this.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing automated discovery systems score actions myopically (e.g., expected information gain per unit cost). The authors identify that this fails when the cheapest path to a confident answer requires a chain of constructive actions — actions that build epistemic capabilities (instruments, assays, pipelines) yielding zero immediate information. Bounded-horizon planners cannot value such actions because they appear indistinguishable from doing nothing within the horizon.

Method: The problem is formulated as a stochastic shortest-path problem in belief space where constructive experiments modify the downstream action graph. The authors prove a capability-indistinguishability lemma showing that within horizon d, acquiring a capability is observationally indistinguishable from a null action. They establish approximation-ratio lower bounds (unbounded for any fixed d) and prove instances where myopic planners never reach the goal. CG-Plan is introduced as an incremental replanner using a composite heuristic h = h_cap + h_exp that accounts for both capability-building cost and experimental information gain.

Result: The performance gap between myopic and capability-aware planning appears only under gating conditions, persists for every fixed horizon, and manifests when near-miss hypotheses come from a data-consistent proposer. The capability-indistinguishability mechanism is shown to be a distinct axis of difficulty from curvature (submodularity) and information order (adaptivity gaps).

Conclusion: Capability gating constitutes a fundamental reachability challenge for automated discovery systems. Myopic information-maximizing strategies are provably insufficient; planners must incorporate explicit reasoning about the future action-graph value of constructive experiments. CG-Plan demonstrates a tractable approach via capability-aware heuristics.

Abstract: Systems that automate scientific discovery must repeatedly decide which experiment to run, which hypothesis to test, which tool to build, and when to stop. Many systems make these decisions by maximizing a myopic score such as expected information gain per unit cost or a learned plausibility score. We identify a structural limitation of this approach. Some actions are constructive: they acquire an epistemic capability (an instrument, assay, pipeline, simulator, or abstraction) whose value lies not in the information returned immediately but in the future actions it makes available. When the least-cost route to a confident answer requires a chain of such constructions, a planner that scores actions only by information obtainable within a bounded horizon cannot value the first construction: it yields no information within the horizon and is dominated by any measurement with positive information, however small. We formulate goal-directed discovery as a stochastic shortest-path problem in belief space in which constructive experiments change the downstream action graph, and prove that for every lookahead depth d there is an instance on which every myopic information-maximizing planner has an unbounded approximation ratio, and a related instance on which it never reaches the goal. The mechanism is a capability-indistinguishability lemma: within the horizon, acquiring a capability can be observationally indistinguishable from paying for a null action. This establishes capability gating as a reachability axis of difficulty distinct from curvature (submodularity) and information order (adaptivity gaps). We introduce CG-Plan, an incremental replanner with a capability-aware cost-to-go heuristic h = h_cap + h_exp. In a controlled testbed, the performance gap appears only under gating, persists for every fixed horizon, and arises when near-miss hypotheses come from a data-consistent proposer.

</details>


### [256] [MALT: Lightweight Curvature-Aware Muon via Diagonal Preconditioning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05088)
*Tongle Wu,Huanyu Dong,Ying Sun,Ziye Ma*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MALT extends the Muon optimizer by adding lightweight two-sided diagonal preconditioners to account for loss landscape curvature, and MALTER adds adaptive stepsize rescaling for robustness to gradient noise. Both outperform Muon on GPT-2 pretraining with negligible overhead.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Muon orthogonalizes momentum via Newton-Schulz iterations to mitigate gradient anisotropy, but it ignores the curvature geometry of the loss landscape, leaving it vulnerable to curvature anisotropy. The authors aim to address this gap without sacrificing Muon's memory and computational efficiency.

Method: MALT applies two-sided diagonal preconditioners (low memory/compute overhead) to approximately capture curvature geometry. The preconditioned momentum is then orthogonalized via Newton-Schulz iterations and mapped back to define the update direction, with norm grafting controlling update magnitude. MALTER further adds adaptive stepsize rescaling to improve robustness against stochastic gradient noise. Convergence guarantees are established for the stochastic non-convex setting.

Result: Experiments on GPT-2 Small, Medium, and Large pretraining demonstrate that MALT and MALTER consistently outperform Muon while maintaining nearly identical memory footprint and wall-clock time.

Conclusion: Incorporating lightweight curvature-aware preconditioning into the Muon framework yields meaningful improvements in language model pretraining performance. The MALT family of optimizers offers a practical, low-overhead alternative to Muon that is both theoretically grounded and empirically superior.

Abstract: Muon has recently emerged as a promising alternative to AdamW for language model pretraining by orthogonalizing momentum matrices using Newton-Schulz iterations. Although Muon mitigates gradient anisotropy, it does not explicitly account for the curvature geometry of the loss landscape and may therefore remain sensitive to curvature anisotropy. We bridge this gap by proposing MALT (Muon Augmented by Lightweight Two-sided Preconditioning), which uses lightweight diagonal preconditioners to reduce the sensitivity of Muon to curvature anisotropy. Specifically, MALT uses two-sided diagonal preconditioners with low memory and computational overhead to approximately capture the curvature geometry of the loss landscape. It orthogonalizes the preconditioned momentum using Newton-Schulz iterations and maps the result back to define the update direction, while norm grafting controls the update magnitude. To improve the robustness of MALT to stochastic gradient noise, we further propose MALTER (MALT with Adaptive stEpsize Rescaling). Convergence guarantees are provided for MALT in the stochastic non-convex setting. Experiments on GPT-2 Small, Medium, and Large pretraining show that the proposed methods outperform Muon while maintaining nearly the same memory footprint and wall-clock time.

</details>


### [257] [Multimodal Spatiotemporal Atmospheric Data Assimilation with Latent Flow-matching](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05103)
*Dibyajyoti Chakraborty,Romit Maulik*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes a unified atmospheric data assimilation framework using latent video flow-matching to generate temporally consistent state trajectories from ERA5 reanalysis, combined with posterior sampling for real observation assimilation, enabling flexible filtering/smoothing and competitive observation-to-forecast performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional data assimilation methods rely on iterative Bayesian updating of numerical forecast models. The authors seek a fundamentally different, unified approach that can naturally handle both filtering and smoothing tasks while propagating information across time without requiring an explicit forecast model during assimilation.

Method: The method has two core components: (1) A generative prior trained via latent video flow-matching on ERA5 reanalysis data (69 variables, 8-day windows) that produces temporally consistent atmospheric trajectories. (2) Posterior sampling to assimilate real observations (e.g., from NOAA IGRA and ISD). The continuous trajectory prior naturally propagates information between observed and unobserved frames, allowing filtering and smoothing simply by changing which frames are treated as observed.

Result: The approach generates full-state ensemble forecasts directly from sparse observations and achieves performance competitive with state-of-the-art observation-to-forecast models.

Conclusion: A unified, forecast-model-free DA paradigm based on learned video priors and posterior sampling is viable and competitive, offering flexibility across DA tasks and opening new directions for generative AI in atmospheric science.

Abstract: Data assimilation (DA) uses Bayesian inference to update the state of a numerical forecast model with observed data. In this study, we propose a fundamentally different, unified approach to atmospheric data assimilation. We use latent video flow-matching to sample temporally consistent trajectories from a prior trained using ERA5 reanalysis (69 variables over an 8-day window). We also use posterior sampling to assimilate real observation sources, such as those from the NOAA Integrated Global Radiosonde Archive and the Integrated Surface Database. Because the prior generates a continuous trajectory, it naturally propagates information between observed and unobserved frames. Therefore, we can perform various DA tasks, such as filtering and smoothing, simply by changing the observed frames. Moreover, we generate full-state ensemble forecasts directly from sparse observations, achieving performance competitive with state-of-the-art observation-to-forecast models.

</details>


### [258] [BnBERT-iPET: Sparse Few-Shot Language Modeling for Bengali via Lottery Ticket Pruning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05104)
*Sajib Hossain,Md Kamrus Samad,Anan Ghosh,Labib Imam Chowdhury,Nabeel Mohammed*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces BnBERT-iPET, a sparse few-shot language model for Bengali that retains only 10% of BERT's edges. Using Lottery Ticket Hypothesis pruning and iterative pattern exploiting training (iPET), it achieves competitive performance against state-of-the-art models like Bangla Electra, Indic-BERT, and XLM-RoBERTa on Bengali NLP benchmarks, while drastically reducing computational cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Training large pre-trained models like BERT is expensive, time-consuming, and environmentally costly, creating barriers for resource-constrained languages like Bengali. The authors aim to demonstrate that sparse, few-shot-learned models can match or rival larger models, lowering the barrier to NLP research for low-resource languages.

Method: The authors propose BnBERT-iPET, which combines two techniques: (1) Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (LTH) pruning to identify and retain only 10% of the most impactful edges in a BERT-based model (achieving 90% sparsity), and (2) iterative pattern exploiting training (iPET), a few-shot learning paradigm that enables effective learning from limited labeled data through iterative knowledge distillation across multiple generations of models.

Result: The 90% sparse BnBERT-iPET model performs competitively ("neck and neck") with much larger, fully dense models — including Bangla Electra, Indic-BERT, and XLM-RoBERTa — on standard Bengali downstream benchmark datasets.

Conclusion: Lightweight, sparse, few-shot-learned language models can rival large state-of-the-art models for resource-constrained languages like Bengali. This approach significantly reduces memory footprint, training time, and carbon emissions while maintaining competitive performance, making advanced NLP more accessible for under-resourced languages.

Abstract: Deep neural networks have shown impressive success in NLP tasks owing to their complex structure and huge number of edges. Achieving state-of-the-art performance in natural language processing with a large pre-trained model such as BERT is expensive and time-consuming, carries a large carbon footprint, and is difficult to realize on machines with minimal computational capability. This creates a barrier to training complex models for resource-constrained languages such as Bengali. However, in a complex neural model, not all edges are equally impactful, and the contributions of some of them can be neglected. Pruning promises to reduce the memory footprint of regular networks, shorten the training time of ever-growing networks, and increase inference efficiency without sacrificing comparable performance. In this work, we introduce BnBERT-iPET, a sparse few-shot language modeling approach for Bengali, and experimentally show that a lightweight few-shot-learned language model retaining only 10% of the edges of an initial model such as BERT can perform neck and neck with much larger models on challenging tasks for a resource-constrained language such as Bengali. By learning from few shots through iterative pattern exploiting training and achieving 90% sparsity with the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis pruning technique, our pruned BnBERT-iPET model proves to be a tough competitor to state-of-the-art language models such as Bangla Electra, Indic-BERT, and XLM-RoBERTa on downstream tasks over standard benchmark datasets of the Bengali language.

</details>


### [259] [Reward Structure Shapes the Interaction Between Episodic Exploration and Neural Memory in Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05111)
*Jai Malegaonkar,Rohan Patil,Henrik I. Christensen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper presents a controlled study showing that exploration bonuses and memory architectures in partially observable RL interact in non-trivial ways governed by reward structure—not reward density. The authors identify three interaction regimes (amplification, equalization, null) and introduce observation-anchored reward machines to formalize sparsity into structural and potential components.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Exploration bonuses and memory architectures in partially observable RL are typically evaluated in isolation, leaving their interaction poorly understood. Additionally, standard notions of "sparse reward" conflate temporal signal density with what the reward actually supervises, creating confusion about when bonuses help or hurt.

Method: The authors conduct a controlled crossover experiment: they pair episodic exploration bonuses (specifically Never Give Up / NGU-style) with diverse neural memory architectures (LSTM, Transformer, Fast Weight Programmers, etc.) across three carefully designed POMDP environments. Each environment manipulates how memory content is acquired (actively discovered and retained unsupervised vs. reward-supervised cue vs. purely scheduled observation stream). They further perform controlled reward manipulations and formalize sparsity using observation-anchored reward machines, decomposing it into structural sparsity and potential sparsity.

Result: The same bonus yields three distinct interaction patterns: (1) amplification of architectural differences when memory content must be actively discovered unsupervised; (2) equalization of architectures to a shared ceiling when memory content is a single reward-supervised cue; (3) null effect when observations are purely scheduled. Dense rewards neutralize bonuses only when they directly supervise required latent memory. A small avoidable penalty on exploration induces suboptimal convergence that bonuses resolve. The reward-machine formalism separates structural sparsity (automaton reproduces return without task-required history) from potential sparsity (one-step reward misprices local exploratory actions).

Conclusion: Exploration and memory are complements, not substitutes: a bonus induces exposure to rewarding states, but only memory converts that exposure into return. The interaction between exploration bonuses and memory architectures is governed by the retention burden exposed by each task's reward structure, not by reward density alone.

Abstract: In partially observable reinforcement learning, agents face a dual bottleneck: they must explore to encounter rewarding states and retain that experience in memory to optimize their policies. Exploration bonuses and memory architectures are traditionally evaluated in isolation, leaving their interaction unmeasured, and standard notions of sparse reward conflate temporal signal density with what the reward actually supervises. We present a controlled study crossing episodic exploration bonuses with diverse neural memory architectures across three environments that vary how the content of memory is acquired. An identical bonus signal yields three distinct interaction patterns: it amplifies architectural capacity differences where memory content must be actively discovered and retained unsupervised; equalizes architectures to a shared ceiling where the content, once sought out, is a single reward-supervised cue; and is null where the observation stream is purely scheduled. Controlled reward manipulations verify that these patterns track reward structure rather than density: a dense reward neutralizes a bonus only if it directly supervises the required latent memory, and a small avoidable penalty on exploratory actions (leaving the optimum unchanged) induces policy convergence to suboptimal stationary states, which either bonus resolves. We then formalize reward sparsity with observation-anchored reward machines, separating structural sparsity (an automaton reproduces the return without the task-required history) from potential sparsity (the one-step reward misprices local exploratory actions); the resulting vocabulary organizes the three regimes by the retention burden each task exposes. Together, these results show exploration and memory are complements, not substitutes: a bonus induces exposure, and only memory converts exposure into return.

</details>


### [260] [DASyR-LLM: Domain-Aware Symbolic Regression with LLMs for Kinetic Model Discovery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05120)
*Roberto Aliaga Medina,Paulina Quintanilla,Antonio del Rio Chanona*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: An LLM-guided symbolic regression framework is introduced for kinetic model discovery, where the LLM critiques candidate models and proposes new rate expressions. Tested on four in silico case studies, it reduces iterations to ground-truth by 41.7–79.3% versus standard SR, while maintaining equivalent predictive performance (R²>0.98).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Symbolic regression for kinetic model discovery typically operates without physicochemical domain knowledge, leading to exploration of implausible models. LLMs offer a way to inject chemical engineering expertise into the search process, potentially accelerating discovery and reducing experimental effort.

Method: An LLM module is embedded within an iterative SR algorithm. At each iteration, the LLM performs two roles: (1) qualitative physicochemical critique of the best SR-generated candidates, and (2) proposing new candidate rate expressions informed by both SR outputs and embedded chemical knowledge. The framework is evaluated on four in silico case studies of heterogeneous catalysis and bioprocess systems, with ablation studies isolating contributions of SR and LLM components.

Result: The LLM-guided framework reduced iterations to identify the ground-truth model by 41.7–79.3% compared to state-of-the-art SR. The LLM directly proposed the correct model structure in >50% of guided runs. Predictive performance on validation sets was equivalent (R²>0.98). Ablation studies showed both SR and LLM components contribute to performance, and a reduced-size LLM largely retained discovery efficiency.

Conclusion: LLMs can effectively inject domain knowledge into scientific model discovery, significantly accelerating kinetic model identification while maintaining accuracy. This enables more efficient experimental design and points toward fully automated, domain-aware kinetic modeling pipelines.

Abstract: Kinetic model discovery is a central challenge in chemical engineering, as accurate rate expressions are essential for understanding and controlling chemical and biological processes. Symbolic regression (SR) has emerged as a powerful data-driven approach for identifying interpretable kinetic models, but usually operates without domain knowledge, often exploring physicochemically implausible models. Large language models (LLMs) offer a promising avenue for injecting domain expertise into this search. Here, we introduce an LLM-guided SR framework, embedding an LLM module within an iterative SR algorithm for automated kinetic model discovery. The LLM performs two roles at each iteration: (1) a qualitative physicochemical critique of the best SR candidates, and (2) the proposal of new candidate rate expressions guided by the SR-generated models and embedded chemical knowledge. Our framework is evaluated on four in silico case studies of increasing complexity, spanning heterogeneous catalysis and bioprocess systems. Results show the LLM-guided framework reduces iterations to identify the ground-truth model by $41.7-79.3\%$ versus a state-of-the-art SR framework, with the LLM directly proposing the correct model structure in over half of the guided runs. In practical settings, where each iteration typically requires a new wet-lab experiment, this translates into a substantial reduction in experimental effort. Predictive performance on an independent validation set is equivalent between both approaches, with $R^2>0.98$ in all case studies. Ablation studies indicate that both the SR component and the LLM scale contribute to this performance, with a reduced-size LLM largely retaining discovery efficiency. These findings demonstrate that LLMs can effectively inject domain knowledge into scientific model discovery, paving the way toward fully automated, domain-aware kinetic modelling pipelines.

</details>


### [261] [SSTQ:Privacy-Preserving Vector Quantization via Subsampled Stochastic TurboQuant](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05127)
*Adel Javanmard,David P. Woodruff,Vahab Mirrokni*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SSTQ combines overcomplete tight frames, coordinate subsampling, and 1D quantization to achieve local differential privacy in distributed optimization with optimal MSE scaling using only ⌈log₂N⌉+b bits per client, outperforming prior vector quantization methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing local DP methods for distributed optimization suffer from high communication cost or dimension-dependent variance. Vector quantization like vqSGD uses high-dimensional geometric constructions but incurs unfavorable dimension-dependent variance, motivating a more efficient approach.

Method: SSTQ framework with two variants: (1) Flat Randomized Response and (2) Metric-Aware Laplace. Core components: overcomplete equal-norm tight frames for preprocessing, coordinate subsampling to reduce dimensionality, and privacy-aware 1D quantization. Also introduces a surrogate privacy-aware codebook objective that improves MSE scaling from O(4^b) to O(2^b).

Result: SSTQ achieves optimal MSE scaling with ⌈log₂N⌉+b bits per client (N=Θ(d)). The surrogate codebook objective reduces codebook-dependent MSE scaling from O(4^b) to O(2^b). Empirical evaluation on CIFAR-10 and Fashion-MNIST federated learning tasks shows favorable utility and communication efficiency against established baselines.

Conclusion: SSTQ effectively resolves the communication–privacy–utility trade-off in locally private distributed optimization by combining tight frames, subsampling, and 1D quantization, supported by both theoretical guarantees and empirical validation.

Abstract: Achieving local differential privacy in distributed optimization while maintaining low communication cost remains challenging. Existing vector quantization methods, such as vqSGD, use high-dimensional geometric constructions but incur unfavorable dimension-dependent variance. In this work, we propose Subsampled Stochastic TurboQuant (SSTQ), a framework that combines overcomplete equal-norm tight frames, coordinate subsampling, and privacy-aware one-dimensional quantization. SSTQ includes two variants: a Flat Randomized Response version and a Metric-Aware Laplace version, the latter being better suited to higher codebook bit-width regimes. We show that SSTQ achieves optimal mean squared error scaling while using only $\lceil \log_2 N \rceil + b$ bits per client, where $N = Θ(d)$ is the frame size. We also derive a surrogate privacy-aware codebook objective that reduces the codebook-dependent MSE scaling from $O(4^b)$ to $O(2^b)$. Finally, we empirically evaluate SSTQ against established baselines on federated learning tasks using CIFAR-10 and Fashion-MNIST, demonstrating favorable utility and communication efficiency.

</details>


### [262] [The Loss Does Not See the Basis, but Adam Does](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05136)
*Devender Singh*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Adam lacks the low-rank implicit bias that gradient descent exhibits on factored models due to its lack of gauge equivariance; equivariant optimizers preserve this bias, and a spectral schedule reconciles conflicting reports on Muon's performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Gradient descent on factored models (W=UV^T) is known to be implicitly biased toward low-rank solutions, but Adam does not share this property. The authors aim to understand the mechanistic cause of this discrepancy and characterize which optimizers preserve the low-rank bias.

Method: The authors analyze the gauge symmetry of the loss under (U,V)→(UQ,VQ) and define gauge equivariance as a necessary condition for preserving gradient flow's low-rank mechanism. They prove a structure theorem characterizing memoryless equivariant update rules as Gram-determined left preconditioners, and a transfer theorem linking gradient flow to common-scalar flows. Empirically, they test nine update rules on underdetermined matrix sensing, evaluate a one-parameter family interpolating between coordinate-wise and shared-scalar preconditioning, study transformers to measure per-head invariant discrepancies, and assess held-out error on hyperspectral datasets.

Result: Gauge-equivariant optimizers (gradient descent, momentum, shared-scalar Adam, Muon, Shampoo) preserve low-rank bias; coordinate-wise methods (Adam, RMSProp) do not. A one-parameter interpolation shows anisotropy is the cause, with monotonic restoration of bias. The "spectral schedule" reconciles opposing Muon reports: equal-rate updates recover exact low-rank targets but degrade as spectral tail grows. In transformers, Adam causes per-head invariants (W_Q^T W_K) to diverge by 56% relative Frobenius distance, which no per-head rotation can close. On hyperspectral data, gradient descent reduces held-out error by 43–44% over Adam at matched training loss and low sampling density.

Conclusion: Basis choice is not a mere tuning detail but a decision about which interpolant the optimizer selects. Gauge equivariance is the key property determining whether an optimizer inherits gradient flow's low-rank implicit bias.

Abstract: Gradient descent on a factored model $W = UV^\top$ is implicitly biased toward low-rank solutions, while Adam, starting from the same small initialization, is not. We trace the difference to the gauge symmetry of the loss, its invariance under $(U, V) \mapsto (UQ, VQ)$. Gradient flow's low-rank mechanism is available to an optimizer only if that optimizer is gauge-equivariant, a condition necessary for the transfer but not sufficient for low-rank recovery. Gradient descent, momentum, "shared-scalar" Adam, Muon, and Shampoo satisfy it. Adam, RMSProp, and the other coordinate-wise methods do not. A structure theorem characterizes the memoryless equivariant rules as exactly the Gram-determined left preconditioners, and a transfer theorem carries gradient flow's pathwise properties to common-scalar flows. We then sort nine update rules on underdetermined matrix sensing by recovery error against the planted ground truth. A one-parameter family from coordinate-wise to shared-scalar preconditioning restores the bias monotonically, isolating anisotropy as the cause. A "spectral schedule" reconciles two opposing reports about Muon: equal-rate updates recover exactly low-rank targets but lose their edge as the spectral tail grows. In transformers, Adam separates two gauge-equivalent initializations at the first step, where the equivariant optimizers stay at float precision, and ends with the per-head invariants $W_Q^\top W_K$ 56% apart in relative Frobenius distance, a gap no per-head rotation can close. On two hyperspectral datasets at matched training loss, gradient descent cuts held-out error by 43-44% at the lowest sampling density, and at lower effective rank. Basis choice is therefore not a tuning detail but a decision about which interpolant the optimizer selects.

</details>

### [263] [Strategic Evaluation of Planning Strategies for LLM Agents in Cyber-Physical Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04265)
*J. de Curtò,I. de Zarzà*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: This paper introduces a physics-grounded benchmark for evaluating LLM planning agents in cyber-physical systems (specifically smart-grid demand-response), showing that execution architecture matters more than mode agreement, and that feasibility filtering substantially reduces regret, with remaining challenges isolated to within-feasible quality selection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM planning evaluations focus on binary task success or plan adherence, but in strategic cyber-physical systems, a deeper question is whether the planning architecture remains robust after autonomous participants respond and physical constraints bind. The authors argue for a controlled, physics-grounded benchmark that exposes how planning-induced control trajectories interact with other agents and physical processes.

Method: The benchmark implements predefined, sequential, hierarchical, and search-based execution architectures in a smart-grid demand-response system with 40 heterogeneous prosumers and an independently simulated radial feeder. The LLM is constrained to typed policy declaration and short operator messages, while schedule construction, prosumer dynamics, and power flow remain explicit code. The protocol uses paired forced-mode counterfactuals, common random response draws, and event-level deadline feasibility. A 144-scenario, 576-episode evaluation bank is constructed, with stress-held-out ridge analysis, ablation studies, and a five-model extension examining latency tails.

Result: Three key findings: (1) Architecture materially changes outcomes — forced search serves as the oracle across all five baseline seeds. (2) Execution fidelity requires more than mode agreement — objective substitution achieves 1.0 agreement yet increases voltage shortfall by 2.68×. (3) The stress-held-out ridge yields mean regret 90.7 (95% CI [73.8, 108.6]) with no detectable value over fixed sequential; applying deadline feasibility before quality prediction reduces regret to 29.0, a 61.1 improvement. An all-feasible ablation fails to beat fixed search, localizing the remaining challenge to within-feasible quality selection. The five-model extension reveals stress-conditioned, state-blind, and invariant declarer classes, with latency tails indicating probabilistic treatment of live feasibility is necessary.

Conclusion: Evaluating LLM planners in cyber-physical systems requires going beyond task success to assess architectural robustness under physical constraints and agent responses. Feasibility filtering dramatically improves outcomes, but the core open problem is quality selection among feasible options. Future work should treat live feasibility probabilistically given latency concerns.

Abstract: Evaluations of LLM planning agents largely ask whether a task succeeds or a declared plan is followed. In strategic cyber-physical systems, a stronger question is whether the planning architecture remains appropriate after autonomous participants respond and physics constrains the outcome. We introduce a controlled, physics-grounded benchmark built around planning-induced control trajectories: the ordered planning operations and directives through which an execution architecture acts on other agents and the physical process. It implements predefined, sequential, hierarchical, and search executors in a smart-grid demand-response system with 40 heterogeneous prosumers and an independently simulated radial feeder. The LLM is bounded to typed policy declaration and short operator messages, while schedule construction, prosumer dynamics, and power flow remain explicit code. The protocol uses paired forced-mode counterfactuals, common random response draws, and event-level deadline feasibility. Three properties follow. Architecture materially changes outcomes: forced search is the oracle in all five baseline seeds. Execution fidelity needs more than mode agreement: objective substitution holds agreement at 1.0 while increasing voltage shortfall by 2.68x. A 144-scenario, 576-episode bank has feasible oracles from three of the four architectures. A prespecified stress-held-out ridge has mean regret 90.7 (95% interval [73.8, 108.6]) and no detectable value over fixed sequential; applying known deadline feasibility before quality prediction cuts regret to 29.0 and improves over fixed sequential by 61.1. An all-feasible ablation does not beat fixed search, localising the remaining challenge to within-feasible quality selection. A five-model extension separates stress-conditioned, state-blind, and invariant declarers; latency tails show that live feasibility should be treated probabilistically.

</details>


### [264] [Responsibility in Multi-Agent Sequential Decision-Making: Comparing Human Judgments to Formal Models of Causal Attribution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04318)
*Nripsuta Ani Saxena,Stelios Triantafyllou,Goran Radanović*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: A large-scale survey using a modified Goofspiel card game evaluates how formal definitions of responsibility attribution (based on actual causality) align with human judgments in multi-agent sequential decision-making. No single method consistently matches human responses, but agent-specific biases and information availability significantly shape responsibility judgments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As AI is increasingly deployed in high-stakes decision-making, understanding who or what is responsible for failures is critical. Existing formal definitions of responsibility attribution exist but their alignment with human intuitions is poorly understood, creating a gap between theoretical frameworks and practical accountability.

Method: The authors conducted a large-scale human survey using a modified version of the card game Goofspiel to elicit responsibility judgments in multi-agent sequential decision-making scenarios. They then evaluated multiple formal responsibility attribution methods grounded in actual causality against these human judgments to measure alignment and identify influencing factors.

Result: No single responsibility attribution method consistently aligned with human judgments. Key factors shaping human responsibility attribution included agent-specific biases (e.g., blaming certain agents more than others) and the amount of information available to agents during decision-making.

Conclusion: Formal responsibility attribution methods do not yet reliably mirror human judgments. Designing future accountability frameworks requires accounting for cognitive biases and informational asymmetries that influence how humans assign responsibility in multi-agent settings.

Abstract: With the growing adoption of artificial intelligence in high-stakes decision-making, identifying the causes of outcomes--particularly failures--and determining who is responsible has become a critical concern. In this work, we examine how well formal definitions of \textit{responsibility attribution}, grounded in the framework of \textit{actual causality}, align with human judgments of responsibility. To this end, we conduct a large-scale survey to elicit human judgments of responsibility in multi-agent sequential decision-making scenarios, using a modified version of the card game Goofspiel. We evaluate multiple responsibility attribution methods, assess their alignment with human judgments about responsibility, and identify factors that significantly shape responsibility judgments. While no single responsibility attribution method consistently aligns with human responses, our findings highlight key factors that influence human responsibility judgments, including agent-specific biases and amount of information available to agents during decision-making.

</details>


### [265] [Continuous Improvement and Parallel Autonomous Exploration: An LLM-Agent Framework for Searching Large Solution Spaces](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04341)
*Dulmini Hettiarachchi,Andre Rusli,Julio Christian Young,Sho Akiyama*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: A framework enabling LLM agents to autonomously explore large solution spaces via a leaderboard-based reward loop and parallel multi-agent execution, demonstrated on product-to-catalog matching with significant performance gains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM agents typically rely on a single seeded paradigm and lack mechanisms for broad, autonomous exploration of large solution spaces. The authors aim to provide both iterative refinement within a paradigm and qualitatively diverse exploration across paradigms, without human intervention.

Method: A two-mechanism framework: (1) a leaderboard scored on held-out data provides a reward signal for continuous self-refinement through repeated submissions; (2) multiple agents run fully autonomously in parallel — analyzing, surveying methods, implementing, self-evaluating, submitting, and revising — while a moderator agent handles logistics. The shared reward across parallel agents broadens solution-space exploration. Instantiated on product-to-catalog matching as selective prediction with a precision-coverage operating point.

Result: Best qualified coverage (≥95% P@1 per category) reached 47.8–57.4% with a single agent and 62.8–69.4% with five parallel agents, versus a 33.3% baseline. Parallel agents surfaced qualitatively different solutions rather than converging on a single paradigm.

Conclusion: The core contribution is the framework itself: a continuous-improvement reward loop paired with a substrate for fully autonomous parallel exploration, validated by case-study evidence showing both refinement within and diversification across solution paradigms.

Abstract: We present a framework that gives LLM agents two mechanisms for searching large solution spaces autonomously. First, a leaderboard scored on held-out data acts as a reward signal that drives each agent to refine its solutions over repeated submissions, a loop that operates even with a single agent. Second, the framework enables running many agents in parallel, fully autonomously, with no human in the loop: agents independently analyze, survey methods, implement, self-evaluate, submit, and revise, while a moderator agent handles only logistics. Running agents in parallel under the shared reward broadens the explored region of the solution space rather than refining the single seeded paradigm. We instantiate the framework on product-to-catalog matching (a core e-commerce retrieval task with a large, category-structured solution space), posed as selective prediction with a precision-coverage operating point. A single agent refines within its seeded paradigm, whereas parallel autonomous agents surface qualitatively different solutions. On this testbed, best qualified coverage (>=95% P@1 per category) reaches 47.8-57.4% with a single agent and 62.8-69.4% with five, against a 33.3% baseline. Our contribution is the framework itself: a continuous-improvement reward loop and a substrate for fully autonomous parallel exploration, backed by case-study evidence.

</details>


### [266] [Emergence of Reputation-Based Cooperation in LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04507)
*Kazuya Horibe,Kenji Itao,Wataru Toyokawa*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: LLM agents playing indirect reciprocity games evolve cooperation, but their robustness to free-riders depends on Image Scoring-like discrimination rather than more sophisticated Leading-Eight norms. Only defector exclusion stringency predicts resistance to invasion, revealing a fundamental vulnerability in culturally evolved LLM cooperation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To investigate whether cooperation among LLM agents can be evolutionarily stable against free-rider invasion in indirect reciprocity settings, and to understand the mechanisms underlying robustness or vulnerability.

Method: An indirect reciprocity donation game where LLM agents observe behavioral traces and donate on a continuous scale. Strategies are represented as natural language prompts and evolve through cultural transmission across generations. Four LLM backends are tested, with robustness to free-rider invasion measured and correlated against discrimination patterns (Image Scoring, Leading-Eight norms) and punishment/reward behaviors.

Result: Robustness to free-rider invasion varies by more than an order of magnitude across LLM backends. The strongest predictor is opponent endowment sensitivity (Image Scoring). Adherence to Leading-Eight L1 norms does not predict robustness. Only the stringency of defector exclusion — not cooperator reward — predicts resistance to free-rider invasion.

Conclusion: LLM agents are confined to Image Scoring-like discrimination and fail to develop more robust Leading-Eight norms, revealing a fundamental vulnerability in culturally evolved LLM cooperation. This motivates bottom-up approaches to norm construction.

Abstract: Can cooperation among large language model (LLM) agents be evolutionarily stable against free-rider invasion? We study an indirect reciprocity donation game where LLM agents observe behavioral traces and donate on a continuous scale. Strategies, represented as natural language prompts, evolve through cultural transmission across generations. Across four LLM backends, robustness to free-rider invasion varies by more than an order of magnitude. The strongest predictor of this robustness is opponent endowment sensitivity, the degree to which agents discriminate between cooperative and uncooperative opponents, operationalizing the classical Image Scoring mechanism. By contrast, adherence to the Leading-Eight L1 norm does not predict robustness. Robustness depends on defector exclusion: while both cooperator reward and defector punishment vary across models, only the stringency of defector exclusion predicts resistance to free-rider invasion. These findings reveal that LLM agents are confined to Image Scoring-like discrimination and fail to develop the more robust Leading-Eight norms, highlighting a fundamental vulnerability in culturally evolved LLM cooperation and motivating bottom-up approaches to norm construction.

</details>


### [267] [HELENA:Hierarchical Sparse Coordination over a Union of Complementary Topologies for MAS](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04634)
*Zhifang Mao,Linyao Zheng,Xuhang Shi,Xiuquan Hou*

Main category: cs.MA

TL;DR: HELENA proposes a hierarchical sparse coordination framework for LLM-based multi-agent systems that combines multiple complementary topologies via MCTS and DPP, then activates only sparse task-relevant subgraphs during execution to suppress noise propagation, achieving SOTA across 8 benchmarks with up to 10.34% improvement on MMLU-Pro.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM-based multi-agent systems optimize a single topology, limiting reasoning to narrow trajectories. Naively merging multiple topologies into a composite graph introduces redundant noise propagation across irrelevant connections, degrading solution quality. The dilemma is balancing diverse reasoning paths with efficient, noise-free execution.

Method: HELENA operates in three stages: (1) Union graph construction using Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) and Determinantal Point Process (DPP) to select complementary candidate topologies; (2) Hierarchical Sparse Coordination, which activates only a sparse subgraph at each reasoning step while agents exchange compressed latent briefs to suppress redundant noise; (3) Local Self-Refinement, which identifies decision units with discrepancy evidence and rewrites them only when contrastive evidence simultaneously confirms a solution-side failure and a challenger-side improvement.

Result: HELENA achieves state-of-the-art results across 8 benchmarks, with an average gain of 3.47% over the strongest baseline and up to 10.34% improvement on MMLU-Pro. Larger improvements are observed on harder benchmarks, at reasonable additional cost.

Conclusion: Hierarchical sparse coordination over a union of complementary topologies effectively balances diverse reasoning trajectories with noise suppression, demonstrating that selectively activating task-relevant subgraphs while pruning irrelevant connections is a viable strategy for scaling multi-agent reasoning to complex problems.

Abstract: LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) typically optimize a single topology, restricting reasoning to a narrow trajectory and limiting comprehensive analytical capacity. Naively merging multiple topologies into a composite graph introduces redundant noise propagation across irrelevant connections, degrading solution quality. To address this dilemma, we propose \textbf{Hierarchical Sparse Coordination over a Union of Complementary Topologies for MAS (HELENA)}, a multi-agent framework that balances diverse reasoning paths with sparse task-dependent execution. \helena{} constructs a union MAS graph from complementary candidate topologies selected via Monte Carlo Tree Search and Determinantal Point Process, broadening the reasoning trajectory for comprehensive analysis of complex problems. A Hierarchical Sparse Coordination module then activates only a sparse subgraph at each step while agents exchange compressed latent briefs to suppress redundant noise propagation. Finally, a Local Self-Refinement stage identifies decision units with discrepancy evidence and rewrites them only when contrastive evidence simultaneously confirms a reliable solution-side failure and a challenger-side improvement. Experiments across eight benchmarks show that \helena{} achieves state-of-the-art results on all benchmarks, with an average gain of \pctup{3.47} over the strongest baseline and up to \pctup{10.34} on MMLU-Pro, achieving larger improvements on harder benchmarks at a reasonable additional cost.

</details>

### [268] [Securing Contrastive mmWave-based Human Activity Recognition against Adversarial Label Flipping](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04029)
*Amit Singha,Ziqian Bi,Tao Li,Yimin Chen,Yanchao Zhang*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: First systematic study on label flipping poisoning attacks against mmWave-based Human Activity Recognition using supervised contrastive learning. Three attacks are identified and corresponding countermeasures proposed, validated experimentally on a prototype system.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Wireless HAR using mmWave technology is increasingly deployed in critical sectors (healthcare, VR, surveillance), yet its vulnerability to adversarial data poisoning — specifically label flipping attacks in contrastive learning frameworks — remains unexplored. This gap threatens system reliability and security.

Method: The authors systematically investigate label flipping poisoning attacks in supervised contrastive learning for mmWave-based HAR. They design three distinct label poisoning attack strategies targeting the contrastive representation learning pipeline, and develop corresponding defense countermeasures. All attack and defense methods are evaluated on a real prototype mmWave HAR system.

Result: All three label flipping attacks successfully degrade the HAR system's performance. The proposed countermeasures effectively mitigate the attacks and restore recognition accuracy. The findings generalize beyond mmWave to other wireless HAR systems.
