Conclusion: mmWave-based HAR systems using supervised contrastive learning are susceptible to label flipping poisoning attacks, but practical countermeasures exist. The work advocates for proactive security considerations in wireless HAR system design and deployment.

Abstract: Wireless Human Activity Recognition (HAR), leveraging their non-intrusive nature, has the potential to revolutionize various sectors, including healthcare, virtual reality, and surveillance. The advent of millimeter wave (mmWave) technology has significantly enhanced the capabilities of wireless HAR systems. This paper presents the first systematic study on the vulnerabilities of mmWave-based HAR to label flipping poisoning attacks in the context of supervised contrastive learning. We identify three label poisoning attacks on the contrastive mmWave-based HAR and propose corresponding countermeasures. The efficacy of the attacks and also our countermeasures are experimentally validated on a prototype system. The attacks and countermeasures can be easily extended to other wireless HAR systems, thereby promoting security considerations in system design and deployment.

</details>


### [269] [SoK: How Frontier AI Reshapes System-Level Security Risk Dynamics in Critical Infrastructure](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04033)
*Chandra Thapa,Mohan Baruwal Chhetri,Marthie Grobler,Shahroz Tariq,Tooba Aamir*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: This SoK paper proposes a five-dimensional risk-dynamics framework for understanding how frontier AI reshapes critical infrastructure security across the AI lifecycle, highlighting recurring mechanisms of capability emergence, infiltration, cross-system propagation, degraded control authority, and strained response capacity, while revealing a mismatch between academic research and operational needs and outlining a deployment-oriented research agenda.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing AI-security literature organizes risks by attack type, lifecycle stage, or asset class but fails to capture system-level dynamics—how risk emerges, spreads, and is controlled—through which frontier AI fundamentally reconfigures critical infrastructure security outcomes. There is also a structural mismatch between prevailing academic AI-security research and the operational constraints faced by CI operators.

Method: The authors conduct a Systematization of Knowledge (SoK), synthesizing existing literature to construct a novel five-dimensional risk-dynamics framework. The five dimensions are: (1) Capability Emergence, (2) Infiltration Pathways, (3) Cross-System Propagation, (4) degradation of Control Authority, and (5) strain on Response Capacity. The framework identifies recurring causal mechanisms rather than enumerating individual threats. The authors then map the gap between academic research and CI operational constraints to derive a deployment-oriented research agenda.

Result: The framework reveals that FAI reconfigures CI security through interconnected dynamics that jointly determine system-level risk. Key findings include a structural mismatch between model-centric academic robustness research and the lifecycle-structured, system-level assurance needs of CI operators. The paper produces a deployment-oriented research agenda grounded in system-level assurance criteria.

Conclusion: CI security must shift attention from model-centric robustness to lifecycle-structured, system-level assurance in interconnected environments. The five risk-dynamics dimensions provide a unified language for analyzing—and ultimately governing—how FAI reshapes CI security, and the proposed research agenda bridges the gap between academic AI safety and real-world CI operational requirements.

Abstract: Frontier artificial intelligence (FAI), encompassing large-scale, general-purpose AI systems, including large language models, multimodal foundation models, and agentic systems, is increasingly integrated into critical infrastructure (CI). This challenges long-standing security assumptions of bounded behavior, segmented networks, component transparency, and human-paced decision-making. Existing AI-security literature typically organizes risks by attack type, lifecycle stage, or asset class, but fails to capture the system-level dynamics, such as how risk emerges, spreads, and is controlled, through which FAI reshapes CI security outcomes. This Systematization of Knowledge (SoK) introduces a five-dimensional risk-dynamics framework that characterizes how FAI reconfigures CI security across the lifecycle: (i) Capability Emergence through new FAI-enabled attack and defense capabilities, (ii) Infiltration Pathways through data, models and AI supply chains, (iii) Cross-System Propagation across interconnected infrastructures and dependencies, (iv) degradation of effective technical and human Control Authority, and (v) strain on institutional Response Capacity under operational pressure. Rather than enumerating threats, the framework identifies recurring mechanisms that jointly determine system-level risk. We further identify a structural mismatch between academic AI-security research and CI operational constraints, and derive a deployment-oriented research agenda grounded in system-level assurance criteria. Collectively, this work shifts attention from model-centric robustness to lifecycle-structured, system-level assurance in interconnected CI environments.

</details>


### [270] [A Multimodal Automatic Redteaming Evaluation based on Atomic Jailbreak Strategy Decoupling and Combination](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04034)
*Shiji Zhao,Yuxuan Zhou,Chen Xiong,Dongxian Wu,Yang Bai,Xun Chen*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: The paper proposes HACA (Hierarchical Atomic Combination Attack), a multimodal automated red-team jailbreak method that decomposes attack strategies into structural, semantic, and syntactic levels across a six-dimensional space, using a cross-modal joint planner and unified executor to generate jailbreak instructions, achieving a 95.48% average attack success rate against five mainstream MLLMs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing multimodal jailbreak attacks lack a systematic, atomic multimodal strategy space and a concise, automated executable framework, relying instead on human-crafted heuristics. This motivates the need for a structured, automated approach to comprehensively cover different attack types.

Method: The authors first decompose the text-image jailbreak strategy space into three levels (structural, semantic, syntactic), constructing a comprehensive strategy set. They then propose HACA, which uses a six-dimensional strategy space with a cross-modal joint planner to select and combine atomic jailbreak strategies, followed by a unified generate executor that directly produces jailbreak instructions based on the selected multimodal strategies.

Result: HACA achieves an average attack success rate of 95.48% against five mainstream MLLMs, demonstrating the effectiveness of the automated red-team approach.

Conclusion: A systematic, hierarchical decomposition of multimodal jailbreak strategies combined with automated planning and execution significantly outperforms prior manual approaches, revealing serious safety vulnerabilities in current MLLMs.

Abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have achieved impressive progress in image-text comprehension and generation, yet they remain susceptible to jailbreak attacks that can trigger harmful outputs and pose serious safety concerns. Existing multimodal jailbreak attacks have shown the feasibility of such attacks, but they still face two fundamental challenges: the lack of a atomic multi-modal strategy space, the absence of a concise and efficient executable framework beyond human-craft experience. To address these challenges, we first decompose the text-image jailbreak strategy space into three levels: structural, semantic, and syntactic, constructing a jailbreak strategy set encompassing both text and image modalities to systematically achieve combined coverage of different attack types. Then we propose a multimodal automated red team jailbreak method named Hierarchical Atomic Combination Attack (HACA). Specifically, based on a six-dimensional strategy space, a cross-modal joint planner is used to select and combine the different atomic jailbreak strategy for subsequent jailbreak command generation. Finally, at the implementation level, we explore to apply a unified generate executor to directly generate jailbreak instructions based on the selected multi-modal strategies. A series of experiments show that our automated red team method can achieve an attack success rate of average 95.48\% against five mainstream MLLMs.

</details>


### [271] [AMD SEV-SNP: A Confidential Computing Primer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04039)
*Amean Asad,Patrick McClurg,Patrick Woodhead*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: A technical primer on AMD SEV-SNP, a hardware-based confidential computing technology that creates Trusted Execution Environments for VMs by encrypting memory and register state, detecting tampering, and enabling remote attestation — all while treating the hypervisor as an untrusted adversary.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The hypervisor in traditional virtualization has full access to guest memory and state, making it a single point of compromise. The paper addresses the need for confidential computing where guests can run securely even when the hypervisor is adversarial, protecting data-in-use from privileged software attacks.

Method: The paper builds SEV-SNP's guarantees bottom-up from hardware: (1) the AMD Secure Processor and memory controller encryption engine encrypt guest memory and registers with hypervisor-inaccessible keys; (2) the Reverse Map Table enforces memory integrity against page-table-level attacks; (3) VM Privilege Levels, encrypted VM Save Area, and the GHCB protocol enable controlled guest-hypervisor cooperation; (4) an attestation pipeline chains hardware-signed initial-state measurements to AMD's certificate chain for remote verification.

Result: SEV-SNP delivers three core guarantees: memory confidentiality (encryption), memory integrity (tamper detection at access time via the Reverse Map Table), and remote attestation (cryptographic proof of the guest's identity and initial code to a remote verifier), all under an active hypervisor threat model.

Conclusion: SEV-SNP represents a practical, hardware-rooted confidential computing architecture that shifts trust from the hypervisor to the CPU vendor (AMD), enabling secure VM execution in untrusted cloud environments through layered mechanisms for encryption, integrity, privileged communication, and attestation.

Abstract: This paper is a technical primer on AMD Secure Encrypted Virtualization with Secure Nested Paging (SEV-SNP), a hardware confidential computing implementation that provides Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs) for virtual machines. SEV-SNP treats the hypervisor as adversarial. It encrypts guest memory and register state with keys the hypervisor never possesses, detects any tampering with guest memory at the point of access, and lets a guest prove to a remote verifier exactly what code it is running. The paper constructs each of these guarantees from the hardware up. It opens with the threat model that drives the design and the hardware that enforces it, the AMD Secure Processor and the encryption engine in the memory controller. It then develops the mechanisms that make a confidential guest practical. The Reverse Map Table provides memory integrity against an adversary who controls the page tables. The privilege and communication machinery (VM Privilege Levels, the encrypted VM Save Area, and the GHCB protocol) lets the guest cooperate with a hypervisor it does not trust. The attestation pipeline binds a hardware-signed measurement of the guest's initial state to AMD's certificate chain, so a remote verifier can confirm independently what is running.

</details>


### [272] [Beyond the QBER Threshold: A Temporal QBER Based Machine Learning Framework for Multi Attack Detection in BB84 QKD](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04047)
*Isha,Deepak Singh,Devesh Kumar,S. K Pal,Praful Hambarde,Amit Shukla*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: A temporal QBER-based machine learning framework using 63 physics-informed features substantially outperforms the conventional fixed 11% QBER threshold for detecting eavesdropping attacks in BB84 QKD systems, with XGBoost achieving 88.01% accuracy and reducing false negatives from 0.8477 to 0.0198.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Conventional BB84 QKD monitoring uses a fixed 11% QBER threshold, but stealthy eavesdropping attacks can operate below this threshold while still compromising security. There is a need for more sensitive, multi-attack detection capable of identifying subtle temporal patterns that threshold-based methods miss.

Method: The authors extract 63 physics-informed temporal features from QBER data, capturing burst behavior, temporal instability, basis-dependent asymmetry, and QBER-loss interactions. These features are fed into Random Forest, XGBoost, and SVM-RBF classifiers, evaluated across seven eavesdropping attacks plus a normal channel scenario under noisy and lossy conditions. SHAP analysis is used for model explainability, and performance is benchmarked against the conventional 11% QBER threshold.

Result: XGBoost achieves the best performance: 88.01% accuracy (0.47% standard deviation) and a macro F1 score of 0.8803, with SVM-RBF performing comparably. The fixed 11% QBER threshold yields only 25.82% accuracy with an FNR of 0.8477, whereas the proposed framework reduces FNR to 0.0198. SHAP analysis confirms that physics-informed temporal and channel-derived features are highly discriminative for identifying specific eavesdropping strategies.

Conclusion: Temporal QBER-driven ML provides an accurate, explainable, and practical framework for multi-attack security monitoring in BB84 QKD systems, substantially outperforming static threshold-based detection, particularly against stealthy attacks.

Abstract: Conventional BB84 Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) systems rely on a fixed 11% Quantum Bit Error Rate (QBER) threshold to detect eavesdropping. However, stealthy attacks can remain below this threshold while still compromising channel security. This paper proposes a temporal QBER based machine learning framework for detecting and classifying eavesdropping attacks in BB84 QKD systems. Rather than relying on average session level QBER, the framework extracts 63 physics-informed temporal features capturing burst behavior, temporal instability, basis dependent asymmetry, and QBER loss interactions. Random Forest, XGBoost, and Support Vector Machine with a Radial Basis Function kernel (SVM-RBF) classifiers are evaluated on seven eavesdropping attacks and a normal channel scenario under noisy and lossy conditions. Averaged over ten independent runs, XGBoost achieves the best performance with 88.01% (0.47%) accuracy and a macro F1 score of 0.8803, while SVM-RBF performs comparably, confirming the robustness of the proposed features. Evaluated as a binary attack-versus-normal detector for comparison with conventional monitoring, a fixed 11% QBER threshold achieves only 25.82% accuracy with a False Negative Rate (FNR) of 0.8477, whereas the proposed framework reduces the FNR to 0.0198, substantially improving detection of stealthy attacks that evade threshold-based monitoring. SHapley Additive exPlanations based (SHAP) explainability shows that physics-informed temporal and channel derived features are highly discriminative for identifying eavesdropping strategies. These results demonstrate that temporal QBER driven machine learning provides an accurate, explainable, and practical framework for multi attack security monitoring in BB84 QKD systems.

</details>


### [273] [When Modalities Fail to Tango: Conformal Backdoor Detection in Multimodal Contrastive Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04052)
*Yiming Chen,Kemou Li,Haiwei Wu,Jiantao Zhou*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: Existing backdoor detection in multimodal contrastive learning relies on CLIPScore, which suffers from overlapping score distributions and lacks statistical guarantees. The authors propose CASCADE, a two-stage conformal prediction framework that provides provable confidence bounds for detecting poisoned image-caption pairs, achieving strong empirical performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current detection-based defenses against backdoor attacks in MCL depend on CLIPScore, assuming poisoned pairs have lower image-caption semantic similarity. This approach is fundamentally flawed due to: (1) substantial distribution overlap between benign and poisoned CLIPScores, undermining reliability, and (2) fixed-threshold methods lacking statistical guarantees for ambiguous samples in overlapping regions.

Method: The authors propose CASCADE, a two-stage Coarse-to-Fine Conformal Backdoor Detection framework. Stage 1 (coarse-grained) uses cross-modality consistency to identify high-confidence benign and poisoned pairs. Stage 2 (fine-grained) constructs a reference set from high-confidence poisoned pairs, computes instance-level nonconformity scores (NCSs) based on text-space similarity for unidentified samples, measuring conformity to the poisoning distribution to precisely detect latent poisoned pairs. The framework integrates conformal prediction to provide provable confidence bounds.

Result: On the large-scale CC3M dataset, CASCADE achieves an average false positive rate (FPR) of 5.79% at 100% true positive rate (TPR) and an average AUROC of 0.9867 across diverse attacks. The method also remains effective against adaptive attacks.

Conclusion: CASCADE effectively addresses the fundamental limitations of CLIPScore-based backdoor detection by leveraging conformal prediction for statistically grounded detection, demonstrating superior and robust performance across various attack scenarios.

Abstract: Backdoor attacks in multimodal contrastive learning (MCL) have garnered growing attention in recent years, as many downstream tasks critically depend on pre-trained MCL models. Existing detection-based defenses predominantly rely on the CLIPScore metric, under the assumption that poisoned pairs exhibit lower semantic similarity between the image and the caption. However, we identify two critical flaws remaining in existing methods: (1) the substantial overlap between CLIPScore distributions of benign and poisoned pairs undermines the reliability of this metric, and (2) fixed-threshold detection cannot provide statistical guarantees for ambiguous samples within overlapping regions. To overcome these limitations, we propose integrating conformal prediction (CP), a statistical framework that quantifies uncertainty through nonconformity scores (NCSs), to establish provable confidence bounds for detecting poisoned image-caption pairs. Building on CP, we introduce CASCADE, a novel two-stage Coarse-to-Fine Conformal Backdoor Detection framework. The coarse-grained stage uses cross-modality consistency to identify high-confidence benign and poisoned pairs. In the fine-grained stage, a reference set is constructed from high-confidence poisoned pairs, and instance-level NCSs based on text-space similarity are computed for each sample in the unidentified subset. These NCSs measure conformity to the poisoning distribution and enable precise identification of latent poisoned pairs within the unidentified subset. Extensive experiments on the large-scale CC3M dataset demonstrate that CASCADE achieves an average FPR of 5.79% at 100% TPR and an average AUROC of 0.9867 across diverse attacks, while remaining effective against adaptive attacks.

</details>


### [274] [AgentAntibody: An Adaptive Immune System for Defending LLM Agents against Prompt Injection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04053)
*Shihao Weng,Yang Feng,Xiaofei Xie,Jiongchi Yu*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: AgentAntibody introduces a self-evolving immune system for LLM agents that learns the user's security boundary across encounters, building a persistent antibody library to defend against prompt injection while preserving legitimate task completion.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing defenses treat each prompt injection encounter independently, ignoring that user requests are often underspecified—describing desired outcomes without specifying acceptable behavior. Attackers exploit this ambiguity. As users clarify expectations through concrete cases, defenses should learn and adapt across encounters, analogous to adaptive immunity in biology.

Method: AgentAntibody maintains a persistent library of "antibodies" that encode the evolving understanding of the user's security boundary. At runtime, this library recognizes threats and mounts immune responses. Across encounters, the system evolves—updating its antibody library based on user feedback or observed outcomes—to strengthen immunity against future attacks.

Result: Experiments across three benchmarks and four backbone LLMs demonstrate that AgentAntibody outperforms existing defenses in preventing harmful actions while preserving legitimate task completion, even when both harmful and legitimate actions are compatible with the stated task.

Conclusion: By learning the user's security boundary through experience, AgentAntibody provides a more robust, adaptive defense against prompt injection that improves over time, unlike static, per-task approaches.

Abstract: Prompt injection remains a critical threat to LLM agents, yet existing defenses treat each task as a self-contained problem, independent of previous encounters. In practice, user requests are often underspecified: they describe the desired outcome without fully specifying acceptable behavior. An injection can exploit this ambiguity, causing the agent to complete the task in a way the user would reject. As the user's expectations become clearer through concrete cases, a defense should learn from each encounter and apply what it learns to the next. Inspired by adaptive immunity, we propose AgentAntibody, which equips LLM agents with a self-evolving immune system against prompt injection. AgentAntibody represents its evolving understanding of the user's security boundary as a persistent library of antibodies. At runtime, the library recognizes threats to this boundary and mounts corresponding immune responses. Across encounters, it evolves to strengthen the agent's immunity to future attacks. Extensive experiments across three benchmarks and four backbone LLMs show that, by learning the user's boundary through experience, AgentAntibody outperforms existing defenses in preventing harmful actions while preserving legitimate task completion, even when the harmful and legitimate actions are both compatible with the stated task.

</details>


### [275] [Trident : How to Break Deep Reinforcement Learning Cyber Defenses (Agentic)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04317)
*Ryozo Masukawa,Ian Bryant,Armita Kazeminajafabadi,Sanggeon Yun,Hyunwoo Oh,SungHeon Jeong,Nathaniel D. Bastian,Mahdi Imani,Mohsen Imani*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: Trident is an agentic LLM-based red-teaming framework that uses RLVR with a "Code-as-Policy" architecture to train adaptive attackers against DRL-based cyber defenses, revealing that static defenses suffer up to 522% performance degradation when facing intelligent, adaptive adversaries.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing DRL-based autonomous cyber defense systems are almost exclusively evaluated against static, heuristic red agents, leaving their robustness against adaptive threats critically underexplored. Meanwhile, RLVR has advanced LLM reasoning but lacks suitable cybersecurity benchmarks and interaction datasets for integration.

Method: Trident consists of three components: (1) a dynamic benchmark with isolated sandbox servers spanning CybORG CAGE 4 and CyberWheel; (2) a dataset of 13,000+ red-blue interaction trajectories for RLVR; and (3) a "Code-as-Policy" agentic architecture that reformulates red agent training as a contextual bandit using a tripartite Log Summarizer–Planner–Coder design, where a trainable Planner generates attack strategies from compressed logs and a frozen Coder translates them into executable Python policies.

Result: With a single trainable 7B Planner, Trident reduces blue agent defensive performance by an average of 522% compared to static red agent baselines, and autonomously discovers emergent behaviors such as decoy avoidance and adaptive state prioritization that static heuristics completely fail to uncover.

Conclusion: Current DRL-based cyber defenses exhibit fundamental brittleness when confronted with adaptive, LLM-driven adversaries. Trident establishes a rigorous evaluation paradigm and exposes the inadequacy of static red-teaming, underscoring the urgent need for more robust defensive strategies.

Abstract: Autonomous cyber defense systems based on Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) have attracted significant research attention, yet remain evaluated almost exclusively against static, heuristic red agents, leaving their robustness against adaptive threats critically understudied. Meanwhile, recent advances in Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) have improved LLM reasoning, but their integration into cybersecurity remains elusive due to the absence of suitable benchmark environments and interaction datasets. To bridge this gap, we introduce Trident, an agentic LLM red teaming framework comprising three components: a dynamic benchmark with isolated sandbox servers spanning CybORG CAGE 4 and CyberWheel, a dataset comprises over 13,000 high-fidelity red-blue interaction trajectories for RLVR, and a ``Code-as-Policy'' RLVR agentic architecture Trident Agentic). The latter reformulates red agent training as a contextual bandit via a tripartite Log Summarizer--Planner--Coder design, where a trainable Planner generates complete attack strategies from compressed execution logs, which a frozen Coder translates into executable Python policies deployed against live DRL defenders. Empirical evaluations reveal a fundamental brittleness in existing defenses: with a single trainable 7B planner, Trident reduces blue agent defensive performance by an average of 522% compared to static red agent baselines while autonomously discovering emergent behaviors such as decoy avoidance and adaptive state prioritization that static heuristics entirely fail to uncover.

</details>


### [276] [An Inline Control Architecture for Language Models in Intelligent Transportation Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04065)
*Narendra Kumar Dewangan,Mounira Msahli*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: Guarded-V2X proposes an inline semantic guardrail architecture to secure LLM-enabled V2X services by combining rule-based filtering, safety classification, constrained generation, trusted retrieval, and post-decision adjudication, demonstrating reduced adversarial vulnerability within V2X latency budgets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are increasingly deployed in V2X systems for semantic tasks (message summarization, operator assistance, decision support) at RSUs and edge nodes. While not in safety-critical control loops, these LLM components introduce prompt-level attack surfaces that traditional V2X security (authentication, message integrity) cannot address. There is a gap in protecting LLM-integrated V2X services from adversarial prompt-based exploits under real-time constraints.

Method: Guarded-V2X is an inline guardrail architecture with five integrated components: (1) rule-based ingress filtering, (2) a lightweight safety classifier, (3) policy-constrained structured generation, (4) trusted-only retrieval, and (5) post-decision adjudication. Evaluation follows a four-stage pipeline: intrusion vulnerability analysis, calibration and latency benchmarking, guardrail validation, and adversarial stress testing, using a V2X-aligned simulated dataset built from RSU advisories, operator messages, and annotated V2X message summaries.

Result: Unguarded and prompt-only baselines showed residual vulnerability under multi-turn adversarial trials. Guarded-V2X consistently reduced intrusion acceptance success rates and eliminated all observed unsafe completions in two-turn settings, while remaining within acceptable latency budgets for V2X semantic advisory paths.

Conclusion: The Guarded-V2X architecture effectively mitigates prompt-level adversarial threats in LLM-enabled V2X services without violating real-time latency constraints, offering a practical security layer complementary to traditional V2X authentication and integrity mechanisms.

Abstract: Vehicle-to-everything (V2X) systems increasingly incorporate large language models (LLMs) for semantic tasks such as message summarization, operator assistance, and decision support at roadside units and edge nodes. Although these components are not part of safety-critical control loops, they introduce prompt-level attack surfaces that are not addressed by traditional V2X security mechanisms focused on authentication and message integrity. This paper presents Guarded-V2X, an inline semantic guardrail architecture for securing LLM-enabled V2X services under real-time constraints. The proposed system integrates rule-based ingress filtering, a lightweight safety classifier, policy-constrained structured generation, trusted-only retrieval, and post-decision adjudication to enforce machine-checkable safety boundaries prior to downstream execution. Guarded-V2X is evaluated using a four-stage experimental pipeline encompassing intrusion vulnerability analysis, calibration and latency benchmarking, guardrail validation, and robustness under adversarial stress. Experiments are conducted on a V2X-aligned simulated dataset derived from RSU advisories, operator messages, and annotated V2X message summaries. Results show that unguarded and prompt-only baselines retain residual vulnerability under multi-turn adversarial trials, while Guarded-V2X consistently reduces intrusion acceptance success rates and eliminates observed unsafe completions in two-turn settings, without exceeding latency budgets for V2X semantic advisory paths.

</details>


### [277] [FBID: Adaptive Personalized Federated Learning for Robust Out-of-Distribution Attack Detection in IoT Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04073)
*An Khanh Bui,Cong Thanh Nguyen,Hoang-Anh Pham,Hoang Thai Dinh,Diep N. Nguyen*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: FBID is a federated learning framework for IoT intrusion detection that uses a server-side contextual bandit to dynamically tune personalization, plus a trust-based blending mechanism to balance global and local models, achieving up to 7.66% improvement in OOD detection rate over baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing PFL methods for IoT intrusion detection rely on client-side self-adjustment, causing over-personalization that degrades out-of-distribution (OOD) attack detection. A server-side control mechanism is needed to prevent this degradation while retaining the benefits of local adaptation under non-IID data.

Method: FBID uses a contextual multi-armed bandit at the server to dynamically regulate each client's local training intensity based on behavior and update quality. It also introduces a trust-based blending mechanism that computes client-specific interpolation coefficients between global and local models, preserving global knowledge while allowing beneficial specialization.

Result: On the CICIoT2023 dataset under heterogeneous non-IID distributions and OOD stress tests, FBID improved individual client OOD Detection Rate by up to 7.66% and F1-Score by up to 5.08% (relative) over the strongest stable baseline, with enhanced robustness to unseen attack classes.

Conclusion: Server-side personalization control via bandit learning effectively mitigates over-personalization in PFL for intrusion detection, yielding superior OOD detection performance and robustness without sacrificing local adaptation benefits.

Abstract: Personalized Federated Learning (PFL) has emerged as a promising solution for intrusion detection in heterogeneous IoT environments, as it can improve local adaptation under highly Non-Independent and Identically Distributed (non-IID) data distributions. However, existing PFL methods often rely on client-side self-adjustment, which may lead to over-personalization and substantial degradation in out-of-distribution (OOD) attack detection. In this paper, we propose Federated Bandit Intrusion Detection (FBID), a novel adaptive PFL framework to address this limitation through server-side personalization control. In particular, FBID employs a contextual multi-armed bandit at the server to dynamically regulate each client's local training intensity according to its observed behavior and update quality. Moreover, FBID introduces a trust-based blending mechanism to derive client-specific interpolation coefficients between the global and local models, thereby preserving global attack-detection knowledge while still allowing beneficial local specialization. Through extensive experiments on the CICIoT2023 dataset under heterogeneous client distributions and OOD stress-test settings, we show that FBID improves individual client OOD Detection Rate (DR) by up to 7.66% and F1-Score (F1) by up to 5.08% (relative) over the strongest stable baseline, while also improving robustness to previously unseen attack classes.

</details>


### [278] [NEBULA: A Language - Independent Specification for Opaque Rotating Refresh Tokens](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04115)
*Matteo Teodori*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: NEBULA provides a precise, language-independent specification for RFC 9700 OAuth 2.0 refresh token rotation with replay detection, backed by ten reference implementations and a machine-readable conformance suite of 38 scenarios, closing a concurrency bypass in reuse detection and ensuring cross-language behavioral consistency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: RFC 9700 mandates refresh token rotation with replay detection for public clients but specifies only policy, not mechanism — leaving wire format, storage schema, verification ordering, concurrency contracts, and edge-case semantics undefined. This ambiguity risks security-relevant implementation divergence in corner cases.

Method: NEBULA defines opaque tokens (128-bit public selector + 256-bit secret verifier from CSPRNG) with server-side validity. It specifies a compare-and-set rotation contract to prevent concurrency-based replay bypass. A machine-readable behavioral suite of 38 scenarios is executed by thin per-language runners against ten reference implementations (TypeScript, Python, Go, Rust, Java, PHP, C#, Ruby, Elixir, Dart), structurally excluding transcription drift.

Result: The specification closes a reproducible concurrency bypass in refresh token reuse detection via its compare-and-set contract. All ten implementations conform to the 38-scenario behavioral suite. The opaque, non-cryptographic token design confers post-quantum security posture.

Conclusion: NEBULA demonstrates that multi-implementation conformance testing via machine-readable behavioral suites is an effective methodology for security specifications, moving beyond prose to executable, verifiable correctness across languages. All artefacts are open-source (Apache 2.0).

Abstract: Refresh tokens are among the most sensitive credentials in modern authentication systems: long-lived, bearer-style, and sufficient to mint access tokens for days or weeks. RFC 9700, the current Best Current Practice for OAuth 2.0 security, mandates that refresh tokens issued to public clients be rotated on every use with replay (reuse) detection, or be sender-constrained. But the BCP specifies policy, not mechanism: it prescribes no wire format, no storage schema, no ordering of verification steps, no concurrency contract, and no semantics for edge cases such as lost-response retries or key rotation. Implementations may therefore diverge in precisely the corner cases that determine security outcomes.
  We present NEBULA, a precise, language-independent specification of the RFC 9700 refresh-token model, together with ten conformant reference implementations (TypeScript, Python, Go, Rust, Java, PHP, C#, Ruby, Elixir, Dart). NEBULA tokens are opaque -- a 128-bit public selector and a 256-bit secret verifier, both CSPRNG output, carrying no claims and no signature -- so token validity is a property of server-side state rather than of cryptographic verification. Its conformance methodology publishes the behavioural suite as data rather than as prose: 38 scenarios in one machine-readable file that every implementation executes through a thin per-language runner, so that drift by transcription is structurally excluded. We describe the specification -- including a compare-and-set rotation contract that closes a reproducible bypass of reuse detection under concurrent refresh -- analyse its security properties including its post-quantum posture, and report on cross-language conformance as a method for multi-implementation security specifications. The specification, implementations, and conformance artefacts are open source under the Apache License 2.0.

</details>


### [279] [Behavioral Information Leakage in Darknet Traffic: A Multi-Channel Analysis Across Anonymity Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04143)
*Javeriah Saleem,Rafiqul Islam,Md Zahidul Islam*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: This paper proposes a behavioral information leakage framework to analyze darknet traffic across Tor, I2P, FreeNet, and ZeroNet, decomposing flows into control, structural, and rhythmic descriptors. Results show Tor exhibits the highest service separability (Macro-F1 0.7165), while FreeNet shows the lowest leakage. Structural-rhythmic representations yield the strongest within-network performance, but cross-network transferability is limited.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing darknet traffic classification research prioritizes predictive accuracy without explaining the underlying behavioral mechanisms that enable encrypted services to be distinguished. The authors aim to systematically quantify and characterize what types of behavioral information leak from different anonymity networks, moving beyond classification performance to understand leakage causality.

Method: The framework decomposes flow-level traffic into three descriptor groups: control (e.g., packet-size organization, directional exchange imbalance), structural, and rhythmic (e.g., packet tempo, silence-burst behavior). It applies normalized mutual information analysis combined with Random Forest-based predictive validation, structural-rhythmic interaction analysis, and cross-network service-variability evaluation. The proposed Service Variability Index and Leakage Variability Index quantify separability patterns. All evaluations use leakage-safe repeated stratified cross-validation, including leave-one-network-out testing.

Result: Tor achieves the highest service separability (Macro-F1: 0.7165, cumulative normalized leakage: 3.9461), while FreeNet exhibits the lowest combined leakage (0.8744). Packet-size organization, directional exchange imbalance, packet tempo, and silence-burst behavior emerge as primary leakage mechanisms. Combined structural-rhythmic representations yield the strongest within-network performance. Leave-one-network-out evaluation shows limited cross-architecture transferability. Video services exhibit consistent network-specific separability; chat and email show greater variability across anonymity-network pairs.

Conclusion: Behavioral information leakage varies significantly across anonymity network architectures. The findings suggest that traffic analysis defenses should be tailored to specific network designs, as leakage mechanisms are not universal. The proposed indices provide a systematic way to quantify and compare leakage across networks and services, highlighting that certain application types (e.g., video) leak consistently while others (chat, email) are more network-dependent.

Abstract: Existing darknet traffic classification studies largely emphasize predictive accuracy while offering limited insight into the behavioral mechanisms that make encrypted services distinguishable. This paper proposes a behavioral information leakage framework that decomposes flow-level traffic into control, structural, and rhythmic descriptor groups across Tor, I2P, FreeNet, and ZeroNet. The framework combines normalized mutual information analysis with Random Forest-based predictive validation, structural-rhythmic interaction analysis, and cross-network service-variability evaluation under leakage-safe repeated stratified cross-validation. Results show that behavioral leakage varies considerably across anonymity networks. Tor achieves the highest service separability, with a Macro-F1 of 0.7165 and cumulative normalized leakage of 3.9461, whereas FreeNet exhibits the lowest combined leakage of 0.8744. Packet-size organization, directional exchange imbalance, packet tempo, and silence-burst behavior emerge as the main leakage mechanisms. The combined structural-rhythmic representation consistently provides the strongest within-network performance, while leave-one-network-out evaluation reveals limited transferability across anonymity architectures. The proposed Service Variability Index and Leakage Variability Index further show that video exhibits consistent network-specific separability, whereas chat and email demonstrate greater variability across anonymity-network pairs.

</details>


### [280] [Open-World Darknet Traffic Recognition Under Leave-One-Service-Out Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04167)
*Javeriah Saleem,Rafiqul Islam,Md Zahidul Islam*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: Existing darknet traffic classification research relies on unrealistic closed-world evaluation. This paper introduces an open-world framework using leave-one-service-out evaluation and uncertainty-aware classification, revealing that closed-world settings vastly overestimate real-world robustness. Behavioral overlap between known and unknown services causes severe misclassification, highlighting a fundamental challenge for reliable darknet traffic analysis.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Most darknet traffic classification studies assume closed-world evaluation — where all service categories are known during both training and testing. This assumption is unrealistic for real-world deployment, where novel or unseen services frequently appear. The paper aims to quantify the performance gap between closed-world and open-world settings and identify the root causes of degradation.

Method: The authors propose an open-world darknet traffic classification framework employing leave-one-service-out (LOSO) evaluation combined with uncertainty-aware classification using Random Forest and XGBoost models. Uncertainty-based rejection mechanisms are applied to filter low-confidence predictions. Additionally, semantic absorption analysis is conducted to examine how unknown services are misclassified into known categories.

Result: Transitioning from closed-world to open-world settings causes severe performance degradation: XGBoost Macro-F1 drops from 88.8% to 46.1%, and Random Forest from 87.4% to 45.7% on I2P traffic. Uncertainty-based rejection provides only marginal improvement. Semantic absorption analysis reveals FreeNet video traffic is absorbed into browsing (88.1% rate) and I2P P2P traffic into FTP-related behavior (83.4% rate), indicating strong behavioral overlap as the root cause of misclassification.

Conclusion: Closed-world evaluation significantly overestimates darknet traffic classification robustness. Behavioral similarity between known and unknown services remains the primary obstacle to reliable open-world classification, and current uncertainty-based mitigation strategies are insufficient to address this challenge.

Abstract: Darknet traffic recognition is critical for cyber threat intelligence, as anonymity networks are often used to conceal malicious activity. However, most existing studies rely on closed-world evaluation, assuming all service categories are known during training and testing, which is unrealistic in real-world environments. This paper presents an open-world darknet traffic classification framework using leave-one-service-out evaluation and uncertainty-aware classification with Random Forest and XGBoost models. Experimental results demonstrate significant performance degradation when transitioning from closed-world to open-world settings, demonstrating that closed-world evaluation substantially overestimates deployment robustness. For example, XGBoost Macro-F1 decreases from 88.8% to 46.1% in the I2P environment, while Random Forest performance drops from 87.4% to 45.7%. Although uncertainty-based rejection slightly improves robustness, strong behavioral similarity between known and unknown services leads to frequent misclassification. Semantic absorption analysis further shows that FreeNet video traffic is classified as browsing traffic with an 88.1% assignment rate, while I2P peer-to-peer traffic is absorbed into FTP-related behavior with an 83.4% assignment rate. The findings demonstrate that behavioral overlap remains a major challenge for reliable open-world darknet traffic classification.

</details>


### [281] [Behavioral Skill Reconstruction: Reconstructing Hidden Functionality from LLM Agent Skills](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04192)
*Peichun Hua,Haoxuan Xu,Mengyuan Li*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: Attackers can clone black-box agent skills through legitimate interactions alone, without accessing hidden files. SkillClone uses structured probing and iterative repair to reconstruct functional equivalents of proprietary skills, bypassing disclosure-focused defenses. File secrecy does not guarantee functional secrecy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing defenses for closed-source agent skills focus on preventing direct file/prompt disclosure, but preventing file leakage does not prevent users from recovering the functionality those files implement. The paper investigates whether functional reconstruction is possible through ordinary, legitimate use alone—a threat model that disclosure-focused defenses cannot address.

Method: The authors introduce SkillClone, a black-box attack with four stages: (1) forming an interface hypothesis from the skill's public advertisement, (2) issuing structured benign probes to the victim skill, (3) synthesizing an executable replica from observed input-output pairs, and (4) iterative repair through differential validation—comparing replica outputs against the victim skill and requerying to close gaps. The attack uses only legitimate task requests, never attempting direct disclosure.

Result: Evaluated across 30 skills spanning rules, tables, procedures, and algorithms, SkillClone achieves exact or partial functional recovery on held-out inputs for multiple targets. Iterative requerying successfully closes gaps missed by single-round reconstruction. Less detailed skill descriptions (a potential defense) offer limited protection against the attack.

Conclusion: File secrecy alone does not ensure functional secrecy. Defenses must evolve beyond preventing direct disclosure to also limit cumulative information leakage from ordinary, legitimate use of agent skills.

Abstract: Closed source agent skills may encode proprietary instructions, scripts, constants, and data. Providers may offer their capabilities as services while keeping the underlying packages hidden. Prior work focuses on prompt injection attacks that directly disclose these artifacts, and existing defenses accordingly aim to prevent such leakage. However, preventing file disclosure does not prevent users from recovering the functionality those files implement. This raises a fundamental question: can a user reconstruct a skill's functionality through ordinary use while its files remain hidden?
  We study behavioral skill reconstruction (BSR), in which an attacker uses valid task requests and observed responses to build a functional clone of a hidden skill. We introduce SkillClone, a black-box attack that clones a target skill by forming an interface hypothesis from its public advertisement, issuing structured benign probes, synthesizing an executable replica, and iteratively repairing it through differential validation against the victim skill. Across 30 skills spanning rules, tables, procedures, and algorithms, SkillClone achieves exact or partial recovery on held-out inputs for several targets. Iterative requerying closes gaps missed by single-round reconstruction. Because SkillClone uses only legitimate interactions, disclosure-focused defenses provide limited coverage, and less detailed skill descriptions offer limited protection. These results show that file secrecy alone does not ensure functional secrecy. Defenses must also limit cumulative information leakage from ordinary use.

</details>


### [282] [PriDyG: Privacy-preserving Dynamic Graph Inference with LLM-GNN Collaboration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04255)
*Yuyang Xia,Ruixuan Liu,Li Xiong*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: PriDyG is a differentially private dynamic graph inference framework that combines GNN structural learning with LLM semantic reasoning. Its key innovation—incremental private multi-hop aggregation—processes each edge exactly once, making total privacy cost equal to a single static release regardless of update frequency, while incorporating LLM predictions from node text adds no extra privacy cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Graph inference over relational data risks exposing sensitive edge information, with the risk compounding in dynamic graphs where repeated model updates cause privacy loss accumulation. Existing approaches using geometrically decaying budget allocation introduce exponentially increasing noise. The authors aim to design a framework that decouples privacy cost from the number of updates while maintaining utility.

Method: The authors propose PriDyG with two core components: (1) Incremental private multi-hop aggregation that buffers newly arrived edges and processes each edge exactly once, leveraging parallel composition so total privacy cost equals one static release. This preserves exact one-hop signals and at least half of two-hop information transfers. (2) LLM-based semantic reasoning that complements privatized GNN outputs using predictions from node text alone, incurring zero additional edge-level privacy cost.

Result: Experiments on four benchmarks for node classification and link prediction show PriDyG consistently outperforms geometrically decaying baselines under identical privacy budgets. It matches the utility of naive per-update retraining while reducing cumulative privacy cost by up to three orders of magnitude.

Conclusion: PriDyG demonstrates that combining incremental private aggregation with LLM-based semantic reasoning effectively decouples privacy cost from update frequency in dynamic graph inference, achieving strong utility-privacy trade-offs without the noise accumulation problem of prior methods.

Abstract: Graph inference over relational data can expose sensitive edge information, and this risk becomes more severe in dynamic graphs, where repeated model updates cause privacy loss to accumulate. We formulate Edge-level Differentially Private Dynamic Graph Inference (EDG) and propose PriDyG, a private inference framework that combines GNN-based structural learning with LLM-based semantic reasoning. PriDyG introduces incremental private multi-hop aggregation, which buffers newly arrived edges and processes each edge exactly once. By parallel composition, the total privacy cost equals that of a single static release, independent of the number or schedule of model updates. Compared with geometrically decaying budget allocation, incremental aggregation avoids exponentially increasing noise while preserving exact one-hop signals and at least half of two-hop information transfers. PriDyG further complements privatized GNN outputs with LLM predictions derived solely from node text, incurring no additional edge-level privacy cost. Experiments on four benchmarks for node classification and link prediction show that PriDyG consistently outperforms geometrically decaying baselines under the same privacy budget and matches the utility of naive per-update retraining while reducing cumulative privacy cost by up to three orders of magnitude.

</details>


### [283] [Adversarial Attacks for Good: A Survey of Proactive Protection across the Visual Content Lifecycle](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04314)
*Jiaming Zhang,Boyang Chen,Zherui Li,Fuyao Zhang,Xinyu Yan,Hong Xi Tae,Wenwen He,Xuan Wang,Siqi Guo,Junhao Dong,Kun Wang,Hanxun Huang,Yige Li,Xingjun Ma,Yang Cao,Lingjuan Lyu,Wei Yang Bryan Lim*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: This survey unifies five research communities that independently developed "adversarial attacks for good" — perturbations applied by data owners to protect visual content across its lifecycle: privacy filters, unlearnable examples, generative safeguards, adversarial CAPTCHAs, and provenance mechanisms. It evaluates them on transferability, adaptability, and deployment readiness, finding most validated only against static adversaries, and consolidates cross-stage countermeasures and open problems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Once visual content enters an AI pipeline, owners lose technical control. Legal remedies act post-hoc, but technical interventions must be applied at release/access time. Five communities independently converged on using adversarial perturbations protectively, yet work in isolation with incompatible success criteria. The paper aims to unify these paradigms, enable cross-community comparison, and assess whether the approach remains viable as models evolve toward multimodality and autonomous agents.

Method: The authors conduct a comprehensive survey organizing protective adversarial attacks by the stage in a visual asset's lifecycle: (1) privacy filters at sharing, (2) unlearnable examples against unauthorized training, (3) generative safeguards against malicious editing/imitation, (4) adversarial CAPTCHAs for access control, and (5) provenance mechanisms for post-circulation attribution. They evaluate all five families along three shared axes: transferability (across models), adaptability (to adaptive adversaries), and deployment readiness (real-world viability). They also consolidate cross-stage countermeasures and identify open problems.

Result: The survey finds that most protections are validated primarily against static or weakly adaptive adversaries, with scarce evidence beyond controlled benchmarks. Despite independent development, many methods exploit persistent perception gaps between humans and machines. Deployment readiness varies significantly across the five families, and cross-stage composability remains largely unexplored. The paradigm's relevance persists as pipelines evolve toward multimodal models and autonomous agents.

Conclusion: The protective adversarial attack paradigm is a coherent, cross-community phenomenon with persistent relevance. However, the field needs stronger evaluation against adaptive adversaries, real-world deployment evidence, and composable protections spanning multiple lifecycle stages. The authors call for robust, deployable, owner-side protection mechanisms and highlight open problems for future work.

Abstract: Once visual content enters an AI pipeline, its owner often retains little technical control over how it is used. Legal and regulatory remedies can address misuse, but many technical interventions must be applied earlier, when content is released or accessed. This survey examines the protective paradigm that has grown around this intervention point, which we call \emph{adversarial attacks for good}. Perturbations and structured signals long studied as attacks on learned models are instead applied by data owners, creators, platforms, or auditors to disrupt unauthorized automation or support later accountability. Five research communities have arrived at this inversion largely independently, each addressing a different stage of a visual asset's lifecycle: privacy filters against unwanted recognition at sharing time, unlearnable examples against unauthorized training, generative safeguards against malicious editing or imitation, adversarial CAPTCHAs for access control against automated agents, and provenance mechanisms for post-circulation attribution. Although developed in separate venues with incompatible success criteria, many of these methods exploit persistent gaps between human perception, semantic interpretation, and machine inference, suggesting that the paradigm remains relevant as visual pipelines evolve toward multimodal models and autonomous agents. To make their claims comparable, we evaluate all five families along shared axes of transferability, adaptability, and deployment readiness. Across the lifecycle, we find that most protections are still validated mainly against static or weakly adaptive adversaries, while evidence beyond controlled benchmarks remains scarce. We close by consolidating cross-stage countermeasures and open problems for robust, composable, and deployable owner-side protection.

</details>


### [284] [Combating Knowledge Corruption in Agent Systems: A Byzantine-Tolerant Secure Collaborative RAG Framework](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04366)
*Zhaoqi Wang,Daqing He,Zijian Zhang,Ye Liu,Jiamou Liu,Zhirui Zeng,Zhan Qin,Zhen Li,Xin Li,Hongwei Yao,Jincheng An,Yong Liu,Yi Li,Qi Sun,Xiulei Liu,Liehuang Zhu*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: SecureCollaRAG proposes a Byzantine-tolerant collaborative retrieval-augmented generation framework that uses a Multi-source Knowledge Validation Mechanism with dynamic GNN-based credibility scoring to defend against knowledge corruption attacks on RAG systems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: RAG systems reduce LLM hallucinations but introduce new vulnerabilities to knowledge corruption attacks, where adversaries poison retrieved documents to manipulate model outputs. Existing defenses are insufficient against stealthy attacks, particularly under non-IID data distributions.

Method: A Byzantine-tolerant collaborative multi-agent RAG framework featuring a Multi-source Knowledge Validation Mechanism. The core is a dynamic Graph Neural Network (GNN)-based credibility scoring system that verifies document provenance across multiple sources to detect poisoned documents while preserving legitimate domain knowledge.

Result: Through extensive evaluations and formal analysis, SecureCollaRAG demonstrates robustness against attackers under non-IID data distributions, effectively preventing stealthy knowledge corruption attacks.

Conclusion: SecureCollaRAG provides a viable defense mechanism for RAG systems against knowledge corruption attacks, maintaining domain knowledge integrity while achieving Byzantine tolerance through collaborative multi-agent validation.

Abstract: While retrieval-augmented generation systems partially address the hallucination issues in large language models, it also introduces new vulnerabilities to knowledge corruption attacks. Adversaries exploit these vulnerabilities by poisoning documents provided by RAG system to manipulate LLM outputs. To counter this threat, we propose SecureCollaRAG, a Byzantine-tolerant collaborative RAG framework leveraging Multi-source Knowledge Validation Mechanism. Our approach enables agent system to securely verify document provenance through dynamic GNN-based credibility scoring, effectively preventing stealthy knowledge corruption attacks while preserving essential domain knowledge integrity. Through extensive evaluations and formal analysis, we demonstrate that SecureCollaRAG maintains robustness against attackers under non-IID data distributions.

</details>


### [285] [Large Language Models and Social Media Information Integrity: Opportunities, Challenges, and Research Directions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04375)
*Junjie Xiong,Zhengyuan Jiang,Xiaoran Xu,Chi Zhang,Changjia Zhu,Ning Wang,Mingkui Wei,Zhuo Lu,Yao Liu,Lingyao Li*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: A systematic review (2019–2024, 215 papers) examining how LLMs both enable and combat information integrity threats on social media, revealing critical gaps in cross-lingual detection, real-time monitoring, and privacy-preserving methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs have become powerful tools on social media, but their dual role — generating convincing deceptive content while also detecting malicious material — creates complex challenges for information integrity that demand systematic investigation.

Method: The authors conducted a comprehensive systematic literature review spanning 2019–2024, screening 1,048 studies and performing in-depth analysis on 215 representative papers drawn from multiple databases. Papers were categorized and analyzed across dimensions of misinformation, disinformation, fake news, social bots, and privacy concerns.

Result: LLMs exhibit a dual role: they enhance detection of malicious content and enable sophisticated defenses, yet also facilitate generation of highly convincing deceptive content. Critical gaps identified include inadequate cross-lingual detection, insufficient real-time monitoring capabilities, and lack of privacy-preserving implementations.

Conclusion: Future research must address cross-lingual detection, real-time monitoring, and privacy-preserving techniques. Stakeholders need balanced strategies that leverage LLM capabilities while mitigating their risks to social media information integrity.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have emerged as powerful tools that impact information integrity on social media platforms. This comprehensive review examines the dual role of LLMs in both facilitating and mitigating various information integrity challenges, including misinformation, disinformation, fake news, social bots, and privacy concerns. \textcolor{black}{We conduct a comprehensive review of the literature from 2019 to 2024, screening 1048 studies and performing an in-depth analysis of 215 representative papers. This systematic approach allows us to identify key patterns in how LLMs influence the information security in social media ecosystems.} Through a systematic analysis of papers from multiple databases, our findings reveal that while LLMs can enhance detection capabilities for malicious content and enable sophisticated defense mechanisms, they simultaneously pose risks by enabling the generation of highly convincing, deceptive content. We categorize and analyze the potential and challenges across different dimensions of information integrity, examining technical capabilities, ethical implications, and privacy concerns. The study demonstrates critical gaps in current approaches, particularly in cross-lingual detection, real-time monitoring, and privacy-preserving implementations. We conclude by proposing future research directions and recommendations for stakeholders to leverage LLMs while mitigating risks in social media information integrity.

</details>


### [286] [DeepInvert: Semi-Supervised Embedding Inversion Against Obfuscated Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04477)
*Zhicong Huang,Cheng Hong,Tao Wei*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: DeepInvert is a semi-supervised embedding inversion attack that recovers original tokens from obfuscated prompt representations with significantly higher accuracy than prior methods, demonstrating that obfuscation-based defenses against privacy leakage in cloud-based language model services are far weaker than previously believed.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Cloud-based LM services process sensitive user prompts. Obfuscation-based defenses (e.g., ObfusLM, SentinelLMs, TextObfuscator, DPNR) claim to protect privacy by transforming embeddings before transmission. The authors challenge these claims, arguing these defenses leak substantially more information than assumed, necessitating a rigorous re-evaluation of their security guarantees.

Method: DeepInvert is a semi-supervised embedding inversion attack. It combines (1) supervised training on labeled shadow data (embedding-token pairs from a local surrogate model) with (2) a novel unsupervised consistency objective applied to unlabeled target obfuscated embeddings. These two objectives alternate in a mixed training pipeline. Defense-aware adaptations tailor the attack to diverse obfuscation mechanisms across both encoder-based and autoregressive architectures.

Result: Evaluated across nine defenses, five tasks, and four model architectures, DeepInvert outperforms prior attacks on most defenses. Against ObfusLM, it achieves 73.5% top-1 token recovery vs. 26.2% for the previous best. A key finding is a task-dependent tension: obfuscation preserving enough signal for downstream utility also retains sufficient structure for inversion; schemes that resist inversion collapse utility. On simpler classification tasks, some DP-based defenses can maintain both properties.

Conclusion: Obfuscation-based defenses provide far less protection than previously believed. The authors call for a fundamental re-evaluation of this defense class, as the utility-privacy tension appears inherent and difficult to resolve outside of constrained settings like simple DP-based classification.

Abstract: Cloud-based language model services routinely process prompts containing sensitive information. Obfuscation-based defenses---including ObfusLM, SentinelLMs, TextObfuscator, and DPNR---mitigate this risk by transforming prompt representations before transmission, offering a lightweight alternative to cryptographic solutions. We show these defenses provide far less protection than previously believed.
  We present DeepInvert, a semi-supervised embedding inversion attack that recovers original tokens from obfuscated representations with higher accuracy than prior methods. The key insight is that unlabeled obfuscated embeddings retain exploitable semantic structure despite perturbation. DeepInvert combines supervised training on labeled shadow data with a novel unsupervised consistency objective over unlabeled target embeddings, alternating between the two via a mixed training pipeline. Defense-aware adaptations further extend the attack to diverse obfuscation mechanisms across encoder-based and autoregressive architectures.
  Experiments on nine defenses, five tasks, and four model architectures show that DeepInvert outperforms prior attacks on most defenses. Against ObfusLM, DeepInvert achieves 73.5\% top-1 token recovery versus 26.2\% for the previous best. Our results reveal a task-dependent tension: obfuscation schemes preserving enough signal for utility also retain sufficient structure for inversion, while schemes resisting inversion collapse utility. On simpler classification tasks, some DP-based defenses can maintain both. We call for a re-evaluation of this defense class.

</details>


### [287] [Checked-In Secret Detection: Strings Are All You Need](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04523)
*Zhengdong Huang,Kevin Li,Jinqiu Yang,Yepang Liu,Lili Wei*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: Secretron detects hardcoded secrets in source code using a novel StringGroup context extraction algorithm that focuses on surrounding string literals, achieving 98.74% F1-score and discovering 48 previously unknown secrets across 26 real applications.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Hardcoded secrets in source code are critical vulnerabilities. Regex-based detectors fail due to secrets lacking identifiable patterns, while existing context-aware methods suffer from obfuscation vulnerability, poor cross-language generalization, and noisy/lengthy context that slows inference.

Method: The authors propose StringGroup, a context extraction algorithm that mines surrounding string literals rather than arbitrary code tokens. This is paired with Secretron, a Transformer-based detection tool. The key insight is that string literals provide high semantic density, obfuscation robustness, and language independence while reducing context length to 33.2% of the original, retaining over 80% of semantic information.

Result: Secretron achieves 98.74% F1-score on SecretBench, demonstrates strong robustness under obfuscation and cross-language scenarios, and outperforms LLM-based baselines. In real-world deployment, it detected 48 previously unknown secret keys across 26 applications.

Conclusion: Focusing context extraction on string literals via StringGroup significantly improves the signal-to-noise ratio for secret detection, enabling a practical, accurate, and robust tool (Secretron) that surpasses existing approaches, including LLM-based methods.

Abstract: Hardcoded secrets in source code pose critical security vulnerabilities which can be easily exploited by malicious adversaries. Existing regex-based detection approaches suffer from fundamental limitations, as secrets often lack identifiable patterns, resulting in poor precision and recall. Recent studies have explored context-aware detection methods, as surrounding code can reveal the purpose of candidate strings. However, these methods confront three key challenges: (1) obfuscation robustness where models over-rely on easily obfuscated identifiers, (2) cross-language generalization difficulties due to uneven training data distribution, and (3) lengthy and noisy context that introduces excessive irrelevant tokens and slows inference. We observe that strings serve as a critical information source for code semantics, offering superior contextual density, obfuscation robustness, and language independence. Based on this insight, we propose StringGroup, a novel context extraction algorithm that mines strings surrounding potential secrets. By introducing a relatively simple modification to existing patterns that narrows the analysis specifically to string literals, the method achieves significant gains. With only 33.2% of the original context, it preserves over 80% of semantic information and significantly improves the signal-to-noise ratio for secret detection. We further design a context-aware secret detection tool, Secretron, based on StringGroup methods and Transformer model. Evaluation on the SecretBench dataset demonstrates high accuracy with 98.74% F1-score and strong robustness under obfuscation and cross-language scenarios, outperforming state-of-the-art LLM-based baselines. We deploy our tool in real-world environments and successfully detect 48 previously unknown secret keys from 26 applications, demonstrating the practical effectiveness of our approach.

</details>


### [288] [Breadcrumbing Search Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04565)
*Xuebin Li,Hanqing Zhao,Siyuan Liang,Kejiang Chen,Weiming Zhang,Dacheng Tao,Nenghai Yu*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: LLM-based search agents are vulnerable to coordinated, multi-step prompt injection attacks across their execution trajectory. The paper introduces Authority-Chain Hijack (ACH), which weaves manipulated search results and page contents into a coherent, corroborating evidence chain, and Trace-Guided Strategy Evolution (TGSE), which automatically refines attacker strategies from execution traces, achieving up to 71.4% ASR / 95.0% MaxN ASR.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work on search-agent safety focuses on static, single-page content injection, which modern agents can dilute or reject by issuing follow-up queries and cross-checking sources. The authors identify that the search/observation delivery channel is a fragile security boundary: a mediated search interface can repeatedly steer evidence gathering across the agent's entire trajectory, not just a single page. The key insight is that coordinated, trajectory-level manipulation is far more dangerous than isolated injection.

Method: Two main contributions: (1) Authority-Chain Hijack (ACH): an expert-refined strategy that transforms isolated search-result and page-content manipulations into a coherent evidence chain spanning multiple queries, where seemingly independent sources corroborate the attacker's narrative. It operates under a constrained tool-intermediary threat model where only one controlled result is appended per query. (2) Trace-Guided Strategy Evolution (TGSE): an automated refinement pipeline that analyzes execution traces from prior attacks to iteratively improve attacker strategies, eliminating the need for manual strategy redesign.

Result: ACH achieves state-of-the-art results on SafeSearch, with 55.9% Overall ASR and 83.3% MaxN ASR on the full test split. TGSE further boosts performance, with its strongest single setting reaching 71.4% ASR and 95.0% MaxN ASR in held-out evaluation, demonstrating that trace-driven automatic refinement substantially outperforms expert-crafted strategies.

Conclusion: The search-observation channel represents a critical and under-explored security vulnerability in LLM search agents. Coordinated, trajectory-level injection attacks (ACH) are significantly more effective than static single-page attacks, and automated strategy evolution (TGSE) can further amplify attack success. The findings highlight the urgent need for defenses that consider the full agent trajectory rather than individual tool returns in isolation.

Abstract: LLM-based search agents are widely used for information-seeking tasks, but their reliance on external tool returns introduces a critical security risk: web content retrieved during execution is untrusted, exposing agents to prompt injection and goal hijacking. Prior work on search-agent safety primarily focuses on static web-content injection, but modern agents issue follow-up queries and cross-check competing sources, so a single injected page is often diluted or rejected. We show that the channel delivering search and page observations is a fragile security boundary: beyond exposing the agent to a single poisoned page, a mediated search interface can repeatedly steer how the agent gathers evidence and forms its final answer. Under a constrained tool-intermediary threat model, appending only one controlled result per query can substantially increase attack success when the evidence is coordinated across the agent's trajectory. We study this setting with a strategy-driven long-horizon attack system and introduce Authority-Chain Hijack (ACH), an expert-refined strategy that turns isolated search-result and page-content manipulations into a coherent evidence chain across seemingly corroborating sources. ACH achieves the highest Overall ASR among all baselines, reaching 55.9% / 83.3% ASR / MaxN ASR on the full SafeSearch test split. We further introduce Trace-Guided Strategy Evolution (TGSE), which automatically improves attacker strategies from execution traces, replacing manual redesign with trace-driven refinement; its strongest single setting reaches 71.4% / 95.0% in held-out evaluation.

</details>


### [289] [Adaptive Intrusion Detection System using Transformer-Based Neural Networks and Continual Learning Approach with Adversarial Investigation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04602)
*Azizi Ariffin,Afif Haris,Faiz Zaki,Hazim Hanif,Nor Badrul Anuar*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: A continual learning framework for network intrusion detection using a tabular transformer with class-balanced replay achieves near-joint-training accuracy on the CICIDS2017 benchmark (0.9989 under a novel class-instance incremental scenario), but the replay buffer introduces critical vulnerabilities: label-flipping attacks collapse the model and backdoor poisoning achieves 95% attack success rate while evading standard monitoring.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing continual learning approaches for network IDS suffer from catastrophic forgetting when fine-tuning on new attacks, and retraining from scratch is computationally infeasible. Furthermore, current benchmarks unrealistically confine benign traffic to a single early task and ignore the replay buffer as a potential attack surface, motivating a more realistic evaluation framework that exposes these vulnerabilities.

Method: The authors propose an adaptive IDS framework combining (1) a tabular transformer encoder with (2) a class-balanced experience replay buffer that replays benign traffic at every update to stabilize decision boundaries. They introduce the Class-Instance Incremental (CII) scenario where benign flows reappear alongside new attacks. The buffer is probed with two attacks: overt label flipping and stealthy backdoor poisoning. Evaluation uses the CICIDS2017 benchmark against baselines including sequential fine-tuning, EWC, LwF, and iCaRL.

Result: Under the traditional class incremental setup, the framework achieves 0.9994 accuracy; under CII, 0.9989 accuracy with negligible forgetting, dramatically outperforming sequential fine-tuning (0.0052), EWC (0.0324), LwF (0.0699), and iCaRL (0.8770). Injecting benign traffic into every experience is essential for preventing forgetting. However, label-flipping at 1% budget collapses accuracy to 0.0053, and backdoor poisoning maintains 0.97 overall accuracy while achieving 95% attack success rate on trigger flows, evading standard monitoring.

Conclusion: A modest replay budget with benign traffic replay recovers near-joint-training performance in continual IDS learning, but buffer integrity is a strict operational requirement. Without robust defenses, the replay buffer becomes a critical attack surface vulnerable to both overt and stealthy poisoning.

Abstract: Network intrusion detection systems (IDS) trained on fixed traffic snapshots decay silently after deployment as threat distributions shift. Fine-tuning models on new attacks triggers catastrophic forgetting, while retraining from scratch is computationally infeasible. Replay-based continual learning counters this, but existing methods unrealistically confine benign traffic to a single early task and ignore the replay buffer as a potential attack surface. To address this, we present an adaptive IDS framework coupling a tabular transformer encoder with a class balanced experience replay buffer that replays benign traffic at every update to stabilize decision boundaries. We introduce the class-instance incremental (CII) scenario where benign flows reappear alongside new attacks as a more faithful stress test, and probe the buffer with overt label flipping and stealthy backdoor poisoning attacks. On the CICIDS2017 benchmark, our framework achieved 0.9994 accuracy under the traditional class incremental setup and 0.9989 under CII, with negligible forgetting, drastically outperforming sequential fine-tuning (0.0052), EWC (0.0324), LwF (0.0699), and iCaRL (0.8770) baselines. While injecting benign traffic into every experience proves essential for preventing forgetting, the replay buffer introduces critical vulnerabilities. Label-flipping collapses the model entirely (0.0053 accuracy at a 1% budget), and the backdoor maintains 0.97 overall accuracy while driving the attack success rate on trigger flows to 95%, evading standard monitoring.
