Ultimately, while a modest replay budget recovers near-joint-training performance, ensuring buffer integrity emerges as a strict operational requirement.

</details>


### [290] [Hidden Ciphers and Where to Find Them: Static Discovery and Assessment of Cryptographic Assets in Software](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04857)
*Christian Näther,Eduard Hirsch*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: A static analysis scanner classifies cryptographic assets into Material, Artifacts, and Invocations, achieving F1=0.75 on benchmarks and discovering 370 assets (6 CVEs, 52 post-quantum candidates) across 57K files in under six minutes, enabling practical crypto governance and migration planning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Organizations lack structured visibility into cryptography deployed across code, configs, dependencies, and files, hindering security governance and post-quantum migration planning. Existing approaches do not provide a systematic, scanner-independent taxonomy for cryptographic asset discovery.

Method: The authors propose a three-category classification (Crypto-Material, Crypto-Artifacts, Crypto-Invocations), derive an extensible, scanner-independent rule repository from this taxonomy, and implement a static scanner that applies these rules to produce CBOM-formatted output. Evaluation uses a synthetic benchmark with known ground truth and a real-world infrastructure of ten deployed services.

Result: On the synthetic benchmark, the scanner achieves an F1 score of 0.75 for asset discovery and correctly annotates 91% of expected weaknesses/vulnerabilities. In the real-world setting, it processes 57,610 files in under six minutes, discovering 370 cryptographic assets, including 6 CVE-linked vulnerabilities and 52 post-quantum migration candidates.

Conclusion: Classification-driven static discovery provides practical cryptographic transparency, enabling effective security governance and informed post-quantum migration planning at scale.

Abstract: Modern software systems rely on cryptography for data protection, authentication, and trust establishment, yet organizations often lack a structured view of the cryptography deployed across source code, configuration, dependencies, and cryptographic files. This lack of visibility complicates security governance and post-quantum migration planning. This paper presents a static approach for discovering and assessing cryptographic assets in software systems. We introduce a classification of Crypto-Material, Crypto-Artifacts, and Crypto-Invocations, derive an extensible scanner-independent rule repository from it, and implement a static scanner that applies these rules to produce CBOM-oriented output. We evaluate the approach on a synthetic benchmark with known ground truth and on a real-world infrastructure of ten deployed services. The scanner achieves an F1 score of 0.75 for asset discovery and correctly annotates 91% of expected weaknesses and vulnerabilities. In the realworld setting, it processes 57 610 files in under six minutes and discovers 370 cryptographic assets, including six CVE-linked vulnerabilities and 52 post-quantum migration candidates. Real-world coverage is assessed against a manually compiled reference list rather than an exhaustive one. These results show that classification-driven static discovery can provide practical cryptographic transparency for governance and post-quantum migration planning.

</details>


### [291] [Blockchain Empowered Trustworthy Agent Networks: Foundations, Taxonomy, and Future Directions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04626)
*Liehuang Zhu,Yuhang Li,Tianxing Wang,Zhihao Chen,Ke Li,Hongyi Liu,Yajie Wang,Lei Xu,Peng Jiang,Zijian Zhang*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: This survey charts the evolution from classical multi-agent systems to open agent networks of LLM-based autonomous agents, identifies a network-level trust crisis unaddressable by single-agent or closed-system methods, proposes a five-dimensional trust taxonomy, and maps how blockchain can serve as a shared trust layer for identity, authorization, provenance, coordination, and settlement without replacing core agent capabilities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As AI agents transition from isolated executors to networked, cross-organizational autonomous entities, they face a trust crisis spanning identity, authorization, auditability, reputation, and settlement — gaps that single-agent safety and closed multi-agent coordination cannot bridge. The paper aims to provide a structured understanding of these challenges and blockchain-based solutions.

Method: The authors conduct a literature survey spanning 1980–2026, reviewing classical multi-agent systems, LLM-based autonomous agents, agent interoperability protocols, Internet-of-Agents infrastructures, and blockchain-enabled trust mechanisms. They develop a five-dimensional taxonomy of trust (entity/capability, authorization/delegation, information/provenance, coordination/group-robustness, accountability/settlement) and systematically map agent-network risks to blockchain mechanisms.

Result: The paper synthesizes a comprehensive mapping between agent-network trust requirements and blockchain-enabled mechanisms (shared identity, verifiable authorization, tamper-evident provenance, auditable collaboration, incentive alignment, value settlement). It clarifies blockchain's proper role as a shared trust layer, distinct from agent security, semantic verification, privacy protection, or robust reasoning.

Conclusion: Blockchain provides essential infrastructure for trustworthy open agent networks by addressing network-level trust dimensions that single-agent and closed-system approaches cannot, but it should complement rather than replace agent-level capabilities. The taxonomy and mapping offer a foundation for designing decentralized, accountable, and interoperable agent ecosystems.

Abstract: AI agents are evolving from isolated task executors into networked autonomous entities that can communicate, delegate tasks, invoke tools, access external knowledge, and participate in cross-platform service and economic workflows. This evolution gives rise to open agent networks, where heterogeneous agents owned by different stakeholders interact without naturally shared infrastructures for identity, authorization, auditability, reputation, or settlement. This survey and tutorial article reviews the literature over the period 1980--2026 on the evolution from classical multi-agent systems to open agent networks, with a particular focus on LLM-based autonomous agents, agent interoperability protocols, Internet-of-Agents infrastructures, and blockchain-enabled trust mechanisms. We first review this evolution and show how the trust boundary expands from individual execution to cross-agent, cross-platform, and cross-organizational interaction. We then identify a network-level trust crisis that cannot be fully addressed by single-agent safety mechanisms or closed multi-agent coordination techniques, and develop a five-dimensional taxonomy covering entity and capability trust, authorization and delegation trust, information and provenance trust, coordination and group-robustness trust, and accountability and settlement trust. Based on this taxonomy, we examine how blockchain can provide shared identity, verifiable authorization, tamper-evident provenance, auditable collaboration, incentive alignment, and value settlement for trustworthy agent networks. We further synthesize the mapping between agent-network risks, trust requirements, and blockchain-enabled mechanisms, and clarify the role of blockchain as a shared trust layer rather than a replacement for agent security, semantic verification, privacy protection, or robust reasoning.

</details>


### [292] [MOAT: Model-Agnostic Randomized Transformations for preventing Efficiency Degradation Attacks on ViTs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04680)
*Anadi Goyal,Nandish Chattopadhyay,Chandan Karfa,Anupam Chattopadhyay,Norrathep Rattanavipanon*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: MOAT is a model-agnostic input pre-processing defense that applies transformations to protect efficient Vision Transformers from adversarial efficiency attacks, limiting GFLOPs degradation to within 3.4% of the unattacked baseline.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Token pruning is widely adopted to make Vision Transformers (ViTs) viable in resource-constrained settings, but adversaries have developed targeted attacks that undermine these pruning techniques. Existing defenses often require architectural modifications. There is a need for a model-agnostic defense that protects ViT efficiency without altering the model or its pruning mechanism.

Method: MOAT is a pre-processing defense pipeline that applies a combination of input transformations (e.g., spatial transformations, pixel-level perturbations) directly to the input image before it reaches the ViT. It operates in a model-agnostic fashion, requiring no changes to the model architecture, token pruning strategy, or inference pipeline.

Result: Across all evaluated ViT models, MOAT limits the GFLOPs degradation caused by adversarial efficiency attacks to within 3.4% of the original unattacked model's computational cost.

Conclusion: MOAT provides an effective, plug-and-play defense against adversarial efficiency attacks on ViTs, preserving computational efficiency without sacrificing model integrity or requiring architectural changes.

Abstract: To adopt the Vision Transformers (ViTs) in resource-constrained environment, token pruning is widely used to reduce computational cost without impacting accuracy. However, adversaries have developed targeted attacks against said token pruning techniques to undermine such attempts to make ViTs efficient. In this paper, we propose MOAT, a model-agnostic pre-processing defense pipeline that applies a combination of input transformations to protect efficient ViT implementations against adversarial efficiency attacks. MOAT operates directly on the input without requiring modifications to the model architecture or token pruning mechanism. Experimental results demonstrate that, across all evaluated ViT models, MOAT limits GFLOPs degradation under adversarial attacks to within 3.4% of the original unattacked model.

</details>


### [293] [LoginTrap: Uncovering Task-Agnostic Phishing-Style Indirect Prompt Injection Attacks against LLM-based Web Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04741)
*Longtao Guo,Zelin Zhang,Kaifeng Huang,Yang Shi*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: LoginTrap is a black-box attack that manipulates webpage content to induce LLM-based web agents into logging into attacker-controlled pages, leaking private credentials with 86% average end-to-end success across various LLM backbones, agent architectures, and defenses.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-based web agents handle sensitive authentication on real web services, but prior work has not fully examined whether malicious webpage content can induce login and cause end-to-end credential leakage. The authors aim to systematically study login inducement as an authentication boundary risk.

Method: LoginTrap operates under a black-box threat model where the attacker controls webpage context and the induced login flow without knowledge of the user's task or agent internals. It uses a fuzzing-inspired process to generate page-specific indirect injections that frame login as a plausible prerequisite for task continuation, guiding the agent to a controlled login page.

Result: LoginTrap achieves 86% average end-to-end attack success rate across multiple LLM backbones. The attack remains effective across different agent architectures and existing defenses, demonstrating that login inducement is a robust and systematic vulnerability.

Conclusion: Login inducement constitutes a systematic authentication boundary risk for LLM-based web agents. The findings call for authentication-aware defenses specifically designed to protect web agents from credential leakage through induced login flows.

Abstract: LLM-based web agents automate user tasks by observing webpages and executing browser actions on behalf of users. As these agents operate on real web services, login becomes a sensitive authentication boundary because it involves credentials and sensitive information. Existing work shows that malicious webpage content can manipulate web agent actions, but it has not fully examined whether such content can induce login and cause end-to-end private data leakage. We study this attack surface and present LoginTrap, a task-agnostic login-inducing attack against LLM-based web agents. LoginTrap assumes a black box attacker that controls the webpage context and the induced login flow without knowing the user task or web agent internals. Under this threat model, LoginTrap uses webpage context to generate page-specific indirect injections through a fuzzing-inspired process, making login appear as a plausible prerequisite for continuing the task and guiding the agent to a controlled login page. We conduct a comprehensive analysis of LoginTrap across realistic web agent executions. The results show that LoginTrap reaches 86\% average end-to-end attack success across LLM backbones and remains effective across agent architectures and defenses. These findings identify login inducement as a systematic authentication boundary risk and motivate further research on authentication-aware defenses for web agents.

</details>


### [294] [Web Cache Overflow: Exploiting Imprecise Keys for Cache Degradation and Beyond](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04744)
*Matteo Golinelli,Kaan Onarlioglu,Bruno Crispo*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: Web caches can be attacked by exploiting imprecisely defined cache keys, where gratuitous HTTP request fields allow attackers to create redundant cached copies of the same object, degrading cache performance and enabling denial-of-service.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Cache keys in web deployments are often loosely specified by operators, creating a mismatch where semantically identical requests map to different cache entries. This gap opens an abuse vector that has not been systematically studied.

Method: The authors analyze how unnecessary request elements in cache keys enable redundant cache entry generation. They conduct experiments across five standalone caching proxies to reproduce cache degradation, measuring attacker cost and cache hit rate under varying parameters.

Result: Sustained generation of redundant cache copies reduces cache effectiveness and increases origin server load. The experiments demonstrate that this can facilitate eviction-dependent attacks and potentially lead to denial-of-service conditions.

Conclusion: Precise cache-key design is the most direct mitigation against this abuse vector and should be adopted as a security best practice.

Abstract: Web caches support the scalability needs of contemporary web applications by storing frequently accessed objects closer to clients. Web caches are conceptually associative arrays, tracking stored objects using cache keys consisting of HTTP request fields. However, these cache keys are often imprecisely defined by website operators. This allows clients to craft a multitude of requests that target the same object, but map to different cache keys.
  In this work, we show that request elements included unnecessarily in cache keys can be abused to create redundant cache entries. In susceptible deployments, sustained generation of such redundant copies reduces cache effectiveness and increases origin load, facilitating eviction-dependent attacks. Our experiments reproduce cache degradation across five stand-alone caching proxies and characterize how these parameters affect attacker cost and cache hit rate, potentially resulting in denial-of-service attacks. We conclude that precise cache-key design is the most direct mitigation against this abuse vector and should be recognized as a security best practice.

</details>


### [295] ["Allow" to Achieve, Over-Privileged Inadvertently: The Unintended Cost of Task-Completion-Driven Pop-up Decisions in Mobile GUI Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04755)
*Dongsheng Chen,Yuxuan Li,Guanhua Chen,Jiaxin Zhang,Xiangyu Zhao,Lei Ma,Xin Yao,Xuetao Wei*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: This paper introduces "Permission Literacy" — the ability of mobile GUI agents to appropriately grant only task-necessary permissions. Through systematic evaluation of four frontier MLLMs using Android-style permission dialogs, the authors uncover two key biases (App-Trust Bias and Task-Prior Override) and find that prompt interventions are inconsistently effective, suggesting that decoupling task execution from permission authorization is a promising design direction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Mobile GUI agents frequently encounter system permission dialogs during task execution, but their capability to selectively grant only permissions that are necessary for the delegated task has not been systematically studied. This raises safety and privacy concerns, as over-granting permissions can expose users to unnecessary risks.

Method: The authors construct a four-level permission framework based on task relevance and privacy risk, validated by three independent GUI-agent safety experts. They inject Android-style permission popups into real GUI tasks and evaluate four frontier multimodal large language models (MLLMs) using synchronized annotated screenshots and UI-tree hierarchies, ensuring the agent has access to requester identity, permission type, justification, and available actions. Controlled interventions separately vary task context and agent-visible requester identity to isolate biases.

Result: Two systematic biases emerge: (1) App-Trust Bias — switching the requester from Calendar to PiMusic under the same Calendar task caused grants to drop from 26/32 to 0/32; (2) Task-Prior Override — holding a popup fixed while changing task context substantially alters authorization decisions. Prompt interventions can reduce unnecessary grants but are inconsistent across models and risk suppressing legitimate grants.

Conclusion: Separating task execution from permission authorization is a promising design direction for future mobile GUI agents, as current models exhibit systematic biases that make consistent, context-appropriate permission decisions unreliable.

Abstract: Mobile GUI agents routinely encounter system permission dialogs during task execution, yet their ability to grant only permissions that are necessary for the delegated task remains largely unexamined. We present a systematic study of this capability, which we term Permission Literacy. We construct a four-level permission framework based on task relevance and privacy risk and validate the evaluated scenarios with three independent experts in GUI-agent safety. We inject Android-style permission popups into real GUI tasks and evaluate four frontier multimodal large language models using synchronized annotated screenshots and UI-tree hierarchies, making the requester, permission, justification, and available actions accessible to the agent. Beyond the main study, we conduct controlled interventions that separately vary task context and agent-visible requester identity. Under the same Calendar task, changing only the requester from Calendar to PiMusic reduces grants from 26/32 to 0/32, revealing a strong but task-conditioned App-Trust Bias. Holding a popup fixed while changing task context also substantially changes authorization decisions, revealing a systematic Task-Prior Override. Prompt interventions can reduce unnecessary grants, but their effectiveness is inconsistent across models and may come at the cost of suppressing legitimate grants. These results suggest that separating task execution from permission authorization is a promising design direction for future work.

</details>


### [296] [PURPOSE: Poisoning Conflict Resolution in RAG via Proxy-Fact-Grounded Updates](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04756)
*Zijian Wang,Yubo Zhu,Muzhi Dong,Yanjun Lou,Yisheng Li,ZiLiang Zhang,Wei Tong,Yuan Zhang,Jingyu Hua,Sheng Zhong*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: PURPOSE is a black-box poisoning attack against RAG systems that avoids frontal contradiction with the resolver by instead injecting factually-grounded, non-contradicting updates that steer generation toward the target answer, achieving state-of-the-art attack success rates across diverse benchmarks and models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing black-box poisoning methods for RAG rely on asserting the target answer in direct contradiction with the retrieved passages, which triggers the very conflict-resolution mechanisms designed to detect and mitigate such attacks. The robustness of post-retrieval conflict resolution against more sophisticated poisoning strategies remains understudied.

Method: PURPOSE operates by: (1) extracting query-related facts that approximate what the resolver might use as a reference, (2) grounding a pivot event within those facts, and (3) crafting an injection that remains consistent with verifiable context while subtly steering the generator toward the target answer. This reframes poisoning as a conflict-minimizing update rather than a counter-claim.

Result: PURPOSE achieved the highest attack success rate (ASR) in 35 out of 45 experimental settings spanning three QA benchmarks, five generators, and three conflict-resolution methods. It outperformed the strongest prior attack by an average of +9.7 ASR points.

Conclusion: Non-contradicting injection is a highly effective and practical attack mode against conflict resolution in RAG, demonstrating that current resolvers are vulnerable to poisoning that minimizes rather than amplifies conflict signals.

Abstract: In Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), post-retrieval conflict resolution arbitrates among noisy or contradictory retrieved passages. However, the robustness of this safeguard against knowledge poisoning has not been adequately studied. Existing black-box poisoning methods all assert the target answer in frontal contradiction with what the resolver treats as settled, the very signal these methods are built to detect. We propose PURPOSE, a strict black-box poisoning attack that reframes the injection as an update that minimizes conflict, rather than as a counter-claim. PURPOSE extracts query-related facts approximating the resolver's possible reference, then grounds a pivot event in them to keep the injection consistent with what the resolver might verify while steering the generator toward the target answer. Across three QA benchmarks, five generators, and three conflict-resolution methods, PURPOSE attains the highest attack success rate (ASR) in 35 of 45 settings and exceeds the strongest prior attack with +9.7 mean ASR points. These results show that our poisoning method is effective against conflict resolution in RAG and identify non-contradicting injection as a practical mode to enhance poisoning attack.

</details>


### [297] [HoRFFI: High-Openness RF Fingerprint Identification with a Similarity-Enhanced Variational Information Bottleneck](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04881)
*Shuiguang Zeng,Yuxiang Shen,Yuanyu Zhang,Yulong Shen,Zhiyuan Tan,Houbing Herbert Song*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: HoRFFI is a high-openness radio frequency fingerprint identification framework that uses a similarity-enhanced variational information bottleneck (SVIB) to achieve scalable device identification and unknown-device rejection with only a few labeled training devices, significantly outperforming existing methods on LoRa and Wi-Fi datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Practical RFFI systems must enroll new authorized devices and reject unknown ones while trained on only a few labeled base-device classes, creating a high-openness problem. Existing open-set recognition methods require large, diverse known-device classes for feature learning, limiting real-world applicability.

Method: HoRFFI uses a similarity-enhanced variational information bottleneck (SVIB) supervision mechanism that employs feature-space augmentation and clustering to derive inter-sample similarity information. This provides supplementary supervision to regularize the embedding space, reducing encoder dependence on training-class diversity and yielding a more transferable embedding.

Result: On public LoRa and Wi-Fi datasets, HoRFFI achieves absolute improvements of 0.112 and 0.288 in novel-class accuracy, and AUC improvements of 0.029 and 0.060, respectively, over the best-performing baselines.

Conclusion: HoRFFI effectively addresses the high-openness RFFI challenge by learning a transferable embedding space with limited training classes, enabling both scalable device identification and robust unknown-device rejection.

Abstract: Radio frequency fingerprint identification (RFFI) is a promising technique for wireless device authentication. However, practical RFFI systems must enroll newly authorized devices while rejecting previously unseen ones, even when the feature extractor is trained on only a few labeled base-device classes, giving rise to a high-openness RFFI problem. Existing open-set recognition methods typically rely on feature spaces learned from a large and diverse set of known-device classes, limiting their applicability in practical scenarios. To address this challenge, we propose HoRFFI, a high-openness RFFI framework that supports scalable device identification and unknown-device rejection using only a small number of labeled training devices. HoRFFI employs a similarity-enhanced variational information bottleneck (SVIB)-based supervision mechanism, which reduces the encoder's dependence on training-class diversity and learns a more transferable embedding space. This supervision mechanism uses feature-space augmentation and clustering to derive inter-sample similarity information, which provides supplementary supervision for regularizing the embedding space. Experiments on public LoRa and Wi-Fi datasets show that HoRFFI achieves absolute improvements of \(0.112\) and \(0.288\) in novel-class accuracy, respectively, and corresponding absolute AUC improvements of \(0.029\) and \(0.060\) over the best-performing baselines.

</details>


### [298] [When Does Latent Communication Pay? A Causal Audit of Relayed KV Caches in Multi-Agent LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04893)
*Jiaming Cheng,Subhransu Das,Rajiv Ramnath*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: The paper audits whether multi-agent LLM systems genuinely transmit "latent thoughts" (example-specific information via key-value caches) by causally testing with mismatched, zeroed, and random caches. It finds that where private information is needed, performance drops to ceiling (100% reliance), but where it isn't, there is equivalence within 2.8 points. The authors argue that benchmark deltas alone are insufficient to prove latent-thought transmission and advocate for mismatched-cache audits.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior multi-agent LLM systems claim performance gains from relaying key-value caches representing "latent thoughts" rather than text, but these claims conflate correlation with causation. There is no rigorous causal audit establishing whether the relayed caches actually carry example-specific semantic content versus merely providing generic computational benefits (e.g., regularization or extra computation). The paper seeks to fill this gap by causally testing whether cache content matters.

Method: The authors perform causal interventions on relayed KV caches in released multi-agent systems (LatentMAS, KVComm, C2C). They replace the sender's cache with three counterfactual types: (1) deranged/mismatched-example caches, (2) zeroed caches, and (3) moment-matched random caches. Testing occurs under two regimes: (a) where the receiver needs the sender's private information (measuring ceiling dependence), and (b) where it does not (testing for undetected advantage). Equivalence testing uses a pre-registered five-seed protocol with Holm-corrected TOST across multiple model families (Qwen3 at three scales, plus a second family), checkpoints, and benchmarks (GSM8K, ARC-Challenge, MedQA, document-QA).

Result: Under the private-information regime, mismatched caches collapse performance to near-floor levels (ceiling: 100% reliance vs. 23–25% for answer-irrelevant relays), replicated across three families, five checkpoints, and a document-QA surface. Under the no-private-information regime, equivalence is established within 2.8 points across GSM8K and ARC-Challenge (Qwen3) and MedQA at 8B, with one cell showing a small detected advantage within the margin; a second family shows no detected advantage. A striking dissociation emerges: in one cell, zeroing the relay costs 14.7 points but mismatching it costs only 0.4, showing large cache effects need not reflect pairing effects. Delivered channels range from ceiling (LatentMAS native relay) to partial (KVComm layer subset) to no detected example-specific transfer (C2C projector).

Conclusion: Benchmark deltas alone do not establish latent-thought transmission; establishing it requires a mismatched-cache audit. The paper releases this audit methodology, demonstrating that many claimed "latent thought" gains are not driven by example-specific semantic content in the relayed caches.

Abstract: Multi-agent LLM systems relay key--value caches instead of text and credit their gains to exchanged ``latent thoughts''. That credit is a claim about \emph{which} example's cache is relayed, not merely that one is. We audit it causally in released systems. The cache is replaced with deranged (mismatched-example), zeroed, and moment-matched random counterparts, under two regimes defined by whether the receiver needs the sender's private information. Where it does, the battery reads ceiling: 100\% against 23--25\% for answer-irrelevant relays on the primary backbone, a contrast replicated across three families, five checkpoints, and a prose document-QA surface. Where it does not, a pre-registered five-seed protocol establishes equivalence within 2.8 points, a margin anchored to the audited system's reported gain, under Holm-corrected TOST on GSM8K and ARC-Challenge across three Qwen3 scales and on MedQA at 8B (one cell shows a small detected advantage inside the margin); a second family shows no detected advantage. A large cache effect need not be a pairing effect. In one natural cell, zeroing the relay costs 14.7 points; a mismatched cache, 0.4. Nor is need sufficient: under the same test, delivered channels span ceiling (LatentMAS's native relay), partial (KVComm's layer subset), and no detected example-specific transfer (C2C's released projector). Benchmark deltas do not by themselves establish latent-thought transmission; establishing it takes a mismatched-cache audit, which we release.

</details>


### [299] [LLM-Assisted Detection and Repair of Hardware Security Vulnerabilities in Verilog Designs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04907)
*Ethen Santana,Gabriel Gyaase,Hao Zheng*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: This paper proposes using Large Language Models (LLMs) to automatically detect hardware security vulnerabilities categorized under the Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE) framework directly from Verilog hardware designs, offering scalable, automated assistance for pre-silicon security analysis.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Hardware bugs that introduce security vulnerabilities become permanently embedded in silicon after fabrication, making them extremely difficult or impossible to patch — unlike software vulnerabilities. Current hardware security analysis methods need augmentation with more scalable, automated approaches to catch weaknesses like improper access control, sensitive information exposure, and privilege escalation early in the design phase.

Method: The authors propose a methodology that leverages a Large Language Model (LLM) to directly analyze Verilog hardware designs and identify potential hardware-related Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE) entries. The approach is evaluated iteratively on a dataset of single-module Verilog designs.

Result: The iterative evaluation on single-module Verilog designs demonstrates that LLMs have promising potential to detect hardware security weaknesses, showing that they can serve as effective automated assistants for identifying vulnerabilities during the design process.

Conclusion: LLMs show significant potential to augment traditional hardware security analysis by providing automated, scalable detection of CWE-classified vulnerabilities directly from Verilog code, enabling earlier identification of security flaws before tape-out.

Abstract: Hardware designs, like software, are susceptible to bugs that can introduce security vulnerabilities and create opportunities for malicious exploitation. Unlike software vulnerabilities, however, hardware flaws become permanently embedded in silicon after fabrication, making them difficult or impossible to patch. Many of these weaknesses are categorized under the Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE) framework and include improper access control, exposure of sensitive information, and unintended privilege escalation. To improve the detection of such vulnerabilities, we propose a methodology that leverages a Large Language Model (LLM) to identify potential hardware CWEs directly from hardware designs in Verilog. The proposed approach is evaluated iteratively on a dataset of single-module Verilog designs to assess its effectiveness in detecting hardware security weaknesses. Our results demonstrate the potential of LLMs to augment traditional hardware security analysis by providing automated, scalable assistance for identifying security vulnerabilities during the hardware design process.

</details>


### [300] [Toward Practical Decentralized Proof-of-Location via Physical Witnessing Zones](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04957)
*Tamor Tomson,Eduardo Brito,Amnir Hadachi,Ulrich Norbisrath*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: The paper presents a physical prototype of a decentralized Proof-of-Location (PoL) system using low-cost hardware, demonstrating how abstract protocols can be adapted to real-world constraints. The system uses witness-initiated ranging, cross-witness consistency checks, and freshness binding to produce verifiable, tamper-evident proof objects, validated through controlled indoor experiments against replay and malicious-ranging attacks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Digital services increasingly depend on location claims that are currently self-reported, easily falsified, and hard to verify post hoc. Existing Proof-of-Location systems lack practical, physically implemented prototypes that operate under real radio, networking, and timing constraints. The work aims to bridge the gap between theoretical decentralized PoL architectures and tangible, low-cost implementations.

Method: The authors build a physical witnessing zone where fixed nearby devices measure a prover's presence using witness-initiated ranging. Claims are exchanged over a local mesh network and recorded in a tamper-evident ledger. The abstract protocol is adapted to physical constraints via three key mechanisms: witness-initiated ranging, cross-witness consistency checks, and freshness binding to prevent replay attacks. A controlled indoor evaluation tests accuracy, latency, and resilience against simulated replay and malicious-ranging attacks.

Result: The prototype produces accurate, low-latency proof objects in controlled indoor settings and successfully detects simulated replay and malicious-ranging attacks. The system serves as a reusable experimental baseline, while exposing remaining challenges in calibration, verifier independence, radio integrity, and scaling.

Conclusion: A functional, low-cost physical PoL prototype is feasible and effective under real-world radio and timing conditions. The work establishes an experimental foundation for next-generation decentralized location evidence infrastructure, while identifying key areas—calibration, verifier-independence, radio-integrity, and scaling—that require further research before practical deployment.

Abstract: Digital services increasingly rely on claims that a person, device, or asset was in a specific place at a specific time. Today, those claims often depend on self-reported location data, which is easy to falsify and difficult to verify after the fact. Proof-of-Location (PoL) systems address this gap by turning presence claims into evidence that an independent verifier can later inspect. This paper builds upon recent theoretical work on decentralized PoL architectures and demonstrates how they can move from emulation to a physical prototype built with low-cost hardware. We implement a witnessing zone in which fixed nearby devices measure a prover's presence, exchange claims over a local mesh, and record them in a tamper-evident ledger. Building the prototype required adapting the abstract protocol to physical constraints through witness-initiated ranging, cross-witness consistency checks, and freshness binding against replay. Our controlled indoor evaluation shows that the system can produce accurate, low-latency proof objects while detecting simulated replay and malicious-ranging attacks. The result is a reusable experimental baseline for next-generation digital trust infrastructure, that exposes the remaining calibration, verifier-independence, radio-integrity, and scaling requirements for decentralized location evidence, where physical presence claims can be independently checked under real radio, networking, and timing conditions.

</details>


### [301] [When Do PEFT Adaptations Leak Structure? Measuring Black-Box Structural Bounds in Public-Base Model Services](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05036)
*Zhongjiang Yao,Shuangshuang Liang,Chun Yang,LiWei Chen,Gang Shi*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: VectorHijack-SR is a measurement methodology that quantifies structural information leakage from PEFT-adapted public foundation models by analyzing victim/base output residuals. It infers PEFT family, layer locality, and rank with task-dependent accuracy, achieving high known-set performance but limited open-world generalization, revealing a gap between visibility and exploitability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Services increasingly deploy private parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) adaptations on public foundation models, creating a differential leakage risk: adversaries with local access to the base model can observe victim outputs and potentially infer proprietary adaptation details (architecture family, rank, version). Prior work lacked rigorous measurement of what structural properties are actually recoverable under realistic threat models.

Method: VectorHijack-SR converts paired victim/base output residuals into calibrated structural bounds across PEFT family, layer locality, and coarse rank. An estimator aggregates query-level statistics (magnitude, ranking, entropy, margin, length, template, locality, spectral) into service-level representations. A service-disjoint classifier quantifies structural evidence, and a cross-fitted hierarchical rejector evaluates whether a victim lies outside the calibrated LoRA manifold. The framework separates metadata visibility from open-world validity and operational exploitability.

Result: Family leakage exceeds chance on BERT/MNLI (8/12), RoBERTa/MNLI (21/24), DeBERTa-v3/MNLI (12/18) and AG News (15/18). Rank inference is task-dependent: BERT/MNLI and DeBERTa/AG News reach 8/9, DeBERTa/MNLI achieves 4/9 (compatible with chance after correction). The rejector achieves pooled AUROC 0.804 (95% CI [0.660,0.927]) and known accuracy 0.956, but struggles with structurally close DoRA and LoRA+head variants. Exact-version linkage on held-out LoRA-r64 services reaches AUC 0.940. A visibility-exploitability gap persists: two-stage recovery yields no query savings, posterior-selected PEFT underperforms distill-then-convert PEFT (0.356 vs. 0.517), and free-running generation remains near chance.

Conclusion: Known-base, rich-output PEFT services can leak actionable structural and version information, but closed-set confidence alone does not establish universal adapter recovery. The visibility-exploitability gap suggests that while structural metadata is partially inferable, turning this into practical model extraction remains challenging, informing both auditing practices and defensive design.

Abstract: Services increasingly deploy public foundation models with private parameter-efficient adaptations, creating a differential information leakage risk when auditors or adversaries can execute the public base model locally and observe victim outputs. We present VectorHijack-SR, a measurement methodology that converts paired victim/base residuals into calibrated structural bounds over PEFT family, layer locality, and coarse rank, while separating metadata visibility from open-world validity and operational exploitability. Our estimator aggregates query-level magnitude, ranking, entropy, margin, length, template, locality, and spectral statistics into service-level representations. A service-disjoint classifier quantifies structural evidence, and a cross-fitted hierarchical rejector evaluates whether a victim lies outside the calibrated LoRA manifold. Across classification backbones, family leakage exceeds uniform chance on BERT/MNLI (8/12), RoBERTa/MNLI (21/24), and DeBERTa-v3 on MNLI (12/18) and AG News (15/18). Rank inference is task dependent: BERT/MNLI and DeBERTa/AG News reach 8/9, whereas DeBERTa/MNLI achieves 4/9 and is statistically compatible with chance after correction. On a ten-seed BERT open-set grid, the rejector achieves pooled AUROC 0.804 (95% CI [0.660, 0.927]) and known accuracy 0.956, but remains limited on structurally close DoRA and LoRA+head variants. Exact-version linkage on five held-out LoRA-r64 services reaches AUC 0.940. Experiments reveal a visibility-exploitability gap: two-stage recovery provides no fair-budget query savings, posterior-selected PEFT underperforms distill-then-convert PEFT (0.356 vs. 0.517), and free-running generation remains near chance. These results show that known-base, rich-output PEFT services can leak actionable structural and version information, while closed-set confidence alone does not establish universal adapter recovery.

</details>


### [302] [Private Direct Preference Optimization for LLM Alignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05040)
*Yangfan Jiang,Fei Wei,Ergute Bao,Xiaokui Xiao,Yaliang Li,Bolin Ding*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: The paper introduces "preference privacy" for DPO, a label-DP notion protecting only relative preferences (not prompts/responses). It presents PrivDPO, which adds calibrated noise along a one-dimensional preference axis via unbiased randomized rescaling of the DPO objective, avoiding per-example gradient operations. Experiments show strong privacy-utility trade-offs across three benchmarks and three LLM families.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: DPO is widely used for LLM alignment, but the relative preference between paired responses can leak sensitive attributes of annotators or users. Existing privacy-preserving methods (e.g., DP-SGD) are poorly suited to DPO's structure, injecting unnecessary noise into prompt/response representations that are already public or non-sensitive, leading to biased updates and degraded utility.

Method: The authors formalize preference privacy as a label-DP notion where only the binary preference signal is protected, assuming an adversary knows the prompt and both responses. The key insight: for neighboring DPO examples differing only in preference, the gradient difference lies on a one-dimensional preference axis determined purely by the text. PrivDPO exploits this by applying an unbiased randomized rescaling to the DPO loss, injecting calibrated noise solely along this axis without per-example gradient clipping or noising. This avoids the inefficiency and bias of generic DP mechanisms.

Result: Experiments on three alignment benchmarks (TL;DR, Anthropic Helpfulness, UltraFeedback) and three LLM families (Pythia, Llama, Mistral) demonstrate that PrivDPO consistently achieves superior privacy-utility trade-offs compared to privacy-preserving baselines, including DP-SGD and output perturbation methods.

Conclusion: PrivDPO provides a practical, efficient mechanism for preference privacy in DPO-based alignment, matching the structure of the learning problem to achieve better utility under the same privacy budget. The approach is directly compatible with large-scale LLM training pipelines.

Abstract: Direct preference optimization (DPO) is now a standard method for aligning large language models (LLMs) using human preference data. Each DPO example contains a prompt and a pair of candidate model responses. While prompts and responses are often public or model-generated, the relative preference between responses reflects subjective judgments and can reveal sensitive attributes of annotators or end users. Off-the-shelf privacy-preserving approaches are not well matched to this structure, leading to unnecessary noise injection and biased updates in training.
  In this paper, we formalize preference privacy, a label-DP-style privacy notion for DPO that protects only the relative preference between candidate responses, assuming an adversary who already knows the prompt and responses. We then design PrivDPO, a DPO variant that enforces preference privacy while remaining compatible with large-scale LLM training. Our main observation is that, for neighboring examples differing only in their preference signal, the gradient difference lies on a one-dimensional preference axis determined solely by the text; all preference information flows through this axis. PrivDPO adds calibrated randomness only along this axis via an unbiased randomized rescaling of the DPO objective, avoiding per-example gradient operations. Our experiments on three alignment benchmarks and three LLM families show that PrivDPO consistently achieves strong privacy-utility trade-offs compared with privacy-preserving baselines.

</details>


### [303] [Gradient Immunity: Null-Space Resistance to Malicious Fine-Tuning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05045)
*Yuxuan Huang,Xingyu Zeng,Tianhang Zheng,Chaochao Lu*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: USG proposes a release-time defense that inserts a Null Space Cubic Layer and Inverse Adapter after the final Transformer layer to block harmful gradients during downstream fine-tuning, maintaining safety without requiring downstream user cooperation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing safety defenses for aligned LLMs either assume a fine-tuning-as-a-service paradigm or require downstream users to follow safety protocols, leaving a gap for the provider-controlled partially protected open-weight release setting where most weights are trainable but a small safety-critical component must be preserved.

Method: USG consists of: (1) a Null Space Cubic Layer inserted post-final-Transformer-layer that suppresses/blocks gradients from harmful samples whose hidden states fall in a calibrated protected region, and (2) an Inverse Adapter that restores the base model's forward behavior. A threshold is calibrated using defender-held harmful data to generalize protection to nearby in-distribution harmful samples.

Result: Across six model-dataset settings, USG maintains post-finetuning attack success rate close to pre-release levels under a fixed threshold, achieves high safe-pass rates on easier settings, and demonstrates a clear safety-utility trade-off on unsafe BeaverTails samples.

Conclusion: Release-time representation-space blocking via USG can effectively raise the cost of malicious downstream adaptation without requiring downstream cooperation, offering a practical defense for partially protected open-weight releases.

Abstract: Released aligned large language models remain vulnerable to malicious downstream finetuning. Existing defenses are largely designed for the fine-tuning-as-a-service (FTaaS) paradigm or rely on downstream users to follow additional safety procedures, and therefore do not directly address the setting we study: a provider controlled partially protected open-weight (PPOW) release setting in which most weights remain trainable while a small safety-critical component is preserved at release. We propose a Unidirectional Safety Gate (USG), instantiated as a Null Space Cubic Layer together with an Inverse Adapter inserted after the final Transformer layer. During downstream fine-tuning, the cubic layer suppresses or blocks gradients from harmful samples whose hidden states fall in a calibrated protected region, while the Inverse Adapter restores the base model's forward behavior. In practice, we calibrate a threshold using defender-held harmful data, allowing protection to generalize to nearby in-distribution harmful samples. Across six evaluated model-dataset settings, USG keeps post-finetuning attack success rate close to the pre-release level under a fixed release threshold, while maintaining high safe-pass rates on easier settings and exhibiting a clearer safety-utility trade-off on unsafe samples from BeaverTails. These results suggest that release-time representation-space blocking can raise the cost of malicious downstream adaptation without requiring downstream cooperation. The code is available at https://github.com/OpenCausaLab/Gradient-Immunity.

</details>


### [304] [Kerckhoffs-Compliant Watermarking for Physical Design IP Protection: From Placement to Routing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05055)
*Andrew B. Kahng,Yiting Liu*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: PDMarks is a Kerckhoffs-compliant watermarking framework for VLSI physical design that embeds ownership evidence across placement, CTS, and routing stages using HMAC-SHA256-derived markers, achieving coincidence probability below 10⁻³² with minimal PPA overhead.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing PD watermarking methods protect only a single PD stage or rely on hidden construction details (security by obscurity), making them vulnerable to white-box adversaries. As access to PD tools expands, unauthorized reuse of placed-and-routed databases demands a robust, multi-stage watermarking solution whose security relies solely on a secret key.

Method: PDMarks uses a 32-byte secret key with HMAC-SHA256 to deterministically derive all watermark instances and target values. Watermarks are embedded across three physical design stages: placement, clock tree synthesis (CTS), and routing. The framework is integrated into OpenROAD-flow-scripts and follows Kerckhoffs's principle, where security depends entirely on key secrecy rather than algorithmic obscurity.

Result: Experiments on NanGate45 and ASAP7 designs demonstrate that PDMarks provides significantly stronger ownership evidence than prior methods, with all-stage joint coincidence probability below 10⁻³² for every evaluated design. PPA overhead is comparable to or smaller than existing approaches. Wrong-key and attack evaluations confirm that incorrect keys fail to reproduce the ownership proof and that weakening watermarks requires broad perturbation of the protected implementation.

Conclusion: PDMarks establishes a practical, cryptographically grounded watermarking framework for VLSI physical design that is resistant to both white-box and removal attacks, offering robust multi-stage IP protection suitable for open-source PD toolchains.

Abstract: Physical design (PD) intellectual property (IP) is a valuable artifact of modern VLSI implementation. It includes optimized cell placement, clock distribution, and routing decisions produced by carefully tuned PD flows. As access to PD tools expands, unauthorized reuse of placed-and-routed databases becomes an increasing concern. Existing PD watermarking methods either protect only one PD stage or rely on hidden construction details, leaving them vulnerable to a white-box adversary. In this work, we develop PDMarks, a Kerckhoffs-compliant watermarking framework whose security depends only on a secret key. PDMarks embeds ownership evidence across multiple stages of the PD flow, including placement, clock tree synthesis (CTS), and routing. All watermark instances and target values are deterministically derived from a 32-byte secret key using HMAC-SHA256, enabling consistent embedding and verification. PDMarks has been integrated into OpenROAD-flow-scripts. Experiments on NanGate45 and ASAP7 designs show that PDMarks outperforms prior physical design watermarking methods by providing much stronger ownership evidence with comparable or smaller PPA overhead. The approximate joint all-stage coincidence probability is below 10^{-32} for every evaluated design. Wrong-key and attack evaluations further show that incorrect keys do not reproduce the complete ownership proof and that weakening the watermark requires broad perturbation of the protected implementation.

</details>


### [305] [Hardware Design and Security in the Era of Chiplets and LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05063)
*Johann Knechtel,Ozgur Sinanoglu,Paul V. Gratz,Ramesh Karri*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: This paper surveys the security challenges and defenses at the intersection of two trends: heterogeneous 2.5D chiplet systems and LLM-integrated EDA flows. It analyzes attack surfaces across architectural, logical, and physical levels for chiplets, and examines exploits against LLM-driven EDA pipelines. Defenses reviewed include 2.5D split manufacturing with active interposer-based Root of Trust for chiplets and state-of-the-art mitigation techniques for LLM-EDA security. The paper concludes by exploring how LLMs can themselves enhance hardware security.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The simultaneous emergence of chiplet-based heterogeneous integration and LLM-driven EDA tools offers substantial gains in yield, modularity, and design productivity, but radically expands the hardware attack surface. A unified security analysis spanning both these frontiers is absent, motivating this comprehensive review of threats and defenses across both domains and their intersection.

Method: The paper conducts a unified survey-style analysis organized along three axes: (1) attacks on chiplet systems at architectural, logical, and physical levels, including hardware stacks for LLM acceleration; (2) exploits targeting LLM-driven EDA pipelines, with systematic threat identification; (3) defense mechanisms — split manufacturing with active interposer-based physically isolated Root of Trust (RoT) for chiplets, and state-of-the-art techniques for LLM-EDA pipelines. A forward-looking discussion examines how LLMs can reciprocally advance hardware security.

Result: The analysis reveals that chiplet systems face multi-level threats spanning interposer communication, die-to-die interfaces, and physical tampering, while LLM-driven EDA pipelines are vulnerable to prompt injection, model poisoning, and supply-chain attacks. For chiplets, active interposers enabling physically isolated RoT architectures provide a powerful defense paradigm. For LLM-EDA, identified native threats can be countered by emerging defense techniques. The symbiotic relationship between LLMs and hardware security presents opportunities for LLM-assisted vulnerability detection, security verification, and secure design automation for modern chiplet systems.

Conclusion: The convergence of 2.5D chiplet integration and LLM-augmented EDA demands holistic security strategies that span hardware and software boundaries. Active interposer-based RoT architectures and split manufacturing offer robust physical isolation for chiplet security, while LLM-EDA pipelines require both native threat mitigation and the responsible harnessing of LLMs as tools for advancing hardware security itself.

Abstract: The semiconductor industry is undergoing a dual revolution: the shift toward heterogeneous 2.5D chiplet systems and the integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) into Electronic Design Automation (EDA) flows. While these paradigms offer unprecedented benefits in yield, modularity, design productivity, etc., they radically expand the hardware attack surface. This paper provides a unified analysis of these frontiers, ranging from attacks on chiplet systems (including hardware stacks for LLM acceleration) across architectural, logical, and physical levels, to various exploits against LLM-driven EDA pipelines. To secure chiplet systems, we review a powerful defense approach that leverages 2.5D split manufacturing and active interposers for physically isolated Root of Trust (RoT) architectures. To secure LLM-driven EDA pipelines, we first identify native threats and then review state-of-the-art defense techniques. Finally, we discuss how LLM systems can advance hardware security efforts for modern systems, including chiplets.

</details>


### [306] [Agent Against Agent: An Agentic System for Automatic Prompt Injection Red Teaming](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05108)
*Yanting Wang,Chenlong Yin,Runpeng Geng,Jinyuan Jia*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: PIMiner is an agentic red-teaming system for prompt injection that learns a transferable strategy library from training on multiple (dataset, target model) pairs, enabling strong attack success rates on unseen LLMs with minimal queries (≈10 per sample).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing RL-based prompt injection red-teaming methods produce attacker models that generalize poorly to new target LLMs, limiting their practical utility for evaluation and defense training data collection.

Method: PIMiner is trained on a sequence of (dataset, target model) pairs and incrementally builds a strategy library from scratch. At test time, the learned strategy library transfers directly to unseen target LLMs without additional training, requiring only a small number of queries (e.g., 10) per test sample.

Result: On IPIArena: 76.2% ASR against Gemini-2.5-Pro, 61.9% ASR against GPT-5.1, 42.9% ASR against Claude-Sonnet-4.5. On AgentDojo: 86.7% ASR against Gemini-2.5-Pro, 53.3% ASR against GPT-5.1, 40.0% ASR against Claude-Sonnet-4.5.

Conclusion: PIMiner demonstrates that a transferable strategy library approach can achieve strong, query-efficient prompt injection attacks against diverse state-of-the-art LLMs without per-target retraining.

Abstract: Prompt injection poses significant security risks to LLM agents. Efficient and effective red-teaming is therefore critical, both for evaluating these risks and for collecting training data to improve defenses. Existing state-of-the-art prompt injection red-teaming methods primarily rely on reinforcement learning (RL), producing attacker models that often generalize poorly to new target LLMs. In this work, we develop PIMiner, an agentic system for prompt injection red-teaming. During training, PIMiner is trained on a sequence of (dataset, target model) pairs and builds a strategy library from scratch. At test time, the learned strategy library can be directly transferred to a previously unseen target LLM without additional training. PIMiner requires only a small number of queries to a target agent (e.g., 10) per test sample. Experimental results demonstrate that PIMiner achieves strong performance. On IPIArena, it attains a 76.2% ASR against Gemini-2.5-Pro, 61.9% ASR against GPT-5.1, and 42.9% ASR against Claude-Sonnet-4.5. On AgentDojo, it achieves an 86.7% ASR against Gemini-2.5-Pro, 53.3% ASR against GPT-5.1, and 40.0% ASR against Claude-Sonnet-4.5.

</details>


### [307] [Temporal Context Awareness: A Defense Framework Against Multi-turn Manipulation Attacks on Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.15560)
*Prashant Kulkarni,Assaf Namer*

Main category: cs.CR

TL;DR: The paper introduces the Temporal Context Awareness (TCA) framework, a defense mechanism against multi-turn manipulation attacks on LLMs that analyzes semantic drift, cross-turn intention consistency, and evolving conversational patterns to detect adversarial tactics that single-turn methods miss.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are vulnerable to multi-turn manipulation attacks where adversaries use seemingly benign conversational turns to gradually circumvent safety measures. These attacks exploit the temporal, context-building nature of dialogue, evading traditional single-turn detection methods and posing a critical security risk for real-world deployments.

Method: The TCA framework employs three core components: (1) dynamic context embedding analysis to track how conversational context evolves, (2) cross-turn consistency verification to detect inconsistencies in stated intentions across turns, and (3) progressive risk scoring that escalates risk assessments as manipulation patterns accumulate. The framework continuously monitors semantic drift and adversarial progression across the full dialogue trajectory.

Result: Preliminary evaluations on simulated adversarial scenarios indicate that TCA can identify subtle, progressive manipulation patterns that traditional detection techniques typically overlook. The paper also provides an analysis of diverse attack vectors and their progression across multi-turn interactions.

Conclusion: Robust, context-aware defenses are urgently needed for conversational AI systems. The TCA framework represents a promising direction for securing LLMs against multi-turn manipulation while preserving their utility for legitimate applications. Code is made publicly available to support further research.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly vulnerable to sophisticated multi-turn manipulation attacks, where adversaries strategically build context through seemingly benign conversational turns to circumvent safety measures and elicit harmful or unauthorized responses. These attacks exploit the temporal nature of dialogue to evade single-turn detection methods, representing a critical security vulnerability with significant implications for real-world deployments.
  This paper introduces the Temporal Context Awareness (TCA) framework, a novel defense mechanism designed to address this challenge by continuously analyzing semantic drift, cross-turn intention consistency and evolving conversational patterns. The TCA framework integrates dynamic context embedding analysis, cross-turn consistency verification, and progressive risk scoring to detect and mitigate manipulation attempts effectively. Preliminary evaluations on simulated adversarial scenarios demonstrate the framework's potential to identify subtle manipulation patterns often missed by traditional detection techniques, offering a much-needed layer of security for conversational AI systems. In addition to outlining the design of TCA , we analyze diverse attack vectors and their progression across multi-turn conversation, providing valuable insights into adversarial tactics and their impact on LLM vulnerabilities. Our findings underscore the pressing need for robust, context-aware defenses in conversational AI systems and highlight TCA framework as a promising direction for securing LLMs while preserving their utility in legitimate applications. We make our implementation available to support further research in this emerging area of AI security.

</details>
